title: HarborCall Insights
content:
HarborCall Insights

Company snapshot: SMB, building a lightweight call-summary widget sold into SDR teams.
Primary ask: Hosted API for quick integration (frontend + serverless backend).
PII concern: they capture full call audio -> transcript -> summaries. Legal wants explicit redaction flow for SSNs, CC numbers, and optional name-masking.
Retention: prefer 'store transcripts for 30d then auto-delete' but need proof of deletion + logs.
Latency: not ultra-sensitive; 2-3s per chunk acceptable for streaming summaries. Throughput modest (50k tokens/mo initial).
Cost sensitivity high — founder: 'want predictable unit cost, can't afford surprises as we scale to 2000 seats'.
Model preferences: open to small open models for cheaper token cost; willing to test 1-2 variants. Interested in quantization recommendations from Optimize later.
Routing/fallback: want deterministic behavior on failures — prefer simple fallback to smaller model, not degraded summaries.
Security asks: audit log examples, retention policy template, and KMS integration questions (they currently use cloud KMS).
Quote from CTO Mateo: 'If you can show a reproducible PII-redaction pipeline and an easy delete API we're ready to do a short POC.'
Next technical step: SE Liam to share example redaction prompts + sample code, run quick POC with 3 recorded calls (Ava to provide).
PRICING: asked for token-level estimate for a 5-min call -> transcript + summary + embeddings for search. Need a sample calc sheet.
Internal notes: target SMB self-serve motion. If POC goes well, upsell path = Dedicated later for higher throughput/regulatory customers.
Risk: Legal could block if deletion proofs are not concrete; also unsure about long-term ARR if heavy embedding usage.
Action items: 1) Send security FAQ + retention SLA (Ava) 2) SE to provide redaction template + sample code (Liam) 3) Create cost calc for 5/15/30-min calls and share
2026-02-18: Inbound signup from product page; trial request (self-serve) received
2026-02-20: Intro call (15m) w/ AE Ava + CTO Mateo; Fireflies transcript linked
2026-02-24: Follow-up email with onboarding steps + sample prompts (Ava)
2026-03-02: Security questions received from legal — asked for retention & PII redaction details
Legal needs PII redaction proof
Retention SLA & deletion workflow unclear
Need token-level pricing for short transcripts
Send security/retention FAQ + example retention SLA; provide 14-day trial API key and sample redaction prompt templates

title: TypeScript SDK: request abort/cancel support for streaming chat
content:
TypeScript SDK: request abort/cancel support for streaming chat

Customer asks how to cancel an in-flight streaming chat request (e.g., user navigates away). They want AbortController support and docs examples. No bug reported; current workaround is closing the underlying fetch/reader.
Support (Connor): Provided workaround: call controller.abort() on the fetch used to create the stream; noted SDK does not expose it yet.
PM (Avery): Asked customer which runtimes (browser vs node) and whether they need partial transcript handling on cancel. Waiting for response.

title: Experiment metrics backfill plan (schema change to {experiment_id, variant_id})
content:
Experiment metrics backfill plan (schema change to {experiment_id, variant_id})

Context
- We added experiment attribution dimensions to request context + telemetry: {route_id, experiment_id, variant_id} (plus model_id, region) per ADR-048.
- Console “Results” view and guardrails are driven off rollup tables keyed by {route_id, experiment_id, variant_id, window_start}.
- During beta we had a schema change + partial rollout (feature flags + region ramp). As a result:
  - historical windows (and even some recent windows during rollout) are missing experiment_id/variant_id
  - Console results appear stale or “no data” for experiments created before the schema flip
  - support tickets are increasingly about “results not updating” when the underlying traffic clearly existed

Goal
Backfill the minimal set of metrics needed by Console route experiment dashboards/guardrails for a bounded time window after the schema change.

Non-goals (for this backfill)
- Not attempting a full reconstruction of all time-series metrics with full label cardinality.
- Not trying to compute statistical significance.
- Not trying to backfill custom/experimental quality signals (eval score stream) in this job.

What we need to backfill (MVP)
Console requires variant-level rollups per experiment, at 1m + 5m windows (5m for most charts; 1m for guardrail evaluation):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end request latency (and optionally model latency if available)
- Errors: error rate, timeout rate, retry rate
- Throughput: req_count, token_count (input/output if available)
- Cost proxy: total_tokens, billed_tokens (if present) and/or cost_usd_estimate if we have it in the pipeline
- Attribution health: attribution_drop_rate (ratio of requests missing experiment_id/variant_id)

Important: we only backfill the analytics rollup tables used by the Results API (not Prometheus/Mimir series). This is intentional to avoid label explosion and because Console reads from analytics.

Retention / source-of-truth constraints
We have multiple telemetry sources with different retention. This determines how far back we can accurately backfill.

Known/assumed retentions (verify per environment; numbers below reflect current defaults as of Mar 2025):
- OTel traces (full-fidelity spans): 7 days
- OTel metrics (high-cardinality tags are sampled/limited): not reliable for backfill; also label strategy changed (PR-28741)
- Request logs (gateway/router access logs with request_id): 30 days in log store; 90 days in cold storage (slow retrieval)
- Analytics “raw request events” table (if enabled): 14 days (partition TTL)
- Analytics rollups (the target): 13 months

Implication
- Best-quality backfill window is limited to the maximum overlap of:
  1) request-level events containing experiment attribution OR
  2) a joinable key (request_id/trace_id) that can be mapped to experiment assignment
- For >14 days, we will likely have to use access logs + join to assignment debug data (if available) OR accept partial coverage.

Proposed backfill window
- Default: backfill last 14 days from the day we confirm “attribution schema fully deployed” in each region.
- Optional extension: last 30 days if access logs are sufficient quality and join works at scale.
- We should NOT attempt beyond 30 days for beta/GA readiness unless an enterprise customer requires it (cost/benefit is poor and risk of incorrect attribution is high).

Schema/version cutover details (what changed)
- Added experiment_id + variant_id into:
  - request context
  - OTel span attributes
  - analytics ingestion schema
  - rollup grouping keys
- Main breakage modes we observed during the cutover:
  - streaming retries dropped attribution (fixed in PR-28622)
  - missing/low-entropy stickiness key caused skew and inconsistent assignment (fixed in PR-28705 + Console warnings)
  - region-by-region rollout caused mixed populations in rollups (older code paths missing tags)

Backfill strategy (high level)
We will run an offline job that recomputes rollups for a bounded time window using request-level events (preferred) or trace-derived request summaries (fallback), and overwrites rollup partitions.

Option A (preferred): backfill from analytics “request event” stream
Prereq: a request-level fact table exists with request_id and experiment_id/variant_id present for the time window (even if some records are missing).
- Input: request_events partitioned by event_time, containing:
  - route_id
  - experiment_id
  - variant_id
  - model_id
  - region
  - latency_ms
  - status_code / error_class
  - token counts
- Transform: aggregate into rollups_1m and rollups_5m with percentiles
- Output: upsert/overwrite partitions in experiment_variant_rollups_* tables

Option B (fallback): backfill by joining router access logs to assignment decision records
Prereq: we can derive or look up experiment assignment by (request_id or trace_id) + stickiness_key.
- Input 1: access logs w/ request_id, route_id, region, latency, model_id, status
- Input 2: assignment decision logs (or a compact “assignment audit” stream) containing request_id/trace_id -> {experiment_id, variant_id}
- Join: request_id (prefer) else trace_id
- Risk: assignment logs may not be complete for older windows; join might be expensive and drop a lot of rows

Option C (not recommended): try to rehydrate from traces only
- Not feasible beyond 7 days due to retention.
- Also traces may be sampled in high-QPS routes; percentiles become biased.

Decision
Proceed with Option A for a 14-day backfill as the primary plan. Keep Option B as contingency if request_events coverage is incomplete.

Implementation plan (jobs + ownership)
Target platform: analytics batch framework (Dataflow/Spark) writing into ClickHouse analytics cluster (rt_analytics). Exact runner TBD by Mei/Caleb based on existing rollup jobs.

Job 1: backfill_experiment_variant_rollups_5m
- Owner: Mei Lin (implementation), Caleb Johnson (pipeline review)
- Schedule: ad-hoc for backfill window; can be re-run idempotently
- Compute:
  - group by window_start_5m, route_id, experiment_id, variant_id, model_id, region
  - metrics: req_count, err_count, timeout_count, tokens_in/out, latency_p50/p95/p99
- Output table: experiment_variant_rollups_5m
- Write mode: overwrite partitions [start_ts, end_ts]

Job 2: backfill_experiment_variant_rollups_1m (guardrails)
- Owner: Nadia Rahman (metric definitions/cost), Mei Lin (aggregation)
- Same structure as 5m but 1m windows; fewer dimensions if needed for cost (see Cardinality Controls)

Job 3: compute_attribution_drop_rate
- Owner: Logan Wright
- Definition: for each window/route/experiment/region, compute missing-rate:
  - numerator = requests that were eligible for experiment but missing experiment_id OR variant_id
  - denominator = requests on route during window
- Practical note: “eligible for experiment” is hard to determine historically; for backfill we will use a proxy:
  - if experiment_id is present on any request for a route in a window, treat that route+window as “experiment-active” and compute missing-rate vs total requests for that route+window
  - this will slightly understate drop rate when attribution is 0% (i.e., full outage), but we have separate detection for “variant 0 traffic / no tagged traffic”

Partitioning + idempotency
- All output tables are partitioned by date (YYYY-MM-DD). Backfill will overwrite date partitions.
- We need guardrails to prevent overwriting “good” new data with older incorrect logic:
  - store backfill_job_version + backfill_run_id in a sidecar audit table
  - only overwrite partitions within an explicit allowlisted [start_date, end_date]

Cardinality controls (avoid cost blow-ups)
- Per PR-28741 we are limiting tags to prevent high cardinality.
- For backfill tables we must keep the exact dimensions the Results API expects. For anything extra, do NOT add new group-by keys.
- Proposed dimension set for backfill rollups:
  - required: route_id, experiment_id, variant_id
  - strongly preferred: region
  - optional: model_id (only if model_id cardinality is bounded; if not, roll up at “effective_model_family” or omit model_id for backfill)
- Action item: confirm Console queries. If Console requires model-level drill-down for GA, we keep model_id; otherwise we can omit it to keep costs manageable.

Compute cost estimate (rough)
Assumptions (to validate):
- Backfill window: 14 days
- Avg request_events volume: 800M req/day (hosted + dedicated combined), but only a small fraction are on experiment-enabled routes
- Eligible experiment traffic: ~2–5% of total requests during beta (spiky)

Estimate:
- Worst-case rows scanned if we scan full request_events: 11.2B rows
- Mitigation: filter early by route_id in experiment-enabled set (from experiment config service snapshots)
- Expected rows scanned after filter: ~200–600M rows total

We should implement route_id filtering using a daily snapshot of active experiment routes:
- input: experiment_config_snapshots (date, route_id, experiment_id)
- filter: only request_events where route_id in snapshot

Validation plan (must-have)
We will not ship the backfill without data quality checks, because incorrect backfills are worse than “missing data.”

Checks to run per region:
1) Row count sanity
- For each experiment_id and day:
  - sum(req_count across variants) ~= total req_count on route (within expected drift)

2) Split sanity (allocation consistency)
- For fixed split experiments (e.g., 90/10): compare observed variant req_count ratio to configured allocation
- Alert if deviation > 3% absolute over 24h (excluding low-traffic experiments)

3) Percentile sanity
- p50 <= p95 <= p99
- latency percentiles within reasonable bounds vs baseline route dashboards (non-attributed)

4) Join integrity (if we use Option B)
- join success rate >= 99% on request_id path; otherwise abort and reassess

5) Console spot-check
- Pick 2–3 beta accounts (Acme AI, Northbridge) and compare:
  - “No data” -> becomes populated
  - trends match operator expectations from Grafana guardrail dashboards

Operational rollout steps
1) Freeze window
- Choose [start_date, end_date] per region based on deployment completion (feature flag fully enabled + attribution bugfixes deployed).
- Avoid including time where we know streaming attribution was broken (pre PR-28622) unless we accept partial drop.

2) Dry run
- Run jobs in “write to staging tables” mode:
  - experiment_variant_rollups_5m_staging
  - experiment_variant_rollups_1m_staging
- Run validation queries; get sign-off from Observability + Console backend (Chloe) + SRE (Rafael)

3) Production overwrite
- Overwrite partitions in prod rollups
- Monitor:
  - query latency for Results API
  - ClickHouse cluster load
  - attribution_drop_rate time series

4) Post-backfill cleanup
- Drop staging tables after 7 days
- Record run_id + metadata in audit table

Risks / open questions
1) Data gaps due to missing attribution
- If experiment_id/variant_id were missing at ingestion time, we cannot reconstruct without a joinable assignment record.
- If request_events has missing fields but we still have request_id and a deterministic re-eval is possible, we could theoretically re-evaluate assignment offline. BUT:
  - requires exact historical config version + precedence rules + stickiness key used
  - very easy to get wrong; will not do for this backfill

2) Streaming/retry paths
- Pre-fix windows can undercount experiment traffic or misattribute. For those windows, backfill won’t “fix” it.
- Recommendation: choose start_date after PR-28622 is fully deployed to all regions.

3) Region mixing / config propagation lag
- If the same experiment had different configs in different regions, and traffic is region-pinned, we’re ok as long as we group by region.
- If customers use multi-region active-active and assignment is expected to be consistent across regions, we need to be careful interpreting combined results.

4) Cost and cluster impact
- Backfills can saturate ClickHouse merges and impact interactive Console queries.
- Mitigation: throttle writes, run in off-peak UTC windows, set max_threads, and coordinate with SRE.

5) Privacy/compliance
- Ensure we do not backfill any PII fields. The rollups are aggregated; request-level access is only in the batch job and should remain in restricted datasets.

6) Definition drift
- If metric definitions changed (latency definition, token accounting), historical backfills could be inconsistent.
- For this backfill, we will use the same aggregation logic as the current rollup job (pin to commit/tag) and write job_version.

Action items
- [Logan] Confirm which table is canonical “request_events” for hosted/dedicated and whether it retains experiment_id/variant_id for the full 14 days (by 2025-03-25).
- [Mei/Caleb] Prototype filtered scan by route_id snapshot and produce cost estimate for 14-day window (by 2025-03-26).
- [Nadia] Confirm cost/token fields available in request_events; if missing, define the minimal cost proxy for Console (by 2025-03-26).
- [Allison] Confirm required dimensions for Console queries (model_id yes/no) and align with cardinality policy (by 2025-03-27).
- [Rafael] Approve runtime window + throttling plan; add temporary alerting for ClickHouse load during backfill (by 2025-03-28).

Proposed schedule
- Week of Mar 24:
  - confirm data sources + implement staging backfill
  - validation queries and Console spot-check
- Week of Mar 31:
  - production backfill for 14 days (region by region)
  - monitor and adjust

Notes to self / parking lot
- If we later need >30 days for enterprise evidence, consider:
  - a lightweight “assignment decision event” stream with longer retention specifically to enable reconstruction
  - storing daily experiment route snapshots + config versions explicitly for offline replay
- Add a clear customer-facing note in docs: “Results dashboard only guaranteed from <date> forward” unless we commit to systematic long-retention request facts.

title: Hosted API sandbox lab — chat & text-gen basics + retry scenarios
content:
Hosted API sandbox lab — chat & text-gen basics + retry scenarios

Intro demo of Redwood hosted inference for chat/text generation. Walked through streaming behavior, key request params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop tokens), retry/backoff and idempotency considerations, and a short Console tour for per-route latency/cost. Discussed Optimize recommendations (batching, KV cache reuse, quantization) and enterprise concerns (SAML SSO, SOC2, audit logs). Agreed to sandbox access and smoke tests.
Meeting header: 2026-04-09 15:00 UTC — duration 47m. Attendees listed above.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone — thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. We've got Priya, our SE, and Sam who will jump in with the console demo. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Lena: Good thanks, Jordan. Excited — we just want a short hands-on of the hosted API for chat gen, mainly streaming, params and what to do when things error out.
[00:18] Jordan: Perfect that's exactly what we'll show. Priya, you want to intro the lab?
[00:21] Priya: Yeah hi all — real quick plan: 10 minutes on core streaming behavior and request params, 15 minutes live sandbox runs (I'll paste curl and SDK calls), then 15 on retry/backoff, idempotency and Console/Optimize tips and finally Q&A. Sound ok?
[00:33] Marco: Sounds great. We're especially worried about tail latency and cost per token.
[00:37] Priya: Totally. We'll show the console traces so you can see token breakdown and how batching/kv cache affects unit cost.
[00:45] Jordan: One quick administrative note — are there any security or compliance blockers up front? SAML / SSO, SOC2?
[00:50] Aisha: We need SOC2 certificate and we use SAML SSO internally. Also KMS for keys ideally.
[00:55] Jordan: Great — we will share security pack after the call. Redwood supports SSO and KMS/HSM integrations and SOC2. I'll follow up with the docs.

[05:00] Priya: Ok, starting the demo — this is the hosted chat endpoint in the sandbox. First behavior: streaming. When you open a stream you'll get incremental partial chunks — useful for UI latency. Note partials are not final predictions; in speech it's like interim captions.
[05:20] Jordan: One common gotcha — streaming shows partial tokens and can be restarted on retries; your frontend should handle deduping partials vs final.
[05:35] Kenji: If we reconnect and resume, does the service replay the entire context or just deltas?
[05:40] Priya: We replay deltas where possible, but to be safe you should send a conversation snapshot up to the last confirmed user message. We also support KV cache reuse if you're pinning model variants. Some transcriptions will show "K V cache" spelled out in places.

[10:00] Priya: Live curl example: POST to /v1/chat with messages array, set stream=true for SSE. Key params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop tokens. We'll paste this in chat.
[10:20] (Priya pastes curl)
[10:30] Marco: Quick question — which param most affects hallucinations?
[10:33] Priya: Temperature and top_p. Lower temperature reduces randomness; top_p controls nucleus sampling. Also good prompt engineering and stop tokens cut off generation where applicable. For deterministic outputs set temperature ~0 and top_p ~0.0-0.1.

[15:00] Priya: Now a small failure mode — we purposely induced a partial drop mid-stream. Watch how the stream emits a 5xx and then our SDK triggers exponential backoff.
[15:18] Sam: The SDK includes automatic retry for idempotent requests. For non-idempotent generation (streams that have side effects) we recommend client-controlled retries with idempotency keys. We usually attach a client_message_id to each user turn.
[15:40] Aisha: So idempotency key is our responsibility?
[15:42] Priya: Yes — you supply an idempotency_key header. For simple text generation where you can tolerate duplicates, the SDK retry policy is fine; for billing and dedupe we recommend explicit keys.

[20:00] Priya: Backoff: use jittered exponential backoff. Example: base 500ms, multiplier 2x, max 8s, with full jitter. Avoid tight retry loops because they inflate load and cost.
[20:20] Kenji: Any rate limit headers we can read to adaptively backoff?
[20:24] Priya: Yes the API returns x-rate-limit-remaining and a Retry-After when throttled. Console traces also show per-route QPS metrics.

[25:00] Priya: Now let's look at the Console — Sam, can you show the token breakdown?
[25:10] Sam: Sure. Here is a sample route — per-token cost, P95 latency and token counts. The Console groups by model variant so you can see the cost impact if you switch to a quantized variant.
[25:30] Sam: Also we surface prefix cache hits — which we call KV cache reuse — that reduces model work when you've repeated prompts or system instructions.
[25:45] Marco: If we use dedicated capacity versus hosted, how different are the SLOs?
[25:50] Jordan: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and private pools with higher SLAs, hosted is multi-tenant but we still publish performance profiles. For strict latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated or pinning to a lower-latency model variant.

[30:00] Priya: Optimize suggestions: 1) batch short messages to amortize GPU overhead, 2) enable prefix KV caching for repeated system messages, 3) use a quantized variant (8-bit or 4-bit) if high throughput with slightly lower quality is acceptable, 4) tune max_tokens per user turn to the minimum needed.
[30:25] Lena: For batching — how does that affect user perceived latency?
[30:28] Priya: Batching is tradeoff — it improves throughput and lowers cost per token but you increase queuing latency. We recommend adaptive batching: small immediate responses for interactive UI, larger batches for background tasks (summaries).

[35:00] Priya: Quick note on safety: if you use stop tokens, model guarentees for truncation are best-effort. Also we recommend server-side safety filters or a secondary reranker to catch edge cases.

[36:00] Marco: For retries, do we get chargedback for partially generated tokens that then fail?
[36:05] Jordan: You get billed for tokens processed by the model. If a stream fails mid-generation you are charged for tokens consumed. That's why idempotency + conservative retry logic matters. We'll include guidance in the follow-up doc.

[40:00] Priya: Wrapping up — we pushed a small guided exercise: run the sandbox curl we pasted, try toggling temperature and stream=true/false, trigger an intentional error and observe console traces.
[40:15] Lena: We'll run that and get back to you.
[40:20] Aisha: And we'll need the SOC2 and SAML docs.
[40:25] Jordan: Yep I'll send the security pack. Priya will share the Optimize spreadsheet and sample SDK snippets.

[45:00] Jordan: Any other questions?
[45:05] Kenji: One last — can Redwood run a short perf benchmark with our typical token mix?
[45:10] Jordan: Yes we can — that would be a scoped POC. We'll propose a runbook after your smoke test.
[46:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and snippets.

End transcript.

Notes: occasional transcript artifacts e.g., misheard acronyms ("K V cache" spelled occasionally), filler words and overlapping talk. References shared: sandbox curl (link sent in chat), console screenshot (link), security pack (link to drive).

title: Streaming Chat connector patterns and migration guide for Python SDK
content:
Streaming Chat connector patterns and migration guide for Python SDK

Problem: multiple consumer patterns in the Python SDK (callback hooks, iterator-based, and low-level SSE adapters) have led to repeated user confusion and brittle integrations when applications attempt to add telemetry, retries, or partial-resume. Goal: introduce a connector pattern + migration guide that provides a small, typed consumer facade (ConsumerConnector) and a set of adapter recipes so existing customers can migrate incrementally. The connector must support: resumable checkpoints, typed event signals (message, meta, error, watermark), prioritized soft-retries, and clear telemetry hooks. This ticket covers design, reference implementation, migration docs, and 2 integration examples (FastAPI webhook and a serverless consumer).
Spec: a one-page event contract + connector API published in docs and linked from SDK README
Reference implementation added to python/sdk/connectors with unit tests covering resume/replay and retry semantics
Migration guide with code snippets for callback -> iterator -> connector flows
Two example apps updated: examples/fastapi-chat-consumer and examples/serverless-stream-consumer
Bench: latency regression < 5% for typical 16-token responses in CI microbench compared to current iterator baseline
Telemetry: connector emits token-level counters and persisted resume checkpoints to SDK tracing hooks
Connector API: class SyncConnector(consumer_callable) and AsyncConnector(async_consumer_callable) with methods: start(), pause(), resume(checkpoint), close()
Event contract: 'type' in {message, meta, error, watermark, checkpoint}; payload schema versioned (v1); include optional 'id' and 'seq' on message events
Retries: connector will expose soft_retry(retry_policy) hook; default policy = exponential backoff with jitter and idempotency by event id
Resume semantics: checkpoint = {cursor, last_seq, model_variant, kv_cache_snapshot_id}; SDK will persist checkpoint to configured storage adapter (in-memory for examples; external store optional)
Telemetry: emit connector.resume, connector.pause, connector.error, connector.message spans; add counters for tokens_emitted and resume_attempts
Migration helpers: callback_to_connector adapter and iterator_to_connector shim provided; examples in the migration guide
Testing: unit tests + integration playback harness that feeds recorded event streams from /tests/fixtures/streams
Risk: breaking existing integrators who depend on low-level SSE shapes. Mitigation: provide adapter layer and keep old APIs for at least 2 releases with deprecation warnings.
Risk: performance regression from extra event wrapping. Mitigation: microbench target <5% regression; inline event object to reduce allocation pressure.
Risk: incorrect resume leading to duplicate token emissions. Mitigation: add seq-based dedupe in connector and test against recorded streams and race conditions.
Finish PR fixes for cache leak and merge feature-flagged connector to canary branch
Add migration snippets to README + full migration guide in docs
Run CI microbench and smoke tests across macOS/ubuntu py3.11 and publish results
Schedule follow-up tickets for TypeScript and Go adapters after stabilization
2026-03-02 - Kickoff: scoped to Python SDK only; TypeScript/Go adapters deferred to follow-up after API stabilizes
2026-03-04 - Design review: decided to surface a tiny SyncConnector + AsyncConnector pair rather than a single universal type to keep ergonomics simple for sync-first consumers
2026-03-06 - Trade-off: opted for explicit 'Checkpoint' objects instead of opaque cursors to make migration and debugging easier; marginally increases surface area but improves transparency
2026-03-08 - Telemetry: agreed to use existing SDK tracing hooks (span name: sdk.connector.resume) and add token_count and checkpoint_id tags
2026-03-10 - Prototype: initial connector implemented behind feature flag 'connector_alpha' in PR #482; basic resume and error-signal wiring works with local playback tests
2026-03-11 - QA: found an edge-case where aborted soft-retries could leak partial KV cache state — added a sandbox test and flagged as follow-up bug ENG-614730
2026-03-12 - Docs: migration guide draft published to Confluence; example snippets reviewed by DE and approved with minor wording suggestions
Priya Patel (2026-03-02): Added initial scope and acceptance criteria. Linked design doc.
Diego Morales (2026-03-04): Posted initial connector sketch and sync/async API surface. Requesting review from @Avery Chen and @Samir Kapoor for telemetry hooks.
Avery Chen (2026-03-05): Prefer explicit checkpoint objects. Concerned about adoption friction — suggested a migration helper module.
Samir Kapoor (2026-03-06): Asked to ensure connector supports both streaming and non-streaming fallbacks. Will follow up with test plan for fallbacks.
Diego Morales (2026-03-08): Uploaded RFC patch to PR #482. Running microbench locally; results within acceptable range.
Nora Li (QA) (2026-03-11): Reproduced KV cache leak in integration test. Created reproducible test case and attached logs to PR. Marked blocking for merge until fixed.
Diego Morales (2026-03-12): Fixed leak by isolating ephemeral cache per consumer instance. Updated unit tests and docs. Ready for final review.

title: Gullridge Logistics Intelligence
content:
Gullridge Logistics Intelligence

Short summary: POC kicked off strong (reranking + embeddings for freight matching) but stalled after security review and an internal hiring freeze. Engineering lead pulled off the project Nov 2025 — no cycles since. Competitive pressure from ModelServeCorp (they offered an on-prem sandbox) and an internal budget reprioritization put deal on hold. Key quote from Head of Product (11/18): "We like performance but we have zero bandwidth until Q3; security wants audited KMS and explicit residency guarantees."

POC details: lightweight end-to-end test created by our SE; baseline latency targets 60ms p95 for rerank calls, throughput 150 req/s in peak simulations. Initial integration used our Dedicated preview in their VPC; ran into audit gaps (missing artifact-level logging + retention policy mismatch). POC milestone 2 (live traffic shadowing) missed on 2025-12-08 — no engineering resource to wire traffic. Security asked for completed answers to SOC2/ISO questions and a legal review of data residency (response submitted 2026-02-10).

Why stalled: combination of budget freeze for Q1 hiring, security policy items (audit/logging + KMS), and departure of internal champion (Sr. ML Eng left Dec). They also asked for an air-gapped option; that is high touch and would push cost beyond their current commit. Our commercial offer was softened (extended evaluation) but procurement is on hold.

title: Graceful Capacity Degradation: Commercialization and Customer Onboarding Playbook
content:
Graceful Capacity Degradation: Commercialization and Customer Onboarding Playbook

Overview

This playbook defines the product, commercial, and operational approach for "graceful capacity degradation" — an end-to-end feature that lets Redwood continue serving customer traffic under transient capacity pressure by: routing to lower-fidelity model variants, applying short-term batching changes, and issuing customer-facing credits where quality/latency SLOs are impacted. The goal is to keep customer applications online while limiting cost and preserving predictable economics.

Use cases:
- Enterprise customers on Dedicated pools experiencing regional GPU contention.
- Hosted-tier customers during cross-region failover events.
- Migration windows where full-capacity variants are being rolled out.

Who should read this: product managers, solutions engineering, account teams, SRE, billing, and customer success.

Objectives

1) Business: minimize revenue churn from outages by providing a transparent, contractual fallback behavior and straightforward crediting model.
2) Product: expose controls for fidelity vs cost tradeoffs and automated fallback policies per tenant.
3) Ops: give SREs deterministic, observable fallbacks with clear telemetry and rollback procedures.

Scope and Non-Scope

In scope:
- Policy definitions in the control plane for per-tenant fallback sequencing (model variant, quantization, batching).
- Billing credit calculation for short-term fidelity/latency degradations.
- Customer onboarding flows and contract language templates.
- Console UX for visualizing fallback events and credit history.

Out of scope:
- Long-term contract renegotiation (handled by Sales).
- Deep model retraining to recover fidelity (handled by Applied ML).

Product contract and SLO implications

SLO mapping (examples):
- Availability SLO: 99.95% regional for Hosted API (unchanged).
- Latency SLO (TR1 route): p95 < 300ms. During graceful degradation that target may be relaxed to p95 < 700ms per policy.
- Quality SLO: BLEU/ROUGE or embedding distance budget for evaluated prompt sets — a soft guard used to trigger crediting when exceeded.

When a degradation policy is applied, the system will:
1) Record an event in routing-proxy and console (event_id).
2) Flag the tenant for billing-service credit evaluation.
3) Update runtime headers to indicate fallback variant (X-Redwood-Fallback-Variant).

Credit calculation rules (summary):
- Windowed approach: credits are calculated per 5-minute window where observed quality/latency exceeds the configured tenant thresholds.
- Credit basis: fraction of token cost attributable to degraded fidelity + fixed service-level goodwill amount.
- Max credit cap: 20% of the tenant’s billed usage in the affected week unless escalated by CSM.

Operational controls and owner ship

Owners: 
- Product: Aisha Patel (owner for commercial playbook updates)
- Opt-in policy feature flag: eng-platform (feature-flag service)
- Runtime/fallback orchestration: eng-serving-runtime (runtime team)
- Billing & credits engine: finance-and-legal (billing-service team)
- Onboarding & comms: customer-success-and-support (CSM team)

Immediate contacts (escalation):
- Oncall SRE: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations
- Billing escalation: Sana Becker (finance)

Customer onboarding checklist (CSM / Solutions Eng)

1) Pre-signing (Contract/Legal):
   - Insert fallback covenant into Appendix B of the contract (template snippet below).
   - Agree on maximum weekly credit cap and SLA tiers.

2) Initial setup (first 7 days):
   - Enable per-tenant fallback policy default in the Console (DefaultPolicy: standard_fallback_v1).
   - Capture a canonical prompt set (10–20 prompts) for quality monitoring. Add to tenant profile: 'fallback_guard_prompts'.
   - Set tenant-specific thresholds: latency_margin_ms, embedding_distance_threshold.

3) Post-activation (day 7–30):
   - Run a simulated load test using the hosted-sim-runner to validate fallback behavior.
   - Walk through customer Console views showing fallback events and credits.
   - Schedule a QBR within first 30 days to review observed fallbacks and crediting.

Template contract snippet (Appendix B):

"During transient capacity constraints Redwood may route traffic to lower-fidelity model variants or apply batching that can affect latency and output characteristics. Redwood will provide usage credits for material degradations consistent with the Customer’s SLA. The maximum weekly credit is 20% of billed usage for the affected time period unless otherwise negotiated."

Staged rollout plan (recommended)

1) Canary (internal): enable on 10 internal tenants and exercise 3 failure modes (GPU pressure, cross-region network spike, warm-pool exhaustion). Duration: 2 weeks.
2) Beta (select customers): opt-in by invitation to up to 20 paying customers. Monitor for false positives in crediting and UX clarity. Duration: 4 weeks.
3) General availability: automatic opt-in default for new enterprise customers, opt-out for legacy contracts.

Rollout metrics to validate at each stage:
- False positive credit events per 1000 degraded windows < 1.
- Time to detect and apply fallback < 15s from threshold breach.
- Percentage of requests served without failover increased vs baseline (resilience uplift).

Billing and pricing impact examples (table)

| Degradation Level | Runtime change | Billing credit % (windowed) | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Minor | small-quant (int8) | 5% | Quality delta within 3% of baseline on eval prompts |
| Moderate | reduced-fp32-context | 12% | p95 latency > baseline by +300ms OR embedding distance exceedance |
| Major | variant-fallback-to-small | 20% (cap) | Significant quality regression; automatic CSM review triggered |

Example credit calculation (simplified):
- Tenant A had $2,000 billed in the affected week. During a 30-minute incident with moderate degradations affecting 3 five-minute windows, system calculates 12% credit on tokens for those windows: estimated credit = $2,000 * (minutes_affected / total_week_minutes) * 12% (simplified). Final credits are rounded and shown in Console adjustments.

Console UX and telemetry requirements

Required Console elements: 
- Fallback events timeline per-tenant with event_id and reason codes (REASON_GPU_PRESSURE, REASON_COLD_START, REASON_NETWORK_EGRESS).
- Credit calculator preview and audit trail.
- Toggle for opt-in/out and tenant-specific thresholds.

Telemetry and logging:
- routing-proxy: fallback_applied (bool), fallback_variant (string), event_id (uuid).
- runtime-metrics: model_variant, avg_batch_size, effective_qps.
- billing-service: credit_eval_id, credit_amount, reason_code.

Operational runbook (SRE)

Trigger conditions: automated detection when any of the following repeat for N=3 consecutive 1-minute windows:
1) p95 latency > 2x configured latency SLO.
2) evaluated prompt-set quality metric breaches threshold.
3) GPU pool capacity utilization > 92% and queue depth > 50%

Immediate actions (ordered):
1) Confirm detection in routing-proxy and surface to incident channel #fallback-events.
2) If automated policy applied: verify X-Redwood-Fallback-Variant in live requests.
3) Notify oncall and CSM if predicted credit > $5,000 in the next 60 minutes.
4) If false-positive: rollback policy via feature-flag (feature-flag service CLI).

CLI snippets (example):

# Inspect current fallback policy for tenant
redwoodctl tenants get --id tenant_123 --fields fallback_policy

# Force-rollout rollback (engineering only)
redwoodctl feature-flags set graceful_degradation false --scope tenant_123 --reason "false-positive"

Acceptance criteria for GA

- Feature flagged and controllable per-tenant in Console.
- Billing-service integration able to generate provisional credits and surface to Console.
- Automated detection rules validated with < 1% false positives in Beta.
- CSM & Sales trained with playbook and contract template.

Success metrics (product & commercial)

- Reduction in outage-related churn rate by 30% for customers using fallback within 6 months.
- Mean time to apply fallback < 15s.
- Percentage of fallback events with customer-visible credits processed within 24 hours > 95%.

Risks and mitigations

Risk: Customers perceive credits as a license for degraded experience.
Mitigation: Restrict rollout to enterprise customers by default; add explicit contract language and weekly credit caps.

Risk: Over-crediting due to noisy quality signals.
Mitigation: Require N=3 consecutive windows and cross-validate with canonical prompt-set before issuing credits.

Appendix: Implementation notes for eng teams

- routing-proxy should emit structured event payloads to kafka topic: fallback-events (schema v1). Fields: event_id, tenant_id, reason_code, variant, window_start, window_end.
- billing-service will consume fallback-events and join with usage-aggregates to produce provisional credit entries (credit_eval_id).
- Console will render a reversible audit trail entry for each provisional credit and allow CSM to approve final credit posting.

Sample fallback-events kafka payload (human readable):
{
  "event_id": "evt-8f3a2",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_123",
  "reason_code": "REASON_GPU_PRESSURE",
  "variant": "small-variant-quantized-v2",
  "window": "2026-06-09T10:05:00Z/2026-06-09T10:10:00Z",
  "metrics": {"p95_latency_ms": 820, "embedding_distance_delta": 0.12}
}

Note: the actual kafka schema is managed in eng-platform/schemas and must be updated in the schema registry before GA.

Related pages and next steps

- Coordinate with finance-and-legal to finalize crediting algorithm and weekly caps.
- Schedule lab tests with Applied ML to calibrate canonical prompt-sets for Beta tenants.
- Run the Canary starting 2026-07-05 and record validation metrics in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite.

Document revision history

- 2026-03-29: initial draft (A. Patel)
- 2026-04-15: added billing calculation examples and SRE runbook (D. Martinez)
- 2026-06-10: post-beta updates, clarified contract language and Console mockups (P. Narayanan)

title: Auriga MLOps - model selection & tool-calling discovery
content:
Auriga MLOps - model selection & tool-calling discovery

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Auriga - Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Auriga - Platform Eng), Marisol Vega (Auriga - PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):
- Auriga is evaluating model selection for multilingual, long-context customer-facing assistant; they have strict latency targets for chat and require function/tool calling to enrich responses from internal systems.
- Key decision factors: context length (up to 65k in some use cases), multilingual quality (EN/ES/DE), cost/latency tradeoffs, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2).
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to share pricing sheet and run dedicated benchmarks on Auriga sample data; customer to share redacted dataset and schedule security deep dive.

Topics: model selection, context length, multilingual, tool-calling, private vs dedicated hosting, benchmarking, security/compliance

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining—I'm Alex, AE at Redwood. Samira, do you want to intro?
[00:12] Samira Patel: Hey all, Samira here, solutions engineer. We'll probably do 45 to 55 minutes, talk through Auriga's use cases, latency/cost constraints, and then map model candidates and deployment modes.
[00:25] Priya Rao: Hi, thanks. I'm Priya, Head of ML at Auriga. Quick context: we run a customer-facing assistant and an internal search/chat for docs. Currently on prem K8s, vector db is Faiss-ish managed in house, retrieval pipeline is our own microservices. Key asks: long context (sometimes 60k tokens of transcript + docs), multilingual support (EN/ES/DE), and ability to call our internal tools for account lookups.
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: Platform notes — we are sensitive about data residency and keys, prefer VPC or private. We also need predictable p99 latency for chat flows (ideally < 350ms) and clear cost numbers.
[01:12] Alex Chen: Great, that's super helpful. Two big axes we'll discuss: model family and deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private). For models, given long context and multilingual, we typically look at 32k and 64k context LLMs — there are open weights like Llama-3 variants, Mistral mixtral, and also some quantized flavors. We've got Redwood-verified profiles for throughput and token-cost.
[01:36] Priya Rao: When you say Redwood-verified profiles, is that publicly available? And how often do those profiles change based on kernel selection?
[01:44] Samira Patel: We publish benchmarks in the console and docs — they show typical latency/cost on GPU types. Kernel selection is automatic in the runtime; it picks optimized kernels and quantization settings based on the model arch and the request shape. That can change effective perf a bit per model.
[02:05] Priya Rao: Our ML team cares about hallucination rates across languages. Any model recommendations for EN/ES/DE parity?
[02:13] Samira Patel: In our experience, Mistral-family and Llama-3 derivatives with instruction-tuning tend to be stronger for high-quality multilingual outputs. If you need parity, the 64k context Llama-3 variant tuned for multilingual data is a strong candidate, but it's heavier on infra. For cost-sensitive paths, a quantized 32k variant plus retrieval augmentation can be much cheaper and still meet quality targets.
[02:41] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood support function/tool calling like OpenAI-style function calls? We need structured outputs to trigger downstream services.
[02:50] Alex Chen: Yes — we support tool/function calling patterns and structured output. We also provide webhooks and a light-weight reformatting layer in the console. Note that function calling adds some latency depending on the number of round trips and whether you embed tools in the generation loop or post-process.
[03:10] Priya Rao: For our flows we prefer single-shot tool calling: model returns a JSON payload and we trigger APIs. Any constraints around size of tool descriptions or number of tools?
[03:19] Samira Patel: You can register multiple tools; the runtime will include tool schemas as needed. The practical limit is token budget — large tool schemas consume context. We recommend compact schemas and using retrieval for tool docs.
[03:33] Marisol Vega: On deployment mode: what pushes customers to Dedicated vs Private? We want both predictable latency and to keep control of keys.
[03:42] Alex Chen: Good question. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our infra with SLA-backed latency/throughput and data isolation — you bring your workload but it's hosted. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict data residency or air-gapped needs; you run a customer-controlled control plane and we support KMS integrations. Dedicated has faster time-to-value; Private has more control and compliance overhead.
[04:05] Priya Rao: Does Private support on-prem GPUs?
[04:08] Samira Patel: Yes, we have an on-prem package. For on-prem you'll coordinate image versions and kernel builds; our team supports onboarding. There's some Ops lift but it's a fit for regulated workloads.
[04:21] Liam O'Connor: Latency — you mentioned kernel selection. If we pick a 64k context model, do we expect p50/p95 to blow up versus 32k?
[04:29] Samira Patel: Generally, cost and latency scale with context length. 64k sequences will show higher per-token latency and memory pressure; you can mitigate with KV cache strategies, prefix caching for static context, and retrieval to keep the prompt size smaller. For chat p95 targets under 350ms, many customers pick 32k or use hybrid: 64k for batch/document tasks and 32k for chat.
[04:55] Priya Rao: Are there examples of customers who do 65k plus retrieval?
[04:59] Alex Chen: Yeah, a couple verticals — legal and clinical — use long-context models with heavy retrieval and prefix caching. We have published an example case study on our docs where they shard the context and only include top-K passages into the prompt. We'll share that link after.
[05:18] Liam O'Connor: Security — SOC 2? How does Dedicated vs Hosted affect audit logs and SSO?
[05:24] Samira Patel: Hosted can be SOC 2 compliant (we provide audit logs and enterprise SSO). Dedicated also includes enhanced logging and per-customer telemetry. Private gives you full control of logs and SSO integrations. We support SAML/Okta and integrate with customer KMS for key control.
[05:42] Priya Rao: For encryption at rest in Dedicated, do we have customer-managed keys or do you manage them?
[05:48] Alex Chen: We support both. For the highest control you can use customer-managed KMS in Dedicated or Private. We'll note that in the pricing sheet options.
[05:58] Marisol Vega: For benchmarking, what do you need from us to run realistic tests?
[06:03] Samira Patel: Ideally: a redacted sample dataset that mirrors your longest contexts, a retrieval sample (top K), and the typical prompt templates. Also your latency SLO targets and expected concurrency. With that we can run a 5-10 run latency benchmark across candidate models and deployment shapes.
[06:21] Priya Rao: We can provide that. We'll need NDA considerations for sample data — do you have a secure upload?
[06:27] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll share secure upload links and an S3 presigned flow tied to the deal. Also we'll mask PII on our side during testing. We'll include that in the security doc.
[06:38] Liam O'Connor: A technical question — how does Redwood handle KV cache persistence across restarts? We want to avoid cold-start thrash.
[06:46] Samira Patel: The runtime supports persistent KV caching and warm-up policies. In Dedicated you can configure instance warm pools; for Private you control the persistence layer. Note transcription might say KV cash sometimes — it's KV cache.
[06:59] Priya Rao: Tooling: we plan to expose a small set of internal tools (account_lookup, billing_history, policy_fetch). We need type-safety on the outputs. How do you recommend we implement that?
[07:13] Samira Patel: Use strongly-typed function schemas and post-call validators. Our runtime can enforce schema validation on function outputs and reject mismatches. Also consider end-to-end tests in your CI that assert contract expectations.
[07:26] Marisol Vega: Cost — any rough numbers for 32k vs 64k on Dedicated? Ballpark to justify PoC sizing.
[07:33] Alex Chen: Ballpark is tricky without exact workload, but roughly 64k can be 2-3x token-cost compared to 32k for equivalent generated tokens because of memory and compute overhead. Dedicated commitments can reduce unit cost substantially compared to hosted on-demand; we'll include sample SKU pricing in the sheet.
[07:55] Priya Rao: Can you do adaptive serving — route heavy-context requests to cheaper variants if quality threshold met?
[08:02] Samira Patel: Yes, smart routing policy is available: you can route by latency, cost, or region. We also support fallbacks to smaller models with a quality gate — useful for keeping service available under load.
[08:16] Liam O'Connor: How about multilingual evals? We want a reproducible eval harness.
[08:21] Samira Patel: We can run automated evals on your test slices across EN/ES/DE and return BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity metrics plus human evaluation samples. We also recommend running a small human eval on critical intents.
[08:39] Priya Rao: Will you run those evals as part of the benchmark?
[08:41] Alex Chen: We can include a basic multilingual quality run; for deeper human evals we'd collaborate on the rubric and scope.
[08:48] Marisol Vega: Any red flags we should be aware of in the onboarding?
[08:51] Samira Patel: Biggest ops stuff is if you go Private/on-prem — that has more lift. Also large context models need careful batching and memory tuning; we'll help tune batching policy to meet p95 SLOs.
[09:04] Alex Chen: Ok quick recap before Qs: Redwood will send pricing sheet and Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, Samira will run benchmarks with redacted sample data, Auriga to share dataset and schedule security session.
[09:16] Priya Rao: Sounds good. A few quick Qs — how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks?
[09:21] Samira Patel: We have model version pins and rollout controls: canary, A/B, automatic fallback to older pinned versions if error rates spike. Everything is per-route and per-customer.
[09:32] Liam O'Connor: Is there a way to get telemetry into our existing Datadog stack?
[09:36] Alex Chen: Yes, we provide traces and metrics exports; Datadog + OpenTelemetry integrations are supported. We'll share the dashboard JSON for a sample route.
[09:47] Priya Rao: Any common misconfigurations you see?
[09:50] Samira Patel: Too-large prompt templates and not using retrieval — that blows up token cost. Also forgetting to compact tool schemas and over-fetching context.
[09:59] Marisol Vega: Can we see an example of a function-schema and how Redwood validates it?
[10:03] Samira Patel: We'll send an example in the follow-up email; it's a small JSON schema and the runtime enforces types.
[10:12] Priya Rao: One more on data retention — how long are logs kept in Hosted vs Dedicated?
[10:17] Alex Chen: Hosted defaults to 30 days, Dedicated can be configured up to 365 days for enterprise packages, Private you control retention. We'll include these defaults in the security doc.
[10:29] Priya Rao: Perfect.
[10:31] Alex Chen: Anything else from the Auriga side?
[10:33] Liam O'Connor: Not from me.
[10:35] Marisol Vega: No.
[10:36] Priya Rao: One ask — can you include a sample autopilot config for routing heavy-context docs to batch jobs?
[10:42] Samira Patel: Yes, we'll include a snippet of autoscaling and routing policies.
[10:46] Alex Chen: Great. We'll follow-up with the spreadsheet, secure upload link, benchmark plan, and security docs. Thanks everyone.
[10:55] Priya Rao: Thank you.

Auto action items (end of transcript):
- Alex: pricing & SKU sheet, Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, retention/keys options.
- Samira: benchmark plan + run with Auriga's sample data.
- Auriga: share redacted sample dataset, schedule security deep dive.

References/links mentioned (to be attached after call):
- Redwood benchmark doc (console link placeholder)
- Example prefix caching case study (legal vertical)
- Secure upload link (will be emailed)

Notes on transcription quality: medium — some proper nouns and acronyms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache rendered as KV cash), occasional overlap on speakers, minor punctuation issues.

title: Proportional burst allocation and post-facto billing adjustments for Dedicated capacity
content:
Proportional burst allocation and post-facto billing adjustments for Dedicated capacity

Background: Dedicated pools expose reserved throughput (committed capacity) plus opportunistic burst capacity. When pool degradation or preemption occurs we must: 1) fairly attribute reserved vs burst usage per tenant; 2) apply SLA credits if reserved throughput was degraded; and 3) offer deterministic, auditable post-facto billing adjustments so finance and customers can reconcile invoices. Current implementation uses a best-effort leaky-bucket per-tenant counter and applies burst credits at coarse windows which leads to noisy attributions and occasional overcharges during multi-tenant pool events. This ticket designs and implements a proportional, time-sliced usage ledger and a reconciliation job that computes SLA credits and negative-balance adjustments after the fact.
Create a deterministic, time-sliced ledger for Dedicated pools that: (a) attributes reserved vs burst consumption proportionally across tenants for each time-slice; (b) computes SLA credit allocation and negative-balance protections post-facto; (c) is idempotent, auditable, and compatible with existing billing pipelines.
Introduce 1-minute time-sliced ingestion of pool-level telemetry and per-tenant request tokens. For each minute slice, compute theoretical reserved entitlement per tenant (based on their committed throughput at that minute) and classify actual tokens consumed into reserved vs burst proportions using a proportional allocator when aggregate demand > reserved capacity. Persist ledger rows per-tenant per-minute. Run a daily reconciliation job to calculate SLA credits for minutes where actual available capacity < reserved capacity and to generate post-facto adjustments (credits/debits) exposed to billing. Implement a shadow mode for 6 weeks before enabling adjustments to invoices.
Telemetry ingestion: use existing runtime metrics endpoint to emit pool.available_capacity and per-tenant.request_tokens per 10s, aggregate into 1m buckets in the ingestion service.
Allocation algorithm: for each minute M, let R = sum(reserved_capacity_i) for tenants i, A = available_capacity_observed for the pool, and T_i = tokens_consumed_by_tenant_i in M. If sum(T_i) <= R then mark consumption as reserved up to each tenant's reserved share. If sum(T_i) > R then compute reserved_share_i = min(T_i, floor(R * (reserved_capacity_i / R))) and remaining tokens are burst. When reserved_capacity floats (reassignments), use the committed reservation snapshot at minute boundary.
SLA credit calc: for minutes where A < R_expected (expected reserved pool capacity), compute an availability_ratio = A / R_expected. For each tenant, SLA_credit_minutes = (1 - availability_ratio) * reserved_share_i. Convert SLA minutes into monetary credit using the tenant's reserved unit rate at invoice time.
Ledger schema (persisted): one row per tenant per-minute with fields: timestamp_minute, tenant_key, reserved_entitled, tokens_consumed, reserved_attributed, burst_attributed, pool_id, capacity_snapshot_tag. Stored in OLAP as CSV/Parquet and exported to billing pipeline. (Persisted as flat columns; no nested blobs.)
Idempotency: reconciliation job computes adjustments by looking up ledger rows with reconciliation_tag=NULL and emits adjustments with a deterministic hash. If a run fails, it can safely retry without double-applying adjustments.
Performance: aggregation and allocation done inside a streaming job (Flink/kafka-streams) with local in-memory per-pool windowed state to operate at scale. Output to an events topic consumed by reconciliation worker.
Auditability: generate per-adjustment proof payload (ledger_rows included by id) linked in billing records and customer-facing invoice adjustments UI.
Compatibility: provide mapping from new ledger rows to existing billing pipeline fields so finance reports remain consistent. Add feature flag to toggle applying adjustments to invoices while still writing ledger rows.
Edge cases: short spikes (<1s) are captured in 1m buckets; preemption mid-minute uses capacity_snapshot_tag to ensure visibility and later correction via SLA credit logic. Pool split/merge operations include a migration mapping table to re-anchor ledger rows when pool topology changes.
Bucket granularity: 1-minute buckets are chosen as a balance between accuracy and storage/compute cost. Finer buckets (10s) increase accuracy for short preemptions but increase ingestion and storage by ~6x.
Proportional allocation fairness vs. simple first-come attribution: proportional approach is fairer for multi-tenant events but requires committed-reservation snapshots per-minute which increases complexity.
Real-time billing adjustments are avoided; we prefer batch post-facto adjustments to keep invoicing deterministic and allow dispute handling.
Shadow-mode complexity: running two parallel attribution models (current production + new ledger) doubles some compute but is necessary for confidence before switching invoice application.
Streaming ingestion emits per-pool 1m buckets with pool_capacity and per-tenant tokens_consume metrics with >=99.9% success under normal load
Allocation job produces ledger rows for 95% of tenant-minute combinations (allowing small data loss windows) and ledger row schema is exported to billing pipeline consumer test harness
Reconciliation daily job computes SLA credits deterministically and produces adjustments with a deterministic hash; two identical runs on the same input produce identical outputs
Shadow-mode comparison: after 4 weeks of shadow runs, discrepancies between old and new attribution are within expected bounds and documented; finance approves cutover criteria
System-level invariants: sum(reserved_attributed + burst_attributed) == tokens_consumed for all ledger rows, and sum(reserved_attributed) <= pool_reserved_capacity for each minute accounting for rounding tolerances
End-to-end e2e integration test that simulates a pool-wide degradation produces SLA credits visible in test-billing UI and an associated audit trail link
Phase 0: Instrumentation (2w) - ensure runtime emits per-tenant tokens and pool capacity at 10s resolution and add aggregator that writes 1m buckets to topic
Phase 1: Allocation service + ledger writer (3w) - implement proportional allocator in streaming job, write ledger to OLAP and events topic, enable feature flag to start writing rows in production (shadow)
Phase 2: Reconciliation job + billing adapter (2w) - daily job that reads ledger rows, computes SLA credits and adjustments, writes adjustments to billing microservice with idempotency keys
Phase 3: Shadow validation (6w) - run alongside existing system, produce discrepancy dashboards, run stakeholder reviews (Finance, Customer Success, Legal)
Phase 4: Controlled cutover (2w) - enable invoice application for a pilot tenant cohort, monitor closely, then full rollout
Phase 5: Backfill and audit (3w) - backfill historical ledger for rolling window (30d) as allowed by compute budget; apply agreed-upon retroactive credits only after legal/finance sign-off
Unit tests around allocation math (including edge rounding cases)
Property-based tests that assert conservation of tokens across synthetic request traces
Integration test that boots a small dedicated pool in staging and replays recorded production traces to verify ledger outputs
Chaos tests: simulate short preemptions and host-level degradation to validate SLA credit paths
Billing pipeline integration tests that consume adjustments and verify idempotency and balance preservation
Metric: fraction_of_minutes_without_ledger_row_per_pool > 0.1% -> paging alert
Metric: daily_total_adjustment_amount > threshold -> pager to finance-runbook
Dashboard: per-pool discrepancy between old_attribution and new_attribution distributions
Audit logs: reconcile_job_run_id and list of ledger row ids included; unprocessed rows metric
Start as write-only: ledger rows are produced but do not feed billing; run shadow comparisons and produce weekly reports for Finance
Pilot tenants: choose 3 mid-size tenants that represent different reservation topologies for invoice pilot
Backfill window: default to 30 days; longer backfill requires manual approval from Finance due to invoice exposure
Dispute handling: adjustments include a human-review flag and can be suppressed until manual approval for enterprise customers
Rollback: feature flag to disable automatic invoice application; ledger rows can continue to be written for forensics
Should monetary conversion for SLA minutes use the reservation rate at invoice issue date or at the minute timestamp? (Finance preference: invoice issue date to simplify accounting)
Rounding policy for fractional token attribution when many tenants share a pool — use deterministic floor-with-remainder distribution?
How to show micro-credits on customer invoices without confusing UX — condensed line items vs. aggregated monthly credit?
Policy for retroactive credits older than billing cutoff (e.g., >90 days) — require legal sign-off?
Storage and compute costs increase due to per-minute ledger rows (estimated +15% infra cost for ingestion and OLAP storage)
Finance or Legal objections during audit of historical adjustments that could delay backfill/cutover
Complexity in mapping pool topology changes (split/merge) to existing ledger rows could cause orphaned rows if mapping not recorded
Incorrect implementation could double-credit or double-debit invoices if reconciliation idempotency keys are not robust

2025-02-21 Liam Chen: Added allocator pseudocode and notes about 1m bucket choice. Suggest we evaluate 30s in stress tests.
2025-02-24 Mateo Rivera (PM): Finance wants deterministic hashes attached to each adjustment for ledger reconciliation. Added requirement.

title: kms-residency-reconciler-and-audit-anchoring-shim
content:
kms-residency-reconciler-and-audit-anchoring-shim

Motivation: We continue to see edge cases where a subset of operator requests (e.g. cross-zone operator automation and retry plumbing) can surface non-conforming KMS usage that bypasses residency enforcement and produces audit records with missing residency claims. This PR implements a runtime reconciler + audit anchoring shim that (1) intercepts KMS-bound operations, verifies effective region claims against tenant residency policy, and emits canonical anchored audit events, and (2) provides a lightweight reconciliation job for drifted operator credentials to detect and optionally quarantine KMS requests that violate configured residency constraints.

Summary of changes (single-string description):
- Add src/crypto/kms/residency_reconciler.go: middleware that checks KMS request context for tenant-region claim, consults residency cache, and rejects or routes to fallback KMS bindings.
- Add src/crypto/kms/anchored_audit_writer.go: produces compact, canonical audit envelopes with residency assertion, signer meta, and short-proof hash for downstream retention.
- Extend src/auth/rbacv2/policy_loader.go to expose policy TTL and region-assertion helpers; small API surface used by reconciler.
- Helm: deploy/helm/templates/kms-residency-configmap.yaml and values.swagger to enable feature-flagged rollout and tuning knobs (quarantine thresholds, reconciliation window).
- Docs: docs/security/kms-residency.md with operator-facing configuration and migration notes.
- Tests: tests/integration/test_kms_residency.sh and unit tests under internal/crypto/kms for edge-case coverage.

Design notes:
- Residency cache: a read-mostly in-memory cache refreshed via async subscriber to policy service; TTL made configurable to balance timeliness and performance.
- Decision semantics: if tenant policy marks region STRICT and request region mismatches, the reconciler will either reject the request (default) or, if in permissive rollout, tag the request as QUARANTINED and allow it through to a region-fallback KMS provider.
- Audit anchoring: every reconciler decision emits an anchored audit envelope containing request-id, tenant-id, decision, and a short-proof HMAC_SHA256 over the claim digest. Anchored envelopes intended for downstream compliance indexer to dedupe and reconstruct timeline even when upper layers drop tracing.
- Backwards compatibility: rollout behind feature flag kms_residency_reconciler=true. When disabled, code paths are no-op and audit writer emits legacy audit records.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implementation of reconciler and audit writer
- [x] Unit tests for decision matrix (STRICT/PERMISSIVE/UNSET)
- [x] Integration tests exercising helm values toggle and e2e reconciliation path
- [x] Documentation (docs/security/kms-residency.md)
- [x] Migration plan and rollback steps

Commits (high level):
- 1a2b3c4: add residency reconciler middleware and interface to policy loader
- 2b3c4d5: implement anchored audit writer and envelope format; add signer metadata plumbing
- 3c4d5e6: helm chart knobs + values for quarantine window and TTL
- 4d5e6f7: add unit/integration tests and CI job entries
- 5e6f7g8: docs and migration notes; fix linting and address review feedback

Files changed (high-level):
- src/crypto/kms/residency_reconciler.go (new) -- core reconciler middleware and decision matrix
- src/crypto/kms/anchored_audit_writer.go (new) -- audit envelope format + writer shim
- src/auth/rbacv2/policy_loader.go (mod) -- expose GetTenantRegionPolicy(tenantID) and TTL hooks
- deploy/helm/templates/kms-residency-configmap.yaml (new) -- runtime knobs for reconciler
- docs/security/kms-residency.md (new) -- operator guide and migration steps
- internal/crypto/kms/residency_reconciler_test.go (new) -- unit tests
- tests/integration/test_kms_residency.sh (new) -- basic e2e validation harness
- build/ci/kms-residency.yaml (mod) -- add integration stage to CI

Small illustrative snippet (residency_reconciler.go):
    // verifyRegion compares the request's claimed region to tenant policy
    if policy.Strict && reqRegion != policy.AllowedRegion {
        emitAnchoredAudit(ctx, req, "reject", "region_mismatch")
        return nil, status.Errorf(codes.PermissionDenied, "tenant residency violation: request region %s not allowed", reqRegion)
    }

Review conversation (selected threads):
- Marco Diaz (reviewer): "Can you clarify the performance budget here? the reconciler will be on the hot path for token issuance and small RPCs -- we should avoid extra network calls. Consider making policy cache default TTL 30s and prefer local evaluation."
  - Author (Lena Fischer): "Agreed. Default TTL set to 30s, reconciler uses in-process cache and async refresh. Fallback to the policy service only on cache-miss. Added benchmarking numbers in unit test comments."

- Priya Nair (reviewer): "Audit envelopes look good; need to make sure the proof HMAC key rotation is handled. How will old proofs be validated after rotation?"
  - Author: "Added signer_id into envelope and a signer-rotation table in deploy/helm/README; the compliance indexer will accept previous signer public keys for 7 days after rotation. Documented in docs/security/kms-residency.md (section 'Key rotation and proof validation')."

- Ethan Cole (reviewer): "Integration test intermittently fails on CI due to test container time drift. Suggest you make test resilient to up to +-120s offset and use monotonic clocks where possible."
  - Author: "Addressed; tests now normalize time windows and rely on monotonic timers for reconciliation window asserts. Re-ran CI locally and fixed flakiness."

- Security review (automated): "Static analysis flagged potential log injection in anchored audit writer when emitting free-form operator notes."
  - Author: "Sanitized operator notes via auditSanitize() and added a unit test for escaping. See commit 5e6f7g8."

CI summary: 
- build: pass
- unit: pass (all tests)
- integration: initial run failed (test_kms_residency.sh timing), rerun -> pass
- lint: pass with minor style adjustments applied

Rollback / migration plan (short):
- Start feature-flagged rollout in canary region (us-west-2) with permissive mode so that violating requests are quarantined but not rejected. Monitor anchored-audit indexer for QUARANTINED events and false positives.
- If spike in false positives: flip to off and collect samples; apply policy corrections; re-enable with longer TTL or widened quarantine window.
- Full rollout to main after 48hr canary with <0.1% false positive rate and no increase in 5xx for KMS proxy.

Operational notes:
- Adds a new metric: kms_residency.reconciler.decisions{decision=(accept|quarantine|reject)} and a histogram for decision latency.
- Anchored audit events are emitted to the same audit topic but include header X-Audit-Anchored: true; indexer config updated to pick up these events for compliance queries.

Merge outcome: Squash merged by Priya Nair on 2026-01-20. Changelog and release notes entry added under releases/notes/2026-01-20-kms-residency.md.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Performance regression on hot paths. Mitigation: in-process TTL-backed cache, synthetic perf tests included, and rollout behind feature flag.
- Risk: Incorrectly quarantining valid operator automation. Mitigation: permissive rollout and detailed anchored-audit payload for rapid triage.

Contact: For followups contact @lena-f or @security-team. 
Marco Diaz: Can you clarify the performance budget here? the reconciler will be on the hot path for token issuance and small RPCs -- we should avoid extra network calls. Consider making policy cache default TTL 30s and prefer local evaluation.
Lena Fischer: Agreed. Default TTL set to 30s, reconciler uses in-process cache and async refresh. Fallback to the policy service only on cache-miss. Added benchmarking numbers in unit test comments.
Priya Nair: Audit envelopes look good; need to make sure the proof HMAC key rotation is handled. How will old proofs be validated after rotation?
Lena Fischer: Added signer_id into envelope and a signer-rotation table in deploy/helm/README; the compliance indexer will accept previous signer public keys for 7 days after rotation. Documented in docs/security/kms-residency.md (section 'Key rotation and proof validation').
Ethan Cole: Integration test intermittently fails on CI due to test container time drift. Suggest you make test resilient to up to +-120s offset and use monotonic clocks where possible.
Lena Fischer: Addressed; tests now normalize time windows and rely on monotonic timers for reconciliation window asserts. Re-ran CI locally and fixed flakiness.

Lena Fischer: Sanitized operator notes via auditSanitize() and added a unit test for escaping. See commit 5e6f7g8.

title: Capacity signal debrief — regional demand variance and next steps
content:
Capacity signal debrief — regional demand variance and next steps

Meeting: Capacity signal debrief — weekly infra sync
Date: 2026-04-20
Lead: Maya Chen (Infrastructure capacity lead)
Attendees: Maya Chen, Arjun Patel, Sofia Ruiz, Liam O'Neill, Greta Andersen, on-call SRE rotation

TL;DR:
- Last week we observed a 22% demand spike in APAC (asia-southeast) tied to an unanticipated enterprise customer test run plus higher PLG trial traffic in eu-west. Net fleet utilization rose from 68% to 84% during peak windows.
- Patching the autoscaler hysteresis reduced oscillation in US regions but revealed slot contention in the eu-west pod group (slot starvation between 03:00–06:00 UTC).
- Immediate mitigations: temp reservation of 20 GPUs in asia-southeast and manual ramp of burst pool in eu-west. Mid-term actions focus on improving demand signals and automated hedging rules.

Snapshot metrics (rolling 7 days ending 2026-04-20):
- Global GPU utilization (weighted): 72% avg, 95th percentile 89% during peak hours.
- APAC (asia-southeast): 78% avg, 95th 95% (spike window 13:00–16:00 local) — increased by +22% week-over-week.
- EU (eu-west): 81% avg during UTC overnight window; p95 latency for small-chat endpoints rose by ~120ms correlating with slot contention.
- US (us-west/us-east): stable utilization 60–70%; autoscaler smoothing reduced thrash by ~40%.

Incidents & observations:
- Slot leak hypothesis (INF-4223): observed tasks not releasing allocated slots after failed container pulls; correlated with eu-west contention. Logs indicate intermittent Docker image pull errors after node kernel update.
- Autoscaler tuning: reducing scale-down aggressiveness fixed thrash but makes temporary over-provisioning costlier; need cost-bound safety nets.
- Prefix cache pressure: higher PLG trials increased cache miss-rate on large-context jobs; increased tail latencies for dedicated customers running long sequences.

Actions taken this week (what we did):
- Temporarily reserved 20 GPUs in asia-southeast for customer test traffic (Sofia, done).
- Manually increased burst pool in eu-west by 15% for 48 hours (Arjun, done).
- Rolled back the problematic kernel patch on 7 nodes where image pulls failed (Liam, done).
- Enabled extra logging and a short-lived debug mode on the slot allocator for one eu-west pod (Greta, in progress).

Open action items (owners and due dates):
1) Investigate and fix slot leak root cause (JIRA-INF-4223). Steps: reproduce with failing image pull, add guard to free slots on terminal failure, add integration test. Owner: Liam O'Neill. Due: 2026-04-27.
2) Implement hedging rule prototype: if regional demand variance > 15% vs baseline and sustained for > 30m, preposition 10% of burst capacity from global pool. Owner: Arjun Patel. Due: 2026-05-04.
3) Autoscaler safety-net: add cost cap circuit that prefers cheaper-quantized variants before scaling GPU count beyond threshold. Owner: Maya Chen + Product (consult). Due: 2026-05-11.
4) Prefix/KV cache telemetry: add per-tenant cache-hit heatmaps and alert when miss-rate increases > 8% within a 1h window. Owner: Greta Andersen. Due: 2026-04-30.
5) Customer communication: CS to notify affected dedicated customers about transient latency windows and mitigations applied. Owner: Sofia Ruiz (CS partner). Due: 2026-04-22.

Risks & tradeoffs:
- Prepositioning capacity reduces cold-start latency but increases committed utilization and potential cost. Need an ROI signal tied to customer SLAs and expected QPS.
- Conservative autoscaler reduces thrash but increases tail risk during large spikes; hedging rules must be conservative initially and staged via canary.
- Fixing slot leak may require transient node restarts; coordinate with on-call windows and Dedicated customers to minimize impact.

Data & instrumentation gaps identified:
- Lack of a single region-level demand variance signal — currently derived from multiple dashboards. Priority to build a unified metric (variance-over-baseline) exposed to autoscaler.
- No per-customer cache-hit alerts; hampers root cause for tail latency on long-seq workloads.

Plan for next 7 days:
- Triage and patch INF-4223 (slot leak) and run a small canary in eu-west.
- Ship hedging prototype config to staging and run chaos test with synthetic spikes.
- Instrument unified demand-variance metric and surface it in Console (basic chart + alert).
- Evaluate cost impact of current manual reservations and propose a short-term credit/billing offset for the enterprise test customer.

Notes / miscellaneous:
- Observed that PLG trial traffic tends to cluster on weekdays 13:00–17:00 UTC — we should consider time-of-day-aware hedging for eu-west and asia-southeast.
- Suggested short-term runbook addition: "when regional demand variance > 20% and p95 latency spike > 50ms, reserve N GPUs and notify CS". Drafted a runbook stub and linked above.

Next sync: 2026-04-27 11:00 UTC (weekly capacity sync).

Appendix: quick links
- INF-4223: slot leak ticket
- INF-4298: hedging rules RFC
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/318 (autoscaler smoothing changes)
