title: Redwood enterprise procedures kit — company operations (2026)
content:
Redwood enterprise procedures kit — company operations (2026)

Overview

Purpose: This document centralizes company-wide operational policies and ready-to-use process templates covering access & permissions, change management, data management, procurement & expenses, vendor management, and travel. It is intended as the canonical reference for operational owners, approvers, and team leads.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and suppliers who request access, make changes to production systems, handle company data, engage vendors, or incur business travel/expenses. Exceptions must be approved by the owner_team (finance-legal) and recorded in the exceptions register.

Principles
- Least privilege and auditable approvals for access.
- Risk-proportional controls: higher risk => higher review/fail-safe.
- Single source of truth for templates to speed approvals and audits.
- Clear ownership for every control and handoff.

Owners and escalation
- Policy owner: Finance & Legal (owner: Maya Chen).
- Operational owners: People Ops (travel & people-related expenses), Eng-SRE (change management for infra), Eng-Platform (deployment change policies), Procurement (vendor onboarding), Security (data classification & RBAC design).
- Escalation channel: #ops-escalation (Slack); for regulatory incidents notify security@redwood.com and legal@redwood.com.

1) Access & Permissions
Summary: RBAC-based model with centralized requests through the Access Request Portal (ARP). Temporary elevation via Just-In-Time (JIT) access is encouraged.
Responsibilities:
- Requester: provide justification and duration.
- Approver: manager or service owner depending on resource type.
- IAM admin: perform provisioning and maintain audit logs.

Access categories and approval matrix (summary):
| Resource type | Approver | Max default duration | Escalation threshold |
|---------------|----------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Non-prod cloud project | Team manager | 90 days | Security review if > 30 days or cross-team |
| Prod read-only role | Service owner | 30 days | Security review if > 30 days |
| Prod write / admin role | Service owner + Security | 7 days | Required approval from Eng-SRE for > 7 days |
| Vendor access (limited) | Procurement + Service owner | 14 days | Contract/DPAs required for > 30 days |

Request process (high level):
1. Submit ARP form including business justification, requested resources, and duration.
2. Auto-notify approver(s); if multi-approver, require all approvals.
3. IAM admin provisions account/role and tags request id for audit.
4. Access automatically expires at the requested end date; reminders sent 7 days before expiry.

Temporary elevation/JIT steps:
1. Request JIT via ARP with short justification and immediate timeline.
2. Approver reviews and sets a task window; JIT sessions are logged and session recordings retained for 90 days.

Access review cadence:
- Quarterly reviews for all active Prod admin roles.
- Annual certification for vendor accounts.

2) Change Management
Goal: enable fast, safe, and auditable changes across infra and product services.
Change categories:
- Standard change: pre-authorized, repeatable operational tasks (e.g., routine scaling) — no CAB required but must follow runbook.
- Normal change: requires change ticket, impact assessment, approver sign-off, and scheduled window.
- Emergency change: implemented to remediate incidents. Post-implementation review required within 72 hours.

Change request template (short):
- Title
- Owner/Requester
- Change category (standard/normal/emergency)
- Impact assessment (services/users, rollback plan)
- Scheduled window
- Validation plan / smoke tests

Approval matrix:
- Normal change: Service owner + Eng-SRE (for infra) or Product owner (for API) depending on impact.
- High-impact (customer-facing outage risk): CAB approval required. CAB meets twice weekly; use asynchronous voting for low-latency approvals.

Implementation steps (normal change):
1. Open change ticket in Change Management system (link: /tools/change).
2. Fill template, attach runbook, assign approvers.
3. Complete pre-change checklist (backups, canary, synthetic checks).
4. Execute in maintenance window.
5. Run validation tests.
6. Close ticket with outcomes and metrics (latency, error rate).

Emergency change protocol:
1. Tag ticket as EMERGENCY; notify on-call and #incident.
2. Implement mitigation with minimum scope.
3. After stabilization, conduct a post-implementation review within 72 hours.

Change windows and blackout periods:
- Production major releases blocked on high-traffic holidays (list maintained by Product).
- Routine changes allowed in designated windows: Mon–Fri 02:00–06:00 UTC and Sat 08:00–12:00 UTC (exceptions handled by CAB).

3) Data Management
Classification scheme (three levels):
- PUBLIC: no restrictions.
- INTERNAL: default for business documents.
- RESTRICTED: PII, customer data, proprietary model weights.

Data handling requirements:
- RESTRICTED data must be encrypted at rest and in transit, stored in approved buckets, and access controlled via RBAC with explicit justification.
- Export/egress of RESTRICTED data requires a Data Use Request and DSA review (Data Security & Assurance).

Retention and deletion
- Logs (diagnostic): 180 days by default, extendable to 365 days upon SRE request.
- Backups: retention per service SLA; restore tests quarterly.
- Customer data retention: as per contract or 7 years max unless otherwise specified.

Data breach steps (summary):
1. Contain and preserve evidence.
2. Notify Security and Legal within 24 hours.
3. Conduct forensics; follow regulatory notification timelines.

Data labeling and metadata requirements:
- Every dataset must include: owner, classification, retention policy, last updated, and approved uses.

4) Procurement & Expenses
Procurement lifecycle:
1. Need identification and owner assignment.
2. Create Purchase Request (PR) using Procurement template (see Templates section).
3. Competitive sourcing required for purchases > $50k.
4. Procurement team reviews vendor compliance (security, SOC2, DPAs) and negotiates terms.
5. Purchase Order (PO) issued; vendor onboarding completed.

Approval thresholds (summary):
- Up to $2,500: Team lead approval.
- $2,500–$50,000: Department head + Procurement review.
- > $50,000: VP approval + Procurement + Legal.

Card and travel expenses:
- Use corporate card for approved travel with pre-approval.
- Expense report due within 14 days of trip end.
- Receipts required for any individual expense > $25.
- Per diem model: US domestic $75/day (meals & incidental), international vary by country — check Finance portal.

Reimbursements and audit
- Finance reserves the right to audit expense claims for 12 months.
- Non-compliant claims will be remediated with manager and may lead to revocation of card privileges.

Procurement request example (JSON snippet to paste into PR form):
```
{
  "requester": "Name",
  "department": "Engineering",
  "description": "GPU cloud capacity: 4 x A100 reserved for Q1 experiments",
  "estimated_cost": "48,000",
  "vendor": "CloudCompute Inc.",
  "business_justification": "Prototype + evaluation for Dedicated offering",
  "approval_chain": ["team-lead", "procurement"]
}
```

5) Vendor Management
Vendor onboarding checklist:
1. Complete vendor intake form and risk assessment.
2. Verify security posture (SOC 2, ISO, pen-test results if applicable).
3. Data processing addendum (DPA) and contractual terms signed by Legal.
4. Create vendor record in Vendor Registry with owner and contract dates.
5. Provision necessary access and limit by least privilege.

SLAs and monitoring:
- Key vendors must have a documented SLA and escalations.
- Quarterly vendor review for strategic vendors; annual review for others.

Offboarding:
- Revoke all accounts and access within 48 hours of contract termination.
- Verify data return/destruction per contract.

6) Travel Policy (summary)
Pre-approval: All business travel requires a Travel Request in the Travel Portal and manager pre-approval.
Booking: Use preferred travel vendors for corporate rates; personal arrangements reimbursable only with prior approval.
Safety & compliance: Follow local guidance and travel advisories; register high-risk travel with People Ops.
Expense categories and caps:
- Lodging: reasonable nightly rate per city band (see Finance portal).
- Meals: per diem or itemized receipts.
- Ground transport: ride-share or economy car rental.

Travel emergency support: 24/7 travel assistance is available via travel-support@redwood.com.

7) Internal Templates (canonical templates to use)
- Access Request (ARP) template (fields: requester, resource, duration, justification, approver).
- Change Request template (fields: owner, impact, rollback, validation, stakeholders).
- Procurement Request (PR) template (fields: requester, vendor, cost, justification, approvals).
- Vendor Intake form (fields: vendor, controls checklist, contracts, risk rating).
- Travel Request template (fields: traveler, dates, destination, business purpose, manager approval).

Example Access Request (text):
--Start ARP--
Requester: Jane Doe
Resource: prod-ml-models S3 bucket (RESTRICTED)
Duration: 7 days
Justification: Investigate model drift for customer incident #1234
Approver: Service owner (ML Infra), Security (if > 3 days)
--End ARP--

Governance and audit
- All actions (access grants, change tickets, procurement approvals) must be tagged with policy id and retained per retention rules.
- Internal audit cadence: semi-annual for access controls, quarterly for change management evidence, annual for procurement/vendor compliance.

Amendments and exceptions
- To request an exception, submit an Exception Request with rationale, compensating controls, and expiration date. Exceptions expire automatically unless renewed via the same process.

FAQs (short)
Q: Who signs off on vendor DPAs?
A: Legal in coordination with Procurement.
Q: How long are access request logs retained?
A: 365 days for provisioning logs; session recordings for 90 days.

Contacts
- Policy owner: maya.chen@redwood.com
- Procurement: procurement@redwood.com
- Security: security@redwood.com
- Travel support: travel-support@redwood.com

Related pages and references
- Central policy index: /confluence/policies-and-process/central-policy-index-and-core-processes-2025
- Change management runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/change-management
- Data classification guidelines: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention

Revision history
- 2025-11-15: Created by Maya Chen (finance-legal).
- 2026-02-10: Updated access durations and procurement thresholds; added JIT access section.

End of document

title: Cerberus Defensive Retrieval
content:
Cerberus Defensive Retrieval

Topline: large DoD-focused search program, strict air-gapped requirements, procurement-heavy timeline.
- Use-case: enterprise search for classified docs + analyst support; primary workloads: embeddings for dense retrieval + reranking layer to reduce false positives.
- Scale ask: ingest ~120M documents (mix of PDFs, DOCX, scans -> OCR), expected vector store ~30TB, incremental updates daily.
- Performance targets: P95 query (retrieval + rerank) < 350ms in on-prem environment for unclassified/IL2; IL4/IL5 buckets can accept higher latency but must maintain P99 < 2s.
- Cost sensitivity: high for hosted; willing to pay for Dedicated/Private but procurement asks predictable TCO and capex-friendly licensing.

title: Usage Insights: reconciliation suite vs billing totals + CI drift gate
content:
Usage Insights: reconciliation suite vs billing totals + CI drift gate

Title: Usage Insights: reconciliation suite vs billing totals + CI drift gate

Summary
We’ve had a few early beta reports that “console totals don’t match invoice” (see SUP-24811) and a recurring internal concern that aggregation lag + rounding will cause subtle drift. This PR adds a reconciliation suite that compares Usage Insights rollups (route/model aggregates) against billing totals (metering hooks → invoice preview) within a defined tolerance, and wires it into CI + a nightly scheduled run with alert hooks.

Key goals
- Catch drift early (instrumentation regressions, bucketing/alias issues, timezone boundary mistakes, rounding deltas).
- Define and document a tolerance policy that is strict enough to catch real issues but robust to expected effects (late events, FX rounding, minimum billable units).
- Provide a runbook-friendly output: workspace/project, day/hour, route/model slices that contribute most to drift.

What’s included
1) Reconciliation job + report format
- New job: services/telemetry/reconciliation/usage_insights_vs_billing
- Compares totals for a given workspace_id + time range across:
  - usage_insights.route_model_agg (the dataset powering console breakdown tables)
  - billing.usage_totals (billing hook rollups used for invoice preview)
- Outputs both:
  - a single “gate” metric per workspace/time window (pass/fail)
  - a ranked list of top contributing slices (route/model/region/deployment_mode where present)

2) Tolerance policy (documented + implemented)
We gate on both absolute and relative drift, and we avoid evaluating windows likely to be incomplete.
- Windows evaluated:
  - Hourly buckets for last 24 hours (excluding most recent 2 hours)
  - Daily buckets for last 7 days (excluding current day)
- Late-event buffer:
  - Ignore the most recent 2 hours entirely to avoid normal ingestion lag.
  - For daily checks, only evaluate days older than 26 hours.
- Tolerance thresholds:
  - Absolute drift allowed: max($2.00, 2000 tokens worth of cost at the workspace’s effective blended rate) per evaluated window
  - Relative drift allowed: <= 0.50% per evaluated window
  - Gate fails if BOTH absolute and relative drift exceed thresholds (prevents false positives on small totals)
- Currency handling:
  - Compare in USD using billing’s canonical conversion for the period.
  - Usage insights cost uses the same price book snapshot key as billing (price_book_version) to avoid rate drift.
- Rounding:
  - Compare on unrounded micros (int64) where available; rounding only applied in the human report.

Tolerance helper (illustrative snippet):

function isDriftAcceptable({ expectedMicros, actualMicros }) {
  const driftMicros = Math.abs(actualMicros - expectedMicros);
  const rel = expectedMicros === 0 ? (actualMicros === 0 ? 0 : 1) : driftMicros / expectedMicros;
  const absOk = driftMicros <= ABS_TOLERANCE_MICROS;
  const relOk = rel <= 0.005;
  return absOk || relOk; // fail only if BOTH are violated
}

3) CI + scheduled runs
- Adds a Buildkite step (non-blocking in PRs, blocking in main nightly):
  - PR builds: runs reconciliation unit tests + one small integration fixture
  - Nightly: runs full reconciliation across allowlisted beta workspaces with paging
- New pipeline: .buildkite/pipelines/usage-insights-reconciliation.yml
- Artifacts:
  - Uploads a CSV and JSON summary for each run
  - Posts a summary comment to #eng-platform on failures with a link to artifacts

4) Alert hooks + runbook pointers
- On gate failure, the nightly job:
  - Emits metric: usage_insights.reconciliation.drift_exceeded{workspace_id, window_type}
  - Logs structured payload with top slices and suspected causes
  - Posts to Slack: #usage-insights-alerts
  - Creates a lightweight incident event (non-page) unless drift persists 2 consecutive runs, then page the on-call (aligns with SRE feedback from earlier threads)

5) Guardrails to avoid noisy failures
- Workspace allowlist for beta reconciliation (config in services/telemetry/reconciliation/config/beta_allowlist.yml)
- Suppression for known exceptions:
  - If billing is missing a price_book_version for the period (rare), mark “skipped” not “failed”
  - If insights freshness lag > threshold (uses existing freshness metadata), mark “skipped”

Why this approach
- We compare at the same conceptual level as customers: “what billing says you owe” vs “what console says you spent”.
- We still include drill-down slices to make debugging actionable (route/model/region).
- Late-event handling is explicit and conservative; we don’t want to treat expected lag as correctness drift.

Files / areas changed (high level)
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/usage_insights_vs_billing/*
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/lib/tolerance.ts
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/lib/report.ts
- services/telemetry/reconciliation/config/beta_allowlist.yml
- .buildkite/pipelines/usage-insights-reconciliation.yml
- docs/internal/runbooks/usage-insights-reconciliation.md
- libs/billing/pricebook/resolve_pricebook_version.ts (small helper to align snapshots)

Test plan
- Unit tests:
  - tolerance calculations (edge cases: 0 totals, tiny totals, large totals)
  - rounding behavior (micros vs displayed dollars)
  - skip logic (freshness lag, missing pricebook)
- Integration tests:
  - fixture dataset with:
    - retries + fallbacks
    - model alias → version bucketing
    - streaming endpoints
  - verifies:
    - aggregation totals match billing totals within tolerance
    - top-slices ranking is stable/deterministic
- Manual:
  - Ran job for HelioChat staging workspace on 2026-02-16 (7d window) and validated output against invoice preview totals.

Rollout notes
- Nightly reconciliation initially scoped to beta allowlist only.
- If the nightly job is noisy, we can widen the late-event buffer or adjust absolute tolerance; prefer changing absolute tolerance first.
- No change to customer-visible console behavior.

Links
- Linear: ENG-3817
- Related PRs: pr-23114 (aggregation job), pr-23135 (query API)
- Support: SUP-24811

Reviewer notes / questions to focus on
- Tolerance policy: are we comfortable gating on “abs OR rel” instead of “abs AND rel”? (current implementation is intentionally forgiving on small totals)
- Skip windows: is 2 hours sufficient buffer for late events in all regions?
- Alerting: does the ‘2 consecutive runs before paging’ rule match SRE expectations?

---

Conversation (abridged)

Allison Grant (Observability) — 2026-02-11
“Please make sure this does not page on first failure. Also can you include a metric with a ‘skipped_reason’ label so dashboards can separate drift vs ‘data not ready’?”

Cole Summers — 2026-02-11
“Good call. Updated: first failure posts to #usage-insights-alerts + emits metrics; paging only after 2 consecutive failures. Added skipped_reason label to reconciliation outcome metric.”

Nadia Rahman — 2026-02-12
“Double-check retry accounting: billing counts retried requests as billed tokens; insights should too. Your fixture needs at least one retry case where the first attempt generated some tokens.”

Cole Summers — 2026-02-12
“Added fixture scenario: partial generation then retry; billing expected includes both attempts. Reconciliation now compares on metering_event_id aggregation rather than request_id when available to avoid undercounting.”

Logan Wright — 2026-02-13
“Perf: the nightly query looks like it’ll scan too much if we do 7 days across many workspaces. Can we do workspace-by-workspace, partition prune by day, and cap to allowlist?”

Cole Summers — 2026-02-13
“Adjusted: strictly allowlist, query per workspace, partition filter on event_day; added a hard cap of 200 workspaces. Also added a note in the pipeline config to expand gradually.”

Kevin Osei (Security) — 2026-02-14
“Make sure report artifacts don’t include customer prompts/content. I see route/model; ok. But please avoid including raw request IDs if they can be correlated.”

Cole Summers — 2026-02-14
“Removed request_id from exported artifacts; only includes hashed route_key + model_key + bucket timestamps + cost/tokens metrics.”

Chloe Martin — 2026-02-15
“The tolerance uses a blended rate estimate for the token-based absolute threshold. Can we just use a flat USD micros threshold and keep it simple?”

Cole Summers — 2026-02-15
“Switched to flat $2 absolute threshold for now (micros), plus relative 0.5%. Kept the blended-rate note in comments as possible follow-up.”

Dylan Brooks — 2026-02-17
“Looks good. Please add a short section to the internal runbook: common causes (missing route tags, model alias bucketing, timezone boundaries) and first debug steps.”

Cole Summers — 2026-02-17
“Added runbook section + links to dashboards for freshness and metering ingestion.”

Approvals

- Nadia Rahman — Approved (2026-02-18)
- Logan Wright — Approved (2026-02-18)
- Kevin Osei — Approved (2026-02-18)

CI
- buildkite/redwood:unit-tests ✅
- buildkite/redwood:lint ✅
- buildkite/redwood:telemetry-integration-fixtures ✅
- buildkite/redwood:usage-insights-reconciliation-smoke ✅

Merge

title: introduce-targeted-presubmit-slimline-and-dep-pruner-operator
content:
introduce-targeted-presubmit-slimline-and-dep-pruner-operator

Motivation: our presubmit CI has grown noisy and slow due to monolithic lint/test lanes that run across the entire monorepo for non-impactful changes. At the same time, transitive dev-dependencies and stale tooling in package manifests cause intermittent CI cache churn and unnecessary build costs. This PR implements two complementary improvements: (1) a targeted presubmit strategy that runs only lightweight checks and narrowly scoped lint/test shards based on path-aware change detection, and (2) a new dep-pruner operator (action + small CLI) that detects and suggests removal of unused dev-deps and flags version instabilities. The intent is to preserve strong correctness guarantees while giving fast feedback for small changes and surfacing dependency debt for maintainers to triage. Highlights/what changed: - Introduce .github/actions/dep-pruner (composite action) and a minimal Go CLI (tools/dep-pruner) that computes unused dev-deps across package.json / pyproject.toml roots. The action runs in a dry-run by default and posts PR comments with suggested edits. - Add path-aware presubmit runner: .github/workflows/presubmit-slimline.yml. The workflow contains three lanes: quick (fast lint + unit smoke), targeted (pattern-driven test shards), and full (fallback that runs full integration on release branches). Quick runs on push for small changes; targeted is triggered when changed files exceed patterns for a module. - Move heavy lint rules behind a staged lint gate; add 'lint-shadow' job that only runs full lint when more than N files touched or explicit label is set. - Add a lightweight test selector script (scripts/select-tests-by-diff.py) that maps changed files to Jest/Pytest shards via a simple config under ci/test-mapping.yaml. - Introduce dep-stability-probe: a periodic job (weekly) that detects transitive version drift and files an issue with a report. - Add infra docs: docs/ci/presubmit-strategy.md and docs/ci/dep-pruner.md. Checklist: - [x] design doc and implementation for presubmit lanes - [x] composite action + CLI with unit tests - [x] workflow templates and mapping file - [x] docs and contributor guide updates - [x] initial integration tests against a lightweight staging runner - [x] staged rollout plan (canary on selected repos) Rollout plan: 1) Deploy workflows in dry-run mode for 48 hours to gather metrics (CI time, jobs avoided). 2) Enable auto PR comments from dep-pruner for contributors with opt-in flag. 3) After one week of metrics, enable lint-shadow gate for all repos. Backwards compatibility and safety: - Presubmit workflows default to conservative thresholds; full workflow is still the default for release/* branches. - dep-pruner never mutates files automatically; suggestions are comments and draft PRs behind a toggled flag. Related tickets: ENG-7721 (presubmit redesign), ENG-7818 (dep hygiene initiative), SUP-501 (customer-incurred CI cost spike).
feat(ci): add presubmit-slimline workflow and test selector script
feat(actions): new composite dep-pruner action and Go CLI (dry-run only)
refactor(ci): stage lint into quick/targeted/full lanes with lint-shadow job
docs(ci): add presubmit strategy and dep-pruner operational docs
test(ci): add unit tests for dep-pruner and integration smoke for targeted lane
Ethan Park: Nice approach. Can we ensure the test-mapping file is maintained by module owners? Otherwise we risk drift.
Maya Brennan: Added a maintenance note in docs/ci/presubmit-strategy.md and an owner field in ci/test-mapping.yaml.
Sofia Ramirez: dep-pruner output looks good, but please make the CLI less chatty by default (added --quiet).
Anand Gupta: Please add a feature flag so repo admins can opt into automatic draft-PR creation later.
Maya Brennan: Implemented feature flag as INPUT_CREATE_DRAFT_PR for composite action; default off.
Introduce targeted presubmit lanes to reduce CI feedback time and add a dep-pruner operator that surfaces unused dev-dependencies and version instability; no automatic file changes by default.
This PR touches CI entrypoints and a small internal tool; keep an eye on cache key semantics in workflows. If you maintain any test mapping, please verify mappings in ci/test-mapping.yaml. The dep-pruner is intentionally conservative; real removals are manual until we prove stability.

title: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets
content:
Session-cache sizing & target unit economics for Integron pilot

From: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
To: Sara Clark <sara.clark@integronhealth.com>, Tom Ellis <t.ellis@integronhealth.com>
Cc: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 21 May 2027 17:05:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap — session cache sizing & rough $/1M targets

Hi Sara / Tom — thanks for taking time today. Quick recap from our discovery and proposed next steps so we can get a realistic costing model together: 

Key inputs we captured on the call:
- Expected pilot scope: ~12k unique end-user sessions/day, roughly 2.5M tokens/session on peak flows (some sessions are short, median ~120 tokens).
- Session pattern: ~70% of sessions start with a 1–2 message prompt series that is highly repetitive across users (templates + guidance text).
- SLA needs: p95 latency target ~450ms for interactive flows; availability: standard hosted SLA.

Caching assumptions to validate (what we used for the first-pass economics):
- Session-prefix caching (warm prefixes / reusable instruction text) coverage: we modeled a 35% prefix cache hit rate across tokens — this assumes we can capture the common opening blocks and sticky templates.
- Cold tokens (misses) still incur full inference cost; hit tokens are served from cached KV/prefetch and reduce effective per-token GPU work by ~75% in our model.

First-pass unit economics (ballpark, to align expectations):
- Nominal list price used: $120 / 1M tokens (model variant X quantized path).
- With 35% cache hit & batching/quantization recommendations applied, effective cost range we modeled: $48–$70 / 1M effective tokens (depends on sequence length distribution and batching).

Asks / next steps:

title: Novaplane Tech - Security & Hosting Intake
content:
Novaplane Tech - Security & Hosting Intake

Intro discovery on Novaplane's security gates and hosting preferences. Focus on SOC2/ISO posture, SSO/SAML, RBAC model, audit log retention, and customer-managed KMS. Agreed to a follow-up technical deep-dive and a short Dedicated trial for latency/cost validation.
SOC2 / ISO scope and artifacts
SSO/SAML and IdP integration
RBAC and least-privilege model
Audit logs & retention (90/365-day scenarios)
Encryption and KMS: CMK vs Redwood-managed keys
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs
Next steps: docs + trial
Redwood to send SOC 2 Type II redacted report and ISO 27001 scope
Schedule 60-min technical deep-dive with Diego and Maya (week of 11/20)
Provision trial Dedicated environment for benchmarking (2 weeks)
Confirm data residency options and KMS integration model
Alex Chen - email SOC2 summary + security whitepaper by 2028-11-17
Maya Patel - prepare Dedicated vs Hosted perf/cost matrix and share by 2028-11-19
Tom Evans - share Novaplane's data residency and retention policy doc by 2028-11-18
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Evans (Novaplane Head of Security), Sara Li (CTO), Diego Ramirez (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick intake, fairly noisy on one end, some transcription mistakes, but captured main asks.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood inference, i'm the AE on this account, quick round robin?
00:07 Tom Evans: tom evans here yep head of security at novaplane, thanks for making time, sorry if there's a bit of background noise on my side
00:13 Sara Li: sara li, cto, i've got diego on the conn— 
00:16 Diego Ramirez: yo hey, diego, platform eng, we'll mostly listen for the infra bits
00:22 Maya Patel: maya, solutions engineer, i'll cover the technical side, perf, keys, all that.

02:05 Alex Chen: high level, where are you today with inference hosting? are you self-hosting or using public endpoints?
02:13 Tom Evans: currently a mix, core models are private on prem for PII parts, but a lot of experimental endpoints hit mega cloud managed services, cost is creeping up, and we need a clear path for SOC2 and auditability for the customer data flows
02:34 Alex Chen: got it, and what are the non-negotiables for you security-wise?
02:37 Tom Evans: SOC2 Type II is required, ISO 27001 desirable but not immediate, SSO via corporate IdP with SAML, RBAC for separation of duties, strong audit logs with retention we can set, and the ability to use our KMS for CMK, we can't have plain text keys outside our control, also data residency - certain workloads must remain in eu-west-1
03:12 Maya Patel: okay that aligns with typical enterprise asks. quick clarifier — when you say CMK, do you mean customer-managed keys in your cloud KMS, HSM backed?
03:22 Tom Evans: yes, HSM backed, we want envelope encryption where tokens and any logs are encrypted with our key when at rest
03:35 Sara Li: and for latency-critical endpoints we may want dedicated capacity, but we'd like a hosted path for lower throughput features — curious about routing, fallback if dedicated misses capacity
03:49 Maya Patel: yep so redwood supports three modes — hosted api, dedicated reserved gpu pools, and private vpc/on-prem. routing policies can fallback to a compatible variant, we'll auto-failover region-wise, we can also configure model variants for cost vs latency.

06:10 Diego Ramirez: question on SAML: we enforce SCIM-based provisioning and Okta as idp, need group membership mapping into roles. how granular can the RBAC be?
06:24 Maya Patel: we support SAML SSO + optional SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with resource scoping — you can map groups from idp to roles in redwood, and we have audit events tied to tokens and API keys, though sometimes the transcription shows 'token list' as 'tonk' — ignore that.
06:45 Tom Evans: audit logs — retention windows, can we store logs for 12 months and export to our splunk? also need immutable audit trails for compliance
06:58 Maya Patel: yes, we stream audit logs to customer destinations (s3, splunk, bigquery) with signed manifests. retention is configurable per-tenant; immutable trails supported via object lock or WORM on s3. we can also push to your SIEM via forwarders.
07:25 Alex Chen: on SOC2 artifacts — we can share a redacted SOC2 Type II report, our ISO attestation details, encryption whitepaper, and a network diagram for the private control plane, will send those after the call
07:38 Tom Evans: great, do you have a list of controls mapped to customers' purple team checks? like a control-mapping spreadsheet?
07:45 Alex Chen: yes, we have a compliance matrix mapping to common frameworks (SOC2, ISO, HIPAA notes), i'll include that.

09:10 Sara Li: for KMS, can customers bring their key into your hosted offering or only for Dedicated/Private? we prefer bring-your-own-key (BYOK) even for hosted if possible
09:22 Maya Patel: current hosted product supports customer-managed keys in the sense of envelope encryption with root-of-trust in cloud KMS for specific customers — for full BYOK hardware-backed CMK we typically recommend Dedicated or Private, because you need the key material to be under your control end-to-end. but we can engage to scope a hosted BYOK path if it's a hard requirement
09:49 Diego Ramirez: ok that matters, we need HSM-backed CMKs for some pipelines so likely we'll want Dedicated or Private for those models, but maybe host sandbox for non-PII features
10:03 Maya Patel: makes sense, we also have token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards so you can split traffic and cost across hosted and dedicated routes

12:40 Tom Evans: another question, what about pen tests and vulnerability scans? we need third-party pentest reports and annual scans, and we require notification windows for incident response
12:56 Alex Chen: we run internal pen tests annually and vendor scans, and we can provide a summary of third-party engagements; incident response SLA main points: notification within 24 hours for confirmed breaches, and we have playbooks and forensics support on enterprise tiers
13:21 Tom Evans: SLA for uptime and latency for Dedicated? we might need SLOs pinned for customer contracts
13:30 Maya Patel: Dedicated comes with contractual SLAs for throughput and latency tiers; we can pin SLOs in the reserved capacity contract. Hosted offers best-effort with published performance profiles but not the same contractual throughput guarantees

15:02 Diego Ramirez: on the logs again, are system-level logs separated from application logs? we need clear separation and different access controls
15:15 Maya Patel: yes system logs and application logs are separated. system logs are retained in the control plane with restricted access; application logs (your inference request/response traces) can be routed to your storage with the retention you choose. RBAC can gate access to those exports.
15:46 Tom Evans: about data residency — if a region is required, can you guarantee single-region hosting, and what about backups? backups must remain in-region or in a specified set of regions
15:58 Alex Chen: we can pin workloads to regions and control backup replication policies; for Dedicated and Private it's straightforward to limit cross-region replication, hosted can be configured per-account to limit to a region though multi-region failover is an opt-in.

18:30 Sara Li: curious about telemetry — we need obfuscated metrics to be shared with our product team but not contain raw prompts; can you redact or mask PII in logs before exporting?
18:44 Maya Patel: we have built-in redaction filters and tokenization hooks; additionally we recommend a prefix-KV cache to reduce exposure of raw prompts, and we can enable on-prem pre-processing for PII scrub before hitting hosted endpoints
19:06 Tom Evans: that sounds promising. can you show how redaction is configured? we might want to see a sample config and the scrubber rules
19:14 Maya Patel: i'll include sample scrubber config and docs in the follow-up bundle.

22:05 Alex Chen: any blockers to running a two-week dedicated trial for a small model set? what's your internal procurement cadence?
22:20 Tom Evans: procurement is 2-3 weeks but security sign-off is the gating factor, if we get the SOC2 artifacts and a short architecture diagram we can spin up a sandbox approval quickly. cost approvals are easier for a short eval
22:38 Alex Chen: good — we'll aim to deliver docs by friday and propose a trial start the next monday, assuming ok from your security team

28:10 Diego Ramirez: technical nit — how do you handle KV cache and warm starts for latency? we run high qps so cache efficiency matters
28:21 Maya Patel: runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache management; we can tune cache TTLs and shard placement for your workload. note sometimes the transcript will convert 'KV' to 'k v' or 'k v cache', ignore that

31:00 Tom Evans: compliance question — do you provide evidence for keys rotation and access logs to satisfy audits? auditors want a chain of custody for keys
31:12 Maya Patel: yes for Dedicated we can provide rotation logs, KMS access logs, and who/when API calls were made. For hosted, we can provide redacted KMS event logs and access records but full key material audit trails are available when you control the CMK in your cloud provider

34:40 Sara Li: any known integration issues with okta/scim? our provisioning is fairly heavy with nested groups
34:51 Maya Patel: we have customers with large scim deployments, we sometimes hit mapping limits with deeply nested groups; our config guide has patterns for flattening or mapping to role-sets — we'll share that guidance.

38:05 Alex Chen: wrap up — recap: you need SOC2 Type II + ISO docs, sample architecture, KMS integration options, RBAC mapping guide, audit log retention details, and a Dedicated trial proposal. Next step deep technical sync with diego and maya. agreed?
38:26 Tom Evans: yep agreed. please include any known limitations for hosted BYOK in the notes.
38:33 Maya Patel: will do, i'll add clear recommended pathways: hosted sandbox for non-PII, Dedicated for HSM-CMK workloads, Private for full air-gap/on-prem needs

41:00 Sara Li: timeline — security review to complete by end of month? we are aiming to put this into vendor shortlist by early december
41:12 Alex Chen: we'll try to get docs to you by 11/17 which gives you two weeks for review before your shortlist deadline
41:22 Diego Ramirez: also let's add a perf benchmark plan — small throughput tests first then 95th pct latency runs
41:30 Maya Patel: noted, i'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet and runbook.

50:05 Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the bundle and invite for the technical deep-dive, talk soon
50:15 Tom Evans: thanks all
50:18 Sara Li: thanks
50:20 Diego Ramirez: great, bye

End of transcript.

Notes: occasional mis-attributions and minor transcription errors (e.g., 'Sam L' for 'SAML', 'K-M-S' spelled out). Document links referenced during call: SOC2 redacted report (link to be emailed), compliance matrix (link), Dedicated trial proposal (link).

title: Introduce onboarding heuristic ranker and summarized release creator
content:
Introduce onboarding heuristic ranker and summarized release creator

Context and motivation: model intake currently produces raw metadata and full performance profiles but lacks a lightweight, deterministic ranking that helps reviewers prioritize which model versions to certify first. When dozens of candidate variants appear (quantized, distilled, quant+distill), reviewers need a concise, evidence-backed suggestion plus an initial release blurb. This PR adds a small, pluggable heuristic ranker and a summarized release-note generator that drafts short changelog entries tied to onboarding artifacts.

Design: The ranker assigns a score computed from three weighted signals: stability_score (based on rollout probe pass rate), coverage_score (how many canonical workloads the model hit during preflight), and cost_estimate (tokens/sec and quantization hint). We expose a config object for weights so platform teams can tune heuristics per workspace. The summarizer consumes ranked artifacts and: - extracts the top-3 contributing changes (e.g. quantization, sequence-length tuning, prompt-template hints), - generates a 2-3 sentence release blurb with deterministic templates, - attaches a small Impact badge (latency delta and cost delta). The summarizer is intentionally conservative: drafts are marked "DRAFT: auto" and require human sign-off in the console.

What changed (summary of commits): commit 1: add ranker module and unit tests; commit 2: add summarizer and integration tests; commit 3: add CLI preview tool and docs; commit 4: wire into release assembler and CI workflow; commit 5: fix edge-case where coverage_score==0 and add guard rails.

Files / key diffs: registry/intake/ranker.py  (new) - core Ranker class with compute_score(metadata, perf_profile) -> float. Sample snippet: def compute_score(meta, perf):
    stability = min(meta.get('probe_pass_rate', 0.0), 1.0)
    coverage = perf.get('workload_coverage', 0) / float(MAX_WORKLOADS)
    cost = max(1e-6, perf.get('estimated_cost_per_1k_tokens', 0.0))
    score = weights['stability'] * stability + weights['coverage'] * coverage - weights['cost'] * math.log(cost + 1.0)
    return round(score, 4)

registry/release/summarizer.py (new) - small template engine with deterministic slot filling and a safety layer preventing PII or long free-text passthrough. CLI: cli/onboard_preview.py (new) - preview a model's ranked entry and summarizer blurb locally before pushing. Docs: docs/onboarding/heuristics.md - explains config knobs and when to tune weights. CI: workflow/ci.yml updated to run summarizer integration tests in the release stage.

Testing and CI: Unit tests for ranker cover corner cases (zero coverage, absent probe_metrics). Integration test simulates a small intake pipeline with two candidate variants and asserts the summarizer produces consistent drafts. CI initially failed on the e2e integration due to a mock secrets race; I added a retry in the test harness and updated the workflow to use isolated ephemeral buckets for test artifacts. Final CI status: all checks passed (lint, unit, integration, e2e).

Review conversation (high-level single-string aggregation): Marco Nguyen: "Nice incremental approach. Two asks: (1) make weight config pluggable per-organization; (2) add guardrail to avoid creating a release blurb for variants with <50% probe coverage."
Aisha (author): "Both addressed: added org-level config and a coverage threshold check in summarizer that tags drafts as 'insufficient telemetry' if below threshold."
Dana Sokol: "Can we include a concise sample of the generated blurb in the docs?"
Aisha: "Added examples in docs/onboarding/heuristics.md and the CLI prints a preview sample."
Priya Raman: "Unit tests look good. Please add a changelog entry for the release assembler wiring."
Aisha: "Added a small CHANGELOG fragment and a README note; moved the release assembler step to a named hook so downstream consumers can opt-in."

Backward-compatibility and risks: There are no changes to public REST APIs. The ranker and summarizer run as part of the internal intake pipeline; teams who relied on the previous purely manual review flow will now see auto-drafts — they must opt-in to auto-publishing. The main risk is over-reliance on heuristic scores; mitigations: conservative defaults, prominently labelled drafts, and per-org weight overrides.

Operational notes: Added a feature flag onboarding.heuristic_ranker.enabled=false by default; rollout plan: enable for 25% of orgs w/ high-throughput onboarding for two weeks, gather feedback, then increase. Metrics added: onboarding.rank_score histogram, summarizer.draft_generated_count, summarizer.draft_signoff_rate. Alerts: summarizer.error_rate > 1% triggers pager.

Follow-ups (future work): (1) add ML-backed ranker trained on historical signoffs; (2) allow customizable natural-language templates per org; (3) surface draft signoff analytics in the Console.

Merge notes: this PR was squashed on merge, changelog fragment included in commit message. Merge method: squash and merge.
Adds a heuristic scoring stage to the model intake pipeline that ranks candidate onboarding artifacts by stability, telemetry coverage, and estimated cost-per-token. Produces condensed release note drafts per model version and wires them into the release assembler. No public API changes.

Highlights: heuristic scoring config (pluggable), summarized changelog autodrafts, small CLI to preview release blurbs, unit + integration tests.

title: TypeScript SDK retries on HTTP 400 responses, causing duplicate request + billing concern
content:
TypeScript SDK retries on HTTP 400 responses, causing duplicate request + billing concern

Issue summary:
Northwind AI reports that the Redwood TypeScript SDK is retrying requests that return HTTP 400 (Bad Request). They observed multiple request IDs for what they believe is a single client call, and raised concern about duplicate billing and/or duplicated side effects in their application.

Impact:
- Customer observed 2–3 identical requests sent for a single application action when the API responds with 400.
- Customer concerned this could lead to duplicate charges and/or duplicated downstream actions (they log each attempt and tie it to billing / user-visible behavior).
- Support + on-call had difficulty triaging because TS error surface did not clearly indicate whether the error was retryable and what triggered the retry.

Customer report (from email + support portal):
- SDK: @redwood-ai/sdk (TypeScript) v2.8.0 (customer-reported)
- Runtime: Node 18
- Pattern: calling chat.completions.create() with a request that sometimes returns 400 (validation failure). SDK appears to retry anyway.
- Evidence: logs show 3 request_id values within ~2 seconds, all 400, same payload.

Environment:
- Region: us-east-1
- Endpoint: api.redwoodinference.com

Steps to reproduce (internal):
1) Use TS SDK v2.8.0.
2) Send an invalid request that triggers a gateway/service 400 (e.g., missing required field or invalid parameter type).
3) Observe SDK retry loop (backoff) and multiple requests emitted.

Expected behavior:
- 400s should not be retried by default.
- The SDK should return a non-retryable, typed error and include request_id if present.

Actual behavior:
- In certain 400 responses, the retry middleware treats the failure as retryable and retries up to the default max attempts.
- Customer sees multiple request IDs (one per attempt).

Notes / hypotheses:
- The retry middleware appears to misclassify some 400 responses as “network errors” due to an exception during error body parsing (e.g., non-JSON error body or unexpected content-type). When parse fails, status is not propagated to the retry classifier.
- This is aligned with other parity findings: different SDKs handle “error parsing failure” differently; TS path can drop status_code and request_id.

Billing clarification (preliminary):
- Platform billing is token-based for successful generations/embeddings. 400 responses should not bill tokens; however, the customer may still see request counts and/or gateway logs that look like “multiple attempts”, and they may have internal metering tied to request volume.
- Independently of billing, duplicate attempts can create duplicate application side effects if the customer couples the API call to a non-idempotent operation.

Request IDs provided by customer (example set):
- rw_req_01HNTW9VZ9J2R3… (400)
- rw_req_01HNTW9W1P8K5A… (400)
- rw_req_01HNTW9W3F0M2C… (400)
(These were within one client action window; exact IDs stored in the private Zendesk attachment, not reproduced here.)

Ask:
- Confirm whether TS SDK is retrying 400s and under what conditions.
- Provide workaround to customer ASAP.
- Align with SDK parity initiative: retryable codes + typed error taxonomy + conformance tests to prevent regressions.
2026-01-29 09:18 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Acknowledged customer escalation. Asked for: TS SDK version, snippet showing retry config (if any), and 3 request_ids + approximate timestamps. Noted that SDK retries are expected on 429/5xx, but not on 400. Opened as P1 due to billing concern.

Shared immediate workaround: set maxRetries: 0 in client config until we confirm behavior.
2026-01-29 10:02 PT — Customer (Northwind AI) via support portal
Confirmed @redwood-ai/sdk 2.8.0, Node 18, running behind a corporate proxy. They see 3 attempts on a single call when the error is 400. They associate retries with possible double-charging because their internal cost dashboard counts requests. They asked whether Redwood bills for failed requests.

They provided logs showing three request IDs and identical payload hash.
2026-01-29 10:30 PT — Owen Phillips (Support Escalation Eng)
Pulled gateway logs for the provided request_id set. Confirmed: all three requests returned HTTP 400 with ~5–20 ms service time. No streaming involved. Response size small. Error body for at least one attempt was not JSON (content-type text/plain) due to an upstream validation error path.

Conclusion: the client truly sent 3 requests. Not a duplicate server-side processing artifact.
2026-01-29 11:15 PT — Ibrahim Khan (SDK TL) (internal note)
This matches a known parity issue: TS retry middleware can treat “failed to parse error response” as retryable because it throws before constructing the HttpError with status_code. If the retry classifier sees a generic error without status, it goes down the network-retry path. Need to ensure status is captured even if body parsing fails, and never retry 400.

Flagging Dana Lo to investigate in TS repo; also aligns with ENG-5126 error taxonomy work.
2026-01-29 13:05 PT — Dana Lo (TS SDK Owner)
Reproduced locally with v2.8.0:
- When error response is JSON, status=400 is preserved and shouldRetry=false.
- When error response is text/plain (or JSON parse throws), the SDK throws a generic error prior to wrapping it, so our retry middleware sees “unknown error” and retries.

Plan:
1) Refactor error parsing so we always preserve HTTP status + headers and build a typed error even when body parsing fails.
2) Tighten shouldRetry to require an explicit retryable classification (429/5xx/408/504 + network timeouts) rather than defaulting unknown errors to retry.
3) Add conformance coverage: 400 with non-JSON body must not retry.

ETA: patch release within a week; will link PR.
2026-01-29 14:10 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Responded to customer with billing clarification:
- Redwood does not bill tokens for requests that fail with 4xx before generation.
- They may see multiple request records because the client retried.

Provided mitigation until fix is released:
- Configure client retries off (maxRetries: 0) or restrict retryableStatusCodes to [408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504].
- Log request_id + retry_count for correlation.

Asked whether they rely on any side-effectful behavior tied to request submission; recommended idempotency keys where applicable (even though chat/embeddings are typically safe, their surrounding workflow might not be).
2026-01-31 16:42 PT — Dana Lo
Opened fix PR and requested review: sources/github/redwood-sdk-typescript/pr-1298-unify-retry-middleware-and-error-shapes.json
Key changes:
- Ensure HttpError is constructed even when response body parse fails.
- Attach status_code, request_id (if present), and retryable flag.
- Update retry classifier: do not retry when status_code is 400–499 (except 408/429), regardless of parse failures.

Also added tests for non-JSON 400 response body.
2026-02-02 09:05 PT — Allison Grant (SRE/Standards)
Reviewed retry classification against standard. Confirmed retryable defaults should include 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 + network errors/timeouts, and must not include 400. Requested one additional guard: if Retry-After is present on a 4xx that is not 429, ignore it for retries.

Suggested adding telemetry fields (retry_count, status_code, request_id) to align with the parity logging plan.
2026-02-03 11:20 PT — Dana Lo
Merged fix + follow-up for Retry-After parsing/jitter alignment: sources/github/redwood-sdk-typescript/pr-1307-retry-after-parsing-and-backoff-jitter.json
Cut release v2.8.2.
Release notes include: “Fix: do not retry HTTP 400 when error body parsing fails; improved typed errors with request_id + retryable flag.”
2026-02-03 12:00 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Informed customer of v2.8.2 and provided upgrade guidance + confirmation steps:
- Upgrade @redwood-ai/sdk to 2.8.2.
- Run a controlled invalid request; verify only one request_id appears and retry_count remains 0.
- Keep maxRetries: 0 in prod until upgrade completes.

Re-answered billing question: token billing not incurred for these 400s; if they need an invoice-level confirmation, we can route to finance but logs indicate no successful generations on those request_ids.
2026-02-06 15:37 PT — Customer (Northwind AI)
Upgraded to 2.8.2 in staging. Confirmed no retries on 400 anymore. Their internal request counter is now consistent. Asked for a short written statement they can share internally that 4xx validation failures do not incur token charges.

No further issues.
2026-02-10 10:12 PT — Dev Patel (Support)
Provided final billing statement and closed ticket. Customer confirmed resolved in production after rollout.

Follow-ups:
- Ensure conformance suite covers “400 + non-JSON body” across SDKs.
- Ensure docs/migration notes mention the retry classifier change and how to tune maxRetries.
2026-02-10 10:20 PT — Ibrahim Khan (internal)
Logged as an input to SDK parity effort: this bug is a concrete example of why error taxonomy must preserve status_code/request_id even on parse failures. Will reference in parity matrix and conformance fixtures.
Resolved in TypeScript SDK v2.8.2 by ensuring HTTP status/request_id are preserved even when error-body parsing fails, and by tightening retry classification so 400 is never retried by default. Customer mitigated by disabling retries until upgrade. Billing concern addressed: 4xx validation failures did not incur token charges.
Customer upgraded to TS SDK v2.8.2; confirmed 400 responses are not retried and internal metering no longer shows duplicate attempts. Provided written clarification that 4xx validation errors do not incur token billing.

title: Post-repair provision: Wi-Fi profile collision prevents Intune enrollment on ThinkPad T15
content:
Post-repair provision: Wi-Fi profile collision prevents Intune enrollment on ThinkPad T15

Issue summary: After depot repair (Wi-Fi module + SSD replacement) the Lenovo ThinkPad T15 fails to finish corporate provisioning. Intune enrollment stalls at 'Applying Wi-Fi profile' and the provisioning agent exits with a network profile conflict error. Impact: Blocked check-in for two devices returned from depot in the last 48 hours; users cannot complete provisioning and join corp network without manual intervention.
Two devices from depot repair failed provisioning and required helpdesk manual cleanup. Affects internal provisioning SLA for depot returns and delays deskside returns to users.
1) Receive device from depot after Wi-Fi module replacement
2) Run standard depot imaging (autoprov-image-v2) with corporate packages and join steps
3) Boot out-of-the-box and let provisioning agent run (provisioner v1.8)
4) Observe provisioning stall at 'Applying Wi-Fi profile' and agent exit status with "NetworkProfileApplyError: duplicate-profile-id"
2026-03-10T08:32:12Z provisioner[3421]: INFO: Starting network configuration
2026-03-10T08:32:15Z network-manager: ERROR: apply_profile: failed, code=409, message='duplicate-profile-id'
2026-03-10T08:32:15Z intune-client[778]: WARN: Enrollment paused: network profile application failed
netsh wlan show profiles
Profiles on interface Wi-Fi:
Group policy profiles (read only)  : 0
User profiles
-----------------
All User Profile     : Corp-WiFi
All User Profile     : Corp-WiFi-OLD
Helpdesk reproduced failure and captured netsh/profile output showing two profiles for 'Corp-WiFi'.
Depot imaging logs indicate that the post-image script that imports Wi-Fi XML profiles (scripts/wifi-import.sh) ran twice due to an edge-case restart when the WLAN driver enumerated after image completion.
Hypothesis: Replaced Wi-Fi module caused interface name/NetCfgInstanceId to change, triggering the wifi-import script to re-apply an already-present profile under a slightly different identifier resulting in duplicate profile metadata in the Windows WLAN store.
We also observed that if a docking station is attached during first boot the system enumerates an additional virtual interface, and the current depot script does not de-duplicate profiles by SSID, only by GUID, so duplicates were created.
No evidence of DHCP MAC duplication or network-level collision; issue isolated to local WLAN profile store and provisioning agent's strict validation.
Reproduced locally by intentionally interrupting imaging after driver install to force a re-run of wifi-import.sh; observed duplicate profile GUIDs and provisioning failure match.
Related artifact: staging depot image had older wifi-import logic that used netsh wlan add profile filename=... without checking for existing SSID - this was the immediate trigger.
2026-03-09 10:12 - Depot completed hardware swap and pushed device to imaging pool
2026-03-09 11:03 - Imaging completed; device returned to user.
2026-03-10 08:30 - User reported provisioning stalled; ticket opened.
2026-03-11 09:15 - Helpdesk reproduced failure on staging depot machine.
2026-03-12 14:40 - Eng confirmed root cause and deployed depot script change.
2026-03-13 10:30 - Workaround applied to affected devices and provisioning completed.
Workaround: Helpdesk removed duplicate Wi-Fi profiles and re-ran provisioner on affected devices: commands used: 'netsh wlan delete profile name="Corp-WiFi-OLD"' and 'provisioner --enroll'.
Permanent fix: Updated wifi-import.sh in depot image to be idempotent and to clear stale NetCfg registry keys prior to profile import. PR gh/pr/infra/1384 merged and new depot image built (autoprov-image-v2.1).
Follow-up: Added a depot smoke test that verifies Intune enrollment completes within 5 minutes of imaging; updated depot runbook (confluence/redwood/depots/runbooks/wlan-cleanup) with manual steps if failure occurs.
Rollout notes: Image v2.1 deployed to central depot on 2026-03-12; regional depots scheduled for staggered rollout over next 3 days.
Closure: Affected devices were re-provisioned and validated on 2026-03-13. No further incidents reported by end of day
Helpdesk (J. Sullivan) 2026-03-10: User tech reported provisioning stuck on Wi-Fi. Collected logs and moved device back to depot for inspection.
Depot Technician (M. Lee) 2026-03-11: Reimaged device and reproduced issue. Noted 'Corp-WiFi-OLD' lingering in profiles after imaging. Suspect script ran twice post-driver install.
Eng (Diego Martinez) 2026-03-11: Investigating. Will instrument wifi-import.sh to log invocation count and skip if SSID exists.
Eng (Diego Martinez) 2026-03-12: Confirmed repro on staging. Pushed branch gh/pr/infra/1384 to add idempotency and pre-clean step (netsh wlan delete profile name="Corp-WiFi-OLD" /all) plus registry NetCfgInstanceId clear for stale entries.
Helpdesk (Aisha Kaur) 2026-03-13: Applied manual cleanup to the two affected devices (netsh wlan delete profile name="Corp-WiFi-OLD" and re-run provisioner) - enrollment completed and devices joined domain.
Depot Lead (R. Patel) 2026-03-13: Deployed updated depot image with wifi-import idempotency. Added a post-image smoke test to validate Intune enrollment completes before marking as ready.

title: Cust VPC Change Simulator and Sample Audit Corpus
content:
Cust VPC Change Simulator and Sample Audit Corpus

Purpose and scope:

This is a working PRD / engineering sketch for a lightweight customer VPC change simulator and a curated sample audit corpus intended to: (1) exercise our approval gate logic, sampling and retention heuristics, and attestation bundling; (2) validate telemetry shape and queryability for forensic playback; (3) produce realistic rejection/rollback/rollback-recovery scenarios for SRE and support drills.

Why this exists (problem statement):
- Customers performing private deployments manage their own networks and will occasionally make configuration changes (SG, route, peering, NAT). These changes must flow through our approval gates or be captured fully in audit evidence when done out-of-band.
- We need a reproducible test harness that can generate varied, realistic change traces (benign changes, configuration drift, misapplied firewall rules, partial peering failures) and an associated audit corpus that represents evidence bundles (logs, netflow, sha-signed change manifests).
- Current PRDs focus on policy and retention; we lack a repeatable way to validate operator experience, failure modes, and query patterns for downstream tooling (search, timeline, forensics).

Goals (what success looks like):
- Deliver a CLI-driven simulator that can synthesize change events with parameters (change_type, scope, operator_role, approval_path, evidence_quality).
- Produce a set of 120 sample audit bundles across 6 classes (approved, auto-approved, rejected, emergency-bypass, partial-apply, rollback) that cover our expected query surface (by tenant, by operator, by timeframe, by change hash).
- Ensure each bundle contains a compact set of artifacts: change-manifest.json, operator-assertion.sig (simulated HSM signature), agent-syslog tail, network-trace (pcap-lite), and a compact summary.json with canonical fields for quick indexing.
- Define compatibility tests for Console playback, SIEM-forwarder ingestion, and on-prem observability export.

Non-Goals:
- This project will not implement a hardened HSM signing pipeline — signatures are simulated but schema-compatible with future KMS-backed receipts.
- We are not building a full traffic generator; pcap-lite will be synthetic, small, and focused on metadata that our parsers exercise.

Key definitions and canonical fields (summary.json schema):
- tenant_id: string (redwood tenant namespace id)
- change_id: string (uuid v4)
- change_type: string (route_update | security_group_update | peering_add | peering_remove | nat_delta)
- operator: string (email)
- operator_role: string (tenant-admin | delegated-operator | support-bridge)
- request_time: iso8601
- approval_path: string (console-canary | api-reserved | delegated-approval | emergency-bypass)
- approval_result: string (approved | rejected | timed_out | bypassed)
- manifest_hash: sha256
- evidence_quality: string (complete | partial | truncated)
- forensic_tags: list of short strings (we will store as comma-separated string in the corpus)

Simulator design (CLI + engine):
- Entry: rd-vpc-simulate run --profile PROFILE --seed SEED --count N --outdir /tmp/corpus
- Profiles (examples):
  - small-change-fast: single SG rule add, operator role delegated-operator, expected approval path console-canary
  - cross-region-peering-failure: peering_add with simulated partial propagation and route-ads update; evidence_quality=partial
  - emergency-rollback: nat_delta that triggers emergency-bypass; approval_result=bypassed, with post-facto attestation bundle
- Engine components:
  - event-synthesizer: creates change-manifest.json and deterministic operator actions from seed
  - evidence-generator: emits artifacts (syslog snippets, pcap-lite, manifest.sig) and synthesizes manifest_hash
  - timeline-builder: produces chronological event stream (request -> approval request -> approval decision -> apply steps -> monitoring alerts -> rollback)
  - corpus-packager: zips each scenario into an evidence bundle and writes summary.json (index-friendly)

Sample audit bundle (human-readable example for review):
- summary.json
  {
    "tenant_id": "tenant-82f3",
    "change_id": "9f2c8b4a-3a1d-4e2e-9a0b-1111111",
    "change_type": "security_group_update",
    "operator": "ops+alice@acme.example",
    "operator_role": "delegated-operator",
    "request_time": "2024-10-28T18:22:40Z",
    "approval_path": "console-canary",
    "approval_result": "approved",
    "manifest_hash": "sha256:...",
    "evidence_quality": "complete",
    "forensic_tags": "sg-change,login-from-nonprod"
  }

(above is stored inside each bundle; real JSON in artifact file — here we show for reviewers)

Acceptance criteria for product and infra teams:
- Simulator binary (or Python script) runs in CI producing deterministic bundles when a seed is provided; artifacts are small (<5MB each bundle) and stored under s3://redwood-evidence-dev/sim-corpus/<release> for retrieval.
- Console can ingest a bundle and render a playback timeline (request -> approval -> apply -> alerts -> rollback) without schema changes to the Console timeline UI.
- SIEM-forwarder can index summary.json and extract manifest_hash, tenant_id, and approval_result into a test index.
- A small test harness exists that asserts queries: counts by approval_result, counts by operator_role, and latencies from request_time to approval decision.

Test matrix and scenarios (high level):
- Categories: approval_behaviour (approved/rejected/timeout/bypass), evidence_integrity (complete/partial/truncated), application_impact (no-service-impact, partial-failure, outage), operator_timeline (single-op, multi-op-handoff), scale (single change, bulk 50 changes).
- For each scenario we define EXPECTED_CONSOLE_STATE and EXPECTED_SIEM_EVENTS (documented in test matrix CSV in repo).

Operational considerations and retention experiments:
- Bundles will be compact (summary + minimal binary artifacts). We will evaluate retention and S3 cost for 6 months of generated corpus at scale 10k bundles/day.
- Propose a TTL experiment: store full bundles for 30 days, archive compact summary-only records for 365 days. Evaluate usefulness to support during a simulated incident.

Security and privacy notes:
- All simulator-generated tenant IDs and operator emails are synthetic and labeled "sim" to avoid accidental cross-contamination with customer data.
- Signature artifacts are simulated. Avoid using this simulator as a certifying tool; it is only for UX/telemetry/forensics testing.

Console / UX playback requirements (short):
- Timeline view should be able to accept a bundle endpoint (local file or s3 path) and step through events. Improve timeline to show "evidence_quality" indicator and link to artifacts (view syslog snippet, download pcap-lite).
- Provide a compact summary card in rollouts page that highlights approval_path and approval_result and links to bundle manifest_hash.

Open questions and decisions needed:
- Do we standardize the compact summary JSON schema now (breaking change for Console)? Proposal: adopt the schema above and version it as v1.0-summary. Decision due by 2024-12-05.
- Where to publish simulator artifacts for reuse? Proposal: s3://redwood-evidence-dev/sim-corpus/<branch> + a simple index endpoint maintained by infra.
- What are acceptable sizes for pcap-lite? Proposal: cap at 200KB per event to keep bundles small.

Implementation plan (quarterly roadmap):
- Week 1-2: prototype CLI and simple profile templates (Marcus, Jules)
- Week 3-4: produce first 30 bundles and run Console ingest smoke tests (Aisha, product)
- Week 5-6: integrate SIEM-forwarder test harness and prepare test matrix (Priya)
- Week 7-8: iterate on schema and produce acceptance test coverage in CI (all)

Risks and mitigation:
- Risk: simulated evidence might accidentally differ from customer artifact shapes. Mitigation: collect anonymized example shapes from recent support tickets (security review) and incorporate into profile templates.
- Risk: corpus grows and costs escalate. Mitigation: TTL policy and compact-summary archival.

Next steps / action items:
- [Aisha] PR the initial repo with CLI skeleton and one profile (due 2024-11-25) — PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy/pull/312
- [Marcus] Draft schema proposal and VersionedSummary RFC (due 2024-12-01) — link to confluence: confluence:PD-4321-cust-vpc-simulations
- [Priya] Draft SIEM ingestion test cases and expected mapping to logs pipeline (due 2024-12-10)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and intended to land quickly as a test harness that improves our ability to validate approval gates and forensic UX. Expect several follow-ups: schema tightening, larger corpus generation, and integration with the attestation service.

Raw brainstorming snippets (notes-to-self preserved):
- consider embedding deterministic anomaly triggers so one can fire a "silent-misapply" where manifest says success but netflow shows block
- simulate operator-network-latency for distributed approvals (two-step OK flow)
- think about a tiny DSL for profiles: change:sg add {cidr} -> approval:console-canary -> monitor:flow-drops

References and related docs:
- Confluence: PD-4321-cust-vpc-simulations (design notes)
- Jira: PD-789-change-sim (epic)
- GH: private-deploy PR 312 (starter)

End of doc.

title: Event Log Mapping Playbook (v0.7 exploratory)
content:
Event Log Mapping Playbook (v0.7 exploratory)

Purpose:
This playbook captures a working approach to mapping runtime events into a compact, SIEM-friendly audit log schema and to surface a minimal evidence set for automated compliance workflows. It is intentionally pragmatic: close-to-runtime fields, conservative growth of the schema, and clear migration steps.

Context & constraints (quick):
- Need one canonical event model used by hosted API, Dedicated control plane, and Private deployment tooling.
- RBAC v2 introduces resource-scoped roles and ephemeral role bindings; logs must record enough to reconstruct authorization decisions without leaking PII.
- SIEM exports should align with common ECS-like conventions to ease ingestion by Splunk/Elastic/QRadar.
- Evidence automation (for audits) will pull a deterministic subset of fields per event-class.

Scope for this doc:
- Event naming conventions, core field set, severity mapping, and basic SIEM export map.
- RBAC v2 field guidance (what to log vs what to redact).
- Versioning and migration strategy v0.7 -> v1.0 candidate steps.
- Implementation checklist and open questions.

1) Event naming and taxonomy (short):
- Use dotted, lower-case nouns: auth.login.success, auth.login.failure, resource.access.denied, model.request.start, model.request.complete, model.fallback.
- Prefixes: auth.*, resource.*, model.*, deployment.*, system.*. Keep verbs to the rightmost segment.
- Event families should be broad; fine-grain detail lives in attributes map to keep index cost predictable.

2) Core audit schema (flat, SIEM-friendly):
- event_id: unique UUID for the event (string)
- event_ts: ISO8601 UTC timestamp (string)
- event_type: taxonomy name (string)
- severity: info|notice|warning|error|critical (string)
- outcome: success|failure|unknown (string)
- actor_id: opaque user id (redactable) (string)
- actor_role_ids: list of role ids applied during decision (list of strings)
- actor_role_names: OPTIONAL human-friendly names, redaction recommended in high-sensitivity customers (string)
- resource_type: e.g., model, dataset, project (string)
- resource_id: canonical resource identifier (string)
- request_id: request correlation id (string)
- service: product surface (hosted-api|dedicated|private-controlplane) (string)
- host_region: region tag (string)
- client_ip: IP or proxy tag (redact per policy) (string)
- user_agent: client user-agent (string)
- duration_ms: numeric-ish as string for indexing (string)
- payload_summary: small JSON blob-as-string summarizing request (trim to 1024 chars) (string)
- error_code: canonical error code if any (string)
- linked_evidence_ids: list of evidence artifact ids (list of strings)
- schema_version: semantic-ish v0.7 (string)

Notes: keep top-level fields flat. Extra diagnostic detail should be stored in an attached evidence artifact rather than in the main event body to reduce event size.

3) Event severity & outcome mapping guidance (examples):
- auth.login.failure: severity=warning, outcome=failure
- auth.login.success: severity=info, outcome=success
- model.request.start: severity=info, outcome=unknown
- model.request.complete (with fallback): severity=notice, outcome=success and set attribute fallback=true
- model.request.error (OOM, inference failure): severity=error, outcome=failure, attach stacktrace evidence id

4) SIEM export mapping (ECS-like suggested fields)
Purpose: a straightforward one-to-one mapping to accelerate ingestion. We recommend shipping both the raw event and the mapped ECS envelope. Minimal mapping:
- ecs.timestamp <- event_ts
- ecs.event.id <- event_id
- ecs.event.type <- event_type
- ecs.event.outcome <- outcome
- ecs.event.severity <- severity
- ecs.user.id <- actor_id
- ecs.user.name <- actor_role_names (only if permitted)
- ecs.network.client.ip <- client_ip (apply redaction rule)
- ecs.url.path <- resource_id (when resource is an API endpoint)
- ecs.service.name <- service
- ecs.duration.ms <- duration_ms
- ecs.stack_trace <- error evidence artifact (link)

Implementation note: produce a lightweight flattened ECS view for high-throughput consumers and store the full raw event for internal investigations.

5) RBAC v2 considerations (what to log):
- Log role ids and the binding id used for the decision. Role bindings are often ephemeral; record binding_ts to make the audit reconstructable.
- DO NOT log token values, full credentials, or private keys. Replace with token_hash if needed for correlation.
- For high-sensitivity customers (HIPAA/PII), default to recording role ids only, not role names. Provide a retrieval API (audit-only) to resolve role names via require-auth.
- Record policy version or policy-check-id to tie a decision to a policy revision.

6) Evidence automation (how events trigger evidence collection):
- Evidence levels: minimal, diagnostic, full. Each event_type maps to a required evidence level. Example mapping:
  - auth.login.failure -> minimal (auth headers sans tokens, timestamp, actor_id) + diagnostic on repeated failures
  - model.request.error -> diagnostic (request payload summary + model logs + stack trace)
  - deployment.rollout.failed -> full (deployment manifest, rollout diff, operator id)
- Evidence artifacts should be stored in a tamper-evident store (S3 versioned + KMS + immutable tags) and referenced by linked_evidence_ids.
- Evidence TTLs: evidence level drives retention class. Minimal: 90d; Diagnostic: 365d; Full: 7 years (enterprise customers may override).

7) Schema versioning and migration strategy (v0.7 -> v1.0):
- Semantic intent: vX.Y where X increments for breaking changes, Y for additive backwards-compatible fields. v0.7 is exploratory. v1.0 freeze planned when: RBAC v2 fields approved, evidence taxonomy stabilized, and SIEM mapping vetted by 2 customers.
- Backwards compatibility rules: always accept older schema_version values when reading. New fields must be optional and default to null/empty.
- Migration steps:
  1) Deploy ingestion that accepts both v0.7 and v1.0.
  2) Start emitting v0.8 with authoritative actor_role_ids list and binding_id.
  3) After 60 days of dual-emit, flip default to v1.0.
  4) Deprecate old fields with 90-day notice and maintain a translation layer for SIEM exports.

8) Performance & cost tradeoffs (practical):
- Keep event payload < 2KiB for high-traffic endpoints. Move large artifacts to evidence store.
- Index only the small subset of fields used in SLOs/alerts (event_ts, event_type, actor_id, outcome, severity).
- Batch-export to SIEM — use compressed NDJSON and incremental checkpoints.

9) Implementation checklist (short-term work items):
- [ ] Add schema_version to all event emitters (API surface, runtime, control plane).
- [ ] Implement actor_role_ids logging in auth middleware and include binding_id.
- [ ] Build evidence artifact API with put/get and immutability markers.
- [ ] Produce an ECS-mapped export transformer and integration test with SIEM partner.
- [ ] Draft RBAC v2 logging policy for customers (redaction defaults).
- [ ] Run load test on event sizes and SIEM export throughput.

10) Open questions / unresolved decisions (for sync):
- Should we include anonymous session tags (session_id) by default for model requests? Pros: easier correlation. Cons: increases PII surface.
- How aggressively do we redact user_agent and client_ip for on-prem customers vs hosted? Policy needed.
- Do we require immutable storage for evidence by default or opt-in per customer?
