title: Console API: create and query Shadow Experiments (CRUD, aggregates, example sampling) with RBAC
content:
Console API: create and query Shadow Experiments (CRUD, aggregates, example sampling) with RBAC

Goal
Implement the Console backend API surface for Shadow Experiments so the Console UI and SDKs can:
- Create/update/delete shadow experiments attached to routes and/or rollouts
- Query experiment status, targets, and sampling config
- Fetch aggregated quality deltas (with confidence intervals) and core health counters
- Fetch sampled examples (prompt/response pairs + score breakdown) in a cardinality-safe and privacy-safe way
- Enforce RBAC/tenant boundaries and audit relevant actions

Context
Shadow traffic duplicates a sampled subset of production requests to one or more candidate variants (“shadow targets”) while returning the control response to the user. Shadow outputs are scored asynchronously (eval-harness adapter + rubric runner) and results are surfaced in Console alongside latency/cost/error metrics.

Non-goals (this ticket)
- Implement routing/mirroring in the data plane (ENG-5402)
- Implement telemetry ingestion/event schemas (ENG-5404)
- Implement scoring pipeline mechanics (ENG-5405/ENG-5406)
- Build UI pages (ENG-5408)

API shape (v1)
Note: exact route prefix may vary based on Console gateway conventions; below uses /v1/console for clarity.

1) CRUD
- POST /v1/console/shadow-experiments
  - Creates a shadow experiment definition.
  - Required inputs:
    - tenant_id (derived from auth context)
    - display_name
    - route_id OR rollout_id (at least one)
    - control: (implicitly the live route config at time of run; stored as a snapshot ref for auditability)
    - shadow_targets: list of variant refs (model_id/model_version OR policy_variant_id depending on rollout integration)
    - sampling: percent + bucketing salt/seed policy (seed stored, salt derived from tenant + experiment id)
    - fail_open: true (hard default; can’t be disabled in v1)
    - retention_profile: default (short) or dedicated/private override (validated)
  - Validations:
    - sampling_percent must be within [0.1, 20] by default (hard cap configurable per tenant; see guardrails)
    - max shadow targets: 3 (v1)
    - cannot target same variant as control snapshot
    - must match route request type constraints (chat vs completions vs embeddings)
    - streaming requests allowed only if shadow_streaming_mode is supported for the route (see ENG-5414)

- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments
  - List experiments for a tenant.
  - Filters:
    - status (draft/running/paused/stopped)
    - route_id
    - rollout_id
    - created_by
    - updated_at range
  - Pagination:
    - cursor-based (opaque cursor) + limit (default 25, max 100)

- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}
  - Returns experiment definition + current state.

- PATCH /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}
  - Allows updates to:
    - display_name, description
    - sampling_percent (within guardrails)
    - paused flag
    - shadow_targets (restricted; requires “experiment:editTargets” permission)
  - Immutable after start:
    - route_id/rollout_id binding
    - bucketing seed

- DELETE /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}
  - Soft-delete (archival) in v1; actual artifacts are handled by retention policies.

2) Aggregates
- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}/aggregates
  - Purpose: power the “Quality deltas” and “Health” panels.
  - Query params:
    - window: 1h | 6h | 24h | 7d (default 24h)
    - segment: optional pre-defined segment key (e.g., region, request_type, route_variant_bucket). Must be from allowlist.
    - metrics: optional list of metric keys; defaults to v1 bundle.
  - Response conceptually includes:
    - sample counts (n_control, n_shadow per target)
    - pass/fail rates (format adherence, refusal rate, etc.) per target
    - deltas vs control with confidence intervals (method per Observability Standard)
    - pipeline health indicators (scoring lag p50/p95, missing score rate)
  - Cardinality guardrails:
    - only allow breakdowns on dimension allowlist (no raw prompt_id, no user_id, no customer internal ids)
    - enforce max number of series returned per request (e.g., top K + “other”)

3) Examples (sampled)
- GET /v1/console/shadow-experiments/{experiment_id}/examples
  - Returns a paginated list of scored examples with a stable sampling strategy.
  - Query params:
    - shadow_target_id (required)
    - window (default 24h)
    - outcome filter (regressed | improved | neutral | missing_score | shadow_error)
    - metric_key (optional; used to sort/filter by “worst offenders”)
    - limit (default 20, max 50)
    - cursor
  - Privacy & retention:
    - response payload should return redacted prompt/response fields per retention_profile.
    - examples may include only references (artifact ids) when prompt/response storage is disabled for the tenant.
  - Ordering:
    - default sort: most recent
    - optional sort: highest absolute delta contribution (requires precomputed index; if unavailable, return 400 or fall back)

RBAC & permissions
- All endpoints scoped to tenant derived from auth token.
- Required permissions (names are placeholders; align with Console RBAC system):
  - experiment:read for list/get/aggregates/examples
  - experiment:write for create/edit/pause
  - experiment:delete for archive
  - experiment:editTargets for updating targets after creation
- Additional checks:
  - If route_id is provided, caller must have route:read (and route:write for binding changes).
  - If rollout_id is provided, caller must have rollout:read (and rollout:write if attaching to an active canary).
- Audit logging:
  - Create/update/pause/archive actions emit audit log events with experiment_id, actor, tenant, and diff summary (detailed diff stored server-side; response returns a safe summary).

Data sources / storage
- Control-plane stores experiment definitions (source of truth), but Console API will read from Console DB read model for latency.
- Aggregates are backed by analytics tables derived from shadow telemetry + scoring results (ENG-5404/5405). This ticket includes query-layer plumbing + guardrails, not pipeline creation.
- Examples use a pointer-based model:
  - metadata in analytics store
  - payload in artifact store (if enabled)
  - redaction at write-time + additional redaction at read-time based on role/tenant settings

Edge cases
- Scoring pipeline lagging: aggregates should include “incomplete” flags and missing_score_rate; UI should surface “data still processing.”
- Shadow target errors: count separately (shadow_error_rate) and do not treat as “quality regression,” but do include in health panel.
- Streaming requests: examples may contain partial captures; surface capture_status (partial/complete/timeout) and only compute certain metrics when capture_status=complete.

Acceptance criteria
- CRUD endpoints implemented with validation + proper error messages.
- Aggregates endpoint returns correct values for internal dogfood experiments (validated against notebook queries by Applied ML).
- Examples endpoint respects retention/redaction settings and does not expose raw PII fields.
- RBAC enforced at route/rollout and experiment object levels.
- Audit logs emitted for create/update/pause/archive.
- Load: endpoints remain responsive under high-cardinality tenants; enforce allowlists and series caps.
- Unit + integration tests covering:
  - pagination correctness
  - RBAC denial cases
  - sampling cap enforcement
  - dimension allowlist enforcement

References
- GitHub: sources/github/redwood/pr-24933-console-api-shadow-experiments-crud.json
- Related tickets: ENG-5408 (UI), ENG-5417 (audit logs), ENG-5410 (cardinality guardrails)
- ADRs: shadow routing architecture + telemetry data model/cardinality (Confluence ADRs)

Open questions (tracked here until resolved)
1) Do we allow attaching a shadow experiment to a route without a rollout object in beta? Proposed: yes (route_id supported), but rollout_id required for “show in rollout timeline.”
2) Example payload shape: do we return raw text (redacted) or only artifact refs by default? Proposed default: return redacted text when tenant retention allows; otherwise artifact refs.
3) Confidence intervals: computed in query-time vs precomputed. Proposed: precompute common windows; query-time only for small series counts (guarded).

2026-01-16 (Dylan Brooks): Creating as P0 for Phase 2 Console beta. UI work (ENG-5408) is blocked until we have stable endpoints + pagination + RBAC semantics. Please coordinate with Jonas/Selene on what metrics must be in aggregates v1.
2026-01-18 (Chloe Martin): Drafted initial API contract (aligning with Drive: shadow-experiments-api-contract-draft). Main concern: aggregates query must be dimension-allowlisted to prevent support escalations like the earlier cardinality incident. Will sync with Allison (Obs) on series caps.
2026-01-22 (Allison Grant): +1 on allowlist + cap. Please do NOT allow arbitrary “tags” query param in v1. We can add a small set of segment keys (region, request_type, model_family) and bucket anything else. Also: include scoring_lag_ms p50/p95 in the aggregates response so dashboards and UI can show “processing delay.”
2026-01-23 (Jonas Weber): For v1 metrics, we need at least: format_adherence_rate, refusal_rate, instruction_following_score (model-graded), safety_flag_rate, and missing_score_rate. Also include sample sizes; we’ve seen small n produce misleading deltas. Confidence intervals should follow the observability standard (Wilson for rates, bootstrap for rubric scores if precomputed).
2026-01-26 (Marcus Lin): Security review note: examples endpoint must enforce retention_profile; do not return raw prompts if the tenant disables storage. Also ensure authZ checks happen before any artifact store lookup to avoid metadata side channels.
2026-01-29 (Chloe Martin): Implemented CRUD + list/get with cursor pagination. Added hard caps: max_targets=3, limit<=100 for list, limit<=50 for examples. Drafted RBAC checks using existing Console policy engine hooks (route:read/rollout:read). Starting aggregates query implementation next; blocked on final metric key names from Applied ML.
2026-02-03 (Selene Huang): Metric keys finalized for v1 bundle: format_adherence_rate, refusal_rate, rubric_overall_score, safety_policy_violation_rate, missing_score_rate. Please expose both absolute values and delta_vs_control + ci_low/ci_high (as floats). If your response schema is strongly typed, ensure we can add new metric keys without breaking older SDKs (map/dictionary).
2026-02-04 (Chloe Martin): We can’t return a map/dictionary in our public API without committing to a schema; but this is Console API (not data plane). Proposal: return metrics as a list of rows {metric_key, control_value, shadow_value, delta, ci_low, ci_high, n}. That keeps it extensible without a map. Will confirm with Monica (SDK).
2026-02-05 (Monica Patel): List-of-rows is good for SDKs. Please ensure metric_key is a stable enum-ish string and add a display_name field in server response for UI convenience (or keep display logic in UI). Prefer not to put display strings in API long-term, but ok for beta if needed.
2026-02-07 (Chloe Martin): PR up for review: implements aggregates + examples endpoints with allowlisted segment keys and series caps. Examples endpoint supports outcome filter and uses artifact refs when payload storage disabled. Added integration tests for RBAC denial + retention gating. PR: redwood/pr-24933.
2026-02-10 (Jada Williams): Rollouts integration: if experiment is created with rollout_id, we should store rollout_phase_id (canary phase) when available so we can later pin metrics to the phase timeline. Not required for beta but please add optional field to create request and store it if present.
2026-02-11 (Chloe Martin): Added optional rollout_phase_id and validated it belongs to rollout_id. Also added audit log hooks behind feature flag (audit schema work in ENG-5417). Merged after approvals.
2026-02-12 (Dylan Brooks): Marking Done. Next: UI integration (ENG-5408) and SDK bindings (ENG-5418). Please ensure docs mention that examples may return artifact refs only depending on tenant retention.

title: Lexana POC: model shortlist & workload scoping
content:
Lexana POC: model shortlist & workload scoping

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Connor (Redwood); Sofia, Omar, Elena (Lexana)
---
Summary:
Sofia wants a 6-week POC to validate open-model options for multilingual contract clause extraction and risk scoring. Primary constraints: legal-grade accuracy, low hallucination, Spanish/Portuguese/Russian support, and on-prem/VPC options for sensitive files. Redwood to propose 3-model shortlist (+quantized variants), run small hosted benchmark, and provide cost/latency projections and security docs.
Topics covered:
- Workload sizing: tokens per contract, QPS, concurrency, retention policy
- Success criteria: precision/recall targets for clause extraction, acceptable latency, failure modes
- Model shortlist: candidate open models and size tradeoffs
- Benchmarks: dataset, metrics, evaluation cadence
- Timeline & next steps
---
Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:06] Sofia (Lexana): hi hi, Sofia here. Head of ML.
[00:09] Omar: Omar, lead counsel. i'll mostly listen but will flag legal constraints.
[00:12] Elena: Elena, PM. focusing on scope and timelines.
[00:15] Connor (Redwood): Connor, infra/SE. i'll run the bench and the hosting setup.
[00:20] Maya: Cool. high level — Lexana wants to run a POC to compare model options for clause extraction and risk scoring across english, spanish, portuguese, and russian. Is that right, Sofia?
[00:29] Sofia: Yes, exact. we also want to measure hallucination rates when models are asked to synthesize missing clauses, and false positives on liability clauses.
[00:35] Omar: also data residency — some contracts from EU clients require data remain in our VPC or an on-prem instance. SOC 2 is baseline, but some customers ask for ISO or audit logs and HSM/KMS.
[00:45] Maya: that's helpful. we can do Hosted for initial runs but will propose Dedicated / Private for production. Redwood has audit logs and KMS integrations; we'll send the security brief. sorry — our security deck.
[00:53] Elena: timeline constraint: we want results before the legal review cycle in mid July, so roughly a six-week window.
[01:00] Connor: noted. to scope infra: can you give rough workload numbers — average contract length, number of docs per day, peak concurrent reviewers?
[01:08] Sofia: average contract is ~3,500 tokens, some long ones up to 12k. we'll pilot with 200 anonymized contracts (mix of standard NDAs, SOWs, supplier contracts). Daily throughput target for POC ~500 documents, peak concurrent users maybe 40.
[01:20] Connor: ok that maps to qps and token throughput. for early bench we can simulate 50 QPS with batching. production expectations?
[01:27] Sofia: production could be 2k docs/day, but POC should demonstrate we can meet ~500/day with sub-second-ish latency per clause extraction call.
[01:35] Maya: let's talk success criteria — what metrics will you use to decide go/no-go?
[01:40] Elena: primary: clause extraction F1 >= 0.85 for key clause types (termination, indemnity, liability). secondary: hallucination rate < 2% on generative answers, latency < 800 ms for single-document extract endpoint, and cost per document under $0.05 for hosted.
[01:55] Sofia: and multilingual performance: for Spanish/Portuguese we want within 5 percentage points of English performance; russian is lower priority but should not be catastrophic.
[02:05] Omar: compliance: all PII must be redacted and logs should be configurable to avoid storing full text in Redwood logs.
[02:12] Connor: we support redaction and KV/prefix cache controls; will note retention config and masking.
[02:17] Maya: model shortlist — based on your domain we recommend testing a small, medium, and a larger open model variant. initial candidates: 1) LlamaX-13B (quantized 4-bit), 2) Orion-33B (unoptimized), 3) JurisGPT-70B-open (if available) — plus distilled / quantized variants. any concerns?
[02:36] Sofia: JurisGPT — is that an external community model? i've heard inconsistent results.
[02:40] Maya: yes community-sourced, tends to be best-in-class for legal prompts but can be less stable on hallucinations. that's why we'll include a medium-sized generalist model as a control.
[02:49] Connor: tradeoffs — 13B quantized will be cheapest and fast with decent accuracy; 33B is a middle ground; 70B likely best accuracy but higher cost and may need Dedicated or higher GPU to meet latency. we can also test smart rerouting: run extractors on 13B and fallback to 70B for low-confidence cases.
[03:05] Elena: fallback policy sounds promising. can we measure reroute latency?
[03:08] Connor: yes we'll instrument trace — expected extra latency if fallback is invoked, but only for small percent of requests.
[03:14] Sofia: what's Redwood's approach to model quantization? are we losing crucial legal nuance?
[03:18] Connor: quantization degrades some subtlety but with instruction-tuning and careful prompt engineering it's often acceptable for extraction tasks. for scoring/risk we might need the larger model. we'll include a quality delta table in the bench.
[03:29] [crosstalk] Omar: and what about fine-tuning vs prompt engineering?
[03:32] Maya: for POC we recommend prompt & eval-first to avoid long fine-tune cycles. If results plateau, we can do a small instruction-tune or RLHF later — which would change timeline.
[03:41] Elena: budget? we have limited budget for this quarter. can you give rough cost brackets?
[03:45] Maya: ballpark for 2-week hosted bench: small model runs maybe $800-$1.2k, mid model $2k-$3k, large $6k+. Production cost depends on tokens and model—we'll provide per-doc estimates.
[03:58] Sofia: ok that's fine as a preliminary.
[04:00] Connor: benchmark plan:
- Week 0: ingest and sanitize 200 contracts (Sofia)
- Week 1: run smoke tests on 13B quantized and 33B baseline (hosted) for extraction metrics
- Week 2: run larger 70B test and fallback policy sim
- Week 3: stress tests for throughput (simulate 500/day, peak 40 concurrent)
- Week 4: compile results, meeting to review and recommend production config
[04:25] Elena: that fits the 6-week window if we start asap.
[04:28] Maya: security items — we'll send SOC 2 summary, encryption at rest/in transit, SAML SSO, and KMS docs. any extra certs?
[04:36] Omar: for certain clients we may need on-prem or private deployment and HSM integration. also legal wants to see data deletion audit trail.
[04:44] Connor: Private deployment is supported; scheduling and hardware planning would add ~4–6 weeks after POC if you choose that route.
[04:52] Sofia: can Redwood provide a sample evaluation script so we can reproduce metrics?
[04:55] Connor: yes we'll share our benchmark harness and a reproducible notebook (will include tokenization, metrics, and conf intervals).
[05:01] Maya: any competitors or internal constraints we should be aware of?
[05:04] Sofia: we did preliminary tests with Bedrock and OpenAI; Bedrock was cheaper but we had trouble with fine-grained extraction, OpenAI had best out-of-the-box but cost is a worry.
[05:15] Omar: legal also flagged vendor lock-in risk.
[05:18] Maya: that's a good point — Redwood's exportable prompts and pinned model versions help reduce lock-in. we'll document the model artifacts and configs.
[05:25] Elena: final recap and next steps?
[05:27] Maya: recap: Lexana provides 200 anonymized contracts + label set by 2026-05-18. Redwood shares benchmark spreadsheet, security brief, and sample notebook by 2026-05-16. Connor to provision hosted trial and run initial 13B/33B smoke by 2026-05-20. We'll target a POC kickoff run week of 2026-05-25.
[05:45] Sofia: sounds good. Omar — any final?
[05:48] Omar: just please include deletion audit detail in the security brief.
[05:52] Maya: will do. thanks all.
[05:55] End of call.
---
References & shared artifacts mentioned:
- Deck: drive.lexana/POC/lexana-poc-deck.pdf
- Bench harness: github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness (notebook link to be provided)
- Security brief: redwood.com/security/lexana-brief.pdf
---
Recorded with moderate transcription fidelity; speaker turns accurate but some technical names may be mis-transcribed.

title: eng-platform
content:
eng-platform

Nina Petrova: looping in eng-platform folks — we need to nail down the integration points between the new VPC terraform modules and platform/installer config. Today we’re doing a lot of “paste subnet ids here” in pilots and it’s brittle.

Victor Alvarez: +1. main question from my side: what outputs do we want to be part of the “contract” for alpha? if we change names/shape every PR it’ll be chaos.

Irene Choi: yep. for alpha I’d like a minimal stable set that redwood-private-installer can consume (either flags or a config file). optional extras can be “best effort” outputs.

Bruno Silva: current modules output the basics (vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, public_subnet_ids, nat_gw_ids) but we haven’t standardized endpoint outputs. also log sinks.

Sean Gallagher: from SRE standpoint: the only things we *must* know to validate networking before we start are: subnets for nodes, cluster SGs, and whether required VPC endpoints exist + private DNS enabled where expected. (we’re adding preflight checks in installer; it needs something deterministic).

Allison Grant: observability angle: we need to know where to send/expect logs. at minimum: cloudwatch log group names/arns for flow logs (if enabled) and any S3 bucket used as sink (flow logs / access logs). plus tags so we can discover.

Rafael Mendes: +1 on deterministic. installer preflight should not scrape AWS too much without inputs; but we can also do discovery if we have VPC ID and region and explicit “I expect endpoints ON”.

Nina Petrova: what’s the preferred format? terraform output -json can be consumed by installer? or we want the terraform to render a yaml file?

Irene Choi: preference: don’t generate files in terraform for alpha. keep it as outputs, then docs say: `terraform output -json > networking.json` and pass to installer.

Victor Alvarez: okay so define a single composite output? e.g. `redwood_private_networking` containing everything.

Bruno Silva: we can, but then we have to keep object shape stable. also some people want individual outputs for reuse.

Sean Gallagher: composite is fine as long as it’s additive-only in alpha. but note: in terraform output -json you’ll get nested structures. installer can parse that.

Allison Grant: I’m fine w nested, but we should keep the “leaf values” as IDs/ARNs/strings. no giant lists of objects unless needed.

Simran Kaur: from RA review: docs should clearly map outputs -> installer flags/values. a table would help. also call out which are required vs optional.

Victor Alvarez: concrete proposal for v0.1 contract:
- required:
  - aws_region
  - vpc_id
  - private_subnet_ids (list)
  - cluster_node_security_group_id (or sg_ids list if pattern module returns multiple)
  - vpc_endpoints_required (map service->endpoint_id?)
- optional:
  - public_subnet_ids
  - nat_gateway_ids
  - flow_logs: enabled + destination (cw log group arn OR s3 bucket arn)
  - interface_endpoint_security_group_id
  - resolver / private hosted zone info (if we ever create)

Bruno Silva: we don’t currently create cluster SG in the VPC module; that’s in SG patterns module. but we can wire outputs through example.

Nina Petrova: for EKS private control plane constraints: installer/cluster will need the endpoint access pattern too. do we need to output whether EKS endpoint private/public is allowed? (or is that out-of-scope since modules aren’t creating EKS)

Irene Choi: out of scope for modules, but we should include “assumptions” in outputs/docs. i.e. “private subnets have route to NAT or endpoints for ECR/S3/Logs”.

Rafael Mendes: installer needs to know ecr endpoints specifically. we already have PR to detect + warn when missing.

Sean Gallagher: yeah PR-19110 is exactly this. it currently checks:
- `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api`
- `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr`
- `com.amazonaws.<region>.s3` (gateway)
plus `logs` and `sts` depending on mode.
We should align the terraform endpoints module defaults to match what the installer expects, then output “expected endpoints list” so preflight error messages can be explicit.

Victor Alvarez: re: “expected endpoints list” — do we output actual endpoint IDs or just booleans?

Bruno Silva: actual IDs are useful for debug. but installer can also query by service name + VPC ID.

Irene Choi: I’d like both: output the service names we *intend* to have and whether private DNS is enabled for each interface endpoint. then installer can cross-check reality.

Allison Grant: +1. private DNS misconfig is a common pilot issue (ECR). if we output the intended `private_dns_enabled=true` for ecr endpoints, that maps nicely to a preflight message.

Nina Petrova: can we keep it simple like:

```
output "redwood_network" {
  value = {
    region = var.region
    vpc_id = aws_vpc.this.id
    private_subnet_ids = module.subnets.private_ids
    public_subnet_ids  = module.subnets.public_ids
    endpoints = {
      ecr_api = { service = "ecr.api", endpoint_id = module.endpoints.ecr_api_id, private_dns = true }
      ecr_dkr = { service = "ecr.dkr", endpoint_id = module.endpoints.ecr_dkr_id, private_dns = true }
      logs    = { service = "logs",    endpoint_id = module.endpoints.logs_id,    private_dns = true }
      sts     = { service = "sts",     endpoint_id = module.endpoints.sts_id,     private_dns = true }
      s3      = { service = "s3",      endpoint_id = module.endpoints.s3_gateway_id, private_dns = "n/a" }
    }
    flow_logs = {
      enabled = var.flow_logs_enabled
      destination = var.flow_logs_destination
      cw_log_group_arn = try(aws_cloudwatch_log_group.flow.arn, null)
      s3_bucket_arn    = try(aws_s3_bucket.flow.arn, null)
    }
  }
}
```

Victor Alvarez: yes-ish. minor: service names should be full AWS service strings or standardized keys? i’d prefer full: `com.amazonaws.${region}.ecr.api` to avoid ambiguity.

Bruno Silva: agreed. and keep `endpoint_type` too (Interface/Gateway) so installer messaging can be better.

Rafael Mendes: re: `private_dns = "n/a"` — better to omit or set null. :)

Allison Grant: for log sink naming: can we output a “recommended log group name” even when not created? (customers sometimes bring their own). maybe:
- `flow_logs.destination_type` = `cloudwatch|s3|none`
- `flow_logs.log_group_name` OR `flow_logs.s3_bucket_name`

Irene Choi: careful: we shouldn’t output customer-provided values in a way that looks like Redwood-managed. but if it’s an input and we just echo it, that’s fine.

Sean Gallagher: also add `tags` output? not required but helps SRE inventory.

Victor Alvarez: tags in terraform output can be noisy. i’d skip for alpha contract.

Simran Kaur: +1 skip tags, but doc should say we tag everything with `redwood:component` etc.

Nina Petrova: question: should installer accept `--networking-json` path? or will it be `--terraform-outputs-json`? naming matters.

Rafael Mendes: i vote `--networking-outputs` or `--network-config`. `terraform-outputs-json` sounds too terraform-y.

Sean Gallagher: installer side can accept a JSON file with just the subset we need. but docs can recommend generating it with terraform output.

Bruno Silva: we can add an example script in the repo:

```
terraform output -json redwood_network > redwood-network.json
redwood-private-installer install --network-config ./redwood-network.json
```

Irene Choi: this is good. action items:
1) Victor/Bruno: standardize a `redwood_network` (or `redwood_private_network`) output in the examples (not necessarily in every module) with: region, vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, endpoints (service_name + endpoint_id + private_dns_enabled + endpoint_type), flow_logs destination info.
2) Sean/Rafael: confirm which fields installer will read in alpha and what’s optional; we can update preflight messaging to reference service names.
3) Allison: provide the minimal log sink fields SRE wants surfaced (cw log group arn/name and/or s3 bucket).
4) Simran: update RA/deployment guide mapping table outputs -> installer inputs.

Victor Alvarez: works. i’ll post a proposed schema in the PR description when we wire it.

Sean Gallagher: please also make sure endpoint keys match installer checks. we’ve been bitten by “logs” vs “cloudwatch-logs” naming.

Bruno Silva: noted. i’ll align to full service names:
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.ecr.api`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.ecr.dkr`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.logs`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.sts`
- `com.amazonaws.${region}.s3` (gateway)

Allison Grant: for flow logs, if destination is CloudWatch we should output retention days too (defaults matter for security/compliance). if it’s customer-owned log group, we can output “unknown”.

Irene Choi: ok but keep it optional. don’t block alpha on it.

Rafael Mendes: :thumbsup: once we agree schema, we should freeze names for v0.x and only add fields. breaking changes require bump and release note callout.

Nina Petrova: +1. also if we can, add a “schema_version”: "0.1" in the output so installer can warn if incompatible.

Victor Alvarez: good call. we can set `schema_version = "0.1"` at top-level.

Sean Gallagher: :+1: that will save us in pilots.

Irene Choi: cool. let’s do it. please link the PR here when ready.

title: 2026-05-22-rate-fencing-and-tenant-split-patterns-livestream-demo-tidewave-systems
content:
2026-05-22-rate-fencing-and-tenant-split-patterns-livestream-demo-tidewave-systems

Intro demo focused on multi-tenant rate fencing, org/project key strategies and handling bursty payments-like traffic. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated with strong security requirements. SE showed console flows for org keys, burst quotas, fairshare, and sticky routing; discussed fallback to lower-cost variants and KV/prefix caching implications. Agreed to run a scoped POC to validate 99th latency under mixed traffic and to share pricing options.
[00:00] Maya (AE): okay good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood Inference. we got Jonah our systems engineer and Priya on product, um we'll run through rate-fencing patterns and then open for Q&A.
[00:14] Aisha: afternoon, thanks. traffic is kinda spiky for us, we have a payments notifications pipeline that has big bursts during settlement windows. we're trying to figure out how to prevent noisy tenants from chewing up our tokens.
[00:28] Jonah (SE): yeah and that's exactly where org/project keying helps. we'll show two topologies: single org key with per-project metadata, and dedicated project keys mapped to quotas. each has tradeoffs for billing and routing.
[00:41] Luis (SRE): quick Q, is the billing then per-project key? we want per-customer chargeback.
[00:47] Maya: yes you can map billing to project keys so accounting is clean. if you use org-wildcard keys you can still do tag-based usage but it's trickier for invoice line-iteming.
[01:02] Jonah: starting demo, pulling up Console -> Governance -> Key topology. this view shows active tokens, associated projects, and current concurrency slices. note that the console has a live QPS heatmap, and you can set soft/hard quotas.
[01:18] [screen share noise] Jonah: here I'm configuring a "burst fence" policy. the idea: each key gets a base rate, a burst bucket, and a cooldown window. when a key hits hard limit we can either queue, drop, or route to a cheaper model variant as a fallback.
[01:33] Ben (Security): about the fallback to cheaper variants — are we sure that's safe for PII? we can't degrade to a public model for regulated traffic.
[01:43] Priya (Product): great point. policies can be annotated with data classification. you can configure policy rules to never fallback for keys marked PHI, and those keys can be pinned to Dedicated or Private deployments.
[01:57] Nora (CTO): timeline question — our procurement needs to know if Dedicated is required for compliant PII handling or if hosted with VPC+KMS will suffice.
[02:08] Maya: depends on control plane expectations. many customers use Hosted + VPC peering + customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest and are SOC2 happy, but some prefer Dedicated for stronger tenancy isolation. we'll add a comparison doc.
[02:22] Jonah: back to live traffic — here's a sample rule I'm simulating: fairshare across projects, with a reservation of 20% capacity for gold tenants then best-effort for others. see the graph — under heavy spike, gold stays within SLO, others throttle.
[02:40] Aisha: can we set preemptive throttles for a tenant before they cross the threshold? like soft limits that warn then hard limit?
[02:47] Jonah: yes soft alerts, then automated throttling. soft is metric-based alert with webhook, and the system supports gradual ramp-down policies so you don't see sharp failures.
[02:58] Luis: what about backpressure to our clients? any recommended client-side patterns?
[03:03] Jonah: yes recommended patterns: client should implement exponential retry with jitter, observe Retry-After header, and use sticky routing keys to maintain KV cache locality. KV caching reduces per-token compute for repeated contexts.
[03:20] Aisha: sticky routing, can you expand? is that per-project key pinned to a pool?
[03:25] Jonah: exactly. when you pin a project key to a pool, subsequent requests hit the same serving nodes which preserves KV cache and lowers p95/p99 latency. downside is less global load balance and possible hotspots; we expose pool-level autoscaling to mitigate.
[03:42] Priya: and we have a sticky-aware scheduler that moves warm state proactively during planned outages.
[03:49] [small crosstalk, typing]
[04:02] Maya: let's talk about unit economics quickly — batching, prefix KV caching and quantization all reduce per-token cost. Jonah did a quick numbers calc for a chat workload — enabling KV cache cut per-token cost by ~18% in our last benchmark.
[04:18] Jonah: the catch is cold starts for new routing keys — first request pays warmup. so our burst buckets and warmup TTL settings are important.
[04:28] Nora: curious about SLO verification — can you run a benchmark that simulates our peaks and show 99th latency?
[04:35] Jonah: yes we can. that's one of the POC items — we'll run a simulated arrival model with your traffic curves. please share the curves.
[04:44] Aisha: we'll export a week with per-minute QPS and 95th/99th token lengths.
[04:49] Ben: security — how are audit logs produced, retention, and encryption? also SSO and RBAC?
[04:56] Priya: audit logs are streamed to your S3 or GCS with AES-256 and tie into customer KMS; retention is configurable. we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and RBAC roles at org/project levels.
[05:09] Ben: any certifications for the hosted environment?
[05:12] Maya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II; we can share the report under NDA. Dedicated/private deployments have additional contractual controls.
[05:22] Luis: what about multiregion failover for low-latency routing? we can't tolerate 200ms spikes for EU customers.
[05:28] Jonah: routing policies support region preference and geo-failover. you can define latency SLOs per customer and the smart router will pick nearest healthy pool.
[05:40] Aisha: okay demo makes sense, show me one more: how do we quickly revoke a compromised key and re-route traffic?
[05:46] Jonah: revocation is a one-click in Console -> Keys -> Revoke; you can also rotate keys via API. after revocation, you can optionally create a temporary fallback key mapped to a different pool to drain state.
[05:59] [sound of a message ping]
[06:05] Nora (joined): sorry, timezone mix up, jumped in. quick Q: if a tenant is on Dedicated but occasionally wants to burst to Hosted, do you support hybrid routing?
[06:15] Maya: yes hybrid is supported via policy-based routing; you can allow overflow to a hosted pool when dedicated is saturated with data-compliance annotations preventing PHI from overflowing.
[06:29] Maya: recap: we showed topologies, burst fences, sticky routing, and fallback policies; action items are benchmark run, pricing deck, and security pack.
[06:38] Aisha: sounds good. any blockers on Redwood side?
[06:41] Maya: we need your traffic curves and list of keys that will be PHI-bound. Jonah will draft the benchmark plan.
[06:48] Luis: one last question on observability — can we get token-level tracing and costs per trace?
[06:54] Priya: yep token-level cost breakdown per request is available, plus trace IDs you can join to your APM, and per-route dashboards.
[07:05] Maya: excellent okay we'll follow up with the POC scoping invite for 06/02 and share the docs. thanks all.
[07:12] [meeting ends]

title: maria_support: FYI — Customer (Acme Health) opened an escalation: API responses after a failover are mangled (weird tokens, truncated JSON). They say it started when their requests were routed to another region.
content:
maria_support: FYI — Customer (Acme Health) opened an escalation: API responses after a failover are mangled (weird tokens, truncated JSON). They say it started when their requests were routed to another region.
kevin_infra: can you drop the request_id and sample response? I want to grep the routing logs
maria_support: request_id=req_01H8Z7K4. Example request (sanitized):

```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \ 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_xxx" \ 
  -H "X-Region: eu-west-1" \ 
  -d '{"model":"rwd-bison-v1","input":"Summarize patient intake form"}'
```
response snippet:
```
{"id":"resp_9abc","text":"Ġ<|role|>patient\n\nĠ<|content|>Name: John Doe\n<|pad|> ..."}
```
maria_support: customer says sometimes they get eloquent answer, then suddenly outputs with raw token markers and broken JSON — happens during higher traffic periods.
deploy-bot: traffic-policy service rolled out config `allow_cross_region_fallback=true` in rollout `routing-2026-02-14` (commit 8e3b2d4) at 2026-02-14T03:12Z
emily_sre: :eyes: that rollout could explain cross-region fallbacks. Did we validate model-variant compatibility mapping with that change?
luca_eng: Noticed that routing fallback currently picks any "compatible_architecture" variant, but we don't check tokenizer/version metadata. That can cause fallback to quantized/legacy variants with different tokenizers.
kevin_infra: grepping logs for req_01H8Z7K4 shows:
```
[2026-03-09T14:22:11Z] req=req_01H8Z7K4 route=euw1 -> fallback=usw2 variant=rwd-bison-quant8
[2026-03-09T14:22:11Z] tokenizer_mismatch=true token_scheme=bytepair expected=cl100k_base got=cl100k_legacy
```
kevin_infra: so the router fell back to `rwd-bison-quant8` in us-west and that variant uses an older tokenizer (cl100k_legacy) — mismatch flagged in logs.
maria_support: customer pasted one of the broken outputs, includes literal `<|pad|>` and some control bytes that break their JSON parser. They flagged as high severity.
luca_eng: immediate mitigation options:
- revert `allow_cross_region_fallback` rollout (prevents cross-region fallback while we patch)
- blacklist specific variants from fallback unless tokenizer_version matches
- update routing preflight to validate tokenizer metadata before sending
emily_sre: revert first please, we need to stop new incidents. I'll coordinate oncall to approve.
maria_support: customer wants ETA and escalation to CSM — any estimate if we can stop this within the hour?
luca_eng: if infra agrees, we can rollback the rollout in ~10-15m. For long term we need a small router change (~2h dev + 30m deploy) to enforce tokenizer compatibility in fallback selection.
kevin_infra: rolling back now. running: `trafficctl rollback routing-2026-02-14` — will post updates in 5.
deploy-bot: rollback of `routing-2026-02-14` started by kevin_infra at 2026-03-09T14:29Z
emily_sre: good. After rollback, please run a targeted replay for the request id and confirm outputs stable.
kevin_infra: replayed req_01H8Z7K4 against euw1 primary -> response clean, no tokenizer markers. replayed forced fallback -> response had markers. Logs updated.
luca_eng: I'll open a small PR to add tokenizer_version checks to the fallback matcher and add a unit test that simulates different tokenizers (PR: rrdw/routing#452). ETA 2 hours for patch and staging test, then can canary to 5%.
maria_support: please include sample text we can send CSM to explain cause/mitigation. Customer asked for reason: why did requests go to us-west and why variant changed?
luca_eng: suggested message:
"We traced this to a recently enabled cross-region fallback policy; the router selected a lower-latency fallback variant in another region that had an incompatible tokenizer. This caused token markers and malformed JSON in some responses. We rolled back the policy to stop new incidents and are patching the router to validate tokenizer/version compatibility before fallback."
maria_support: perfect. tagging CSM.
emily_sre: action items:
- kevin_infra: confirm rollback fully rolled out (in progress)
- luca_eng: PR for tokenizer check + tests
- maria_support: update customer and log incident ticket
- ops: monitor spike in cross-region traffic
maria_support: updating ticket INC-2026-318 and CSM. will keep thread updated. thanks team :heart:
luca_eng: once PR merged will create a short runbook snippet: "if cross-region fallback is enabled, ensure `tokenizer_version` in model metadata matches before routing" — will attach to incident.
kevin_infra: rollback completed at 2026-03-09T14:36Z. monitoring for reruns.
emily_sre: :thumbsup: closing escalation until we see reoccurrence. maria, please post if customer still sees issues.


maria_support: FYI — Customer (Acme Health) opened an escalation: API responses after a failover are mangled (weird tokens, truncated JSON). They say it started when their requests were routed to another region.
kevin_infra: can you drop the request_id and sample response? I want to grep the routing logs
maria_support: request_id=req_01H8Z7K4. Example request (sanitized):

```

title: Release Conservatory Runpad — 24hr Stabilization Log & Compact Checklist
content:
Release Conservatory Runpad — 24hr Stabilization Log & Compact Checklist

Context / goal:
This is a compact runpad for the Jun release (codename: conservatory). Primary goal: move traffic to v2 routing with staged canary while preserving 99th percentile latency SLO and keeping per-token unit cost within projection. Use this doc as the single-source quick checklist + 24h stabilization log for on-call and release stewards.

Summary of change:
- Routing layer change: traffic-aware fallback to quantized-compat model when Dedicated pool is saturated.
- Small model upgrade: model-v2 (attention perf patches + kv-cache improvement).
- Operator-visible flags: route.weight, batch.max_tokens and cache.prefetch.

Quick runpad (hour-by-hour highlights)
- T-2h: final preflight (smoke tests, bench against staging, notify CS + infra-watch). Check: smoke/generate endpoint, embeddings sample, auth tokens.
- T-1h: apply route.weight=0.05 for cohort A (10 hosts), open watch channels (#release-conservatory and #sre-nightwatch).
- T+0m: increase cohort A -> 5% global traffic for 15m, verify success criteria (p95 latency <= 180ms, error rate <0.2%).
- T+15m: cohort A -> 20% if green, else abort and revert to previous route config.
- T+45m: cohort B rollout ramp (20% -> 50% over 30m) with telemetry sampling increased.
- T+90m: full ramp to 100% if all gates pass. Begin 24h stabilization log.

Preflight checklist (must be green before any traffic shift)
- [ ] Canary config checked in Git and validated: linear INF-4122 status = ready.
- [ ] Deployment artifact SHA verified and pinned in release manifest.
- [ ] Staging smoke matrix run: basic LLM generation, streaming, embeddings, tool-calling samples.
- [ ] Bench script executed: median and p95 token/sec within 10% of baseline.
- [ ] Observability hooks active: tracing, token-level cost metrics, KV cache hit rate instrumentation.
- [ ] Rate-limit backstop configured for safety-lane and windowing.
- [ ] Pager rotation and guardrails briefed; primary steward (Asha), secondary (Diego), SRE (Maya).
- [ ] Customer success pre-notice sent to top-10 accounts with SLA triggers.

Canary schedule (compact calendar)
- Window: 2026-06-12 18:00–20:00 PT (quiet window, low release collision).
- 18:00 PT: cohort A 5% for 15m -> validate telemetry.
- 18:15 PT: cohort A 20% for 30m -> validate.
- 18:45 PT: cohort B gradual ramp 20% -> 50% over 30m.
- 19:15 PT: pause 15m to inspect signal.
- 19:30 PT: ramp to 80% -> 100% between 19:30–19:45 PT if green.
- 19:45 PT: final commit and mark release-flag active.

Success criteria / gating signals (explicit)
- Latency: p95 request-to-first-byte <= 220ms for Hosted API and <= 350ms for Dedicated in worst-case region.
- Errors: 5xx rate < 0.5% of requests, user-facing API error rate < 0.2%.
- Cost: per-token unit cost delta <= 12% against projection.
- Quality: automated prompt-set eval regressions <= 2% on BLEU-like metric and prompt fidelity checks.
- Observability: KV cache hit-rate not falling > 10% vs baseline.

Telemetry / dashboards to watch (primary widgets)
- api.latency.p95 by region and model variant (hosted vs dedicated).
- infra.gpu.utilization by pod and pool (watch for hot spots).
- token_cost.per_request and token_cost.daily_rate.
- gen.error_rate and gen.exception.classifications (top-10 stack traces).
- kv_cache.hit_rate and kv_cache.evictions/min.
- Traces: sampling for slow requests (p99 > 1s).

Immediate mitigation & rollback criteria (if any of these happen -> trigger rollback)
- Any sustained p95 above threshold for > 10m configured alarm -> immediate pause and scale down new route weight.
- Error spike: 5xx rate > 1% for 5m -> rollback to previous manifest.
- Cost runaway: token_cost running 30% above projection for 2 consecutive 1h windows -> rollback and open postmortem.

Rollback steps (fast path)
1) Revert route config to pinned manifest (git rollback command in infra/runbooks).
2) If rollback fails: trigger hotpatch with global route override (ops emergency toggle).
3) Notify slack: #release-conservatory, escalate to SRE Lead and Product.
4) Keep rollback annotated in ticket INF-4122 and fill the stabilization log with timestamps and signals.

24h stabilization log (template for entries)
- Timestamp | Operator | Action | Signal observed | Notes
- Example: 2026-06-12T18:07Z | Asha | increased A to 20% | p95=172ms, 5xx=0.06% | green
- Keep concise entries; prefer timestamped bullets.

Post-rollout checks (first 24h priorities)
- Hourly snapshot of p95/p99 for first 6h, then 3h cadence until 24h.
- After 4h: run mini-eval suite against our canonical prompt set (regression detection).
- After 12h: verify cost runtimes vs projected model/quantization benefit.
- 24h: finalize release notes and switch status from draft->final in release manifest.

Compact release notes (draft - to be expanded for external changelog)
Title: model-v2 routing upgrade (conservatory) — staged rollout
Short blurb: We rolled out model-v2 with improved attention kernels and routing fallbacks to optimize for latency and cost. This release uses staged canaries and monitored rollouts; no action required for most customers.
Key changes:
- Routing: traffic-aware fallback to quantized model-compat variants when Dedicated pool saturates.
- Model: v2 improves long-sequence KV cache hits and reduces tail latency on typical prompts.
- Ops: improved telemetry for token-level costing.
Known limitations / notes:
- There is a small expected cost delta for heavy prefix workloads; we are monitoring and will publish guidance if we adjust batching defaults.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self)
- Q: Should we pre-warm dedicated pools for accounts with heavy context length? (Maya to advise)
- Q: Do we enable auto-fallback based on predicted latency per-request or keep the deterministic routing policy? (product decision)
- TODO: add a short demo snippet for CS to explain fallbacks in customer-facing notes. (Jonah)
- TODO: check PR #1783 for an optional telemetry tag that isn't merged yet — defer if not in manifest.

Postmortem trigger policy (quick)
- Any rollback causes automatic postmortem with SLO review. Owner: release steward.

Appendix: quick commands & references (cheat)
- Rollback manifest: infra/deployments/releases/2026-06-12/manifest.yaml
- Canary toggle CLI: infra/cli route set-weight --route conservatory --weight 0.2 --cohort A
- Smoke run: scripts/release_smoke.sh --model v2 --sample 50
- Pager oncall: https://oncall.redwood/rota (primary: Asha, secondary: Diego)

Notes: rough, expect edits. This is intentionally compact — put details into the main runbook if we need extended debugging steps.

-- end of runpad --

title: Stripe prefetcher and per-CPU pin highways for block manager
content:
Stripe prefetcher and per-CPU pin highways for block manager

Motivation: Reduce early-warmup p99 tails and allocator contention in the paged KV block manager for mixed small/large request patterns. Current freelist grabs and opportunistic prefetch lead to head-of-line contention on high core counts and bursty workloads. This PR introduces two complementary mechanisms: a stripe-based prefetcher that issues clustered prefetch ahead-of-use, and a light-weight per-CPU pin highway that serializes pin/unpin bookkeeping per core to avoid global freelist races.

Design summary: stripe-prefetcher: maintains short-lived 'stripes' (small contiguous sets of blocks) discovered by scanning hot prefixes and allocation traces. Prefetch issues are batched into a vector-friendly path that emits contiguous async IO/KV-loads to warm the cache and prime KV block pin state. Prefetch budget is adjustable per-tenant and per-route; aggressive mode is disabled by default.

per-CPU pin highways: instead of a single freelist hot path with atomic handoffs, pins/unpins are shuttled through a per-CPU ring (highway) which batches releases and performs coalesced freelist returns. This reduces CAS storms on the global freelist and keeps hot allocations local to the CPU that consumed them. A global slowpath remains for cross-core steals.

Kernel-friendly hints: prefetcher emits 'kernel hints' that are consumed by the serving runtime path to select a vectorized copy kernel when contiguous stripes are available; this reduces per-block bookkeeping overhead when moving KV payloads into GPU-visible memory. The runtime selects the hint-aware kernel only when contiguous runs exceed a threshold to avoid fragmentation penalties.

Backward compatibility and safety: no on-disk format changes. Feature gated behind two runtime flags (kv.stripe_prefetcher.enabled, kv.percpu_pin.highways_enabled) and a dynamic prefetch_budget param. If either flag is disabled, behavior falls back to the existing allocator. We added a runtime guard to disable prefetch on constrained memory nodes and a throttler for background prefetch work to preserve latency SLOs.

Benchmarks: microbenchmarks on a 32-vCPU canary with 4 A100s show: +12% aggregate throughput for mixed small/med gen workloads, p99 latency down 18% on short-response chat-style requests, and a 22% reduction in CAS contention observed on the global freelist counter. End-to-end cost-per-token reduced ~6% under synthetic steady-state due to fewer reissued cache misses. Detailed numbers and methodology are in docs/ops/prefetcher.md.

Testing and rollout: unit and integration tests added; bench harness extended with a 'stripe' scenario. Rollout plan: gated canary -> region grayscale -> global enable with telemetry thresholds. Feature flags are on by default only for internal dev clusters.

Checklist:
- [x] Implementation of stripe prefetcher and per-CPU pin highways
- [x] Unit tests for allocator fastpath and slowpath
- [x] Integration tests covering prefetch budget and disable guards
- [x] Bench harness scenario and raw results attached
- [x] Telemetry (contention, prefetch hits/misses, highway occupancy)
- [x] Docs: ops guide and rollout notes

Related: ENG-4821 (allocator contention reduction), ENG-4923 (prefetch controls and telemetry).
Arjun Patel: Request change - add a unit test for cross-core steal path and validate highway fallback under preemption.
Maya Chen: Added cross-core steal test and stress harness; pushed follow-up commit f7a8b9.
Liam O'Neill: Suggestion - expose prefetch_budget via runtime API for on-the-fly tuning. Please add metrics for budget utilization.
Maya Chen: Exposed budget via configs/feature_flags.yaml and added kv.prefetch.budget_used metric.
Hannah Brooks: Noted an intermittent CI failure on integration tests (timing); reran CI and added small delay in test to stabilize.
CI Bot: integration-tests failed on first run due to race in highway_ring; fixed in commit c0d1e2 and re-run passed.
Introduce stripe prefetcher and per-CPU pin highways to reduce allocator contention and improve early-warmup p99. Controlled by kv.stripe_prefetcher.enabled and kv.percpu_pin.highways_enabled flags. No on-disk changes. See docs/ops/prefetcher.md for benchmarks and rollout guidance.

title: scalable-reserve-droplet-and-tenant-saturation-detector
content:
scalable-reserve-droplet-and-tenant-saturation-detector

Motivation: production tenants with bursty traffic patterns occasionally drive node-level saturation that triggers aggressive autoscaler decisions and SLO violations for adjacent tenants. This PR introduces a lightweight per-tenant saturation detection signal and a small, bounded 'reserve droplet' allocation mechanism that provides short-lived, spillover capacity to tenants that are about to hit sustained saturation. The goal is to reduce noisy-neighbor-induced autoscale churn, protect tail latency, and improve utilization signals used by downstream accounting. Design summary: 1) Saturation detector: a new sampler that computes a tenant_saturation_score by combining per-pool occupancy, queue-depth percentiles (P90/P99), and recent scheduling rejections. The detector emits a short TTL score (30s window) and a smoothed score for admission logic. 2) Reserve droplet allocator: small reserved allocations (1-3 slot droplets depending on tenant tier) that are liquid — they are granted for short intervals (default 45s), charged to tenant allocation, and reclaimed aggressively on preemption. Allocation decisions are conservative: total droplets per pool capped at 8% of pool capacity and subject to headroom budget. 3) Autoscaler/Admission integration: the admission controller consults the tenant_saturation_score to prefer droplet granting over immediate scale-up when a tenant shows transient saturation but the cluster still has headroom. When cluster-wide pressure persists, the fallback is the regular autoscaler path. 4) Telemetry and reporting: exports tenant_saturation_score, droplet_allocated{tenant,pool}, droplet_preempt_count, and a derived tenant_saturation_class (OK/WARM/CRITICAL). These feed the utilization rollup and a new tenant-level heatmap in Console. Rollout plan and safety: staged rollout toggled by feature flag fleet.reserve-droplet.enabled. Canary on two non-critical us-west pools for 48h, then expand to 25% of pools with increased sampling. Safety knobs: hard cap on droplets per pool, per-tenant max-droplet-per-minute, and opt-out via tenant config. Backwards-compatible: if the feature flag is off, no control path changes. Linear/Jira: relates to ENG-3419 (reduce autoscale churn), PM-4128 (tenant latency regressions), and SUP-1221 (customer incident follow-up). Checklist: - [x] unit tests for detector scoring and edge cases - [x] integration test with admission controller sim in bench-lab - [x] telemetry metrics + Grafana dashboards (draft) - [x] migration docs and tenant opt-out documented - [x] e2e dry-run in canary region - [x] rollout feature flag and safe defaults Known limitations: detection window tuned conservatively; may under-react to extremely short microbursts (sub-100ms). Future work: adaptive droplet sizing, budget-aware droplet pooling across zones.
Marco Ruiz (2026-02-14): Nice incremental design. Two asks: add a metric for droplet-request-latency and ensure the droplet reclaim path cannot starve node-level evictions.
Aisha Kumar (2026-02-15): Added droplet_request_latency metric and tightened reclaim window; added additional unit test for eviction safety.
Dana Lee (2026-02-18): Request changes: the default droplet TTL of 45s seemed long in the sim — can we make it adaptive? Suggested config: min/median/max TTL and conservative default 30s.
Aisha Kumar (2026-02-19): Made TTL configurable with defaults changed to 30s. Left TODO for adaptive TTL in follow-up (ENG-3428).
Priya Shah (2026-02-22): Approve after CI green. Noted that dashboard wording should make it clear droplets are temporary and billable.
CI bot (2026-02-20): Lint failure on reserve_droplet_controller.go: gofmt issues. (fixed in f6a7b8c).
Marco Ruiz (2026-02-26): Squash-merged after canary run; leaving post-merge follow-ups for dashboards and SLO guardrails.
Introduce tenant saturation detector and reserve droplets: reduces autoscaler churn by providing short-lived spillover capacity for tenants approaching sustained saturation. Feature off by default; enable via fleet.reserve-droplet.enabled. See ops docs for knobs and tenant opt-out.

title: Kestrel Ventures Tokenflow & p95 Throughput Discovery
content:
Kestrel Ventures Tokenflow & p95 Throughput Discovery

Discovery call focused on p95 latency targets and token/sec throughput for streaming chat workloads. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private due to compliance and burst traffic. Agreed to run benchmark and share pricing + security docs.
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-04-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Reilly (CTO, Kestrel), Sana Patel (Platform Lead), Markus Li (SRE), Ana Gomez (Product)

Auto-summary (auto): Customer wants p95 under 600ms for streaming token flow during peak, tolerates slightly higher during cold starts; interested in Dedicated for burst windows but wants private for regulated pipelines.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros, then we'll dive into traffic shapes and p95 goals.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Liam): Hey, thanks. Our primary thing is realtime summarization in the product, so streaming latency is the big one. We're trying to get p95 of, like, under 500ms for user visible tokens, otherwise the UX feels laggy.
00:35 Speaker 3 (Maya): Got it. When you say "user visible tokens" do you mean partial token flushes per streaming chunk or end-to-end response p95?
00:42 Speaker 2 (Liam): Partial streaming. We stream as the model generates. So p95 per token chunk is the key number.
00:50 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Okay, good. Can you share expected concurrency? tokens/sec peaks?
01:02 Speaker 4 (Sana): We see about 250 concurrent active sessions in the EU region during peak; average request length is 120 tokens prompt + 300 tokens response historically. Burst can go up to ~700 concurrent for a marketing campaign.
01:20 Speaker 3 (Maya): Quick note: that response length is substantial. For 300 tokens response, sustained token/sec and KV cache reuse matter a lot. Do you have any prefix reuse across requests?
01:34 Speaker 4 (Sana): Yes, lots of repetition—system prompt and a few contextual turns are similar across sessions. So KV cache should help.
01:42 Speaker 5 (Markus): Our constraints: infra is hybrid — primary in-cloud but some workflows must run on-prem for regulated customers. Also strict key management, we need HSM/KMS integration and audit logs.
01:55 Speaker 3 (Maya): That's fine. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs; Dedicated has isolated capacity but still managed control plane, and Hosted is the fastest to get started. We can walk through lat/throughput tradeoffs.
02:10 Speaker 1 (Jordan): For p95 goals, are you targeting single-digit token latency or end-to-end?
02:16 Speaker 2 (Liam): Realistically we want p95 per partial chunk under 400–600ms during non-burst, and under 800–1,000ms acceptable during big bursts as long as we don't drop sessions.
02:28 Speaker 3 (Maya): Good benchmark to aim at. For a 300 token response streamed, you'll hit token/sec limits depending on model size and GPU type. What model families are you planning to run?
02:40 Speaker 2 (Liam): We're evaluating open models right now; want something high-quality but quantized for cost. Probably an LLaMA-derivative, 34B-ish.
02:52 Speaker 3 (Maya): Okay, that maps well to Redwood Dedicated profiles. We typically recommend 8xA100-equivalent for heavy streaming, but with quantization and kernel selection we can increase throughput. With prefix caching you can reduce effective compute per request.
03:07 Speaker 5 (Markus): Network jitter is a big factor for us; sometimes inter-region routing adds spikes. Do you do region pinning or fallback?
03:16 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes — smart routing can pin traffic to a region and we have automatic fallback to adjacent region/model-variant to preserve availability. But that adds a little latency on failover.
03:26 Speaker 6 (Ana): Question on KV cache: how much does it actually buy us in real traffic?
03:32 Speaker 3 (Maya): In our experience with similar customers, when there's high prefix reuse you can see 30–60% reduction in consumed tokens and 20–40% latency improvement on p95, depending on model and batch sizes. But depends on hit rates.
03:48 Speaker 2 (Liam): Important for us: we can't accept any logs being stored in a shared control plane for regulated flows. Private offering needs to support air-gapped or VPC-only control.
03:58 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Understood. For Private we do offer on-prem packages; control plane can be customer-managed and logs kept behind your VPC. We'll share the security pack after this call.
04:10 Speaker 3 (Maya): Back to numbers — can I confirm your p95 target: 400–600ms per streaming chunk at 250 concurrency typical, with 700 concurrency burst up to 1,000ms p95 acceptable?
04:22 Speaker 2 (Liam): Yes that's right. Also want to look at token/sec throughput per GPU and cost.
04:29 Speaker 3 (Maya): For a 34B quantized model on an 8-GPU Dedicated pool, rough rule of thumb: sustained aggregate throughput ~6k–10k tokens/sec depending on kernel/quantization. With a single request producing 300 tokens, that implies X concurrency before you saturate — we can run a precise token/sec run with your prompt set.
04:50 Speaker 4 (Sana): Can you also test streaming tail-latency (first-token vs steady-state)? Our UI is sensitive to first-token latency.
04:58 Speaker 3 (Maya): Absolutely, we capture first-token latency and p95 for stream chunks. We'll include that in the benchmark.
05:05 Speaker 5 (Markus): For Dedicated, what's the autoscaling behavior during bursts? We don't want cold-starts that make p95 spike.
05:14 Speaker 3 (Maya): We have configurable autoscale with warm pool and burst capacity. You can keep a minimum number of instances warm to meet p95 SLOs; During sudden spike we have fallback policies to smaller model variants to keep latency bounded.
05:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Pricing note: Dedicated commits give you reserved capacity with lower per-token cost but you pay for baseline. Hosted is usage-based, higher unit cost but zero management. Private is a license plus ops. I'll send a cost model.
05:45 Speaker 6 (Ana): How do you measure p95 in streaming scenarios? Token boundaries vs chunk boundaries?
05:53 Speaker 3 (Maya): We measure both: first-byte latency, chunk p95 (n tokens), and end-to-end response p95. For dashboards we break them down per route/model.
06:06 Speaker 4 (Sana): Network: our egress limits may mean we need to colocate inference near customers. Do you support regional deployments?
06:13 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes, Hosted has multiple regions; Dedicated can be provisioned in a chosen region; Private can obviously be on-prem. We'll document region options in the follow-up.
06:22 Speaker 2 (Liam): Can Redwood run a mixed strategy: Hosted for general traffic, Dedicated reserved for peak sessions, and Private for regulated customers?
06:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Absolutely — hybrid routing is a core pattern. You can route by policy: percent to Dedicated, failover to Hosted, and direct-regulated flows to Private.
06:39 Speaker 5 (Markus): Curious on observability — can we get token-level cost breakdown and per-token latency?
06:45 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route p95, and trace hooks; you can export logs to your SIEM.
06:55 Speaker 4 (Sana): Anything about model fallbacks — is content and safety preserved when you downgrade to a smaller model during burst?
07:04 Speaker 3 (Maya): We recommend a canary test and quality gating; fallbacks preserve prompt context but quality will vary. We can set rollback thresholds based on evals.
07:13 Speaker 2 (Liam): Okay, high-level makes sense. Next, can you run that benchmark you mentioned with our prompt set? We want numbers: first token p95, streaming chunk p95, aggregate tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens on Dedicated vs Hosted.
07:31 Speaker 3 (Maya): Yes. We'll need sample prompts and a small dataset of representative sessions. Also, network conditions are important — if you can replicate jitter we'll do it in the run.
07:42 Speaker 4 (Sana): We'll provide a subset of 500 sessions and a synthetic burst plan.
07:49 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Great. I'll attach the cost model and SLA comparatives. Also sharing SOC 2 / ISO docs and PKI/KMS notes.
07:58 Speaker 6 (Ana): One last ask — can you show P95 drift over time? We need to know how p95 behaves under model updates.
08:06 Speaker 3 (Maya): We can set up quality monitoring tied to eval prompt sets and alert on regressions. That's part of Redwood Optimize.
08:15 Speaker 2 (Liam): Cool. Timing: we want to make a decision in two weeks if benchmarks show we can meet p95 at peak with reasonable cost.
08:23 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Sounds achievable. We'll aim to deliver benchmark results and pricing within 5 business days.
08:30 Speaker 5 (Markus): Small note: encryption in transit and at rest must conform to our compliance list — we'll email legal.
08:40 Speaker 3 (Maya): We'll include the compliance checklist.
08:45 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Recap — Jordan shares pricing + security pack, Maya runs benchmark with Kestrel prompts, Kestrel provides prompts + network profile, schedule Private architecture deep-dive if needed.
08:59 Speaker 2 (Liam): Thanks everyone, talk soon.
09:05 Speaker 1 (Jordan): Thanks, bye.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions where product names heard as "Redwood Privatee" or "KV cash". Speakers sometimes labeled generically. There was overlap at 03:30 with cross talk.

Customer is risk-averse on data residency. Strong candidate for hybrid approach: Dedicated for cost-sensitive steady-state and Private for regulated pipelines. Benchmarks will drive final commit.

content:

Agreed next steps include sending a concise security playbook, a baseline benchmark plan, and scheduling a short on-prem/VPC install walkthrough.
Owner: Maya Patel - Send SOC 2 + ISO executive summary and Redwood private deployment checklist - Due: 2027-02-16
Owner: Ethan Cole - Draft benchmark plan (latency p50/p95, tokens/sec, cold vs warm cache) and sample test harness scripts - Due: 2027-02-18

Meeting: 2027-02-11 16:00 UTC - Duration 42m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Rina (CSM) -- Nina (VP Eng), Omar (SecOps), Priya (ML Eng), Tom (Procurement)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros and then we'll jump to acceptance criteria. Uh, Nina are you leading on the success criteria side?
[00:12] Nina: Yeah thanks, hi all, hi Maya, Ethan. So for LucentGrid we need to validate three things in the pilot: first functional parity for routing and prompt handling, second performance under our 250 concurrent sessions peak, and third security and auditability - SOC 2 style controls and SSO integration.
[00:30] Ethan: Great, can I ask a quick clarifying q, when you say 250 concurrent, is that hard concurrency or sessions with long polling? Like are these streaming sessions?
[00:40] Priya: Mostly short-turn chat like 60-120 token responses, some longer 600-800 token generation for summarization, and yes streaming is important for UX. Concurrency is around 250 active connections, QPS about 120 sustained, bursts to 300 for a minute or two.
[01:01] Maya: good, that's helpful. We'll propose a baseline benchmark that includes p50/p95 latency, and throughput targets. Our typical private deployment config for that footprint is-- sorry Rina interjects--
[01:12] Rina: and just to note we have autoscale + burst on Dedicated but for Private VPC it depends on infra.
[01:18] Omar: security front, a few must-haves: SOC 2 type II equivalence, ISO 27001 evidence preferred, SSO with SAML2.0 and SCIM for provisioning, RBAC scoped to environment and model, and full audit logs with immutable retention for at least 1 year. Also KMS integration for envelope encryption.
[01:36] Ethan: Understood. For SOC 2 / ISO we can provide our audit artifacts and an executive summary. For KMS, we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM in Private deployments and can outline key rotation flow.
[01:48] Omar: How granular are your audit logs? We need token-level attribution back to the user identity and model version, plus tamper-evidence.
[01:55] Ethan: We capture request id, caller identity (via token claims or SSO subject), model id/version, full request/metadata and, depending on config, truncated payloads. We can retain logs on the customer's S3/GCS bucket with lifecycle policies. There may be redaction options for PII in transit though that's part of the workload design.
[02:14] Nina: retention - we can't keep raw content beyond 90 days in some markets, but audit metadata must stay 1 year. Is redaction configurable so we can keep logs for auditing but redact text?
[02:25] Maya: Yes, we typically separate audit metadata from payload. We can discuss a configuration where full payloads are off by default, metadata retained longer; also we can support routed copies to customer-owned bucket for retention policies.
[02:38] Tom: procurement question, timeline - we need an internal security review first before a PO. What's a realistic pilot start date if we move quickly?
[02:45] Maya: If all artifacts are shared promptly, we can start benchkick in ~2 weeks and have a 4-week pilot. So start date target week of 2027-02-22 and wrap by mid-March.
[02:56] Priya: on benchmarks can you lay out cold vs warm cache numbers? Our models are GPT-style decoder models, KV cache matters for warm starts.
[03:07] Ethan: Absolutely. Bench plan will include cold start latency (first token), warm cached latency (p50/p95), and throughput tests with continuous batching. We'll also test prefix caching for repeated prompts. We'll attach scripts - note sometimes transcribe as redwood runtime does continuous batching which lowers per-token cost.
[03:26] Nina: about environment isolation - we want a VPC-deployed private control plane. Is there a lightweight control plane that still gives us RBAC and tracing hooks?
[03:35] Ethan: The Private offering runs a control plane that can be customer-hosted in your VPC. It exposes RBAC, per-model routes, and tracing hooks (trace id injected). We can provide SSO mapping to Azure AD or Okta and SCIM provisioning.
[03:49] Omar: any third-party pen test or do you provide SOC 2 report only? We might require a pen test summary for the specific setup.
[03:57] Maya: We have a SOC 2 Type II report and can share redacted pen test summaries. For on-prem/private deployments we offer assistance during our onboarding pen test window and can coordinate a scoped test with your team.
[04:12] Priya: data residency — we have EU customers; for this pilot data must stay in eu-west-1. Can Private run in their region?
[04:20] Ethan: Yes we can deploy in customer VPC in eu-west-1 region or on-prem; we'll note network egress requirements in the checklist.
[04:27] Tom: SLAs - during pilot we don't need a formal SLA but need reliability targets for acceptance.
[04:33] Maya: Acceptance criteria doc will include uptime thresholds (>=99% over bench window), p95 latency <= 500ms for short responses, and throughput targets per your sample workload. We'll put those into the success criteria spreadsheet.
[04:46] Nina: Can you also capture cost estimate per 1M tokens and per-hour reserved capacity so we can budget?
[04:53] Maya: Yes, we'll provide rough unit economics for both hosted and private (GPU-backed) configurations and show sensitivity to batching and quantization.
[05:02] Omar: SSO integration detail - we need SAML metadata and SCIM for group sync into RBAC. Also, audit trail must show which group made changes to model versions.
[05:12] Ethan: We'll map SAML attributes to RBAC and log admin actions with subject and group info. Model rollouts are logged as events with before/after model ids.
[05:21] Priya: any gotchas with HSM/KMS in private - rotation frequency and access patterns?
[05:28] Ethan: Customer KMS supports envelope keys, we don't hold plaintext root keys. Rotation is handled per your KMS policy; we document the handshake and access control. If you require HSM-backed keys in your HSM we can integrate via standard KMS providers.
[05:42] Rina: quick note, we'll share a short 1-pager that maps compliance asks to artifacts we can provide.
[05:48] Maya: Okay to recap - Redwood sends security pack (SOC2/ISO exec summary + private deployment notes), Ethan sends bench plan and test scripts, LucentGrid sends workload samples and IdP metadata, Omar sends retention/KMS specifics. We aim to kick bench the week of 2/22.
[06:04] Tom: sounds good, I'll start procurement gating and let you know PO timeline.
[06:09] Nina: thanks, one last question, competitors - we're also testing a Bedrock path and an internal inference stack. How do you help compare cost/perf?
[06:18] Maya: We'll include a short comparison matrix and run the same benchmark harness so apples-to-apples. We'll also highlight where our routing and caching gives unit cost benefits.
[06:28] Maya: Alright we'll follow up with the pack and schedule the benchkick. Thanks everyone.
[06:33] End meeting

title: Add staged prompt-authoring watch-mode quickstart with structured-output linter
content:
Add staged prompt-authoring watch-mode quickstart with structured-output linter

Introduce a compact developer quickstart that demonstrates staged prompt authoring with an iterative watch-mode workflow and an integrated structured-output linter. Motivation: teams authoring RAG/agent prompts need a low-friction local loop to iterate on prompt stages (context assembly, skeleton generation, tool-call gating, final formatting) while validating structured outputs against a small contract. This quickstart provides: 1) a minimal file layout with a staged prompt pipeline, 2) a watch-mode devserver that hot-reloads prompt stage files and runs fast contract checks, 3) TypeScript and Go example adapters that show tool-calling guard rails, 4) an opinionated structured-output linter (StrucLint) with example contracts and fixes, 5) devcontainer + docker-compose for reproducible local runs, and 6) lightweight telemetry presets for the Console (span tags and step timing) so teams can instrument authoring iterations. The PR includes docs and a short site integration guide so the quickstart appears under "Local authoring" in the docs site nav.

Checklist completed: - scaffolding and README - TS and Go samples - watch-mode implementation and tests - StrucLint rules and example contracts - devcontainer/devops runbook - docs landing and metadata for docs site - e2e smoke CI job (headless run)

How to try locally (summary): 1) git clone && cd quickstarts/staged-prompt-authoring 2) ./dev up (starts watch-mode + local indexer stub) 3) edit stages/*.prompt.json -> watch-mode runs lint and emits structured diffs 4) open http://localhost:4000/playground for a minimal REPL that shows intermediate stage outputs and tool-call proposals. See README for full commands and examples. This quickstart is intentionally minimal: it wires Redwood SDK calls via examples/samples.ts and examples/main.go but uses a stubbed indexer and a local in-memory tool adapter for safe local experimentation.
Evan Li (reviewer): Nice scaffolding. Two asks: (1) Add a short note about security when running local tool stubs; (2) Can the watch-mode avoid full-restart on linter-only changes?
Marisol Vega (author): Added security note in README and switched the linter to run in-process so watch-mode does not restart the server (see runner.js change).
Priya Nair (reviewer): Please include a minimal test for the StrucLint rule engine to protect against regressions.
Marisol Vega (author): Added a small mocha test (ci/smoke/struclint.test.js) that asserts contract failures emit a compact diff and exit code 2. Tests pass locally; pushed fix for a race on startup.
Tomás Rodríguez (reviewer): Docs landing looks good. One minor nit: consider a tiny screenshot in the landing page to show the REPL output.
Marisol Vega (author): Added a compact CLI screenshot and updated the landing paragraph. Ready to merge.
Evan Li (reviewer): Approving — nice iterative loop.
