title: Introduce prefill-decode concurrency harmonizer with kernel time-slicing and opportunistic KV reclaim
content:
Introduce prefill-decode concurrency harmonizer with kernel time-slicing and opportunistic KV reclaim

Summary: This PR implements a "harmonizer" layer in the serving scheduler that time-slices GPU kernel execution between prefill and decode stages, introduces microburst quotas, and adds an opportunistic KV-cache reclaim path during decode idle windows. Motivation: In mixed workloads (large prefill bursts followed by many short decodes) we observed priority inversion and tail-latency spikes when prefill kernels monopolize compute for long slices. Existing chunked-prefill and speculative prefill approaches reduce some tail effects but either increase decode stall frequency or over-fragment work. Harmonizer goal: provide deterministic, low-latency decode windows while preserving aggregate throughput by slicing long prefill kernels into bounded time quanta and reclaiming KV-cache slots opportunistically during decode-dominated micro-windows. Key changes and rationale: 1) Kernel time-slicing: the scheduler now enforces a per-kernel timeslice (default 8ms, adaptive) for prefill kernels above a configured duration threshold. Long prefill work is split into logical continuations; the runtime kernel adapter exposes a continuation token so the GPU kernel can resume without extra host-side model reinitialization cost. This reduces blocking time for decode kernels and reduces tail latency. 2) Adaptive timeslice estimator: a lightweight moving-window estimator adjusts timeslice size based on recent decode tail P95/P99 and prefill throughput. The estimator biases toward smaller slices when decode tail is increasing and toward larger slices when decode latency is healthy. 3) Microburst quotas: decode requests are granted short-run quotas (number of tokens or microseconds) that guarantee a minimum execution window before prefill resumptions. This prevents tiny decodes from being starved. 4) Opportunistic KV reclaim: when the harmonizer detects decode idle intervals inside a timeslice boundary (e.g., waiting on network/IO), the runtime performs a soft-evict hint on cold KV entries and background-prefetch low-cost priming for imminent prefill continuations. This reduces cold-KV misses when prefill resumes. 5) Metrics & observability: new metrics harmonizer.timeslice_ms, harmonizer.prefill_splits, harmonizer.decode_quota_acquired, kvcache.soft_evictions, and harmonic.prefill_continuations were added. Tracing hooks mark harmonizer decisions so we can correlate decisions with latency outcomes. 6) API/Config: exposed config knobs in runtime config: harmonizer.enabled, harmonizer.base_timeslice_ms, harmonizer.max_splits, harmonizer.decode_quota_us. These are gated behind an opt-in feature flag for staged rollout. Performance summary (internal bench): - Mixed workload (50% large prefill 50% small decodes): p99 decode latency reduced by ~12% (from 310ms to 275ms), p95 by ~9%. - Aggregate token throughput for prefill-heavy runs decreased by ~3% worst-case; in practical settings we saw throughput flat or +2% due to reduced KV thrashing. - For steady-state decode-only workloads, no measurable regressions. Compatibility and risk: The continuation token requires small changes to the kernel entry path but keeps ABI stable; fallbacks in place for older kernels (no splitting). KV soft-evict is conservative and uses a background thread with rate limits to avoid noisy eviction. Testing and rollout: Unit and integration tests added for scheduler behavior and continuation correctness. Microbench harness extended to validate timeslice adaptation. Canary rollout plan: opt-in flag -> small fleet in europe region (low RPS) -> ramp to all hosted runs over 2 weeks while monitoring new metrics and regressions. Checklist: - [x] Scheduler time-slice implementation - [x] Kernel adapter continuation token - [x] Adaptive timeslice estimator - [x] Microburst decode quota enforcement - [x] Opportunistic KV reclaim path - [x] Metrics + tracing hooks - [x] Unit/integration tests - [x] Benchmarks and perf report - [x] Feature-flag gate and config knobs Commits: (summary) - a1bf3d4: harmonizer: core scheduler loop & timeslice enforcement - c2d9e01: kernel-adapter: continuation token & split/merge helpers - e4f7ab2: kvcache: soft-evict hint and background reclaim worker - 9b2c7d1: config: harmonizer feature flags and runtime knobs - 5d7a9ef: metrics + tracing for harmonizer decisions - 3f8bd44: tests: unit and microbench harness updates - 7ea5d2c: docs: runtime config reference and migration notes Files changed (high level): - runtime/scheduler/harmonizer.cpp (new) - runtime/scheduler/harmonizer.h (new) - runtime/kernel/adapter.cc (continuation token + resume interface) - runtime/kernel/kernel_entry.S (small glue changes for continuation fast-path) - runtime/kv/soft_reclaim.cc (new) - runtime/config/feature_flags.yaml (opt-in knobs) - runtime/metrics/harmonizer_metrics.cc - tests/harmonizer_scheduler_test.cc - benchmarks/microbench/harmonizer_mixed_workload.py - docs/runtime/harmonizer.md - docs/config/runtime_flags.md - scripts/canary_rollout.md Review summary and decisions: Reviewer Ethan Zhao: "High level: this direction looks promising. Two immediate concerns: (1) contiguity of KV eviction — we must not evict hot KV while prefill is mid-continuation; (2) timeslice tuning defaults may need to vary by GPU architecture." Author reply (Nina): "Both addressed: soft-evict respects 'do-not-evict' tags set at prefill slice boundaries and rate-limits are per-GPU; added arch-weighted default table (A100=8ms, H100=10ms, V100=6ms) and config override." Reviewer Priya Sinha: "We need signal / guardrail alerts for when harmonizer is throttling prefill heavily (throughput regression)." Author response: "Added metric harmonizer.prefill_throttle_ratio and alert playbook entries in scripts/canary_rollout.md." Reviewer Marco Valdez: "Edge case: extremely long single-token prefill ( > 300ms ) — splitting might add visible overhead due to repeated kernel launches." Author: "We added a threshold to only split kernels above 32ms and a fast-resume path that avoids host-side model re-setup; microbench shows overhead < 1% for this case." CI / checks: - unit-tests: pass - integration-tests: pass - lint: initial run flagged style in harmonizer.h -> fixed - benchmarks/regression: pass (bench harness comparisons attached) - canary-sanity: pending during initial PR, green pre-merge Performance artifacts: attached benchmark output (benchmarks/microbench/results/214450-mixed.json) and flamegraph samples (benchmarks/microbench/flamegraphs/214450-prefill-slice.svg) Merge: PR was squashed and merged by Priya Sinha after CI turned green and a 48-hour canary in eu-west. Merge method: squash. Post-merge actions: - release_notes: "Add harmonizer scheduler to reduce decode tail latency in mixed prefill/decode workloads; opt-in via harmonizer.enabled; see runtime/harmonizer.md for tuning." - Incremental rollout scheduled and post-release metric dashboards created (runtime/harmonizer-dashboard). Known limitations and follow-ups: - Follow-up ENG-7612 will add model-aware timeslice (longer slices for transformer configurations that pay high resume cost). - Experiment ENG-7688 will evaluate merging harmonizer with the speculative prefill controller for further gains. Overall notes: This PR trades bounded prefill kernel slices for improved tail decode latency and steadier decode QoS. Implementation favors conservative defaults and is gated by feature flag to allow observational rollout.
Ethan Zhao: High level: this direction looks promising. Two immediate concerns: (1) contiguity of KV eviction — we must not evict hot KV while prefill is mid-continuation; (2) timeslice tuning defaults may need to vary by GPU architecture.
Nina Park: Both addressed: soft-evict respects 'do-not-evict' tags set at prefill slice boundaries and rate-limits are per-GPU; added arch-weighted default table (A100=8ms, H100=10ms, V100=6ms) and config override.
Priya Sinha: We need signal / guardrail alerts for when harmonizer is throttling prefill heavily (throughput regression).
Nina Park: Added metric harmonizer.prefill_throttle_ratio and alert playbook entries in scripts/canary_rollout.md.
Marco Valdez: Edge case: extremely long single-token prefill ( > 300ms ) — splitting might add visible overhead due to repeated kernel launches.
Nina Park: Added threshold to only split kernels above 32ms and a fast-resume path that avoids host-side model re-setup; microbench shows overhead < 1% for this case.
CI Bot: lint: style issue in harmonizer.h (fixed in c2d9e01).
Bench Reviewer: Please add a comparison vs chunked-prefill baseline; initial bench attached shows harmonizer improves p99 decode vs chunked-prefill by ~6% for our mixed scenario.
Merged via squash by Priya Sinha after canary and CI green. Feature gated behind harmonizer.enabled; docs and playbook updated.
Add harmonizer scheduler to reduce decode tail latency in mixed prefill/decode workloads. Opt-in via runtime config harmonizer.enabled. Default timeslice tuned per GPU architecture. Follow-up work planned for model-aware timeslicing.

title: Lighthouse alignment - radical transparency & Q3 priorities
content:
Lighthouse alignment - radical transparency & Q3 priorities

Company all-hands focused on Q3 operational priorities, transparency on hiring and budget, product performance investments (latency/cost tradeoffs), and security/compliance updates. Leadership introduced a new "Lighthouse" initiative to centralize strategic bets and clarified canary rollout rules. Open Q&A covered SOC2 timeline, Dedicated vs Hosted guidance for large customers, and planned changes to on-call rotation and observability dashboards.
1) Lighthouse initiative + definition of success
2) Q3 priority areas: performance, reliability, go-to-market enablement, hiring cadence
3) Budget & hiring: tradeoffs and runway considerations
4) Security & compliance: SOC2, KMS, audit logs
5) Observability improvements and developer ergonomics
6) Open Q&A
[00:00] Ava: okay hi everyone, welcome to the all hands, thanks for joining. I'm Ava. Uh today we want to be a little bit shorter than usual, 70-ish minutes, got a tight agenda.
[00:16] Marcus: hey folks, Marcus here, quick heads up — we'll go through tech highlights first then product then q&a.
[00:30] Priya: hi, team — quick update from eng: we've been dogfooding the continuous batching improvements, seeing about 12 to 18% token cost reduction on average for web traffic but — uh — not uniformly across long-form bursts. so there is more tuning to do.
[00:55] Jamal: quick context, the "Lighthouse" idea is basically to pick three strategic bets for Q3 where we concentrate product, infra, and GTM so we don't spread thin. the bets are: 1) extreme latency SLOs for interactive apps, 2) Dedicated capacity for mid-market enterprise, 3) verticalized solutions for search & customer support.
[01:18] Ava: i want to emphasize transparency — we'll publish a dashboard that shows progress on each lighthouse bet weekly. not the whole payroll but high level metrics.
[01:34] Lena: also want to call out changes to how we prioritize hiring requests — there will be a short rubric, it's about impact on lighthouse bets and critical operational risk.
[01:50] Diego: from sales, customers keep asking about dedicated vs hosted overhead and what signals should push a POC into a Reserved capacity conversation. we'll share a decision tree.
[02:08] Nora: security quick — SOC2 phase 2 kickoff is next month, KMS integration for private deployments is in design, and we will publish an FAQ for Sales and SEs.
[02:27] Samir: observability — rolling out token-level tracing in staging this week, which should make it easier to correlate latency spikes to model/version.
[02:40] Audience (mic): applause / cheers (brief)
[03:00] Ava: ok now demo highlight — Marcus, you want to show the latency profile?
[03:08] Marcus: sure; so we ran a 1,024 token tail experiment across our 80/20 load split and found that the new kernel selection reduces p95 by around 30ms for small seqs but adds about 10ms for some quantized paths. there's a trade — cost decreases, sometimes latency edges up.
[03:38] Priya: yeah there's a tradeoff matrix in the doc. the key is we can make profile-based routing pick the lower-latency path at the cost of some throughput.
[03:50] Audience question: any updates on private/on-prem customers and air-gapped installs?
[03:57] Nora: yes, we have two pilot customers for private on-prem and both have unique networking needs. the package will include a local control-plane option and KMS hooks. still early.
[04:18] Jamal: product rollout policy update — canaries will default to 10% for major model switches, with automatic fallback to previous variant on error spikes. we'll add a warmup period for KV cache priming to reduce cold-start regressions.
[04:45] Diego: on pricing, we will not change public hosted pricing this quarter but for Dedicated we are looking at more granular bundles to match mid-market patterns.
[05:00] Audience comment (murmur): "how will this affect current pilots?"
[05:05] Ava: good question — pilots shouldn't be negatively impacted; SEs will get recommended settings per pilot.
[05:12] [05:12] Marcus: quick note about kernels — some model families still show instability with the quantized path on A100 gen2 earlier this week; we rolled a patch but need a follow-up.
[05:30] [06:00] Priya: ops update — we will adjust on-call rotations to reduce pager fatigue, moving to 48 hour handoffs for infra owners and adding an extra backup on high-traffic days. feedback pls to people ops.
[06:22] [06:40] Lena: yes please fill the anonymous pulse if you are affected, we'll revise.
[07:00] Audience question: "what's runway and hiring status?"
[07:08] Ava: runway is healthy but we have to be deliberate; hiring will be prioritized for lighthouse bets and critical ops. teams must submit requests with clear impact statements.
[07:28] Diego: tying to GTM — we'll focus inbound motion for self-serve but allocate SEs for mid-market Dedicated POCs.
[07:44] [08:00] Nora: security Q — some folks asked about encryption at rest for hosted API. we already encrypt at rest and in transit; the KMS integration gives additional customer-managed key options for Dedicated/Private.
[08:20] Audience: "timeline for SOC2?"
[08:25] Nora: target is to complete Type II readiness audit by Q1 next year; phase 1 documents will be out mid-August.
[08:40] [09:00] Jamal: product clarifying — "verticalized solutions" means we will publish starter packs for search and support use-cases: prompts, evals, and quantization settings tuned per workload.
[09:20] Priya: engineering will deliver quantization recommendations and a lighter 8-bit runtime for small VMs by mid-Q3.
[09:36] Audience: "how do we measure success for lighthouse?"
[09:40] Ava: success metrics: latency p95 improvement, gross margin impact from cost reduction, number of customers on Dedicated, and number of closed-loop regressions detected by our evals.
[09:58] [10:15] Samir: observability will expose a weekly lighthouse dashboard: traffic share, p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, rollback events.
[10:30] Audience follow-up: "can we see the dashboard before public release?"
[10:35] Ava: yes leaders will get access and we'll ask for feedback.
[10:45] [11:00] Diego: sales playbook update — we'll publish a one-pager for AEs on when to recommend Dedicated and a checklist for procurement items.
[11:16] Audience question: "Any change to compensation or headcount?"
[11:22] Lena: compensation stable; headcount prioritized; we will not hire across the board.
[11:35] [12:00] Open Q&A (rapidfire):
[12:05] Employee 1: will we extend free credits for startups?
[12:08] Diego: probably yes, but with tighter qualifying signals.
[12:12] Employee 2: will the new batching change affect latency-sensitive customers?
[12:15] Marcus: we'll allow per-route overrides so sensitive customers can opt out of aggressive batching.
[12:28] Employee 3: can we have more clarity on regional capacity?
[12:32] Ava: we're expanding EU and APAC regions; details in the infra update next week.
[12:44] Employee 4 (mumble): requests for more async docs and runbooks.
[12:48] Priya: noted. docs team — we'll add sprint to backlog.
[13:05] [13:30] Final recap by Ava: recap: lighthouse bets, hiring rubric, SOC2 timeline, observability dashboard, canary policy. next steps: leadership doc next week, team leads submit resource asks, security FAQ. thanks all, meeting adjourned.
[13:50] (end)

title: Pool fallbacks and tenant throttle investigation — nightshift tactical slate
content:
Pool fallbacks and tenant throttle investigation — nightshift tactical slate

Purpose
- Capture the on-call notes and quick runbook for the 2024-10-29 evening GPU pool disruption that cascaded into route fallbacks and tenant-level throttling. This is a lightweight, tactical doc for SRE night crews; follow-up postmortem to be authored in Confluence once root cause final.

TL;DR
- 2024-10-29 ~20:40 UTC: p95 token latency for dedicated-pool-east-1 increased from 120ms -> 2.2s; internal autoscaler triggered multiple replenishments but pool offered degraded capacity (GPU kernel stalls). Traffic routing system paged fallbacks to compatible pools; fallback rate exceeded safe quota and triggered tenant-throttle rules, causing sustained client errors for some customers.
- Immediate mitigation: scaled affected pool manually to 0.8x (drain low-priority slots), disabled cross-pool fallback for 10m window, and applied short-term tenant throttle relaxation for high-SLA customers. Visible recovery by 21:12 UTC.

Impact summary
- Affected: Dedicated capacity customers on pool gamma-east-1 (approx 12 tenants).
- Symptoms: elevated request queue length, increase in model-infer errors and timeouts, surge in KV-cache miss amplification.
- Client visible: timeouts (504), transient 5xx spikes in hosted routing logs, and slowdown in streaming responses.

Detection and alerting
- First signal: p95 latency alert from /metrics/route/p95 (threshold 800ms) at 20:39:48 UTC.
- Secondary signals: allocator eviction spikes, GPU driver interrupt counts, autoscaler thrash events.
- Dashboards: gpu-pair-health, route-fallbacks, tenant-errors (see linked Grafana).

Timeline (concise)
- 20:39:48 UTC: p95 latency alert fired (oncall dispatcher -> SRE pager).
- 20:41:10 UTC: Oncall (Maya) confirmed increased queue depth and 90%+ kernel wait in pod logs.
- 20:42:05 UTC: Autoscaler attempted two scale-ups; new pods failed readiness due to driver timeouts.
- 20:45:30 UTC: Routing service started cascading fallback assignments to beta/pool-west-2. Fallback rate jumped to 320/min (normal < 30/min).
- 20:48:02 UTC: Tenant-throttle engine applied backpressure — rules triggered due to high fallback error rate. Customer support tickets begin.
- 20:50:00 UTC: Manual mitigation: disabled inter-pool fallback for gamma-east-1 -> recovery of routing state.
- 20:55:00 UTC: Began manual eviction of confirmed noisy tenant (suspected tenant id T-3401) from pool.
- 21:08:30 UTC: Queue depth falling, p95 back to ~180ms.
- 21:12:00 UTC: Traffic normalizing; keep watch for recurrence.

Initial hypotheses considered (notes)
- hypothesis A: GPU driver/firmware glitch causing stalls under specific kernel patterns. Evidence: driver interrupts spiked, and new pods failed readiness with driver timeouts.
- hypothesis B: A single tenant started heavy KV-cache-miss pattern causing cache amplification and forcing kernel work leading to eviction/thrashing. Evidence: tenant T-3401 showed 8x normal token throughput and repeated model-cache flushes.
- hypothesis C: Autoscaler hysteresis misconfiguration combined with fallback aggressiveness created a feedback loop where fallback assignments overloaded target pools. Evidence: fallback rate metric high and autoscaler logs show repeated scale events without adequate cool-down.

Triage checklist (quick, for night crews)
1) Confirm scope
   - run: curl -s "https://grafana.redwood.com/api/annotations?panelId=..." (or open gpu-pools dashboard)
   - check p95 and queue length for affected pool (gamma-east-1) and target pools.
2) Look at pod-level GPU signals
   - kubectl -n inference logs <pod> | grep -E "driver timeout|stall|KERNEL_WAIT"
   - nvidia-smi dmon (if accessible) or check prometheus: node_gpu_kernel_wait_seconds_total
   - note GPU util vs kernel-wait ratio; kernel wait > 40% is red flag.
3) Evaluate autoscaler behavior
   - check autoscaler events: kubectl -n infra describe hpa/pool-gamma-autoscaler
   - look for rapid scale in/out and short cool-down violations.
4) Routing & fallback checks
   - query route-fallback-rate metric: sum(rate(route_fallbacks_total[1m])) by pool
   - if >100/min, consider temporary fallback disable for affected pool.
5) Tenant isolation
   - identify tenants with >3x baseline request rate (metric: tenant_request_rate)
   - if identified, note tenant ID and consider immediate eviction/soft-throttle.

Immediate remediation playbook (fast-mode)
- Priority order: (1) stabilize routing and avoid amplifying fallback loops, (2) isolate candidate noisy tenants, (3) reduce pool pressure by draining lower-priority workloads.
Steps: 
1) Disable inter-pool fallback for impacted pool (one-liner):
   - curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN" https://routing.internal/api/v1/pools/gamma-east-1/fallbacks/disable
   - (This prevents cascade until pool health restored)
2) Relax tenant-throttle for high-SLA tenants only (temporary):
   - POST to throttle config with safe window and revert timer 15m.
3) Evict identified noisy tenant(s):
   - mark tenant T-XXXX as low-priority -> drain from pool via placement-api
   - run: placementctl evict --tenant T-3401 --pool gamma-east-1 --reason "noisy-amplification-night"
4) If driver stalls persist, cordon affected nodes and rotate GPU nodes through maintenance image rollback (see infra runbook).

Actions taken during incident (what we did)
- Disabled inter-pool fallback at 20:50 UTC.
- Evicted tenant T-3401 at 20:55 UTC and observed immediate queue depth improvement.
- Relaxed throttle for top 3 SLA tenants for 15m to avoid customer impact.
- Opened emergency support ticket with GPU host vendor (case #VND-112233) due to driver interrupt patterns.

Data collected / artifacts
- pod logs archived: s3://redwood-ops/incident-2024-10-29/gamma-logs.tar.gz
- grafana snapshots linked in linked_artifacts above
- coredumps (if any) uploaded to artifacts bucket and referenced in JIRA-RED-9876

Follow-ups / remediation backlog (short-term)
- Revisit autoscaler cool-down and hysteresis: increase stabilization window from 30s -> 120s for dedicated pools (owner: Omar).
- Adjust fallback aggressiveness: cap fallback-rate per-minute to 50 and add exponential backoff (owner: Priya).
- Add an automated detection for kernel-wait > 30% triggers temporary routing quarantine (owner: SRE-runbook team).
- Confirm driver/firmware upgrade plan with infra and vendor and schedule a canary (owner: Alex).

Longer-term ideas to prevent recurrence
- Implement tenant scoring for KV-cache miss amplification and proactively throttle before eviction.
- Build a routing-simulator to validate fallback policies under noisy-tenant scenarios.
- Create an autoscaler simulator that runs against recorded traffic traces to reveal hysteresis misconfigurations.

Open questions (need engineering input)
- Exact root cause of driver interrupts: firmware bug vs load pattern. Vendor input pending.
- Was eviction of T-3401 an appropriate mitigation or would soft-throttle been sufficient? (data needed: request replay & model call profile).
- Do fallback limits break expected multi-region failover SLAs for Dedicated customers? Need product alignment.

Retrospective quick notes (for the eventual postmortem)
- The outage was a compound event: hardware/driver instability amplified by aggressive fallback policy + autoscaler hysteresis. Single fix likely insufficient; need layered mitigations.
- Night crew response: > good, manual mitigations applied quickly but several actions lacked automation (disable-fallback, tenant-evict) that could be scripted.

Immediate next steps (this doc owner)
- Draft formal postmortem on Confluence (link placeholder) — due 2024-11-09.
- Assign autoscaler and fallback follow-ups in JIRA-RED-9876 before end of week.
- Schedule vendor call (Alex) to review driver logs and coordinate canary.

Notes to self / shorthand (nightshift)
- If you see kernel-wait spike + fallback rate rising -> hit fallback disable early.
- Evict only when you have telemetry showing tenant >3x baseline sustained >2m.
- After mitigation, leave a 30m watch window and capture histograms at 1s resolution.

Appendix: quick command cheats
- Check fallback rate: curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(route_fallbacks_total[1m])) by (pool)" | jq
- Identify hot tenants: curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/v1/query?query=topk(10, sum(rate(tenant_requests_total[1m])) by (tenant))"
- Evict: placementctl evict --tenant T-3401 --pool gamma-east-1 --force --reason "noisy-night-evict"

-- end of notes --

title: Helix strategy and ops deconflict
content:
Helix strategy and ops deconflict

Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-04-18
Start: 10:00 PT
Duration: ~74 minutes
Location: Zoom - company all-hands
Attendees: Elena Park, Marco Alvarez, Priya Desai, Samir Khan, Lina Torres, plus open Q&A from company

Summary:
- Leadership reviewed "helix" initiative (cross-functional push to tighten product/ops cadence).
- Discussed recent incident, reliability mitigations, and tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted routing.
- Agreed on hiring priorities and a conservative rollout plan for canary/traffic shaping.
- Next steps: prioritized action items for product, infra, and people.

Topics covered:
- Helix initiative overview and desired outcomes
- Incident review highlights and short/medium term mitigations
- Cost control: batching, quantization, region routing, dedicated pools
- Hiring cadence and org resourcing
- Customer & enterprise posture: SOC 2 timing, audit log retention

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Elena Park (CEO): Hey everybody, good morning, thanks for joining our helix update, we'll keep it tight, we got a lot to cover and then open q and a. um Marco, quick microstate of infra?
[00:18] Marco Alvarez (CTO): yeah, morning. so we've been tracking that spike last week, the incident, turns out it was a combo of an autoscaler bug and a kernel selection mismatch on the newest gpu nodes, uh, and that caused very uneven tail latency, and then a the fallback routing didn't kick fast enough.
[00:35] Speaker 4 (Engineering lead - Samir): to add, the KV cash — sorry, KV cache priming logic was racing with the cold starts, so lots of cache misses when we hit long sequences, so token costs spiked.
[00:50] Elena: ok, that's the gist. i'm hoping we can walk through short-term mitigations first, then product priorities. Priya?
[01:02] Priya Desai (Head of Product): yeael, so helix is meant to be the cross-team cadence — product builds, infra optimizations, and ops guardrails. high level targets: reduce P99 latency by 20%, keep per-token costs flat, and cut incident recovery time in half by Q3. those are our north stars.
[01:25] [01:25] Lina Torres (Head of People): and tangentially hiring: we need to line up three infra senior ICs and two SREs by end of Q2 to hit these numbers, otherwise we won't make the throughput work without cost overruns.
[01:40] Marco: yea the capacity plan is tight, and our vendor quotes for extra reserved capacity are... not great, so we need to balance dedicated pools versus smarter routing.
[01:54] [01:54] Audience Question (Speaker X): hi could you clarify what dedicated pools mean for existing hosted customers, any pricing changes?
[02:03] Elena: good question — in short, dedicated is reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput, it's opt-in for enterprise customers, pricing considered as a monthly commit. won't change hosted pricing for existing users. we'll send a short FAQ later.
[02:20] Priya: also important, for helix we want more canary control: traffic shaping by region, by tenant tier, and automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if latency SLOs break.
[02:38] Marco: the automatic fallback needs to be model-aware though; not every variant has the same function-calling or structured-output behavior, so we'll need compatibility checks. some of the autogen tests failed because of that.
[02:56] Samir: yes and there's a product-quality tradeoff — fallback to a quantized 8-bit variant gives cost savings but sometimes the hallucination rate nudges up, which our evals catch but customers might see.
[03:13] Elena: we need to balance unit economics with trust metrics. Priya, keep eval thresholds tight.
[03:21] Priya: noted.
[03:24] [03:24] Marco: quick point on the incident root cause: the new kernel selector we pushed assumes consistent sequence length distribution. during a customer experiment, sequence lengths skewed long and that pushed a codepath we hadn't exercised in staging. staging datasets didn't cover the churn.
[03:42] Speaker 7 (Product PM): so we should expand staging replay and add stress tests for long sequence tails, yes?
[03:48] Marco: exactly. we'll add a sequence-tail stress harness.
[03:51] [04:00] Audience (Volunteer): will this affect the private deploys and VPC customers?
[04:06] Samir: private customers are on a different upgrade cadence, but the same runtime code flows. for private we can schedule staggered upgrades and extra canaries since they control their infra. the main worry is the private on-prem customers that are air-gapped — their kernel backports take longer.
[04:25] Elena: we'll capture those timelines separately with CSMs.
[04:28] [04:30] Lina: hiring note — compensation for the infra hires is tight, we've got to move offers by May 3rd to meet joiners in June. otherwise Q3 headcount will slip.
[04:43] Priya: on product roadmap, the helix MVP is three features: 1) traffic shaping UI in console, 2) explicit model-variant compatibility checks, 3) improved rollout telemetry and tracing per request. those are our first deliverables.
[05:03] Marco: on telemetry, we need token-level tracing that ties back to route config and to the KV priming state. right now traces are coarse.
[05:13] Samir: that telemetry will also let us tune batching better — we can identify request shapes that benefit from bigger batch windows. bigger batches reduce cost but up latency for short requests; so routing rules need to be aware.
[05:30] [05:30] Audience (Q): do we have new SOC 2 timelines?
[05:35] Elena: good timing — audit kickoff is next month, target completion end of Q3. Lina and security will share specifics. we'll publish an FAQ.
[05:44] Lina: security readiness is in parallel; we have two key gaps: long-term log retention policy and more formal RBAC in the console. both are on the board for May sprints.
[05:57] [05:57] Priya: quick product concern — if we enforce stricter RBAC it may change how we do customer-level rollouts for early access features. need product and security handshake.
[06:09] Marco: yes, and for the canary we need a fallback policy that prioritizes continuity over feature parity — meaning if a canary fails we keep customers online on last-known-good model variant.
[06:22] Samir: on the ops side, the short term mitigation is to revert the autoscaler change for the hot path and add safer thresholds; medium term is to revamp our kernel selector testing and expand mix of real traffic in staging.
[06:36] [06:36] Audience: any customer impact notices sent?
[06:40] Elena: we sent a brief to affected customers with a high-level postmortem and said we were executing mitigations. follow-up will include a more detailed postmortem and timelines.
[06:50] [07:00] Priya: ok timeline for helix: sprints 1-2 (2 weeks) finish telemetry and canary control, sprints 3-4 (4 more weeks) ship console UI and rollout compatibility checks. we want an internal canary by mid-May and public canary in late May if hiring and infra align.
[07:18] Marco: about cost optimization — two levers: smarter batching and model quantization recommendations surfaced in console. the Optimize toolkit will suggest quantization profiles and batching windows per route. we should be careful: not all models are safe at 4-bit, and we need evals for each customer workload.
[07:36] Samir: that said, we can start with non-critical tenants for aggressive quantization to get baseline numbers.
[07:45] [07:50] Audience (Question): are we changing pricing for embeddings?
[07:55] Elena: not today. any pricing adjustments would come with clear customer comms; our priority is stability and predictable unit economics.
[08:05] [08:10] Priya: a small but important ask: product will need example prompts and eval criteria from sales and solutions so our regression alerts are meaningful — please send the top 10 prompt sets by next Tuesday.
[08:24] Lina: people update — org health looks good in most teams but infra is stretched. hiring freeze lifted for critical roles; recruiters will prioritize infra and SRE. also we want to remind managers about offer flexibility for counteroffers.
[08:42] [08:45] Audience: are we going to centralize the benchmark sheets?
[08:49] Marco: yes, a single benchmark spreadsheet will be the source of truth; infra will own it with read perms broadly but edit perms limited. we'll put it in the shared drive and link in the console docs.
[08:59] Samir: action on incident owner mapping: we'll publish a runbook with clear owners for autoscale, kernel selection, and KV priming.
[09:10] [09:10] Priya: ok let's take live questions.
[09:15] Audience Q1: will this change our roadmap for Dedicated customers?
[09:20] Marco: Dedicated still gets priority for capacity; any region routing changes will be backwards compatible. Dedicated customers can still pin versions and we will offer a rollback window.
[09:31] Audience Q2: what's the customer-facing SLA change?
[09:35] Elena: no SLA change today; we will only adjust SLAs with clear product and infra readiness and after legal signs off.
[09:44] Audience Q3: can we get an incident dashboard?
[09:50] Samir: yes, we will publish an internal incident dashboard and a high-level customer-facing timeline for affected customers.
[10:00] [10:00] Elena: brief recap — Priya product plan and eval thresholds; Samir postmortem and runbook; Marco hardware/cost review; Lina hiring and offers. big ask: leaders to empower their teams to escalate when telemetry shows odd tails.
[10:18] Marco: last thing, competitor note: BigCloudAI rolled out a cheaper dedicated option last month; their fallback behavior isn't as mature as ours but their price looks aggressive. watch for sales objections and we'll prepare battlecards.
[10:33] Priya: and FastServe is pushing a private-edge pitch in EMEA, we should coordinate partner messaging.
[10:40] Elena: alright, thanks everyone. we'll post slides and the canary plan. meeting closed.

Post-meeting notes:
- Slides: link (internal) - "Helix initiative overview and canary plan"
- Shared artifacts: incident summary (link), benchmark spreadsheet (link), hiring slate (link).

title: Control plane decomposition & regional routing playbook
content:
Control plane decomposition & regional routing playbook

Purpose:
This is a working playbook sketch to clarify service boundaries for the control plane components we own, and to capture a regional routing decision model people can copy into RFCs and runbooks. Focus: API gateway responsibilities, orchestration (control-plane core), runtime adapters (GPU/CPU pools), and how ownership shifts when we run multi-region.

High-level service decomposition (intended):
- API gateway (edge team): ingress, auth, tenant scoping, initial request validation, short-circuiting (rate limits, quota), and primary routing hints (region preference, model / variant selector). Not responsible for model compatibility checks beyond surface level (e.g., model id exists).
- Orchestration / Control-plane core (platform-engineering): policy evaluation, placement decision, global state (capacity map), rollout policies, deployment metadata, canary logic, route fallbacks and A/B selection. Exposes policy API consumed by gateway and autoscaler.
- Runtime adapters (serving-runtime interface): translate placement decisions into concrete fleet operations (allocate GPU slot, pin model binary, configure quantization profile). Responsible for per-cluster capacity accounting and local health signals.
- SRE / Observability: owns incident runbooks, cross-region outage detection, and the tracing/metric dashboards; collaborates on SLA targets for each component.

Routing decision model (step-by-step):
1) Gateway receives request -> extracts tenant & model intent + optional region hint. Apply auth & quota.
2) Gateway requests placement from orchestration service with (tenant, model, region_hint, latency_slo, cost_tier).
3) Orchestration evaluates:
   - Preferred region availability (capacity map)
   - Latency SLO vs estimated p99 for candidate clusters
   - Cost tier (e.g., on-demand vs reserved)
   - Canary/rollout policy binding for tenant/model
   - Model compatibility (via model metadata cached from model catalog service)
   - Fallback rules (force cross-region if no compatible capacity)
4) Orchestration returns route: {target_cluster, adapter_endpoint, expected_latency_ms, fallback_list}.
5) Gateway forwards request to runtime adapter endpoint. If adapter rejects (capacity/health), gateway retries orchestration for next fallback.

Region-aware ownership rules (practical callouts):
- Gateway must be region-aware but stateless in terms of global policy (does not hold authoritative capacity map).
- Orchestration is authoritative for capacity/rollout but must tolerate eventual consistency; ownership includes sharding logic for regional caches and a single leader for write operations (per-region leader + global coordinator).
- Runtime adapters own local health + exact placement operations; they must expose a stable contract (health, tokenized lease, eviction reasons).

Failure scenarios & responsibilities (who acts first):
- Regional control-plane control-loss (leader unresponsive): orchestration should promote standby leader; gateway should consult regional fallback list and route to next region. SRE triggers incident and capacity borrowing.
- Adapter-level eviction (OOM / model crash): adapter emits structured event -> orchestration marks slot unhealthy and triggers reschedule; gateway retries with adapter-suggested fallback.
- Model rollout causing regression across region: orchestration can globally pause rollout and trigger global rollback; rollback owner: product + platform-engineering to coordinate.

Operational boundaries (TL;DR ownership matrix):
- Auth & quotas: API gateway (policy enforcement), but quota counters replicated to orchestration for global quotas.
- Routing decision (final): Orchestration returns canonical route; gateway executes.
- Telemetry ownership: adapters emit raw metrics; orchestration normalizes and tags; observability owns storage/alerts.

Design constraints & rationale (why split this way):
- Keep gateway lightweight & horizontally scalable; avoid embedding long-running policy logic to minimize cold-start surface.
- Centralize policy in orchestration so we can evolve rollout semantics without changing gateway code across many languages.
- Let adapters be the narrow hardware-specific translation layer so new hardware types (e.g., future accelerators) only need adapter changes.

Practical runbook snippets (to copy into ops docs):
- "If region X reports >30% slot error rate for >5m, mark as degraded, remove from primary routing, and notify SRE. Orchestration will drain canary traffic automatically"
- "When promoting regional leader: validate global state snapshot is less than 2m behind; otherwise run snapshot catchup job."

Open questions / TODOs (working list):
- How much policy should live in gateway for fast failover vs. central orchestration latency? (tradeoff: fail-fast vs single source of truth)
- Exact schema for orchestration's fallback_list (should include cost delta and estimated added latency).
- Lease TTL semantics between orchestration and adapters (currently prototyped in PLAT-4121).
- Cross-region data compliance hooks: add a flag in routing response that the gateway logs for audit (GDPR/Paid-region tenants).

Action items (next 3 sprints):
- Sprint A: finalize fallback_list schema + update gateway client (Ethan).
- Sprint B: implement adapter lease TTL enforcement and eviction reason codes (Raj).
- Sprint C: run chaos experiment that kills regional leader and validate fallback behavior (SRE + Platform).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally informal; please annotate sections you want formalized into an RFC. Link any relevant Jira tickets into the TODOs above.

Slack refs / historical context:
- See slack thread: #platform-arch "regional routing sketch" (Nov 2025) for early whiteboard screenshots.
- Prototype work lives in repo: control-plane/placement-v2 (PR linked above).

End.

title: correlated-load-generator-with-e2e-telemetry-export
content:
correlated-load-generator-with-e2e-telemetry-export

Motivation: existing workload runners cover independent request streams (single-sequence throughput, sequence-mix) but do not model correlated cross-stream load spikes that occur in production (e.g., user action fanout, background sync overlapping with foreground traffic). This PR introduces a correlated-load generator harness plus an end-to-end telemetry export pipeline to capture cross-stream latency, queue-growth, and synchronization metrics so that downstream analysis and reporting can reason about tail behavior caused by inter-stream contention. Key deliverables: 1) bench/correlated_runner.py - a new runner that models N interdependent streams with configurable correlation matrices, jitter, and fanout; 2) telemetry/otel_exporter.py - lightweight OTel exporter that emits per-request attributes, cross-stream correlation IDs, and histogram buckets; 3) reporting/cross_stream_reporter.py - post-run aggregator that computes cross_stream_p50/p95/p99, queue_peak_avg, backlog_area (integral of queue length over time), and produces CSV + NDJSON outputs for the existing reporting pipeline; 4) integration test harness (tests/integration/test_correlated_end_to_end.py) that runs the runner against the model stub and asserts telemetry invariants; 5) CI workflow update to run the correlated workload in a short smoke mode on PRs. Design notes: the runner uses event-driven scheduling (asyncio) with a central correlation controller that injects synthetic causality between streams; correlation is parameterized as a matrix of probabilities (float in [0,1]) that governs whether an event in stream A triggers related events in stream B within a time window. Telemetry uses OpenTelemetry traces + custom metric instruments; to avoid high cardinality, correlation IDs are hashed to a bounded dimension and we export representative sample traces at a 1/100 sampling rate in CI mode. Backwards compatibility: the runner is opt-in for the lab (not enabled by default), uses existing bench runner interfaces, and integrates with current reporting consumers. Checklist: [x] add correlated runner and unit tests; [x] add OTel exporter with config; [x] add reporting aggregator and CSV/NDJSON writer; [x] add integration smoke test; [x] update CI workflow; [x] document config knobs (README). Known limitations and future work: higher-fidelity user models (session state), long-running persistence of correlation IDs to simulate multi-minute flows, and a telemetry ingest sidecar for high-throughput on-prem runs. Impact: enables reproducible stress tests for cross-stream tail behavior and provides structured outputs for the dashboarding team to add cross-stream charts.
Priya Narang: This looks useful for the tail investigations we've been missing. Two asks: make the sampling deterministic for CI (so snapshots are reproducible) and add an option to throttle exported telemetry to avoid CI timeouts.
Daniel Chen: Added seed parameter (utils/seed_helper.py) and a --ci-fast-sample flag that reduces sampling to 1/100 for PR runs. Updated tests to assert deterministic outputs when seed is fixed.
Ethan Walker: Can the runner blow up memory if correlation fanout is high? Suggest add a hard cap on queued derived events and emit backlog alerts so the reporter can detect overloads.
Daniel Chen: Implemented queue cap (configurable) and backlog_area metric. Added an integration assertion that backlog_area stays below a threshold in smoke mode. Also added a unit test for queue cap behaviour.
Lena Fischer: Minor: prefer snake_case in metric names and include unit labels (ms) for latency histograms. Also asked to include a short example in docs showing how to reproduce a 5-stream correlated spike.
Daniel Chen: Updated metric names to cross_stream_p95_ms, cross_stream_p99_ms, and included example run command in docs/bench/correlated.md.
Add correlated workload runner and end-to-end telemetry exporter for cross-stream tail analysis. Includes reporting aggregator and CI smoke tests. This enables reproducible correlated spike tests and CSV/NDJSON outputs for dashboards.
Testing guidance: run `python -m bench.correlated_runner --config examples/correlated_small.yaml --ci-fast-sample` for a quick smoke run.
Backward compatibility: default behavior unchanged for existing runners; correlated runner is opt-in.
Follow-ups: add a Jupyter notebook that visualizes backlog_area over time and integrate with perf-canary dashboards.

title: Streaming tool/function output tokens billed on final invoice despite console estimate showing zero
content:
Streaming tool/function output tokens billed on final invoice despite console estimate showing zero

Issue summary: Customer reports that streaming requests which include function/tool calls produced console estimates showing 0 tool-output tokens (console estimate column), but the finalized invoice contains token charges attributed to the tool outputs. Impact: LexiHealth reports a $9,200 unexpected charge on their monthly invoice tied to streamed sessions that used function calls for structured data retrieval. Environment: Production, us-east-1, enterprise account with reserved capacity and hosted fallback enabled. This affects streaming chat endpoints where the model returns tool invocations (function calls) and the tool outputs are streamed back as separate chunks.

Expected behavior: Console and estimate API should include a consistent token estimate for tool outputs (either zero if non-billable or the same token estimate used for invoice attribution). Final invoice should not introduce previously-unestimated token charges for tool outputs.

Actual behavior: Console estimate showed zero tool-output tokens for ~1.5M tokens across all tool invocations during the billing window. Final invoice shows ~1.45M billed tokens under a line labeled "tool-invoke-output" with reserved-rate fallback applied.

Customer impact: Revenue-impacting billing dispute, customer is holding renewal request pending resolution.

Attachments: Customer provided sample request IDs and screenshot of console estimate vs invoice lines.

1) Use a streaming chat request to /v1/chat/stream with function_call enabled
2) Have the model return a function call and stream the tool output as separate chunks using the streaming protocol
3) Observe console estimate and /v1/estimates endpoint showing tool-output token count = 0 for these sessions
4) After billing cycle finalization, inspect invoice line items and see billed tokens attributed to 'tool-invoke-output' with nonzero count
Customer provided request ids: p-req-20260301-7a1, p-req-20260304-2f3, p-req-20260307-9b0
Gateway logs (sample): 2026-03-01T14:12:07Z TRACE request p-req-20260301-7a1 stream chunk tool-output bytes=12456 tokens=478
Estimate API sample response (for p-req-20260301-7a1): {"model":"gptx-8k", "estimated_tokens": {"prompt": 512, "completion": 1200, "tool_output": 0}}
Billing postback shows: line_item id li-202603-lexi-tool-output tokens=1450000 rate=hosted-reserve-fallback
03-10 10:15 - Support: validated customer provided request IDs and fetched gateway traces; traces show tokenized counts at gateway level for tool-output chunks.

03-11 09:02 - Billing team: finalizer job uses ingestion of gateway token events (event-sourced) and included tool-output token events; rate applied based on route at time-of-execution and account fallback settings.
03-11 13:45 - Correlation: estimator uses preflight cost model which receives only model-internal token counts and not post-hook tool-output tokens; billing uses the event stream that includes tool-output tokens emitted after model completion.
03-11 16:00 - Engineering produced a reproducer: streaming tool-output emitted via external adapter produced an extra event with tokens but was not surfaced to estimator API.
03-12 08:20 - Confirmed scope: affects streaming sessions with function_call mode where tool outputs are generated by external adapters and streamed as separate events. Non-streamed (batch) tool outputs are estimated correctly.
2026-03-10 11:04 - Support (Ava Chen): Thanks for the info. We've pulled the gateway traces and escalated to metering and billing. We'll update within 48 hours.
2026-03-11 09:25 - Metering (Rajat Singh): Reproducer created. The estimate pipeline currently subscribes to model tokenizer events; tool-output events are emitted on a different topic 'tool-stream' and are not included in estimate aggregation. Working on a patch to include tool-stream token counts in estimates.

2026-03-12 12:10 - Support (Liam O'Keefe): Ack. Metering has a PR queued (see related_github_prs). Billing team proposed provisional credit; preparing credit memo draft for $9,200 pending sign-off. Next update EOD 2026-03-12.
Provisionally crediting the billed tool-output tokens for the March cycle pending a permanent fix to the estimator. Engineering to land estimator subscription change to include 'tool-stream' events and add an integration test verifying console estimates match billed events for streaming tool outputs. title: Cross-model embedding format incompatibility causing rerank queue buildup and degraded latency
content:
Cross-model embedding format incompatibility causing rerank queue buildup and degraded latency

Issue summary: Customer ClearSight reports that calls to the /v1/rerank endpoint started experiencing long tail latency and queueing beginning 2026-03-10 08:30 UTC. The rerank results also show quality regressions (unexpected ordering) when the customer mixes vectors produced by two different embedding variants in the same request.

Impact: Intermittent timeouts from the customer's service (503/504), increased 95th/99th percentile latency for rerank API in us-west, and customer-facing throughput drops. Several high-volume requests queued, causing rate-limit-like behavior and triggering their dedicated capacity autoscale.

Environment: Dedicated tenant (ClearSight) on prod:us-west using a mix of embed-lite-v2 (512 dims, L2-normalized) and embed-highdim-2025 (1024 dims, raw float) produced by their pipeline. Rerank service is expected to accept homogeneous vectors but did not validate dims in upstream request layer.

Steps to reproduce:
- Construct two embedding arrays: one from embed-lite-v2 (shape N x 512, l2-normalized) and one from embed-highdim-2025 (shape N x 1024, raw).
- Send a single /v1/rerank request containing a candidate list where some candidates include 512-d vectors and others include 1024-d vectors (no explicit embedding_version header).
- Observe immediate enqueuing and a sharp latency increase for that request ID (~>5s p99), occasionally resulting in 503 or rerank returning lower-quality ordering.

Observed logs: Trace IDs: rnk-20260310-8a4f, rnk-20260310-8b11. Error snippets show the rerank evaluator logging "embedding dim mismatch - implicit upcast" and downstream trace showing fallback to CPU quant path. Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rerank/us-west?panelId=7&from=2026-03-10T08:00:00Z&to=2026-03-10T09:00:00Z. Slack thread: #support (thread ts 1700003000.002200).
Generate 512-d L2-normalized embeddings (embed-lite-v2)
Generate 1024-d raw embeddings (embed-highdim-2025)
Combine both types in a single /v1/rerank request payload without embedding_version headers
Send to customer's dedicated endpoint in us-west and observe latency and ordering
2026-03-10T08:34:12Z rnk-20260310-8a4f rerank WARN embedding dim mismatch - implicit upcast
2026-03-10T08:34:13Z rnk-20260310-8a4f rerank INFO fallback to cpu-quant path, estimated token cost +1.9x
2026-03-10T08:34:14Z api-gateway 429 upstream queue depth exceeded for tenant clearsight
2026-03-10 09:02 - Ava Martinez (Support): Acknowledged customer report, requested sample payload and trace IDs. Asked for exact model variants and whether any normalization was applied client-side.
2026-03-10 09:20 - Customer (ClearSight - S. Patel): Provided sample payloads and confirmed the two models above; they said their ingestion pipeline accidentally stitched outputs during a rollout and didn't set embedding_version headers.
2026-03-10 11:05 - Ravi Shah (SRE): Observed sharp p99 increase aligned with trace IDs; rerank service allowed mixed-dim vectors and triggered a slow conversion in the scoring path. Filed INT-4012 to track an internal validation fix.
2026-03-11 07:18 - Eng (L. Chen): Root cause identified: upstream request validator omitted embedding dimension validation when a mixed candidate list is present. Implicit handling attempted to upcast 512->1024 and call into CPU fallback for several heavy kernels, causing latency spike. Created PR #1287 to add strict validation + syntactic hinting for embedding_version header.
2026-03-11 14:30 - Support (A. Martinez): Communicated temporary workaround to customer: ensure homogeneous embedding dims per request or include embedding_version header; If mixing is unavoidable, pad 512-d vectors with zeros to match 1024 length as a short-term mitigation.
2026-03-12 03:05 - Ravi Shah (SRE): Hotfix deployed to prod: validator now rejects mixed-dim requests with clear 400 response and guidance. Gradual rollout completed across us-west. Monitoring shows p99 latency back to baseline.
2026-03-12 10:00 - Customer (S. Patel): Confirmed issue resolved from their perspective; no further timeouts observed in last 24h and quality returned to expected ordering.
Checked Grafana: rerank queue depth spiked at 08:34 UTC, correlated with increase in cpu pathway calls (serving-runtime cpu_binder).
Heap/CPU profiles captured for one trace showed expensive memcpy and zero-padding steps executed under request lock while scoring ran on CPU vector kernels.
Hypothesis: absence of embedding_version header + mixing dims caused system to try compatibility conversion; conversion fallback path is not gated by timeout and increased latency drastically under concurrency.
Confirmed that prior safety check for vector length exists at model-serving layer but the rerank preprocessor path bypassed it during a historical refactor (see commit 6a2f8b3).
Related PR adding strict dims check and clear error messages: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rerank-service/pull/1287
Related internal ticket: INT-4012 for adding e2e tests and SDK validation helpers.
Deployed a validator that rejects mixed-dimension embedding lists with an informative 400 response explaining expected dims and embedding_version header format. Back-ported a short-circuit to avoid implicit upcast/conversion on hot paths. Created SDK guidance and sample code for ClearSight and added an integration test asserting consistent dims. Customer confirmed resolution. Action items: (1) Add automatic recommend-converter utility for customers who need cross-model compatibility; (2) Add telemetry to count mixed-dim attempts and trigger early alerts; (3) Update runbook with exact error messages and workaround steps.
Create conversion utility RFC (owner: L. Chen)
Add mixed-dim detector alert to PagerDuty playbook (owner: Ravi Shah)
Ship SDK helper that fails fast with clear error for mixed dims (owner: Developer Experience)
Customer-facing note provided: 'We temporarily observed elevated rerank latencies when mixing embeddings from different model families. The service now returns a clear error for mixed-dimension requests and we provided migration steps. We apologize for the disruption and are working on an automated converter for mixed workloads.'

title: Clarify operator rights and audit evidence for on-prem pilot
content:
Clarify operator rights and audit evidence for on-prem pilot

From: Sandra Lopez <slopez@acmehealth.com>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
Cc: Procurement Team <procurement@acmehealth.com>
Date: Wed, 4 Aug 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Clarify operator rights and audit evidence for on-prem pilot

Hi Jonas,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Procurement and our security team ran through the draft MSA and the proposed on‑prem pilot language and have two blocks they need clarified before we can sign the Order Form:

- What exact "operator" rights are we licensing for the pilot? Our auditors need a clear boundary (no access to PHI outside the VPC, no remote exec without approval).
- For the audit window (Q3 internal SOC prep), we need evidence that operator access is controlled and auditable — examples they asked for: timestamped operator logs, an immutably signed snapshot of the deployed model + runtime configuration, and an attestation from Redwood that operator keys were rotated after evidence delivery.

Can you point us to an evidence delivery workflow you can commit to, or an alternative approach (e.g., encrypted snapshot to customer S3 + attestation letter)? Also need to know if the MSA/addendum needs changes to license scope to reflect split operator responsibilities during pilot vs. production.

Attached: acme_evidence_req.pdf (list of auditor asks).

Looking to get this to legal by Friday; can you confirm next steps?

Thanks,
Sandra
Sandra Lopez
Head of Security Operations, Acme Health
"Sandra Lopez" signature

-----
From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
To: Sandra Lopez <slopez@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 4 Aug 2027 11:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Clarify operator rights and audit evidence for on-prem pilot

Hi Sandra,

Really appreciate the level of detail — totally reasonable asks. High level options we typically propose for pilots to address auditor requirements:

1) Remote-limited operator (no exec, monitoring-only): Redwood operators have monitoring and read-only metrics access. Evidence: access logs + role-based session logs.
2) Split-ops handover (preferred for customers who want control): deliver encrypted snapshot of model runtime and KV state to customer-controlled storage together with an attestation letter. Operator credentials provided only to named admins for a limited handover window; keys rotated afterwards. Evidence: signed snapshot hash, rotation confirmation, operator access audit trail.
3) Full customer-controlled operator (on-prem handoff): Redwood performs initial install support, then we hand over operator credentials to customer SOC; Redwood commits to a support SLA but not continuous access. Evidence: delivery confirmation + runbook and support tickets.

title: Stuck canary state and version pinning: timeline, root cause, and remediation
content:
Stuck canary state and version pinning: timeline, root cause, and remediation

A model rollout entered a stuck canary state due to an interplay between version pinning and the rollback handler; resulting in residual traffic to the canary and degraded throughput for pinned customers. This ticket tracks the timeline, root cause analysis, and concrete action items to prevent recurrence.
Between 2026-03-02 07:40 and 2026-03-02 09:20 UTC ~15% of production requests to the europe-west1 region were routed to a pinned canary variant that had degraded tokenization performance. Observed effects: 5-10% tail latency increase for affected tenants, error rates for long-sequence generation increased from 0.2% to 1.6%. Two enterprise customers reported degraded response times; no data exfiltration or model output integrity issues identified.
2026-03-02 07:36 UTC - Automated rollout to model-v2-canary begins
2026-03-02 07:40 UTC - Canary healthcheck shows elevated decode latency (alerts fired to SRE)
2026-03-02 07:48 UTC - Rollout controller observes metric regressions and initiates automated rollback
2026-03-02 07:49 UTC - Rollback API call returns 202 accepted but subsequent routing update fails intermittently due to rate-limited control-plane write (cp-worker-3)
2026-03-02 07:50-08:05 UTC - Partial rollback: control-plane applied routing table update for 80% of nodes; remaining 20% retained pin flag in canary_state table
2026-03-02 08:08 UTC - Autoscaler sees unusual connection patterns and scales pools conservatively, amplifying degraded tail latency
2026-03-02 08:18 UTC - On-call manually forces canary unpin (routing-matrix v2 API) and triggers a cleanup job; traffic returns to expected distribution by 08:22 UTC
2026-03-02 09:00 UTC - Post-incident triage call; decision to open this follow-up ticket for long-term fixes
Two contributing defects aligned: 1) The version-pin API writes were not fully idempotent under partial failures: rollback flow assumed the routing-matrix update would be atomic across control-plane shards but control-plane uses eventual convergence and the cp-worker component was rate-limited, leaving stale entries in the canary_state table. 2) The rollout guardrails did not validate global route convergence post-rollback: the canary lived in a half-committed state with pin=true in ~20% of nodes which continued to accept A/B routing binds. The combination allowed residual client sessions and sticky routing to persist to the degraded canary.
Alerts: infra.alerts#latency-tail, rollout.alerts#canary-regression. Customer reports via support noting slow responses. Grafana anomaly detection flagged increased 95th/99th percentile decode time for model-v2-canary. Incident created from paging and support escalation.
Immediate mitigations performed: 1) Manual unpin via routing-matrix v2 API and forced sync job (control-plane job cp-20260302-07) to reconcile canary_state across shards. 2) Temporarily increased capacity in europe-west1 to absorb backlog and reduce tail latency. 3) Short-term rollout freeze for model-v2 variants until follow-ups are implemented.
OWNER: Diego Morales - Implement a post-rollback convergence check that verifies routing-matrix entries across all control-plane shards before marking rollback complete. ETA: 2026-03-18
OWNER: Claire Ng - Add end-to-end test to the rollout pipeline that simulates partial control-plane failures and validates idempotent unpin semantics. ETA: 2026-03-15
OWNER: SRE Team - Add Grafana dashboard panel (rollout.convergence) that shows live shard-level pin counts and a Prometheus metric for 'stale_pin_count'. ETA: 2026-03-12
OWNER: Diego Morales - Rate-limit backoff: make rollback writes use exponential backoff with bounded retries and produce a safety stop if >X% of shards report pending state. ETA: 2026-03-20
OWNER: Product/Platform - Update rollout runbook to include explicit manual unpin steps and verification checklist (who can execute, required logs). ETA: 2026-03-10
OWNER: Security - Verify that canary unpin workflow continues to meet RBAC expectations when executed manually; document audit steps. ETA: 2026-03-22
PM review (Liam O'Rourke): prioritize preflight checks for pin operations in the rollout pipeline.
Design feedback (Nora Blake): consider UX guardrail in Console that surfaces 'stuck canary' state and blocks new rollouts until resolved.
SRE comment: add incident-specific runbook snippet to avoid repeated manual fixes; automate reconcile-job and run as a controlled cron until fixed.
Primary focus is on making rollback and pin/unpin operations observable and strongly consistent from the caller's perspective. Secondary work items include improving Console UX and adding automated reconciliation that only runs under a safe rate-limited mode. We'll re-check incident metrics after completing the first three action items and close this ticket when the convergence check is merged, end-to-end test added, and dashboard live.
No customer data exposure detected. Audit logs for pin/unpin operations retained for 90 days per platform retention policy. Manual unpin steps were performed by SRE and recorded in audit trail cp-audit-20260302-9.

title: FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint epic (runtime perf suite + rollout decisions)
content:
FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint epic (runtime perf suite + rollout decisions)

Epic goal
Deliver a defensible, reproducible FP8/INT8 benchmark matrix across top hosted models and primary fleet GPUs (H100, A100, plus at least one cost SKU where feasible), then translate results into concrete runtime changes: kernel auto-selection heuristics, scheduler knob defaults, and hosted-catalog quantization profile guidance. Changes must be safe to roll out via flags + perf canary with automatic rollback.

Why this sprint
We have kernel-level wins from FP8/INT8 paths that are not consistently realized end-to-end due to scheduling interactions (prefill/decode mix, batching window, backpressure) and shape-specific constraints. We also need reproducibility improvements (driver/CUDA pinning, clock locking, artifact metadata) so results are defensible internally (and selectively externally via PM).

Owners / stakeholders
- Program driver: Talia Benson
- Kernel lead: Hiro Tanaka (primary assignee)
- Scheduling lead: Sofia Ivanova
- Benchmark harness owner: Rina Kobayashi
- Perf/Evals decision owner: Jonas Weber
- Infra capacity sponsor: Neha Kapoor
- SRE canary/rollout owner: Rafael Mendes
- Observability/dashboards: Allison Grant

Scope (in)
1) Benchmark harness updates (microbench + E2E serving)
- Add FP8/INT8 modes, consistent warmup/measurement loops, standardized artifact export and metadata (git SHA, container, CUDA/driver, clocks, model hash, config).
- Add scheduler instrumentation to isolate prefill vs decode and expose queue depth/backpressure for mixed workloads.

2) Execution: benchmark matrix runs
- GPUs: H100 + A100 as required; add one cost-focused SKU (L4) if the harness supports apples-to-apples + we can reserve time.
- Models: “top hosted models” (final list captured in sprint plan / benchmark suite v3). Include realistic workloads: prompt length distributions, prefill/decode mixes, batch sizes, and concurrency profiles.

3) Analysis + decisions
- Kernel-selection heuristics: when to pick FP8 vs INT8 vs baseline by GPU arch and shape regime; include guardrails and correctness fallbacks.
- Scheduler parameter tuning: batching window / backpressure defaults tuned so end-to-end realizes kernel wins without TTFT regressions.
- Quantization policy guidance: which models eligible for FP8 vs INT8 defaults; when eval sign-off is required; calibration requirements and known risks.

4) Shipping + rollout
- Implement changes behind flags; enable per-model/per-region cohorts.
- Perf canary gates: thresholds for TTFT/TPOT/tokens/s with noise handling; automatic rollback triggers.
- Release notes + runbook updates.

Out of scope (explicit)
- Re-architecting the scheduler (we are tuning knobs + instrumentation only).
- Publishing public benchmarks. PM will decide what can be shared and with what footnotes.
- Model training changes (this is serving/runtime only).

Definition of done
- Benchmark matrix produced with p50/p95 latency, throughput, variance (error bars), and cost proxies across the agreed GPU/model/workload set.
- Reproducibility: runners pin driver/CUDA and optionally lock clocks; artifacts include required metadata; reruns on the same setup reproduce within standards variance.
- ADR-level decision captured for kernel auto-selection heuristics + guardrails + fallback.
- Scheduler tuning validated against the benchmark suite to avoid TTFT regressions (or documented trade-offs + gating).
- Perf canary thresholds implemented and dashboards live; rollback triggers tested at least once in staging or via controlled degradation.
- Runtime 1.22.0 changes merged, flagged, and rolled out via canary; release notes drafted.

Milestones / timeline (sprint-style, ~2 weeks)
- Day 1–2: Kickoff + methodology sign-off; reserve GPU capacity; finalize model/workload list.
- Day 3–4: Harness updates + calibration runs; validate measurement stability; address variance.
- Day 5–9: Full benchmark execution across matrix; daily anomaly triage.
- Day 10–11: Analysis + decisions (kernel heuristics + scheduler knobs + quant policy).
- Day 12–14: Implementation + perf canary gates; staged rollout and documentation.

- Scheduler knobs: sources/github/redwood/pr-19911-optimize-scheduler-knob-defaults-for-mixed-workloads.json
- Metrics tagging: sources/github/redwood/pr-19934-metrics-tagging-model-gpu-kernel-mode.json
- Release notes finalization: sources/github/redwood/pr-19955-update-release-notes-runtime-1-22-0.json

Milestone checklist (tracked here for the epic)
- [x] Kickoff held; methodology signed off (Claire + Jonas); list of models/workloads locked.
- [x] GPU reservations approved (Neha/Irene) and window scheduled to avoid Dedicated pool conflicts.
- [x] Harness supports FP8/INT8 toggles; measurement stability within standards on calibration runs.
- [x] Runner pins container/driver/CUDA; clocks lock option exercised for H100 variance issue.
- [x] Full H100/A100 matrix completed for top models; anomalies documented and re-runs performed.
- [x] Quality sanity suite executed for candidate defaults; model-specific caveats documented.
- [x] ADR-019 finalized; heuristics implemented + unit tests.
- [x] Perf canary thresholds deployed; dashboards verified with model/GPU/mode tags.
- [x] Canary rollout executed; one rollback event handled per runbook; follow-up hotfix merged where needed.
- [x] Runtime 1.22.0 notes updated and shared with #eng-runtime / #eng-sre.

Key decisions (summary)
- Kernel selection follows ADR-019: prefer FP8 on H100 for eligible shapes unless long-context quality risk is flagged; INT8 used primarily where matmul shapes align and quality is stable; baseline is default fallback.
- Scheduler knobs adjusted to prevent TTFT spikes under mixed workloads; batching window capped in low-concurrency regimes; backpressure thresholds tuned to avoid decode starvation.
- Quantization defaults require Applied ML sign-off for specific model families and long-context workloads; canary gating remains mandatory for default flips.

Risks + mitigations logged during sprint
- Variance on H100 due to clock drift/thermal throttling and shared-node contention → mitigate by pinning clocks where permitted, enforcing exclusive allocation in runner, and tagging artifacts with clocks + thermals.
- Correctness failures for INT8 on specific shapes → shape guardrails + runtime fallback to baseline + unit tests.
- End-to-end TTFT regressions even when kernel microbench wins → add scheduler instrumentation, tune batching/backpressure, require canary TTFT/TPOT thresholds.
- Customer impact from capacity contention during benchmark windows → reservation plan guardrails + avoid Dedicated pools + explicit SRE/Infra coordination.

Comms cadence used
- Daily 15-min triage (runtime + applied ML + SRE rep) during matrix execution.
- End-of-week readout to performance stakeholders (Jonas/Neha/Aditya/Henry) with “what we can claim” caveats.
- Rollout coordination in #eng-releases for runtime-1.22.0 RC sign-off.

Notes / updates (condensed)
- 2026-02-10: Epic created after kickoff thread; sub-issues opened for harness, kernel flags, scheduler instrumentation, and canary gates.
- 2026-02-13: Calibration run found unacceptable variance on H100; pivoted to driver/CUDA pinning + clock lock support.
- 2026-02-17: First full matrix pass complete for H100; A100 in progress; INT8 correctness failure reproduced → added shape guardrails and reran affected cells.
- 2026-02-20: ADR heuristics review converged; implemented + started canary gating integration.
- 2026-02-24: Canary detected TTFT regression in a narrow prompt regime; auto-rollback triggered; issue triaged to launch overhead + scheduler mix; hotfix landed to disable FP8 for that shape cohort pending deeper kernel work.
- 2026-02-28: Final matrix + eval summary attached in Drive; runtime-1.22.0 release notes updated; epic marked Done.

Follow-ups (not in scope for this epic, but recommended)
- Add L4 coverage and validate INT8 wins in cost SKU regimes (requires updated runner support + reservations).
- Expand quality suite to include more structured-output/tool-calling long-context prompts where FP8 showed sensitivity.
- Extend perf canary baselines per region and add automated drift detection for driver updates.
