Duration: 52 min (recorded)
Attendees: Lena Torres (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (Redwood CSM), Oliver Kemp (Cranemere Head of Platform), Priya Shah (DevOps), Markus Vogel (CTO), Hannah Lee (PM)

Summary:
Quick renewal/expansion check-in focused on: committed capacity uplift, adding EU region (data sovereignty), burst/overage pricing, and pilot timeline for private VPC option. Customer brought new compliance timeline (Q4 audit) and wants clarity on SLA, audit logs and key management. Redwood to provide benchmark run and updated pricing amendment.

Topics:
- Committed capacity increase (baseline + burst)
- EU private VPC / data residency path
- Latency SLOs and canary strategy for multi-region traffic
- Security docs: SOC2, SSO, KMS integration
- Contract amendment process and procurement timeline

[00:00] Lena Torres: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, um just to set the agenda, quick renewal check-in, we have a couple items on committed capacity and then Marcus will talk through the performance benchmark plan. then we'll go into sovereignty and private vpc options. sound good?

[00:18] Oliver Kemp: yeah that works for us, thanks Lena. quick context: we are coming up on our contract renewal window in september and we need to lock in an uplift for the holiday season, and we also have a q4 data residency audit so the eu region is a hard requirement for some customers.

[00:34] Marcus Li: great, hi everyone. i'll keep the benchmark plan brief — objective is to validate token-level latency at your typical prompt mix and measure cost per 1k tokens under both hosted and private scenarios. we'll run 3 workloads: short chat queries (~32 tokens), mixed QA (~120 tokens), and long generation (~600 tokens) to simulate your support and transcript generation flows.

[00:57] Priya Shah: just to flag, our traffic is spiky — we do big batches at midnight in timezone eu-west and then a daytime chat peak in us-east. how does Redwood handle burst beyond committed pools? do we get throttled?

[01:12] Lena Torres: good question. so you have two levers: reserved capacity (committed) and burst capacity we can attach to the plan. if burst is used we bill at the burst rate — we can add a cap/overage policy so you don't go unlimited. also automatic fallback to a lower-cost compatible model is possible if latency SLOs are flexible.

[01:35] Markus Vogel: okay, what about routing? we can't have eu data leaving region, some of our compliance tests check that tokens are processed inside eu.

[01:44] Marcus Li: for that we recommend Redwood Private with a VPC control plane in eu-west. you can pin the model and route traffic locally. we maintain the same API surface so minimal app changes. there's an onprem option if you need air-gap, but that's heavier.

[02:05] Hannah Lee: timeline question — procurement asked whether we can have the private vpc provisioned before Oct 15, because audit is mid-Oct. is that realistic?

[02:14] Lena Torres: provision time depends on contract and infra sizing. for a standard private VPC we typically do a 4-6 week lead time once terms are signed and capacity is committed. given today's date, that puts provisioning mid-September if contract is signed by Aug 18. we should try to aim for that.

[02:36] Oliver Kemp: procurement will need a concrete contract amendment. can you send a commitment amendment with explicit start date, committed GPUs, and burst caps? and also the pricing tiers so our finance can model it.

[02:51] Lena Torres: yes — i'll send the amendment draft and updated pricing sheet today.

[03:00] Priya Shah: another technical point — we use an older transformer model internally; will Redwood's runtime support the kv cache and token streaming we rely on? i've had issues with other vendors dropping the stream after 2k tokens.

[03:16] Marcus Li: Redwood's runtime supports continuous KV cache and streaming; there are a couple knobs — max prefix, session pooling — we'll surface the default config and also run your benchmark to exercise long sessions so you can see any degradation. some transcriptions might have slight errors in names but core behavior should be solid.

[03:42] Markus Vogel: in terms of cost, how does dedicated compare to hosted? we are trying to decide if purchasing a dedicated pool with reserved capacity makes sense versus staying hosted and paying higher per-token price with burst.

[03:54] Lena Torres: typically for sustained throughput — if you have predictable monthly token volumes — dedicated/reserved is 30-55% cheaper vs pure hosted; exact depends on model family and quantization. Redwood Optimize will provide suggestions like lighter quantization for batch jobs and batching config to lower per-token cost. we'll include cost modeling in the spreadsheet.

[04:18] Hannah Lee: can you also include examples of automatic fallbacks? we need documented behaviour if eu capacity is saturated during peak.

[04:26] Marcus Li: yes — fallback policies are configurable: region-fallback (route to another eu cluster), model-fallback (drop to smaller quantized variant), or rate-limiting with 503 and retry headers. we'll show config snippets in the playbook.

[04:44] Priya Shah: security — we need SSO (SAML), RBAC, audit logs shipped to our splunk. do you support customer-managed KMS with HSM?

[04:56] Lena Torres: short answer yes: SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning, RBAC at token/route level, and audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM. for encryption we support customer-managed KMS for private deployments — HSM is an enterprise add-on. i'll attach the security pack link after the call: https://redwood.ai/security-pack (note: link for reference).

[05:20] Oliver Kemp: can we get a copy of SOC2 and penetration test reports?

[05:26] Jared Kim: absolutely — i'll drop SOC2 Type II summary and the latest pen test redacted artifacts, plus architecture diagrams.

[05:35] Markus Vogel: about benchmarks — Marcus, what metrics will you return? p50/p95/p99 latencies, token throughput, and cost-per-1k?

[05:44] Marcus Li: yes p50/p95/p99, tail latencies on long prompts, throughput in tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens under both hosted and private configs. we'll also provide a CSV with request-by-request timings so you can plug into your dashboards.

[06:02] Priya Shah: got it. also, please include a test that simulates our midnight batch job, because that one hits 4x the daytime load.

[06:09] Marcus Li: yep we'll add a spiky workload. question for you: do you have any hard latency SLOs for interactive chat?

[06:17] Oliver Kemp: under 250ms p95 for the short chat path; for long gen we are ok up to 2s p95 but we want predictable tails.

[06:26] Lena Torres: we can tune pooling, batching, and model choice to hit 250ms p95 on short queries; we'll validate in the benchmark. if not we can propose a dedicated reserved slice sized for your peak.

[06:40] Hannah Lee: procurement will probably ask about termination clauses and credit for downtime. what's Redwood's SLA?

[06:47] Lena Torres: hosted offers 99.9% uptime SLA, dedicated private plans have higher SLAs available as enterprise add-on. credits depend on incident severity and are spelled out in the TOS. we'll include SLA section in the amendment draft.

[07:05] Markus Vogel: any chance to pilot EU private cluster before commit? we'd prefer a short validation run with sample traffic before signing a long-term reserved contract.

[07:14] Jared Kim: yes, we can do a 14-day pilot with limited capacity, or a paid PoC that converts to committed capacity. Marcus can stand up a sandbox in eu-west for you.

[07:26] Marcus Li: process: we provision sandbox with limited nodes, run the benchmark, and then iterate. it'll surface any network egress or config changes you need.

[07:36] Priya Shah: do you support customer-side NAT for egress? our infra team needs to control egress IPs for allowlists.

[07:43] Marcus Li: yes for private VPC we can use customer-controlled NAT and IP whitelisting. we'll document the network diagram and firewall rules.

[07:57] Oliver Kemp: a concern — Anthropic offered us a short-term discount to lock in now; how flexible is Redwood on term length and ramped billing? we might want a 6-month ramp to avoid committing full capacity immediately.

[08:12] Lena Torres: we can do stepped commitments (ramped capacity) with a defined ramp schedule in the amendment. pricing will reflect the ramp. if you need a short-term discount we can also propose a limited pilot discount to bridge procurement.

[08:28] Hannah Lee: thanks — that's helpful. one more — can we schedule a deep-dive with networking team to discuss VPC peering and routing specifics?

[08:35] Lena Torres: yes — Marcus and Jared can meet your network folks. i'll let Jared coordinate calendar invites.

[08:44] [Slight crosstalk / someone types in chat]

[08:50] Marcus Li: we'll run the benchmark next Tuesday (Aug 12) unless you prefer a different date. we need a small sample dataset and a list of endpoints to emulate.

[08:59] Priya Shah: Aug 12 works. i'll upload a sanitized sample dataset and a short prompt set by Aug 11.

[09:07] Lena Torres: perfect. recap quick: 1) Redwood to send amendment + pricing (Lena) 2) SE to run benchmarks and share CSV + results (Marcus) 3) CSM to share security docs and SOC2 (Jared) 4) Cranemere to confirm procurement timeline and upload sample dataset (Oliver/Priya). we will reconvene Sept 2 to review amendment.

[09:31] Oliver Kemp: that aligns. any blockers on your side?

[09:36] Lena Torres: none. we'll aim to get materials out today and have the benchmark results by Aug 13.

[09:45] Markus Vogel: thanks everyone — looking forward to results.

[09:51] Jared Kim: i'll create the sandbox project and send invites; expect the security pack link and SOC2 within the hour.

[10:00] [Meeting ends]

Notes on transcription quality: occasional word swaps (e g 'kv' transcribed as 'k v'), some speaker label slippage in a few short segments; overall medium quality.

References / Links mentioned:
- pricing spreadsheet (shared via drive)
- security pack: https://redwood.ai/security-pack
- benchmark template: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/template

Recap / Next steps (repeat):
- Lena: amendment draft + pricing (due 2025-08-10)
- Marcus: benchmark and CSV (due 2025-08-12)
- Jared: SOC2 + pen test artifacts + sandbox invites (due 2025-08-08)
- Oliver/Priya: upload sample dataset and confirm procurement owners (due 2025-08-11)

End of transcript.

title: Unexpected egress affinity shift causing cold TLS handshakes and streaming cancels for BrightRetail
content:
Unexpected egress affinity shift causing cold TLS handshakes and streaming cancels for BrightRetail

Issue summary:
Customer BrightRetail observed repeated streaming cancellations and request timeouts starting 2026-03-09 22:40 UTC. Affected requests show unusually long TLS handshake durations (~2.5-6s) prior to application-level token exchange, causing client SDKs to cancel after 3s. The problem appears correlated with egress routing shifts where a small percentage of connections are routed across regions rather than to the account's pinned local egress pool.

Impact:
- Multiple production endpoints experiencing elevated p95/p99 latency for streaming API calls.
- Customer reports ~6% of requests for their production key are aborted by the client due to handshake/tcp timeout.
- Business impact: degraded chat experiences and user-visible timeouts for BrightRetail storefront search assistants.

Environment:
- Customer: BrightRetail Inc. (dedicated pool, us-west primary)
- Platform: hosted Redwood API (prod)
- Affected routes: /v1/streams/generate and /v1/chat/stream
- Time window: first observed 2026-03-09 22:40 UTC, ongoing as of update.

Steps to reproduce (observed):
1) Issue occurs on first request after connection idle or session cache miss.
2) Client initiates streaming request to us-west endpoint; server logs show egress selection to us-east for ~6% of fresh connections.
3) TLS handshake duration recorded as 2500-6000ms in edge-proxy metrics.
4) Client SDK cancels at ~3000ms, generating client-side cancel and no downstream tokens returned.

Observed behavior / logs:
- Edge-proxy TLS handshake histogram: p50 ~45ms, p95 ~260ms, p99 ~3100ms during window.
- Routing logs: route decision for affected keys shows fallback to remote-pop due to transient affinity tag mismatch.
- Connection traces: new sessions include missing session-id header leading to allocation from warm pool in us-east.
- Error patterns: client-side cancel + server write timeout followed by a short-lived connection reset.

Investigation notes:
- Hypothesis 1: Session affinity tags occasionally not preserved by upstream gateway under burst conditions, causing a small fraction of fresh connections to be routed to a non-local egress pool (cross-region). Cold TLS handshakes on these remote pools are significantly slower due to lack of warm TLS session cache and additional network RTT.
- Hypothesis 2: Edge-proxy warm pool eviction policy combined with NAT SNAT rotation results in different downstream 5-tuple, invalidating L4 affinity for a subset of connections.
- Metrics correlating egress-affinity flips with p99 handshake spikes: confirmed timestamps match customer reports.
- Captured packet-level pcap (redacted) shows TLS ClientHello -> ServerHello delay of ~2.8s for affected sessions.
- No config change recorded in the control plane for BrightRetail during incident window.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- Engineering toggled strictly-local-egress routing rule for BrightRetail on 2026-03-10 03:10 UTC which reduced affected requests from 6% to ~0.3% in the following 6 hours.
- Increased edge-proxy TLS session cache TTL for the customer's egress pool to retain sessions across brief warm-pool churn (safe, short-term change).

Workaround for customer:
- Advise SDKs to increase client-side stream timeout to 6s during ongoing mitigation window to avoid client cancels (BrightRetail accepted temporary change).
- Recommend keepalive to reduce cold-connection rate.

Next steps / action items:
1) SRE: instrument detailed affinity tag propagation at the L4 proxy to capture missing headers and identify where tag removal occurs (assigned INT-7112).
2) Infra: audit warm-pool eviction thresholds; consider pre-warming remote egress for high-tier dedicated customers.
3) Networking: review SNAT churn and NAT table rotation that could be affecting L4 affinity.
4) Product: evaluate permanent local-egress enforcement option for dedicated customers to prevent cross-region cold-handshake regressions.
5) Postmortem: capture timeline and metric deltas; propose long-term fix and rolling deploy schedule.

Resolution notes (temporary):
- Local-egress enforcement and TTL increase applied as mitigations. Monitoring shows p99 handshake times returned to baseline for the majority of traffic. Longer-term fixes pending investigation.

2026-03-10 01:02 UTC - Support (Maya Chen): Customer reported intermittent streaming cancels; attached SDK logs and sample request IDs. Escalating to SRE due to cross-region routing evidence.
2026-03-10 02:15 UTC - SRE (Ethan Morales): Confirmed handshake p99 spike in edge-proxy metrics for BrightRetail key. Suspect affinity misassignment; temporarily enabled local-egress enforcement for account to reduce impact.
2026-03-10 05:20 UTC - Customer (BrightRetail Ops - Jordan Patel): Thanks for the quick mitigation. We'll extend client timeouts as you suggested. Please keep us posted on root cause.
2026-03-11 09:40 UTC - Infra (Priya Narang): Investigating warm-pool eviction logs; seeing correlated churn around 22:30-23:00 UTC. Opening internal ticket INT-7112 to trace SNAT rotation and pool assignment.
2026-03-12 14:05 UTC - SRE (Ethan Morales): Applied TLS session cache TTL bump and validated reduced incidence. Next: full affinity propagation traces scheduled for 2026-03-13. Updating ticket with progress; marking as In Progress.

title: Runtime Scheduler Decision Fabric and Telemetry Playbook
content:
Runtime Scheduler Decision Fabric and Telemetry Playbook

Summary

This document defines the "Decision Fabric" concept for the runtime scheduler: a structured set of decision points, the telemetry signals required to make those decisions, and a practical playbook for evaluating, rolling out, and debugging scheduler policy changes. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and owners of scheduling policy components.

Goals

- Make scheduling decisions auditable and reproducible.
- Ensure telemetry is sufficient to explain why any request took the path it did.
- Provide safe rollout and rollback steps for scheduler changes.
- Define incident triage and escalation steps when scheduling misbehavior impacts SLOs.

Scope

Covers: kernel scheduling policy decision points, admission controllers, priority tags, preemption windows, kernel selection hints, and the telemetry & alerts that validate these decisions.
Does not cover: low-level GPU kernel source code changes or vendor driver instrumentation (those belong to kernel-and-scheduling code docs).

1. Decision Fabric: concepts and nodes

The Decision Fabric is a logical DAG of discrete decision nodes that operate on enriched request context and produce actions or routing hints. Nodes are micro-decision units intended to be small and testable. Example nodes:

- Request Classification: maps incoming request attributes to a class (e.g., interactive, batch, background).
- Admission Gate: enforces concurrency & slot availability budget for class and tenant.
- Priority Arbiter: resolves conflicts between competing requests (SLA, customer tier, emerging emergency).
- Kernel Selector: picks the kernel variant and quantization profile.
- Prefetch/KV Hint: decides whether to fetch KV cache for a session.
- Fallback Router: chooses alternate model variant/region on capacity or error.

Each node emits a standardized Decision Event (see Telemetry section). Nodes are composed into runtime pipelines.

2. Decision Event schema (telemetry contract)

All scheduler decision nodes MUST emit a Decision Event at the moment a decision is made. This makes decisions traceable end-to-end. The near-term schema (text representation):

Example Decision Event (single-line JSON text for logs; the runtime also emits structured proto for the tracing pipeline):
{
  "request_id": "string",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-15T14:12:03Z",
  "node": "PriorityArbiter:v2",
  "input_signals": ["tenancy_tier:standard","seq_len_estimate:32","recent_error_rate:0.002"],
  "decision": "grant:slot-id=slot-42, kernel_hint=gptq-4bit-fp16",
  "reason_codes": ["tenancy_quota_ok","latency_target_50ms"],
  "latency_ms": 0.42,
  "cost_weight": 1.0
}

- Note: Events should be JSON-encoded when landing in structured logging systems; they must also exist as compact binary in the tracing pipeline for high-cardinality sampling.

Required fields (text form): request_id, timestamp (ISO8601), node (string), decision (string), reason_codes (list), latency_ms (number), cost_weight (number), input_signals (list).
Optional but recommended: model_version, kernel_revision, tenant_id, route, sampled_trace_id.

3. Minimal telemetry to support common investigations

To triage scheduling issues within 5–15 minutes, the following telemetry streams are required:

- Decision Events (high cardinality, sampled): ~1 per decision; sample strategy below.
- Request Timeline Trace (distributed trace spanning API -> admission -> kernel dispatch).
- Per-kernel execution metrics: queue_time_ms, kernel_exec_ms, retry_count.
- Admission & slot pool stats: available_slots, inflight_by_tier, eviction_count.
- Request classification histogram: seq_len, token_budget, request_surface_type.

Suggested retention and sampling:

| Stream | Sampling | Hot retention | Cold retention |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|Decision Events|100% for tier=enterprise; 5% for standard/free|7d|180d|
|Request Traces|100% for p99+ tail traces, 1% baseline|14d|90d|
|Kernel exec metrics|Aggregate per-min buckets 100%|30d|365d|

4. Reason-coding taxonomy (short list)

Decision nodes should attach reason codes. We maintain a canonical set to avoid free-form strings. Examples:

- quota_exhausted
- latency_slo_risk
- high_seq_len
- emergency_preemption
- kernel_incompatible
- kvcache_miss
- model_swap_fallback

5. Playbook: safe rollout of scheduler changes

This is the sequential process you must follow when deploying a scheduler policy change (e.g., new PriorityArbiter logic, admission thresholds, kernel selector rules):

1) Design review and unit tests
- Create an ADR (link to decision record). Include decision fabric impact map (which nodes change).
- Unit tests: determinism tests for decision nodes and reason_code coverage matrix.

2) Local and integration testing
- Run deterministic replay of representative request corpus (use the operational workload simulator) and compare Decision Event diffs.
- Validate no new reason codes introduced unintentionally.

3) Canary rollout (safety gates)
- Canary cohort: 0.5% baseline requests or a narrow tenant set of non-critical accounts.
- Observability checks (automated):
  - p50/p95 request latency for canary <= baseline + 5%
  - decision_event.reason_code change rate <= 2x baseline for any single reason code
  - admission.rejection_rate <= baseline + 0.1% absolute
  - kernel_exec_ms median unchanged or improved

4) Gradual ramp and policy checks
- Ramp to 5% after 30m if canary signals pass for 15m rolling windows.
- Run the differential tracer extractor to verify decision path similarity (expectation: >95% of canary decisions match legacy for non-experimental paths).

5) Full rollout and post-mortem observation
- After 24 hours at 100% observe metrics for 72 hours.
- If any SLO regressions occur, trigger automatic rollback and open a postmortem.

6. Incident triage checklist (scheduling-related)

When customers observe increased latency or error rates that trace to scheduler behavior:

1. Confirm alert and scope: check SLO dashboards for elevated p99 and per-route errors.
2. Correlate with Decision Event spike: query decision_event.node aggregated by reason_code in last 15m.
3. Inspect admission pool state: available_slots, pool_eviction_count, queue_time_ms.
4. Query kernel health: dispatch_fail_rate, nvlink_errors, watchdog_restarts.
5. If decision nodes show a sudden change in reason_code distribution (e.g., quota_exhausted spikes), identify the upstream change (policy, config, traffic surge).
6. If root cause is policy regression, execute rollback (see Rollback snippet).

Rollback CLI snippet (example):

# Roll back to last stable policy bundle
redwood-schedctl rollback --bundle-id=rb-2026-0007 --reason="p99-latency-regression"

Wait for slot metrics and decision_event reason_code to normalize, then annotate the incident.

7. Debug recipes and quick checks

- "Why did my request get preempted?"
  1) Search Decision Events by request_id -> look at PriorityArbiter and Admission Gate nodes.
  2) Check reason_codes: if emergency_preemption present, check active incident tags and owner.

- "Why was kernel_variant X chosen?"
  1) Inspect KernelSelector decision event; cross-check input_signals for sequence length and model_version.
  2) Look at kernel_revision compatibility table (see table below).

Kernel compatibility table (text):
| kernel_revision | model_family | quant_profile | notes |
| kv1.4 | gpt-j | 8bit | legacy; higher latency for long seqs |
| gq-2025-4b | llama-family | gptq-4bit-fp16 | low cost; prefer for background tasks |
| vbench-rc2 | opt | int8 | experimental; disable for enterprise tenants |

8. Metric and alert definitions (examples)

- sched.decision.rate (counter): decision events per second. Alert: sustained drop >30% over 5m -> scheduler stall investigation.
- sched.admission.rejection_rate (gauge %): Alert if >0.5% absolute above baseline for 10m.
- sched.kernel.queue_time_p99 (ms): Alert if >250ms for 5m.
- sched.reasoncode.quotas_exhausted.rate (counter): Alert if sudden spike (>5x expected) during deployment windows.

9. Sampling and storage plan for Decision Events

We recommend a two-path approach:
1) High-fidelity path (tracing infra) stores sampled full traces and Decision Events for a narrow sample of requests and all p99 tail traces.
2) Low-cost aggregated path stores per-minute aggregated counters and histograms for long-term analytics.

Sampling knobs (examples):
- sample_by_tier: {enterprise: 100%, standard: 5%, free: 1%}
- tail_capture: p99+ of request_latency || error_rate -> force sample.

10. Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: runtime-scheduler team (oncall rota: runtime-scheduler@pagerduty).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre (for capacity, node-level issues).
- Incident severity mapping:
  - Sev-1: customer-facing outage (SLO > 30m breach) -> notify exec-oncall, start incident bridge.
  - Sev-2: p99 latency spikes without complete outage (SRE & scheduler oncall).

11. Compatibility and migration notes

- When changing reason codes or Decision Event schema, include a compatibility shim for 60 days. Update the schema registry and add transformers in the analytics pipeline.

12. Appendix: example decision event query patterns

- Find the decision path for a request id (pseudo-SQL):
  SELECT * FROM decision_events WHERE request_id = 'req-123' ORDER BY timestamp ASC;

- Aggregate reason code rate by node:
  SELECT node, reason_code, count(*) FROM decision_events WHERE timestamp > now() - interval '15m' GROUP BY node, reason_code ORDER BY count DESC;

13. Change log

- 2024-09-12: initial draft by Riley Chen.
- 2025-03-02: added kernel compatibility table and rollout gates (Aisha Patel review).
- 2026-01-15: updated Decision Event schema and sampling defaults (Marco Silva).

Related material and references

- Scheduler policy language spec (see related pages).
- Request classification and telemetry contract (team-wiki).

Contact

For questions or to request changes to the decision fabric, open a PR against the runtime-scheduler repo and add runtime-scheduler@team as reviewers.

title: Incidents runbook: overload behavior with tiered batching defaults (fast/standard/cost-efficient)
content:
Incidents runbook: overload behavior with tiered batching defaults (fast/standard/cost-efficient)

## Goal
Provide a single on-call runbook for diagnosing and mitigating overload-related latency regressions when tiered batching defaults are enabled (fast / standard / cost-efficient). This runbook covers:
- symptom → likely cause mapping
- immediate mitigations (no code)
- tier-specific guidance
- rollback / kill-switch procedures
- post-incident follow-ups

This is intended for Runtime + SRE on-call during staged rollout (internal canary → hosted subset → Dedicated opt-in → broader default).

---

## Definitions / mental model
**Overload** here means one (or more) of:
- arrival rate > sustainable throughput for the active tier profile
- queue growth that increases time-to-first-token (TTFT) and/or p99 end-to-end latency
- admission control/load shedding triggers (or fails to trigger)
- scheduler behavior that starves some requests under mixed prompt length / mixed streaming

**Tier expectations** (high-level):
- **fast**: protect tail latency; will sacrifice throughput earlier via tighter wait budget + admission control.
- **standard**: balanced; modest batching, modest wait; aims to be stable for general SaaS workloads.
- **cost-efficient**: maximize throughput / $ per token; can tolerate higher tail, but must not allow runaway queue depth.

**Key guarantee:** correctness must be preserved; degrade predictably under overload (backpressure, rate limiting, or load shedding) rather than silent latency collapse.

---

## When to use this runbook
Trigger when any of the following occur after enabling tiered defaults (feature flag on, or tier selection introduced):
1) **Fast tier p99 regression** (especially TTFT) vs baseline.
2) **Queue depth increasing** with p95/p99 latency increasing.
3) **Streaming endpoints** report slower TTFT or irregular chunking (perceived "stalling").
4) Increased **429/503** (load shedding / admission control) after enabling fast tier.
5) Dedicated tenant reports override not applying or unexpected effective tier.

Related tickets/threads to reference:
- Slack: fast-tier p99 regression investigation (eng-runtime/1768501140)
- Slack: overload mode behavior discussion (eng-runtime/1768664305)
- Jira: SUP-48219 p95 regression during canary
- Hotfix precedent: PR-28544 limit tier label cardinality (telemetry blow-up can masquerade as perf regression)

---

## Required dashboards / queries
1) **Tiered batching dashboard** (Observability Pack)
- latency: p50/p95/p99 by {tier, model_family, region, streaming}
- TTFT (streaming vs non-streaming)
- queue depth and time-in-queue
- batch size distribution (prefill batch tokens, decode batch tokens)
- admission control / shed counters
- cache hit rate (prefix/KV) and cache evictions

2) **Reason codes** for profile selection
Check selection reason counts over time to confirm expected behavior.
Common reason codes:
- `tier.default.fast|standard|cost_efficient`
- `tier.override.route_policy`
- `tier.override.customer` (Dedicated)
- `tier.constrained.model_limit` (model/hardware constraint clamps knobs)
- `tier.overload_mode.active` (scheduler entered overload behavior)
- `tier.fallback.compat_variant` (if applicable)

3) **Infra saturation**
- GPU utilization / SM occupancy
- HBM usage / OOM events
- CPU saturation in control plane / streaming gateway
- network egress saturation for streaming-heavy regions

---

## First 5 minutes: decision tree
### A) Is this a telemetry artifact?
- If latency histograms degrade while service-level sampling changes or metrics cardinality spikes, verify metrics ingestion health.
- Check whether tier labels exploded (known early canary issue); if so, apply telemetry hotfix / sampling controls and re-evaluate.

### B) Is the tier actually applied?
- Confirm effective tier for affected routes/tenants.
- Look at reason code mix:
  - if `tier.override.*` dominates unexpectedly → config precedence issue.
  - if `tier.constrained.model_limit` spikes → model/hardware clamp causing different behavior than expected.

### C) Is it localized?
- Compare by region/model family. If one region/model family only, suspect:
  - heterogeneous fleet hardware
  - different concurrency distribution
  - cache behavior differences
  - a single model family with prefill/decode imbalance sensitivity

### D) Is it overload vs regression under normal load?
- If queue depth and time-in-queue increase in parallel with latency → overload/backpressure problem.
- If queue depth is flat but p99 increases → scheduler/kernel regression, model-level issue, or downstream gateway.

---

## Triage steps (deeper)
1) **Identify impacted dimension(s)**
- tier (fast vs standard vs cost-efficient)
- streaming vs non-streaming
- prompt length bucket (short/medium/long)
- model family + quantization variant (if applicable)
- region

2) **Check queue dynamics**
- queue depth trend
- max wait budget usage (esp. fast tier)
- batch formation rate (are we forming too-small batches due to tight wait? or too-large due to aggressive batching?)

3) **Check for starvation under mixed workloads**
Signals:
- long prompts are consistently delayed behind short prompts (or vice versa)
- streaming requests get delayed behind large prefill batches
Mitigation options (no-code):
- shift affected route from cost-efficient → standard, or standard → fast (depending on symptom)
- temporarily cap max batch tokens / max wait via override if available (Dedicated/enterprise)

4) **Check admission control / shedding**
- Rising 429/503 with stable latency may indicate fast tier protecting tail correctly, but upstream rate limits need tuning.
- Rising latency without shedding indicates admission control not triggering when it should (regression or thresholds too lenient).

5) **Confirm cache behavior**
- If cache hit rate dropped coincident with tier change, larger batches may be increasing eviction or changing request interleaving.
- Cache issues can present as sudden prefill time increase (TTFT regression) without obvious queue growth.

---

## Tier-specific guidance
### Fast tier (protect tail latency)
Typical failure modes:
- **p99 TTFT regression** due to queueing from insufficient admission control or too much prefill work per step.
- **increased 429/503** because admission control became more aggressive than expected.

Mitigations:
1) If p99 is rising and queue depth is rising:
- enable/raise fast-tier admission control (if not already) and verify it is active.
- reduce exposure: roll back fast tier defaults for affected model/region cohort.
2) If 429/503 rose sharply but latency stayed healthy:
- validate upstream rate limiting configs; communicate expected behavior (fast tier chooses fail-fast under overload).
- consider shifting high-QPS non-critical routes to standard tier.

Escalate to Runtime if:
- starvation suspected (mixed prompt lengths) despite admission control.
- prefill/decode balancing looks off (high prefill time spikes while decode steady).


### Standard tier (balanced)
Typical failure modes:
- slow creep in p95 under sustained load due to queue depth increasing.
- mixed streaming and non-streaming contention.

Mitigations:
- if streaming routes are impacted, isolate by moving streaming routes to fast tier.
- if batch sizes are too small (low throughput), consider cost-efficient for non-latency-sensitive routes.
- if batch sizes are too large (queue blowups), temporarily clamp max batch tokens via route override (if available) or move to fast.


### Cost-efficient tier (throughput-first)
Typical failure modes:
- **queue blowup** under bursty traffic (tail latency becomes unbounded).
- **timeouts** at gateways due to slow TTFT.

Mitigations:
1) For queue blowup:
- shift impacted route(s) to standard temporarily.
- if overload mode exists, verify it is active and is reducing queue growth (not increasing).
2) For widespread impact:
- reduce rollout scope for cost-efficient tier; disable for streaming endpoints by policy.

Hard rule during incident:
- Do not recommend cost-efficient tier for customer-facing interactive streaming endpoints unless they explicitly accept TTFT risk.

---

## Rollback / kill switch procedures
### Scope options (prefer smallest blast radius first)
1) **Per-route tier override** (Console/policy): change tier for a single route.
2) **Per-tenant override** (Dedicated): enforce tier at tenant/cluster level; ensure precedence (customer override > route policy > tier default).
3) **Disable tiered defaults feature flag** for cohort (region/model family).
4) **Global kill switch**: revert to pre-1.22 manual batching behavior / previous defaults.

### Rollback checklist
- capture incident timestamp window + impacted dimensions (tier/model/region/streaming)
- snapshot key graphs: p99, TTFT, queue depth, batch size distribution, shed counters
- confirm reason codes show the expected effective tier before and after rollback
- post rollback: monitor for 30 minutes (or 2x traffic peak window) and confirm metrics return to baseline band

### Communication
- If customer-facing degradation (Hosted): notify Support + PM on-call with:
  - affected regions/models
  - mitigation (tier shift / rollback)
  - expected time to stabilize
- If Dedicated tenant: coordinate with CSM/Support; document effective tier and override precedence.

---

## Known pitfalls / lessons learned (add as we learn)
1) **Metric cardinality can look like a perf regression**
If tier labels are added without cardinality controls, ingestion pressure can create noisy dashboards and delayed data.
Reference: runtime hotfix PR-28544.

2) **Streaming requires TTFT-first thinking**
Even if end-to-end p95 is stable, TTFT regression is a user-visible incident for streaming chat.

3) **Mixed prompt lengths can induce starvation**
Watch for bimodal latency by prompt-length bucket; consider policy split by route type.

---

## Artifacts / links
- Confluence (design): workload-aware batching defaults design doc (eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling)
- Confluence (SLOs): latency SLO tiers definition fast/standard/cost-efficient
- Confluence (dashboards): batching defaults observability dashboard spec
- GitHub: PR-28480 (feature flag + kill switch plumbing)
- GitHub: PR-28473 (reason codes)
- GitHub: observability-pack PR-933 (tier dashboards)

---

## Acceptance criteria
- Runbook published and linked from:
  - SRE on-call handbook
  - runtime-1.22 launch brief
  - batching defaults rollout checklist
- Includes explicit rollback order + kill switch instructions.
- Includes tier-specific symptom→mitigation guidance.
- References dashboards and reason codes needed for validation.

---

## Follow-ups (not required for closure, but tracked)
- Add a lightweight "incident note template" to the rollout checklist (owner: Rafael Mendes)
- Add an alert annotation when overload mode toggles (owner: Allison Grant)
- Add dedicated override precedence troubleshooting snippet to support playbook (owner: Aisha Bello)

2026-03-11 (Rafael Mendes): Creating this after reviewing the canary plan thread. We need a single place for "what do we do when fast tier p99 spikes" and "when is it appropriate to shed vs roll back". Drafting initial runbook skeleton and will route to Runtime + Observability for review.
2026-03-13 (Sofia Ivanova): Please include explicit checks for starvation under mixed prompt lengths + streaming contention. We’ve seen cases where queue depth doesn’t look terrible, but certain buckets get stuck behind large prefill batches.
2026-03-14 (Allison Grant): +1. Also call out the cardinality incident we hit earlier; dashboards can mislead during ingestion pressure. Recommend first step: validate metrics pipeline health before assuming real latency regression.
2026-03-17 (Sean Gallagher): I’ll own final edit + publication. Suggest we add an ordered rollback ladder (route override → cohort flag off → global kill switch) so on-call doesn’t jump to global rollback immediately.
2026-03-20 (Omar El-Sayed): Added notes on TTFT vs end-to-end for streaming. Fast tier should be evaluated primarily via TTFT p99 + time-in-queue. If TTFT is rising with flat queue, suspect prefill/decode imbalance.
2026-03-24 (Aisha Bello): Please include the paging vs ticketing guidance: page on fast-tier p99 sustained breach + high customer impact; otherwise file ticket with dashboard snapshots. I’ll align alerts once runbook is final.
2026-04-02 (Rafael Mendes): Applied edits from SRE review. Added reason-code validation step and explicit comms bullets for Support/CSM. Linking this from the rollout checklist once merged.
2026-04-18 (Sean Gallagher): Published to SRE handbook + linked from runtime-1.22 launch brief. Marking done. Next incident should paste graphs + selected reason codes into postmortem for quicker feedback loops.

title: Tidecrest dispatch assistant integration journal
content:
Tidecrest dispatch assistant integration journal

Call: Tidecrest Logistics — Dispatch Assistant integration (initial technical capture)
Date: 2025-01-12 10:00 PT
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SRE), Anita Rao (Redwood Solutions), Rajiv Menon (Tidecrest CTO), Priya Kapoor (Tidecrest Product), Luis Ortega (Tidecrest Platform)

High level ask
- Replace current rules engine for short text suggestions and driver instructions with an LLM-backed assistant to summarize incident context and propose routing adjustments. Must be realtime-ish (human-in-the-loop, <200ms p95 preferred for suggestion latency).
- On-prem/VPC-first: Tidecrest wants private deployment inside their AWS account (VPC) for sensitive telematics + PII. Dedicated/private deployment preferred; they may start with Dedicated before migrating to Private.

Key constraints (from Rajiv + Luis)
- Intermittent connectivity: some edge hubs (rural terminals) are behind flaky links. Need offline resilience or graceful degradation.
- Small GPU footprint at edge: can't run large 70B models on-site. Looking for a hybrid: small quantized local model for immediate suggestions, and larger hosted model fallback for complex summarization.
- Data residency: trip logs/driver notes considered PII under their policy — must be encrypted at rest and in transit; need KMS/HSM integration and retention controls (default 14 days, configurable).
- Audit trails: compliance wants per-request audit logs with raw prompt and model response for 30 days (log retention + ability to export for audits).

What Redwood can offer / initial recommendations
- Deployment: Recommend Redwood Private (VPC) so control plane can be in their account; if they want lighter ramp, Redwood Dedicated with private network peering is an interim approach.
- Model routing policy: run a quantized 8-bit ~7B local model for latency-critical suggestions on edge caches, route complex summarization (end-of-day consolidation, incident synthesis) to larger hosted model (e.g., 13B/33B) in Redwood Dedicated. Automatic fallback rules if local inference fails.
- Streaming + partial results: use streaming responses for the driver suggestion UI so partial text appears as tokens are generated (improves perceived latency).
- KV/prefix caching: for repeated route templates and driver-specific prompts, enable KV cache on the driver/session id to avoid recomputing context. Watch out for state drift on frequent TTL updates.
- Embeddings for recall: store embeddings of recent incidents to surface similar past cases. Use per-tenant namespace and encrypted vector store.

Technical gotchas / open risks
- Token accounting for telemetry: telematics JSON blobs (gps traces, events) are large. We need a pre-processing filter to extract salient fields; avoid sending raw telemetry as prompt. Otherwise token cost spikes.
- KV cache invalidation: dispatch state updates are frequent (every few seconds). If we cache too aggressively we serve stale suggestions. Need TTLs or event-driven invalidation from their event bus.
- Partial context vs hallucination: small local models hallucinate more on policy/guidance questions. Must add guardrails and deterministic rule checks before recommending route changes.
- Websocket vs REST: their UI uses websockets for live driver status. Need connector to map websocket events -> Redwood request stream; session affinity is required for KV cache reuse.

Integration requirements (explicit asks from Priya)
- Endpoint: a streaming API endpoint that accepts: {tenant_id, session_id (driver_id), event_summary, recent_telemetry_digest, exigency_level}. Returns tokens as a streaming suggestion and a confidence score.
- Real-time webhook: when suggestion is accepted, Redwood should POST a signed webhook to their /dispatch/apply endpoint including model_id, prompt_id, and delta actions for audit + idempotency.
- Per-tenant rate limits and quotas, and token usage dashboards exposed in console and via telemetry webhooks for billing reconciliation.
- Encryption: integrate with Tidecrest KMS (AWS KMS) for model input/output encryption at rest; support customer-managed keys.

Prompts & eval notes (quick, informal)
- Draft prompt (short): "Driver incident: {one-line summary}. Last 2 events: {e1}, {e2}. Constraints: arrival <= 15m, avoid heavy traffic. Suggest 1 concise instruction and confidence."
- Test scenarios to include: broken down routes (lots of reroutes), long-running congestion (preserve patience in suggestions), privacy redaction (ensure phone numbers/IDs stripped).
- Metrics for acceptance: suggestion usefulness (human accept rate) > 85% after 4-week tuning, p95 suggestion latency < 250ms for edge model, fallbacks < 1% of requests in steady state.

Action items / next steps (owners & rough dates)
- Marcus: prototype websocket -> Redwood streaming bridge (POC) and latency bench (target 1/2 week) — due 2025-01-20.
- Anita: design KV cache TTL strategy + inconsistency mitigation doc (include event-driven invalidation patterns) — due 2025-01-24.
- Sofia (me): build sample prompt set (20 examples) and lightweight eval harness for manual labeling; coordinate baseline accept-rate target with Priya — due 2025-01-18.
- Rajiv/Luis: provide sanitized sample telemetry dataset (anonymized traces, <1000 sessions) and KMS contact for integration — asked by 2025-01-17.
- Joint: schedule technical deep-dive for infra & security with Tidecrest infra team (2 hours) — set for 2025-01-22 (tentative).

Questions to resolve (TBD)
- Will Tidecrest allow outbound connections from edge hubs for fallback to Redwood Dedicated? If not, need an on-prem-only architecture.
- What SLA for suggestion availability do they want? Is occasional delay acceptable if correctness improves?
- Audit log retention: can we meet 30-day raw-prompt retention given their company policy and cost implications?

Quick notes / voice-of-customer snippets captured in call
- Priya: "We want suggestions to feel like a senior dispatcher — short, actionable, not long paragraphs."
- Rajiv: concerned about token bills if we naively send traces: "If you charge per token for every ping, it's untenable."
- Luis: strongly prefers KMS integration before any PII leaves account.

Random scratch ideas for future phases (brainstorm)
- Model personalization: lightweight per-driver context embeddings (driving style, preferred phrasing) to tune tone. Keep vector keys encrypted and per-tenant.
- Cost-control ML agent: suggest when to route to local vs hosted model based on cost/latency prediction and current spend budget.
- Offline summarizer: nightly batch summarization of incidents to reduce need for long-term model queries.

End of capture — keep this as working doc. Will iterate after POC latency numbers and once we get sanitized telemetry.

title: oncall-rotation-onboarding-and-slo-ownership-runbook-2024
content:
oncall-rotation-onboarding-and-slo-ownership-runbook-2024

Overview:
This runbook describes the standard onboarding flow for engineers joining the SRE on-call rotation and the concrete handoff for SLO ownership and error-budget stewardship. It is written for new rotation members, rotation leads, and managers who need a repeatable checklist to verify readiness to carry SLO responsibilities in production.

Purpose:
- Ensure consistent knowledge transfer for SREs joining or re-joining rotation.
- Reduce time-to-first-independent-incident-handling while protecting customer-facing SLOs.
- Establish a clear sign-off process for SLO ownership and capacity remediation privileges.

Scope:
Applies to: core inference platform services (api-gateway, runtime-router, kv-cache, model-host-pool) and SREs who will be primary or secondary on-call. Does NOT replace service-specific runbooks — those remain authoritative for service-level troubleshooting.

Definitions:
- SLO owner: rotation engineer accountable for monitoring, first-response and initiating mitigation for a target SLO.
- Error budget: rolling 30-day percentage (or per-SLO window) of allowable user-impacting failures.

Before you start (prerequisites):
- GitHub access: read/write to infra/playbooks repo.
- Confluence access to eng-sre space and product SLO matrix.
- PagerDuty and Slack access; add yourself to #sre-oncall and service channels.
- Complete the mandatory SRE training module: "SLO Fundamentals and Incident Triage" in LMS.
- Local dev cluster credentials and sandbox project (for safe drill exercises).

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step):
1) Orientation (Day 0–1)
   - Read the SLO matrix: open the SLO dashboard and export the list for your service(s). Verify thresholds for: p50, p95, p99 latency, availability, and correctness metrics used by product.
   - Join recurring oncall handover: attend next rotation change and shadow the outgoing oncall.

2) Tooling and alerts (Day 1–3)
   - Subscribe to alerts: PagerDuty, OpsGenie (fallback), and Slack alert bridge.
   - Verify alert routing: confirm that critical SLO alerts escalate to your primary channel and that low-severity alerts are rate-limited.
   - Walkthrough the telemetry queries:
     - Example PromQL (tail-latency):
       sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime-router\",le=\\\"0.5\\\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{job=\"runtime-router\"}[5m]))
     - Example traces: open the trace link pattern: https://jaeger.company.local/trace/{{trace_id}}

3) Read and rehearse runbooks (Day 2–4)
   - Read core runbooks: SLO rollback, capacity hedge, model-hotpatch, and circuit-breaker reset.
   - Run a table-top drill: simulate a p95 latency spike caused by a KV cache miss storm. Walk through mitigation steps (enable short-circuit cache warm, apply tiered throttles). Document decisions.

4) Capacity and provisioning basics (Day 3–6)
   - Review capacity model: headroom policy, burst pools, and preemption rules for spot instances.
   - Review tenant fair-share rules: how requests are prioritized across Dedicated and Hosted customers.
   - Practice issuing a safe scale action: CLI example (dry-run):
     rfn-capacity scale --cluster runtime-prod --pool inference-pool --count 4 --reason "oncall-drill" --dry-run

5) Error budget stewardship (Day 4–7)
   - Understand error budget windows and burn-rate alarms. Verify the dashboard shows the rolling window used by the SLO (30d by default).
   - Confirm the automated responses enabled for the service: throttling, model-fallback, cross-region reroute.
   - Practice executing an emergency fallback:
     - Step: trigger model fallback to smaller quantized variant (canary first)
     - Command (internal API):
       curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://console.internal/api/v1/rollouts/fallback" -d '{"service":"runtime-router","action":"fallback-quantized","target":"model-v2-q4"}'

6) Incident communication and post-incident responsibility (Day 4–8)
   - Run the incident comms template: copy and post to #incident-comm when practicing. Include: impact, scope, mitigation, ETA.
   - Ownership: the SLO owner must create the post-incident ticket under ENG-SRE > incident-review and ensure attachments: timeline, telemetry snapshots, and decision log.

Acceptance criteria (sign-off):
- Completed checklist items 1–6 and provided evidence (screenshots / links) in the onboarding folder.
- Passed a recorded tabletop drill assessed by rotation lead.
- Demonstrated ability to run three recovery actions in the sandbox (scale, fallback, throttle).
- Rotation lead signs off in Confluence comment and updates rotation roster.

Escalation matrix (who to call):
- Immediate (pager): oncall-sre-primary -> oncall-sre-secondary -> eng-sre-manager.
- For capacity quorums (if >2-hour impact): capacity-ops@redwood.com and cloud-accounts oncall.

Runbook snippets and templates:
- Incident start checklist (first 10 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty.
  2. Post initial impact message (template):
     - Subject: [INC][service] brief title
     - Body: one-line impact, estimated affected tenants, user-visible effect, immediate mitigation in progress.
  3. Attach top-3 telemetry graphs: p95 latency, request rate, error-rate (per-tenant).

- Quick mitigation decision matrix (summary):
  - If error-rate spike and p95 increased -> look for traffic shift or model regression.
  - If traffic surge without elevated error-rate -> provision temporary capacity or enable burst pool.
  - If sustained burn-rate > 2x baseline for 60m -> initiate throttling and notify product.

Ownership and responsibilities table:
| Role | Responsibility | OK to action without manager approval |
|-----|---------------|---------------------------------------|
| SLO owner (oncall) | Triage, execute mitigations, create incident ticket | Yes (scale, fallback, short-term throttles) |
| Rotation lead | Sign-off postmortem, progressive escalations | No (policy changes are escalated) |
| Capacity oncall | Provisioning, permanent capacity changes | No (requires capacity committee approval) |

SLO-specific quick references (examples):
- API-Gateway availability SLO: 99.95% (30d rolling), error budget 0.05%.
- Runtime-router latency SLO: p95 < 200ms for inference path, p99 < 600ms (window: 7d).
- Embeddings service correctness SLO: 98% similarity threshold pass rate (30d).

Training plan and milestones (first 90 days):
- Week 1–2: Complete checklist above and shadow two full rotations.
- Week 3–4: Run two live drills and participate in a capacity rehearsal.
- Month 1–2: Co-own one minor incident under supervision and produce post-incident notes.
- Month 3: Independently manage an escalation and be eligible for rotation lead consideration.

Continuous improvement notes (what to update in this doc):
- Add new commands when automation tooling changes.
- Update SLO thresholds when product SLOs change (owners to file Confluence change note).
- Add examples of new mitigation patterns (e.g., adaptive throttles) after tabletop validations.

Appendix A — Useful commands and links:
- SLO dashboard: https://metrics.redwood.internal/dashboards/slo-matrix
- PagerDuty playbook: https://pagerduty.com/orgs/redwood/services
- Capacity CLI: rfn-capacity (help: rfn-capacity --help)
- Trace UI: https://jaeger.company.local

Appendix B — Post-oncall checklist for outgoing engineer (handover):
1. Document unresolved actions with owners.
2. Export and link current top telemetry graphs.
3. Confirm any temporary mitigations remain or are part of a long-term plan.
4. Hand off any running audits or tickets to next rotation.

Notes and rationale:
- We require a formal sign-off to reduce silent SLO ownership drift. This runbook emphasizes evidence-based progression (drills, recorded actions) rather than ad-hoc approval.

Contact & ownership:
- Document owner: Maya Thompson (SRE).
- Rotation lead (example): Arjun Patel — contact via Slack @arjun.p.

Last reviewed: 2025-02-10 by Hannah Li.

title: Offline bundle signing – threat model brainstorm notes (working)
content:
Offline bundle signing – threat model brainstorm notes (working)

Context / why this exists
- We need to support fully offline/air-gapped installs of Redwood Private.
- Customer installs should be able to verify provenance + integrity of the entire offline bundle without any network access.
- The "formal" threat model will be written in Confluence; this doc is the scratchpad / brainstorming source.

In-scope assets (things we care about protecting)
- Offline bundle contents (examples, not exhaustive):
  - Installer binary / CLI + embedded configs
  - Helm charts / manifests
  - Container image references (and/or image tarballs if included)
  - Runtime/model artifacts, weights, tokenizer files, etc.
  - SBOM file(s) or pointers + checksums
  - Manifest describing bundle contents (version, build id, hashes)
  - Signature over manifest (detached or embedded)
  - Trust roots (public keys) that the installer uses for verification
- Build pipeline outputs:
  - The exact set of artifacts that are considered "the release"
  - The signing step + logs
- Local install state:
  - Previously installed version record used for downgrade prevention
  - Local audit logs/events about verification outcomes

Trust boundaries / threat surfaces
- Redwood build + release pipeline boundary
  - Who/what can influence artifact inputs?
  - Who can sign?
- Artifact publication boundary
  - Where bundles are stored pre-delivery (internal object store, release share)
- Customer transport boundary (high-risk)
  - Bundles moved via USB, secure courier, DVD, etc.
  - Unzip tools, line-ending conversions, antivirus “cleaning”, partial transfers
- Customer install boundary
  - On-prem installer verifies signature + hashes
  - Cluster admission/helm apply
- Post-install boundary
  - Day-2: upgrades, rollbacks, support bundles, audit export

Assumptions (need to confirm)
- Installer is allowed to fail closed (block install) on verification errors by default.
- Some customers will have unreliable time sources (no NTP; manual clocks; time skew).
- Customers may have constraints on crypto: FIPS mode, disallowing certain curves/algorithms.
- Customers might demand evidence: "who signed", "where is the root of trust", "how do you rotate".

Attacker profiles (who/what are we defending against)
- Opportunistic tampering during transport (malicious or accidental)
- Malware on a machine that touches the bundle (pre-install workstation) that can edit files
- Insider threat at Redwood: developer/release operator trying to ship a backdoored bundle
- Compromise of CI runner / build environment
- Compromise of signing key material (catastrophic)
- Customer-side malicious admin (less relevant; they can always bypass if root) BUT we still want strong auditing + safe defaults
- "Downgrade" attacker: pushes older but signed bundle to reintroduce known vuln
- "Confused deputy" via support / break-glass path abuse

Primary goals (security properties)
- Integrity: detect any modification of bundle contents.
- Authenticity/provenance: installer can verify bundle is signed by a Redwood-trusted signing key.
- Anti-replay/downgrade: prevent installing older signed bundles where policy disallows.
- Auditability: produce local evidence of verification + any overrides.
- Resilience: don’t brick customers during key rotation; support multiple keys.

Non-goals (likely)
- Confidentiality of artifacts inside the bundle (bundles are not encrypted). If customer needs encryption-at-rest during transport, that’s separate (e.g., customer-managed encryption).
- Preventing a fully privileged customer admin from installing whatever they want (but we should make bypass explicit and logged).

Attack tree brainstorm (rough)
Root: Customer ends up running a compromised/unauthorized Redwood Private deployment

1) Tamper with bundle contents
  1.1 Modify installer binary
    - Replace binary with trojan, keep filename
    - Patch verification routine to always pass
  1.2 Modify Helm chart/manifests
    - Add malicious init container / privileged pod
    - Change image registries/tags to attacker-controlled
    - Add cluster-admin bindings
  1.3 Modify container images (if images shipped as tar)
    - Swap layers / introduce backdoor
  1.4 Modify model/runtime artifacts
    - Insert payload in runtime plugin
    - Replace weights with watermarked/poisoned version (integrity goal; safety/quality risk)
  1.5 Modify manifest
    - Remove entries so modified artifact is unchecked
    - Swap hash algorithm identifier

2) Trick verification into accepting tampered content
  2.1 Canonicalization mismatch
    - Create a different JSON serialization that verifies under one tool but parses differently in installer
    - Unicode confusables / whitespace / key ordering edge cases
  2.2 Path traversal / symlink tricks inside bundle
    - Hash computed over one file, installer reads another (symlink swap)
    - Zip slip style extraction leading to overwritten trust store
  2.3 Hash collision / weak hash algorithm selection
    - Choose weak digest algorithm (avoid SHA1/MD5)
  2.4 Verification bypass via "break-glass" flag
    - Social engineering Support / customer operator to use override permanently

3) Replay / downgrade
  3.1 Install old signed bundle
    - Bundle is legitimate signature but contains known CVEs / old images
  3.2 Roll back local install state
    - Delete/modify local record so downgrade checks pass

4) Key / trust compromise
  4.1 Signing private key stolen
    - Attacker produces fully valid signed bundles
  4.2 Untrusted public key inserted into trust store
    - Modify installer trust store file in bundle or on disk
  4.3 Build pipeline signs wrong artifacts
    - "Time-of-check" vs "time-of-use" mismatch: manifest generated, then artifacts swapped before signing/publish

5) CI/CD compromise and build provenance gaps
  5.1 Compromised runner injects payload post-tests
  5.2 Dependency compromise (bundle tooling)
  5.3 Human error in release process
    - Signs staging build and publishes as prod

6) Time-based validation failures that cause unsafe workarounds
  6.1 Cert not-yet-valid / expired due to clock skew
    - Customer forced to use override, lowering security

Likely mitigations / design levers (brain dump)
- Sign a single canonical manifest that includes:
  - Bundle version + build_id
  - Hashes (SHA-256 minimum) for every included artifact
  - Explicit relative paths (normalized) and file sizes
  - Possibly a content-type field per artifact (installer/helm/image/model/sbom)
  - SBOM filename + hash (or pointer + hash)
  - Created_at timestamp (careful w/ time skew)
- Detached signature file (manifest.sig) + explicit envelope format
  - Avoid ambiguity: signature covers EXACT canonical bytes of manifest
  - Define canonicalization in spec/ADR (JSON canonicalization rules)
- Trust store strategy
  - Installer ships with embedded trusted public keys (or a trust store file packaged with installer)
  - Support multiple active keys (for rotation)
  - Pin key ids + allowlist
- Key ceremony + custody
  - HSM-backed keys where feasible
  - Two-person approval for signing operations (at least for key usage / release promotion)
  - Audit logs from KMS/HSM and CI
- Reproducible bundle builds (deterministic) where possible
  - Stable ordering of manifest entries
  - Avoid embedding local timestamps into artifacts unless captured as metadata fields and explicitly signed
- Verification behavior
  - Fail closed by default on: invalid signature, unknown key, manifest parse/canonicalization error, hash mismatch
  - Clear error codes and remediation guidance to reduce support pressure for unsafe bypass
- Downgrade prevention
  - Signed version metadata and local "installed version" state
  - Policy: allow rollback only to versions within a signed/approved window (e.g., last N versions) OR require explicit override with audit record
- Break-glass override
  - Should exist for operational continuity but should be gated:
    - require an explicit flag
    - produce loud console warnings
    - emit a local audit event "verification_bypassed"
    - optionally require a "reason" string
    - document approval path (Support + Security/Release)
- Local audit logging
  - On verify success/failure: capture key_id, bundle build_id, manifest digest, failure reason category
  - Ensure logs avoid sensitive data (no full paths if they include customer-specific details? maybe ok; TBD)
- Transport hardening guidance
  - Provide customer guidance for checksum verification post-transfer
  - Recommend tar over zip? Or provide a single bundle file format with predictable extraction
  - Warn about CRLF conversions / "smart" unzip tools
- Symlink and path traversal defenses
  - During bundle build: disallow symlinks in artifacts directory
  - During verification: resolve paths, ensure all paths stay within bundle root
  - Hash the extracted file bytes actually used
- Reduce reliance on wall clock
  - Prefer non-expiring signatures (key rotation handled by trust store updates) OR long validity windows
  - If using certs with validity: provide a controlled time source mechanism (e.g., allow passing explicit current time for diagnostics only)

Questions / open items to validate with Security Eng + Release Eng
- Crypto + envelope:
  - Are we using raw public keys (ed25519) vs X.509 cert chain?
  - If X.509: do we require full chain shipped in bundle? Where do roots live?
  - If ed25519: how do we represent key ids and rotate? (key id = hash of public key?)
  - Do we need FIPS mode compatibility? ed25519 may be problematic for some customers; ECDSA P-256 might be required.
  - Do we need dual-signing during transition/rotation (two signatures)?
- Time handling:
  - Are signatures time-bound? If yes, how do we handle air-gapped clock skew? Any "not-before" issues.
  - If not time-bound, how do we meet customer requirements for revocation? (revocation is hard offline)
- Revocation model:
  - If a signing key is compromised, how do we prevent acceptance in air-gapped envs that can’t receive updates?
  - Do we rely on trust store update distribution as the revocation mechanism?
  - Can we ship an emergency "trust store update" bundle to customers? What’s the operational plan?
- Bundle contents:
  - Are we signing image tarballs or just references? If just references, offline install still needs images somewhere.
  - If images are shipped, do we verify image digests and/or OCI layout signatures?
- Provenance evidence:
  - Do we need SLSA-ish provenance statements for customers? Or just internal evidence (GRC)?
  - What evidence must be kept for audits (build logs, signing logs, approvals)? Where stored and for how long?
- Failure mode UX:
  - What error taxonomy do we want (hash mismatch vs signature invalid vs unknown key vs parse/canonicalization error)?
  - What should be the message for "unknown key" during rotation (actionable: update installer trust store / upgrade installer)?
- Break-glass policy:
  - Who can approve? How do we communicate to customer? How do we ensure follow-up remediation?

Customer-driven constraints heard so far (from SE / calls)
- Air-gapped means no outbound network; sometimes even no internal NTP.
- Security teams want: "Show me your key ceremony", "Where are keys stored", "How do you rotate", "How do I audit that verification happened".
- Some customers require ability to export audit logs to SIEM later (even if offline at install time).
- Transport is messy: bundles often copied via Windows workstations or scanning tools that can alter files.

Potential abuse cases to explicitly call out in final threat model
- "Support tells customer to use break-glass" becomes a default workaround. Need guardrails + training.
- Key rotation that leaves older air-gapped sites stranded -> they disable verification entirely.
- Manifest canonicalization disagreements across versions -> signature verification failures -> customers request disabling checks.

Notes to incorporate into formal mitigations list
- Define canonical JSON rules once and test across languages (Go/Rust/Python) if applicable.
- Add integration tests for tampered bundles (modified manifest, swapped artifact, truncated bundle).
- Consider a separate "bundle inspect" command for Support/SE to diagnose quickly and reduce pressure to bypass.
- Make downgrade prevention explicit: signed "min_installer_version" and/or "min_bundle_version"? TBD.

Action items (rough)
- Marcus: sync with Connor + Sahana on CI threat scenarios (TOCTOU, signing wrong artifacts).
- Kevin: propose audit event schema fields + redaction guidance.
- Hanae: confirm key storage options + what’s feasible for FIPS customers.
- Ethan: confirm installer verification flow, especially symlink/path traversal handling.
- Olga/Daniel: list controls/evidence mapping needed for customer security reviews.

Appendix: quick checklist of "must answer" for threat model doc
- What’s the root of trust?
- What exactly is signed?
- How is canonicalization defined?
- How do we handle key rotation + compromise in offline environments?
- What do we log locally and how can it be exported?
- What are the break-glass conditions and approval flow?
- What is the downgrade policy?

title: Standardize timeout defaults + AbortController plumbing (streaming vs non-streaming)
content:
Standardize timeout defaults + AbortController plumbing (streaming vs non-streaming)

## Summary
Standardizes timeout behavior in the TS SDK and fixes AbortController wiring so cancellation/timeouts are applied correctly for both streaming and non-streaming requests. This brings TS into parity with the timeout model ADR and unblocks conformance tests around streaming idle hangs.

Primary changes:
- Introduce a single `timeouts` configuration block (`timeout_ms`, `connect_timeout_ms`, `read_timeout_ms`) at both client level and per-request override.
- Implement portable enforcement using `AbortController` for `timeout_ms` (overall per-attempt deadline).
- Implement streaming **idle** enforcement for `read_timeout_ms` by aborting the request if no bytes/events are observed for the configured period.
- Ensure we create a fresh AbortController/timers per retry attempt (no controller reuse across attempts).
- Document runtime limitations: granular connect/read enforcement is best-effort; browser fetch cannot reliably enforce connect timeouts, and non-streaming read timeout collapses to the overall timeout.

Refs:
- ADR: SDK Timeout Model (v1) — Overall + Connect/Read Timeouts (published 2026-01-24, updated 2026-02-18)
- ENG-5124: TypeScript retry/timeout refactor

## Motivation
Support + internal dogfooding found multiple edge cases where timeouts and cancellation were inconsistent:
- Streaming requests could remain open indefinitely when a corporate proxy half-opened the connection (no more events, no FIN).
- In Node, we were sometimes creating an AbortController but not consistently plumbing it through both request + stream reader.
- User-provided `signal` + SDK timeout signal were not combined, causing either (a) timeouts to be ignored or (b) user cancellation to be dropped depending on call path.

This PR implements the ADR semantics in TS and makes streaming timeout behavior predictable.

## Design / Behavior
### Public API
New standardized option names (client-level):
```ts
const client = new Redwood({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY,
  timeouts: {
    timeout_ms: 60_000,
    connect_timeout_ms: 10_000,
    read_timeout_ms: 60_000,
  },
});
```
Per-request override (RequestOptions):
```ts
await client.responses.create(
  { model: "redwood/llama-3.1-70b", input: "..." },
  { timeouts: { timeout_ms: 30_000 } }
);
```
Legacy compatibility:
- `timeout` (number) is still accepted (client + request options) and maps to `timeouts.timeout_ms`.
- A deprecation warning is emitted once per process when `timeout` is used.

### Defaults (per ADR)
- Non-streaming default: `timeout_ms=60_000`, `connect_timeout_ms=10_000`, `read_timeout_ms=60_000`
- Streaming default: `timeout_ms=600_000`, `connect_timeout_ms=10_000`, `read_timeout_ms=60_000` (idle)

Disabling:
- `timeout_ms=0` disables overall deadline enforcement (no AbortController timer for overall timeout).
- `read_timeout_ms=0` disables streaming idle enforcement.

### Streaming semantics
- `timeout_ms` is the max wall-clock lifetime of the stream (per attempt).
- `read_timeout_ms` is an **idle timeout** between bytes/events. If we do not observe any bytes/events for `read_timeout_ms`, we abort the request and throw a typed TimeoutError (`phase=read`).
- We reset the idle timer on *any* received chunk, not just fully parsed SSE events, to be resilient to proxy buffering behavior.

### Per-attempt semantics (retries)
Timeouts are applied per attempt. The retry layer instantiates a new controller/timers per attempt to avoid accidental cancellation propagation to subsequent attempts. (Total elapsed time bounding remains the responsibility of retry configuration.)

## Implementation details
### Abort signal merging
We now consistently merge user cancellation with SDK timeout cancellation:
- If `AbortSignal.any` exists (Node 20+/modern runtimes), we use it.
- Otherwise we fall back to a small local `mergeAbortSignals()` helper that forwards abort and preserves a best-effort abort reason.

### Overall timeout timer
- For `timeout_ms > 0`, we create an AbortController and schedule a timer that aborts it with reason `{ type: "timeout", phase: "overall", timeout_ms }`.
- We always clear timers in `finally` blocks to avoid leaks.

### Streaming idle timeout
- For streaming responses we wrap the response body reader and maintain a “last activity” timer.
- When the timer fires we abort the controller with reason `{ type: "timeout", phase: "read", timeout_ms: read_timeout_ms }`.
- We capture `x-request-id` once headers are available and attach it to the TimeoutError when possible (idle timeouts happen after headers, so request_id is usually present).

### Error surface
This PR adds/extends `TimeoutError` (SDK error taxonomy work is ongoing in a separate PR, but we need a stable shape here):
- `name`: `TimeoutError`
- `message`: includes `phase` + `timeout_ms`
- `request_id`: included when available
- `phase`: `overall | read | connect` (connect is currently best-effort / not reliably detected in fetch; set only when we can infer)
- `retryable`: `true`

Non-timeout aborts:
- If the user signal aborts, we surface an `AbortError` mapped to our SDK error wrapper and do **not** label as TimeoutError.

### Runtime limitations (documented)
- Browser fetch cannot reliably implement `connect_timeout_ms` at the network layer; we accept the option for parity but do not enforce it.
- For non-streaming requests, `read_timeout_ms` is effectively equivalent to overall `timeout_ms` with fetch; we keep the knob for parity but document that enforcement is via overall deadline.

## Tests
- Unit tests:
  - Non-streaming request aborts after `timeout_ms`.
  - Streaming idle abort triggers after `read_timeout_ms` of inactivity and yields TimeoutError with `phase=read`.
  - Streaming overall abort triggers after `timeout_ms` even if bytes continue.
  - Merged signals: user abort wins and does not get classified as timeout.
  - Retry attempt isolation: first attempt timeout does not cancel subsequent attempt controller.
- Added fixtures for the conformance suite runner to simulate “no more bytes” on stream bodies (Node test harness).

## Docs / Developer notes
- Updated inline option docs + README snippet in this repo to use `timeouts.*` naming.
- Added a short “Timeouts & streaming” section to `docs/streaming.md` explaining idle vs overall and how to disable each.
- Follow-up docs-site PR will mirror these examples across languages (tracked in ENG-5128).

## Rollout / Compatibility
- No API removals in this PR.
- The only behavior change is the introduction of defaults for streaming overall timeout + idle timeout in cases where callers were relying on “infinite” streams. Callers can set `timeouts.timeout_ms=0` and/or `timeouts.read_timeout_ms=0` to preserve the previous behavior.

---

### Changed areas (high level)
- `src/core/requestOptions.ts`: introduce `Timeouts` type + normalization (legacy `timeout` -> `timeouts.timeout_ms`).
- `src/core/fetcher.ts`: consistent AbortController creation per attempt; signal merging; cleanup.
- `src/streaming/sse.ts`: add idle timer + activity reset on chunk reads; improved cancellation semantics.
- `src/errors.ts`: add `TimeoutError` fields + mapping from abort reason.
- `test/timeouts/*.test.ts`: new coverage for overall + idle timeouts and merged signals.

### Notable snippet (illustrative)
We now abort with a structured reason so we can differentiate user abort vs timeout abort:
```ts
controller.abort({ type: "timeout", phase: "read", timeout_ms: readTimeoutMs });
```
and later map to `TimeoutError` in a single place.

## Review conversation (highlights)
**Ibrahim Khan (requested changes)**: “Please align defaults + semantics exactly to the timeout ADR table (60s non-streaming / 10m streaming; idle=60s). Also confirm per-attempt controller creation under retries.”

**Dana Lo (author)**: “Updated defaults to match ADR; added an explicit `createAttemptSignals()` helper used by both non-streaming and streaming paths so retries always allocate a fresh controller + timers.”

**Allison Grant**: “For streaming idle timeout, reset on bytes read rather than parsed events; proxies can buffer SSE frames and we should treat any bytes as activity.”

**Dana Lo**: “Done. Idle timer now resets on each `reader.read()` chunk. Added a regression test where partial SSE frames arrive in multiple chunks.”

**Sahana Iyer**: “CI is running Node 18 in one workflow; `AbortSignal.any` isn’t available there.”

**Dana Lo**: “Added a polyfill merge helper with feature detection; Node 18 job is green now.”

**Henry Cho**: “Make sure the deprecation warning for `timeout` is non-spammy.”

**Dana Lo**: “Warning is once-per-process (guarded by a module-level flag). Also added a doc note showing the new `timeouts` block.”

### Approvals
- Ibrahim Khan: Approved
- Allison Grant: Approved
- Monica Patel: Approved

## CI
- lint: pass
- unit tests: pass
- integration (node fetch streaming): pass
- build: pass

## Follow-ups
- Wire conformance suite “timeout phase” expectations once error taxonomy PR lands (ENG-5126).
- Docs-site parity update (ENG-5128).
TypeScript SDK now supports a standardized `timeouts` config block: `timeout_ms`, `connect_timeout_ms`, `read_timeout_ms`.
Default timeouts are now consistent with the SDK timeout ADR (non-streaming: 60s overall; streaming: 10m overall + 60s idle).
Streaming now enforces an idle read timeout (no bytes/events) via AbortController to avoid hung streams behind proxies.
Legacy `timeout` option is still accepted but is deprecated; it maps to `timeouts.timeout_ms`.

title: Lodestar Retail AI
content:
Lodestar Retail AI

▶ Summary: POC completed (month-long): integrated personalization model, latency target ~150ms p50 across NA. Results met functional QoE but economics gap large.

▶ What happened:
- AE/SE ran model variants (ffhq-open-65B quantized + 8-bit int8 on dedicated droplet) during POC. Token usage tracked at ~18M tokens/wk for personalization pipelines.
- Finance pushed back: projected monthly GPU burn + per-token costs leave payback >18 months given current ARR profile.
- Procurement flagged minimum commit as too high (preferred smaller commit or spot/usage).
- Internal champion (Dir. ML Ops, Priya Rao) moved to a new role; no replacement champion identified.

▶ Customer quotes / paraphrase:

- "Competitor offered dedicated instance with steep commit discount — procurement liked the guaranteed unit cost."

▶ Economics details discussed:
- Redwood proposal: 2x V100-equivalent GPUs (dedicated) reserved, expected token cost $0.0025/token for generation profile.
- Lodestar finance calc: effective cost after infra overhead ~ $0.004/token; need <$0.002 to hit internal ROI targets.
- They asked for batching/caching recommendations and 3 alternative pricing scenarios: lower commit + autoscale burst, smaller reserved cluster + intelligent routing to cheaper region, and hosted API with tighter rate caps.

▶ Security / deployment notes:

- Next step: craft 2 new commercial options (smaller commit + performance-based uplift; or hosted trial with capped spend) and re-open conversation mid-April after their budget cycle. SE to prepare new cost projection using Optimize suggestions (batching + KV caching) to show path to ~$0.002/token.

Notes tone: terse, CRM shorthand. Repeat follow-ups attempted (email + two voicemails) — no response since 2026-01-20.

Auric Bridge Tech

- Avg tokens/request: 1.6k (system + user + conversation history).
- 70% of calls share common product prefix content. Good candidate for prefix/KV caching.
- Real-time latency target: 200-400ms P95 for single-turn responses; throughput modest (20-60 rps bursts).
- Current model: open-model small-medium sized (customer sampled gpt-like open checkpoint). May accept quantized variants.

- Example prompt compression templates and automated rewrite suggestions.
