title: Thunderbolt AI - Dedicated surge & isolation intake
content:
Thunderbolt AI - Dedicated surge & isolation intake

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lucas Ramirez (Head of Platform, Thunderbolt AI), Priya Singh (SRE), Owen Park (CTO)

Summary:
Thunderbolt AI is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private for a low-latency real-time recommendation service used in multiplayer games. Primary concerns: reserved GPU sizing, tenant isolation, burst-to-4x traffic patterns during events, latency SLOs (95p < 80ms), encryption/KMS (Azure Key Vault), SOC 2 compliance, and on-prem path as contingency. They asked about failover playbooks, warm pools/prewarm behavior, and pricing for reserved nodes + burst credits.

Topics:
- Workload profile and burst patterns
- Isolation and tenancy model (hot pools, tenant fencing)
- Failover and fallback to hosted model
- Prewarm / warm pool strategies and costs
- Compliance: SOC 2, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integration
- Timeline and procurement constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros—I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and with me is Ravi, our SE focused on Dedicated and Private deployments.
[00:12] Lucas: Hey Maya, hey Ravi. Lucas here, Head of Platform at Thunderbolt AI. Thanks for making time.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, SRE. We'll likely be the ones running the fist fights when things go sideways.
[00:22] Owen: Owen, CTO. I'll listen in; happy to answer higher-level questions.
[00:26] Maya: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand your peak patterns and isolation needs so we can recommend reserve sizing and failover options. Roughly 45 minutes, leave some time for next steps. Sound good?
[00:34] Lucas: Sounds good. We'll jump in.
[00:35] Ravi: Quick note—if it helps later I can pull up the docs for prewarming and our warm-pool cost model.

[02:05] Lucas: To give context: we run a real-time recommendation engine for a live multiplayer title. Typical traffic is low steady-state, then during tournaments/events traffic spikes 3-4x for short bursts (10-40 minutes). We need 95th percentile inference latency under 80ms for player-facing calls.
[02:25] Priya: Most requests are short sequences, 32 tokens or under, but throughput is high. We also can't have noisy neighbors; when one tenant runs training or batch jobs, it breaks our tail latency.
[03:02] Maya: Got it. Sounds like isolation and tail latency are the big ones. Have you considered Dedicated pools vs Hosted fallback model?
[03:12] Lucas: We like the economics of hosted for baseline, but we need guaranteed performance for peaks. Thinking about a dedicated reserved pool (or a warm reserved hot pool) for critical traffic and fallback to hosted API for non-critical flows.
[03:29] Ravi: That's a common pattern—dedicated for SLO-critical traffic, hosted for overflow. We support routing policies that prefer dedicated, with automatic fallback to hosted variants when capacity is exhausted. We also support model variants (quantized or smaller models) as fallbacks.

[04:10] Priya: A couple of concrete questions: how fast can you spin up burst capacity? And how does warm pool prewarm behave—do you keep GPUs hot and is there a prewarm cost?
[04:22] Ravi: Prewarm: you can configure a warm-pool size that maintains kernels and KV states warmed. There's a continuous cost for reserved warm nodes; it's cheaper than full-on spare nodes because they can be smaller or quantized for faster resume. We also offer burst credits for short bursts if you have reserved capacity. For spin-up to fully ready, warm pool to fully warmed serving path is typically under 90s; cold spin from zero can be several minutes depending on model size.
[04:51] Lucas: Ninety seconds is ok but sometimes our spikes are sudden—tournament queue opens and we get hit instantly. Can we do instant failover to hosted and still maintain the same model?
[05:04] Maya: You can. We allow routing to point to hosted model variants with compatible behavior. There will be slight differences if the hosted variant is quantized differently; we can test parity with your eval prompts.

[06:10] Owen: Security: we need KMS integration (we're on Azure Key Vault), SOC 2 Type II, SSO via Okta, and audit logs for every inference. How does Redwood handle that?
[06:24] Ravi: For Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via our KMS integrations; Azure Key Vault is supported. We can enable envelope encryption so keys never leave your control. SOC 2 artifacts and the compliance pack can be shared—I'll add them to the follow-up. Audit logs and per-route tracing are available; you can ship logs to your SIEM or retain in Redwood console.
[06:46] Priya: Do the audit logs include per-token traces or just request-level metadata? We need enough detail to debug tail cases.
[06:54] Ravi: Currently request headers, request/response sizes, latency breakdowns and model selection events are logged. Full token-level traces can be enabled in debug mode but with cost and privacy considerations; we usually advise redacting PII.

[08:12] Lucas: Another operational question—how do you enforce tenancy isolation? We want burst traffic from other tenants, or internal batch jobs from our non-prod tenant, to never impact prod.
[08:26] Ravi: Dedicated Reserved can be configured with soft or hard isolation. Hard isolation pins GPUs to your tenancy (no multi-tenancy). Soft isolation uses fenced hot pools where compute is dedicated but control plane can borrow under emergency. For strict SLAs you want hard isolation. Our hot-pool topology supports tenant fencing at node-level.
[08:50] Priya: What's the blast radius if a hardware failure occurs on a pinned node? Do you prewarm standby nodes or have automatic failover?
[08:58] Ravi: For pinned nodes we recommend N+1 standbys. There is an automated failover into standby nodes, but warm standby reduces time to recovery. If you want near-zero impact you can provision hot-standbys that are warmed and ready. That increases cost, but it's the usual trade-off.

[10:12] Lucas: Cost is a big factor—our finance team will push back on always-on hot standbys. We need guidance on sizing so we don't overcommit.
[10:21] Maya: We can do a sizing exercise. If you share typical QPS and token distribution we can model reserved node counts and warm-pool sizing. We also provide a cost/latency tradeoff sheet.
[10:33] Owen: Quick procurement note—we have a 60-day procurement cycle and prefer 12-month committed pricing for reserved capacity. Do you offer monthly vs annual commits?
[10:44] Maya: Yes, reserved commitments can be monthly or annual; annual has better pricing. We'll include both options in the pricing matrix.

[12:15] Priya: What's the difference between Dedicated and Private here? If we need on-prem later, how big a lift is migrating?
[12:26] Ravi: Private is essentially running Redwood control plane in your VPC or on-prem package. The APIs are consistent but Private brings additional network and install controls. Migration is straightforward if you keep model versions and config consistent, but there is an integration cost: networking, KMS, and potential hardware procurement. We have reference on-prem manifests and a runbook.
[12:50] Lucas: For now we're leaning Dedicated but want Private as a contingency in case regulations tighten.
[12:59] Maya: That's a common path—start on Dedicated, then move to Private if needed.

[14:05] Lucas: One more technical—how does the runtime handle KV cache across sequence continuity? We rely heavily on KV cache for context, and eviction can harm latency.
[14:18] Ravi: We manage KV cache per-session and have configurable cache retention policies. For Dedicated we can tune cache sizes and prioritize your tenant's KV allocations to reduce cache churn. There was a minor note in our docs where KV cache got transcribed as 'KV cash' sometimes in automated notes—sorry for the typo in the docs.
[14:34] Priya: Ha, yes I saw that.

[15:44] Lucas: For burst modeling—our peak bursts historically last 15-30 minutes. We might see a 3.5x spike for the first 10 minutes then taper. If we reserve nodes for average peak it's wasteful. Are there hybrid models—like partial reserved + burst credits?
[15:58] Ravi: Yes, hybrid is typical: reserve a baseline of capacity to cover median peaks and then have either warm-pool sizing to cover the initial spike and fallback to hosted for overflow, or reserve a small hot standbys pool plus burst credits. We can also suggest model quantization and smaller model variants to absorb overflow with less cost.
[16:30] Lucas: Can you run a simulated burst with our sample load so we can see tail latency behavior?
[16:40] Maya: Absolutely. If you can share a representative load generator and a small prompt corpus, we can run a hosted simulation or spin up a small Dedicated trial environment.

[18:10] Priya: Networking—we need VPC peering and strict egress controls. Does Redwood Dedicated allow VPC peering?
[18:19] Ravi: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private networking. For Private deployments you'd have full control. For Dedicated hosted in our cloud region we offer VPC peering and restricted egress with customer NAT. We'll share network diagrams.

[19:45] Owen: I want to call out parity of model behavior—if we route to hosted fallback, we must guarantee minimal semantic drift. How do you evaluate that?
[19:59] Ravi: We recommend running an eval suite—sample prompts, quality checks, and A/B comparisons. Redwood Optimize has a regression alerting feature tied to prompt sets; we can run the same tests across variants and give a delta report.

[22:05] Lucas: Are there any hard limitations on model size for warm pools? We use a 30B model currently, but might move to 70B for specific tournament features.
[22:18] Ravi: Warm pools can handle larger models but cost and warm time grow. For 70B the warm-to-ready time is longer and you may need more reserved memory. Another option is a mixed fleet: keep a smaller 30B tuned variant warmed for the common path and enable a slower 70B path only for high-value calls.

[24:30] Priya: How do you price reserved nodes vs warm pool instances? Is warm pool cheaper because of shared memory or is it just a smaller instance type?
[24:44] Maya: Warm pool pricing is typically lower than fully warmed serving nodes because they can be configured to be smaller or use quantized flavors. But the pricing varies by region and GPU type. We'll include detailed per-GPU SKU pricing in the follow-up.

[26:05] Lucas: Any vendor lock-in concerns? If we wanted to move off after a year, how easy is it?
[26:15] Ravi: We provide model and config exports; the runtime uses standard model formats. Network and infra teardown is the main work. We also support pinned model versions and recommend a data egress plan in the contract.

[28:30] Priya: Regarding SLOs—what's Redwood's SLA for Dedicated? We need specifics for uptime and p95 latency commitments.
[28:40] Maya: Dedicated SLA covers uptime of the control plane and your reserved capacity. For latency SLOs we provide guidance and per-route SLO monitoring; contractual latency SLOs are available on enterprise contracts with accepted guardrails. We'll include template SLA language.

[30:05] Lucas: Competitors—someone internally suggested DeepServe because they have pre-baked gaming optimizations. How do you compare?
[30:14] Maya: DeepServe is focused on model-side optimizations for gaming but we differentiate on unified routing, observability, and enterprise controls. We'll share a competitive brief.

[32:20] Owen: On the timeline—if we decide to move forward, what is a realistic ramp for Reserved dedicated capacity?
[32:31] Ravi: From contract to live varies; typically 4-8 weeks including network setup, model onboarding, and warm-pool tuning. If you want quicker ramp we can do a hybrid start on Hosted then flip routes once Dedicated is ready.

[34:10] Lucas: Let's cover a couple of edge cases: sudden peak plus regional outage—can you failover across regions?
[34:21] Ravi: Yes—cross-region routing and automated fallback policies exist. However, model parity and cold-start times differ. We can replicate model artifacts to a standby region; that's an added cost.

[36:00] Priya: For the technical deep dive, Priya will need details on kernel selection, quantization tradeoffs, and batching behavior at short sequences. Who should lead that?
[36:12] Maya: Ravi can lead the deep dive. He'll walk through batching heuristics, kernel choices, and KV cache tuning.

[38:05] Lucas: Can you include an initial sizing sketch in the follow-up? Even rough numbers help our procurement.
[38:14] Maya: Yes—we'll model multiple scenarios: conservative, balanced, and aggressive (covering 4x short bursts).

[40:20] Owen: We should also consider a canary strategy for rollout. We prefer canary -> phased -> full. Does Redwood Console support canary and A/B routing?
[40:32] Ravi: Yes, canary rollouts, weighted traffic routing, and automatic fallback policies are supported. You can set thresholds to auto-rollback on regression alerts.

[42:05] Lucas: Priya—anything we missed from an SRE perspective?
[42:11] Priya: Just two things: our compliance team will likely ask for network flow logs and KMS proofs; and we want a runbook for incident scenarios involving warm pool exhaustion.
[42:23] Ravi: We'll include a runbook template and network flow guidance in the follow-up.

[45:00] Maya: Ok, quick recap and next steps: we'll send pricing and reserve options, KMS/SOC2 artifacts, schedule the technical 60-min deep dive with Priya and Lucas, and run a hosted burst simulation if you can share the load generator.
[45:17] Lucas: Sounds good. We'll share a load generator and sample prompts by EOB tomorrow.
[45:24] Maya: Great—we'll aim to have materials to you by Friday.

[46:50] Owen: One more thought—if we choose annual commit, is there any enterprise discount for multi-year?
[46:59] Maya: Yes, multi-year discounts are part of enterprise negotiations; we'll flag that to the sales ops team.

[48:30] Priya: Small nit: will test harnesses be able to collect p99 traces? We want to see tail behavior; p95 isn't enough for major tournaments.
[48:41] Ravi: You can enable extended tracing in test mode, but it has overhead. For p99 we usually advise dedicated profiling runs with a small set of traced sessions.

[50:05] Lucas: Ok, I think that's everything for now. Thanks all.
[50:12] Maya: Thank you, we'll follow up with docs and pricing.
[50:20] Owen: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

title: Colocation rack power & cooling planning — on-prem GPU pools (Q2 2026)
content:
Colocation rack power & cooling planning — on-prem GPU pools (Q2 2026)

Purpose:
Plan for next-phase on-prem / colo GPU pool growth: define per-rack power and cooling budgets, physical U-space layouts, PDU/amperage constraints, and rollout checklist for Q2 2026. This is an operational planning sheet — rough numbers and open questions are intentionally included.

Summary / goals:
- Add 48 x A800-equivalent GPUs across two colo sites (site A + site B) to support Dedicated surge capacity and private-customer pools.
- Target average rack PUE and cooling capacity so we don’t exceed facility power draw and can keep inlet temps <= 30C under 95th percentile load.
- Prefer 1:1 cold-aisle containment where feasible; evaluate water-cooled trays if density > 40 GPUs/rack.

High-level assumptions (call these out):
- GPU model used for baseline calculations: NVIDIA Hopper-class A800 (nominal max TDP 350W).
- Typical node: 8x A800 per 2U chassis (8 GPUs per node), with dual PSUs and 3U networking overhead for dense configs.
- Node idle draw: ~120W per GPU-equivalent (includes CPU, NVMe, fans under light load).
- Service overhead per rack: 1 top-of-rack switch (800W), KVM, management 200W.
- Facility power deliverable per rack: negotiable; baseline target is 20kW per rack (208V, 3-phase with 80A PDUs), can push to 30kW with water-cooling/engineering signoff.
- Target operating margin: reserve 15% headroom below facility PDU limit for transient spikes.

Detailed capacity math (baseline):
- Per GPU sustained draw estimate: 300W (conservative for mixed inference workloads).
- For 8 GPUs/node, node draw = 8 * 300W + 200W (CPUs/SSD/fans) = 2,600W ≈ 2.6kW.
- With 42U rack and conservative spacing (account for 3U network + PDUs), we can fit 16 nodes (32U used) => total compute draw = 16 * 2.6kW = 41.6kW (too high for simple air-cooled rack).
- Air-cooled safe configuration (20kW per rack): back-calc nodes supported = floor((20kW - 1.0kW overhead) / 2.6kW) = floor(19kW / 2.6kW) = 7 nodes => 56 GPUs/rack at ~300W/GPU seems inconsistent with earlier density numbers because node size assumption must be rechecked.
- Alternative realistic packing: 4 nodes per rack (2U nodes) would be 8 GPUs/node => 16 GPUs/rack? That’s low density but fits 20kW budget.

Candidate rack profiles (quick variants):
- Profile A — Air-cooled standard (priority: simplicity, lower colo cost)
  - Power budget: 20kW per rack (80A 3-phase); usable ~17kW after 15% headroom.
  - Node config: 2U, 4 nodes/rack (8 GPUs/node) = 32 GPUs/rack.
  - Estimated draw: 32 * 300W + 1.2kW overhead = 10.8kW => comfortably under budget; leaves room for bursty workloads or denser nodes later.
  - Pros: widely supported by colo, cheaper. Cons: lower density, higher rack count.

- Profile B — High-density air + enhanced airflow (containment)
  - Power budget: 24kW per rack (requires colo approval).
  - Node config: 2U, 8 nodes/rack = 64 GPUs/rack (if mechanical layout allows).
  - Estimated draw: 64 * 300W + 1.5kW overhead = 20.7kW => within 24kW.
  - Cons: requires cold-aisle containment and higher fan noise/maintenance; risk if cooling fails.

- Profile C — Liquid-assisted high-density
  - Power budget: 30kW+ per rack, water-cooled rear-door or direct-to-chip allowed.
  - Node config: 4U or specialized trays, 128 GPUs/rack feasible with D2C.
  - Use when we need minimal floor space (e.g., enterprise private racks).
  - Draw: depends on vendor; ensure leak-detection and redundancy.

Site-by-site initial plan (two colo sites):
- Site A (primary): 12 racks available; initial commit: 6 racks. Choose mix: 4 x Profile A, 2 x Profile B to balance density.
  - Compute capacity estimate (approx): (4 * 32) + (2 * 64) = 128 + 128 = 256 GPUs initial.
- Site B (secondary / DR): 8 racks available; initial commit: 4 racks of Profile A for predictable cooling.
  - Capacity: 4 * 32 = 128 GPUs.
- Combined initial on-prem/colo pool: ~384 GPUs across sites. Scaling plan: add 6 racks over 6 months as demand grows.

Power & electrical notes (actionable):
- PDUs: prefer 2x 63A 3-phase PDUs per rack (A+B) on separate feeds. Specify monitoring PDUs with per-outlet metering (Vendor quote VC-3321 covers metered PDUs).
- Breaker requirements: ensure dedicated 3-phase breakers; confirm site wiring (is it 208V vs 400V?) — open question for Site B.
- Generator/UPS: target N+1 UPS for racks serving production Dedicated customers; confirm UPS runtime at expected draw (e.g., 10 racks at 20kW each -> 200kW draw).

Cooling & mechanical notes:
- Baseline air-cooled racks: ensure cold-aisle containment and Aisle-Inlet temp sensors at multiple heights (bottom, mid, top).
- Recommend vendor-supplied airflow management hardware (blanking panels, baffles) for dense racks.
- If any rack > 22kW, require cold-door/water cooling conversation. Obtain quote for Rear Door Heat Exchanger (RDHx) for two candidate racks at Site A.
- Facility PUE target: negotiate for <1.6 at site level for racks consumed by GPU fleet.

Space planning (U count):
- Reserve 3U per rack for networking and management (not counted in GPU capacity).
- Cable management: plan 2U front and rear for cable trays in Profile B/C.
- Weight: approximate 80kg per 2U node (incl rails), ensure floor loading > 1500kg per rack. Confirm with colo.

Network and I/O constraints:
- To avoid top-of-rack bottlenecks, provision 2 x 100GbE uplinks per rack (LACP) and optional 1 x 400Gb spine links later.
- Topology: flat fabric for dedicated clusters; per-tenant VLAN segmentation for private pools.

Cost drivers (rough estimates to include in procurement):
- Colo power premium for >20kW racks: +$2,500 / rack/month vs standard 10kW baseline.
- RDHx retrofit: ~$6k–10k per rack + maintenance.
- Metered PDU (2x63A): ~$2k–3k per rack.
- Installation / commissioning labor: ~16–24 hours per rack.

Open questions / risks (to resolve before ordering):
- Confirm Site B phase/wiring and PDU amperage availability (ticket to colo ops).
- Confirm regulatory/compliance requirements for any customer data in private racks (KMS/HSM proximity).
- Failure modes for RDHx: plan for bypass if water cooling offline — automatic fallback to lower-power mode with GPU shedding policy.
- Spare parts: how many spare nodes and spare PSUs to stock per site? Suggest 2 spare nodes per 12 racks.

Immediate next steps (owner / ETA):
- [Sana] Draft vendor RFQ for PDUs and RDHx (ETA 2026-03-08) — link: GH PR above.
- [Ethan] Verify Site B electrical specs with colo rep and upload power diagram (ETA 2026-03-05).
- [Priya] Cost model update for colo tiers and expected monthly burn; incorporate into Dedicated pricing sheet (ETA 2026-03-12).
- [Luca] Run thermal simulation for Profile B racks using baseline workload traces (ETA 2026-03-15).

Appendix: example per-rack quick checklist for install day
- Confirm 3-phase feeds present and separate PDUs installed (A/B).
- Verify rack grounding and bonding.
- Measure floor loading and confirm seismic/anchoring as required.
- Install blanking panels and airflow management hardware before powering nodes.
- Connect and configure metered PDU and integrate with DCIM alerting.
- Run load tests to 95th percentile expected token throughput for 2 hours and confirm inlet temps < 30C.

Notes to self (raw):
- Might need to standardize on a slightly lower-GPU TDP profile (e.g., 260W) for some private customer racks to avoid costly watercooling.
- Check with legal about language for colo contracts referencing liquid-cooling equipment.
- Keep a two-week buffer between receiving racks and provisioning GPUs (cable/PDUs/testing).

End of sheet — comments welcome.

title: cross-SDK stream resume + graceful token refresh bridge (python/ts/go)
content:
cross-SDK stream resume + graceful token refresh bridge (python/ts/go)

Motivation: long-lived streaming sessions occasionally encounter mid-stream 401/403 during token expiry/rotation. Clients either dropped the stream (losing partial results) or had to re-establish and reparse responses, causing UX roughness and higher error rates for interactive apps. This PR introduces a cross-SDK compatibility layer and ergonomics improvements to allow graceful token refresh and optional in-band resume semantics so higher-level applications can recover without full restart. Summary of changes: 1) wire-level: introduce an opt-in resume_token header and an optional resume handshake message for streaming transports. The contract is backward-compatible: servers not advertising resume support simply ignore the header. 2) auth: implement a LeakyTokenRefresh shim that transparently handles 401/reauth during an active stream and attempts a resume when the server supports it. 3) SDK ergonomics: Python adds Stream.as_context() to get automatic refresh + cleanup; TypeScript exposes AsyncIterable.withResume({timeout}) helper; Go adds StreamResumer interface and a small helper in the connection pool to retry with jittered backoff. 4) tests: new integrational mocks that simulate mid-stream expiry and validate exactly-once resume semantics for client-visible events. 5) versions: minor bumps to sdk packages to publish compatibility patches (python 1.8.0, typescript 2.4.3, go 0.9.2). Compatibility notes: the new resume header is optional, and servers must explicitly opt into resume behaviour. Existing SDKs will continue to work unchanged if not using the new helpers. Rollout plan: feature gated behind server-side flag for the first two weeks; telemetry added to monitor resume success/failure and any duplicated events. Checklist: - [x] design doc and sequences (linked) - [x] implementation across python/ts/go - [x] unit & integration tests - [x] e2e harness against mock token rotation - [x] docs snippets for SDKs - [x] version bumps and changelogs - [x] telemetry dashboards and alerts (QA)
Liam O'Connor: Can we ensure resume_token can't be replayed? Suggest tying resume_token to connection-id and short TTL.
Maya Singh (author): Reply: added connection-id binding and enforce 5s TTL server-side in design; client includes connection checksum in header to reduce replay risk.
Priya Raman: Question: how does this interact with function-calling / structured responses mid-stream? We need to ensure partial structured frames are re-emitted exactly once.
Maya Singh (author): Reply: shrunk atomic frame unit boundary in transport; integration tests validate dedupe by frame-sequence id. Added note in docs.
Diego Alvarez: CI flaked on linux/py3.11 matrix; re-run fixed it. Please add a small test that asserts no .close() leak when resuming fails.
Maya Singh (author): Reply: added test and resource cleanup in Stream.as_context() implementation.
SDKs: add optional graceful streaming resume and transparent token-refresh helpers across Python/TypeScript/Go. Backward compatible; opt-in resume header required. Minor version bumps: python 1.8.0, typescript 2.4.3, go 0.9.2. See docs/sdk/streaming-resume.md for migration guide.

title: Dock ACPI _DSM change reorders kernel modules and breaks encrypted-home mount during Linux provisioning
content:
Dock ACPI _DSM change reorders kernel modules and breaks encrypted-home mount during Linux provisioning

Issue summary:
During staging workstation provisioning, machines docked to the new TB4 dock (firmware v1.3.0) intermittently fail to mount the user's encrypted home (LUKS) during first-boot setup. The system stops at 'Waiting for encrypted partition' and drops into emergency mode.

Impact:
- Blocks automated imaging and enrollment for developers receiving docked laptops in staging.
- Affects both Dell XPS and Lenovo X1 hardware when docked during provisioning; undocked provisioning completes fine.
- Slows down depot turnaround and blocks a handful of on-call tasks.

Environment:
- Linux image: Ubuntu 22.04.5 + custom preseed (rd.luks.options set), kernel 6.1.47 (custom patches), initramfs generated by image-scripts v0.15.
- Dock firmware: TB4-dock v1.3.0 (rolled 2026-03-09).
- Provisioning server: staging provisioner behind NAT in us-west.
- Repro rate: ~40% of docked workflows, 0% when same device imaged undocked.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Attach laptop to TB4 dock (firmware v1.3.0).
2) Boot PXE to provisioning image, start automated installer (preseed).
3) Installer reaches disk partitioning and sets up LUKS for /home (automated).
4) Reboot into first-boot initramfs to unlock LUKS.
5) Observe initramfs fails to find underlying block device and drops to emergency shell.

Observed logs (key excerpts):
- journalctl (first-boot) shows: "blk_update_request: I/O error, dev nvme0n1, sector ..." then "udevd: failed to apply ACPI _DSM properties"
- initramfs debug: device nodes present (/dev/nvme0n1p3) but cryptsetup open fails with "Device or resource busy"
- dmesg: new ACPI _DSM object parsed, acpi_device_add changed ordering for USB/PCI hotplug events
- modprobe ordering: sometimes zram, then nvme, then a storage controller module; on successful boots nvme is probed earlier.

Investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: Dock firmware v1.3.0 exposes an ACPI _DSM method that triggers a late rebind of USB-attached NVMe bridges, altering the timing of block device availability during initramfs.
- Hypothesis B: The dock advertises an extra PSCI device and triggers kernel to probe a composite driver which delays nvme driver init order.
- Reproduced in lab with two different docks with v1.3.0; downgraded dock to v1.2.1 and provisioning succeeded for same machines.
- Captured early boot trace with initramfs + kmsg: shows module load order differs between good and bad runs.
- Tried forcing cryptsetup to wait for device (sleep 10s) as a workaround — reduces repro rate but not reliable.

Root cause (working theory):
Dock firmware change introduced an ACPI _DSM entry that causes the kernel to register an additional ACPI device late in early userspace. This shifts probe ordering so the NVMe controller module is loaded after initramfs attempts to open the encrypted partition, causing intermittent "device busy" or missing-device failures. The problem manifests only when the dock is attached because the device tree and ACPI namespace differ.

Temporary workaround implemented:
- Image-scripts: added a patch to initramfs that retries cryptsetup with exponential backoff up to 30s and explicitly triggers udev settle before unlocking. Deployed to staging (image-scripts v0.15.2).
- Procurement/Depot: advised to image undocked devices until dock firmware is rolled back.

Permanent remediation plan:
- Engineering (kernel/infra) to add a udev/kernel probe ordering fix: prefer NVMe controller binding earlier when block devices are expected during initramfs. (ENG ticket target: low-level module ordering patch).
- Work with Dock vendor to supply a firmware patch that removes or corrects the ACPI _DSM behavior (open vendor SR).
- Add an initramfs feature flag to wait for named block devices for critical partitions when docks are present; expose as a config in image-scripts.

Follow-up tasks:
- INT-884421: Create depot SOP to undock units before imaging (assigned to Depot Ops).
- ENG-PRIORITY: Kernel/module probe ordering engineering task (assigned to kernel team).
- Ops: Add automated boot-time diagnostic capture (kmsg + udevadm info) for next 50 failed boots.

Resolution notes (so far):
- Workaround (initramfs retry) reduced failures in staging from ~40% to ~6%.
- Vendor acknowledged a regression in the dock firmware and opened a ticket; vendor ETA for firmware patch: 2 weeks (awaiting confirmation).

Customer-facing impact: None (internal-only).

Next steps:
- Keep ticket In Progress until vendor firmware or kernel patch is deployed and we've validated 7 days of successful provisioning runs in staging (>99% success).
- Once validated, create a small Ops change to schedule dock firmware roll-forward in depots and update provisioning SOP.

2026-03-10 10:12 - Aisha Khan (Support): Initial report from Imaging team. Added logs and early traces. Assigned to Marcus for triage.
2026-03-10 14:05 - Marcus Lee (Infra Eng): Reproduced in lab on two units. Downgraded dock firmware to v1.2.1 and repro disappeared. Collecting kernel module timing traces.
2026-03-11 09:20 - Elena Park (Firmware Eng): Confirmed dock v1.3.0 exposes new _DSM entries. Reached out to vendor to escalate; vendor opened SR# DCK-2026-334.
2026-03-11 15:44 - Marcus Lee (Infra Eng): Deployed initramfs retry workaround (image-scripts v0.15.2) to staging provisioner. Monitoring metrics. Failure rate dropped to ~6%.
2026-03-12 08:00 - Depot Ops (note): Depot imaging temporarily updated SOP: undock devices before starting PXE job. Linked to INT-884421 for longer-term change.
2026-03-12 11:30 - Marcus Lee (Infra Eng): Filed kernel probe-ordering task with Eng and added reproducer notes + kdump artifacts to ENG ticket.
2026-03-12 16:50 - Elena Park (Firmware Eng): Vendor estimated firmware fix in ~2 weeks; requested full ACPI dump and failing kmsg samples (uploaded to vendor portal).
Workaround deployed (initramfs retry + udev settle). Downgrade of dock firmware to v1.2.1 also resolves repro. Awaiting vendor firmware fix and kernel probe-ordering patch. Depot SOP updated to undock prior to imaging.
Keep ticket open until vendor firmware and kernel fix validated in staging for 7 consecutive days. Create follow-up INT for SOP rollout.

title: incident-bot: ALERT: p99 latency breach on dedicated pool eu-west-1-prod-pool-17 for model redwood-7b-quant. p95=870ms, p99=2300ms (SLO=1000ms). Queue depth rising. Paging oncall @alice_oncall. Incident ID: INC-3371234567
content:
incident-bot: ALERT: p99 latency breach on dedicated pool eu-west-1-prod-pool-17 for model redwood-7b-quant. p95=870ms, p99=2300ms (SLO=1000ms). Queue depth rising. Paging oncall @alice_oncall. Incident ID: INC-3371234567

alice_oncall: on it. what's the visible customer impact? which routes/models? :eyes:

clara_runtime: seeing heavy queueing on that pool. per-route: /v1/generate (streaming) shows stall spikes, many requests waiting for slot handshake. current queue depth ~1200, inflight warmups ~18, warmup success rate ~34% in last 10m. handshake_fail=12% (registration timeouts)

dan_sre: any autoscaler events? did the pool try to add nodes and fail?

clara_runtime: autoscaler attempted 3 scale-ups in last 7m but slot registration lagged ~45-90s each — handshake window expired and client requests sat in queue. logs show repeated "slot_registration_timeout" and "image_pull_slow" events.

ben_platform: confirming: cloud provider has transient ECR throttling in eu-west-1. image_pull_timeavg jumped to 70s. that explains slow container readiness.

alice_oncall: ok. immediate mitigation ideas? can we fallback to another pool or margin model variant?

clara_runtime: yes — we have two levers: 1) reroute traffic to eu-west-1-hotshot (has spare capacity) but will add cross-pool network hop. 2) fallback to redwood-7b-quant-light (faster cold start, lower memory) on same pool which bypasses heavy warmup kernels. both will reduce p99 quickly.

eva_support: which customers are impacted? I need a short list for CS to notify.

frank_cs: initial list from traces: cust-ACME, cust-ZETA, cust-ORBIT (high QPS clients). Impact window ~5m and ongoing. Some streaming sessions saw stalls and reconnects.

alice_oncall: execute fallback to light variant and start manual scale up. clara, can you run warmup for additional slots and set routing rule to fallback? I'll coordinate with ben for reroute if needed.

clara_runtime: running commands now:

```
# prewarm 20 slots with light variant
rictl warmup --pool eu-west-1-prod-pool-17 --model redwood-7b-quant-light --slots 20
# add slots (manual reservation)
rictl pools scale eu-west-1-prod-pool-17 --add-slots 20 --force
```

clara_runtime: warmup requests started. logs:

```
[warmup] 00:12:05 warmup(1) start model=redwood-7b-quant-light slot=42
[warmup] 00:12:18 warmup(1) ok slot=42
[register] 00:12:30 slot_registration ok slot=42
```

dan_sre: I'll watch autoscaler metrics and cloud image pull infra. if ECR continues to be slow we should switch to cached image in private registry.

ben_platform: starting a cross-pool reroute plan as backup. small percentage (10%) traffic -> eu-west-1-hotshot, can increase if stable. command:

```
rictl route adjust --from-pool eu-west-1-prod-pool-17 --to-pool eu-west-1-hotshot --percent 10
```

alice_oncall: enabling immediate fallback rule in routing policy (per-request):

```
# set fallback for streaming heavy routes
rictl policies set --pool eu-west-1-prod-pool-17 --fallback-model redwood-7b-quant-light --threshold p95>800ms
```

clara_runtime: fallback rule applied. seeing drop in handshake failures for new requests. p99 trending down: now 1.4s.

frank_cs: notifying customers now: "We're seeing transient stalls in eu-west. We've applied fallback and are scaling; some sessions may have experienced reconnects. We'll follow up with timeline and root cause." :email:

eva_support: posting interim notice to status page and flagging impacted customers for 2hr follow-up.

ben_platform: manual scale completed, 20 slots added, but note: underlying container image pulls still slow for standard image. light variant uses smaller base so quicker.

clara_runtime: queue depth: 1200 -> 420 after fallback and scale. in-flight warmups still finishing, but streaming stalls reduced. p99 now 900ms, p95 650ms.

alice_oncall: great. are there any regression signals (error rates, mispredictions) with light variant? product risk?

harper_product: light variant reduces context window slightly and may change tokenization edge cases for some prompts. product: we'll run quick smoke tests on top-5 customer prompts. prioritize ACME.

clara_runtime: smoke tests OK for ACME sample set. no immediate quality alerts. continuing to watch eval metrics.

dan_sre: I've opened cloud support ticket for ECR throttling in eu-west-1. also spinning up a private image cache in region as a fallback. ticket: CLOUD-9987

alice_oncall: handoff plan: if p99 remains <1.0s and queue drains, we'll keep fallback in place for 30m, then attempt controlled rollback to primary variant with gradual ramp. if image pull throttling resolved, we'll revert.

clara_runtime: monitoring dashboards show sustained p99 <1s for last 6m. queue draining to normal (<50). I'll leave warmup jobs running to fill pool.

frank_cs: posted update to impacted customers. CS requests follow-up note with RCA and timeline once triage complete.

alice_oncall: adding action items:
- (A1) eng-platform: set up regional image cache + improve image pull retry/backoff logic (owner: ben_platform)
- (A2) eng-runtime: improve warmup backoff and registration visibility, add explicit handshake metrics (owner: clara_runtime)
- (A3) SRE: add autoscaler circuit-breaker to avoid repeated partial scale attempts piling queues (owner: dan_sre)
- (A4) docs: update runbook for fallback-to-variant step (owner: harper_product)

ben_platform: acknowledged A1, starting infra change request.

clara_runtime: acknowledged A2. I'll add instrumentation and a small alert for "registration_time > 20s".

dan_sre: acknowledged A3. will draft circuit-breaker playbook.

alice_oncall: final: incident state -> mitigated. p99 at 0.88s, queue depth 28, no active regressions. moving to post-incident review. handing off to night-oncall @pete_oncall for monitoring until 0200 UTC.

incident-bot: INCIDENT INC-3371234567 status=mitigated by alice_oncall, Clara_runtime, Ben_platform, Dan_sre. Participants: alice_oncall, clara_runtime, ben_platform, dan_sre, eva_support, frank_cs, harper_product, pete_oncall. Close time recorded. Please file postmortem in /incidents/postmortems/ with RCA and action items.

alice_oncall: thanks team. I'll create the postmortem and include timelines and customer impact. closing thread.

title: eng-releases
content:
eng-releases

Connor O'Brien: Kicking off key rotation drill dry-run for offline bundle signing. Goal is to walk the runbook end-to-end (generate new key, update trust store, dual-sign, cut RC, verify installer preflight, capture evidence). Drop notes here as we go.

Sahana Iyer: Here’s the sequence I’m following (from draft runbook):
1) create new signing key in HSM slot + export pubkey
2) update installer trust store (ship in next installer build)
3) update CI signing job to dual-sign manifest (`manifest.sig` old + `manifest.sig.new` or combined envelope)
4) verify `rpi bundle inspect --verify` passes with both keys
5) cut a Private RC bundle and test downgrade prevention still works

Devon Price: FYI I pulled the current signing job config from `private-release-signing.yml`. It assumes a single `SIGNING_KEY_ALIAS=offline-bundle-prod` and writes `manifest.sig` only. Dual-sign isn’t wired.

Hanae Suzuki: On key creation: HSM emulator in staging is flaky again. I can generate the new key, but the export step is failing with permission denied (looks like the service account token isn’t scoped for the new alias).

ReleaseBot: CI job `private/offline-bundle/sign` failed on staging.
Step: `redwood-sign export-public-key --alias offline-bundle-2025q4-rot-01`
Error: `403: not authorized for alias offline-bundle-2025q4-rot-01`

Sahana Iyer: That’s already a “what went wrong”: the pipeline role bindings are hardcoded to the old alias. We need an automation path to create alias + bind perms + audit it.

Marcus Lin: +1. Also from a threat model POV, we *want* explicit approval gates on creating a new signing key alias. But it needs to be repeatable and auditable (no ad-hoc console clicking).

Connor O'Brien: We’ll treat this as: key creation is manual w/ approvals, but the permission binding + evidence capture should be scripted.

Hanae Suzuki: I can unblock by adding the alias to the allowed list for the signing operator role in staging, but that’s manual.

Connor O'Brien: Do it for the drill (staging only), and let’s note the gap.

Hanae Suzuki: Done. Alias `offline-bundle-2025q4-rot-01` created, pubkey exported. Where do we want to store the pubkey artifact for the drill? (internal repo vs release bucket)

Devon Price: For now we’ve been embedding keys in the installer repo under `trust/keys/` and shipping compiled trust store. For evidence, we also attach the pubkey + key-id to the release ticket.

Ethan Park: Installer trust store update is the next blocker: current released installer only trusts `offline-bundle-prod-2024` key id. So any bundle signed solely by the new key fails preflight with `UNKNOWN_SIGNING_KEY`.

Ethan Park: I tried locally by swapping the trust store file:
```
$ rpi preflight --bundle ./bundle-rc.tgz --airgapped
ERROR BNDL-VERIFY-002: signing key not trusted
  key_id: offline-bundle-2025q4-rot-01
  trust_store: /opt/redwood/etc/trust-store.json
  remediation: update installer trust store or use break-glass (policy-gated)
```
So we can’t validate the full “rotate key then cut bundle” flow without cutting an installer build first.

Connor O'Brien: Yep, sequencing issue. For the drill we should do the correct real-world order:
A) ship installer update that includes both keys (old+new)
B) start dual-signing bundles
C) after N releases, drop old key

Sahana Iyer: Agree. The runbook draft currently has key generation first, which is fine, but it should explicitly say “don’t publish bundles signed w/ new key only until installer trust store is in the field.”

Olga Petrov: From compliance side, we need a clean story for customers: there is a transition window where installer trusts both keys. Also we should document how air-gapped customers get the updated trust store (new installer media vs separate trust store update package).

Daniel Carter: For evidence mapping: we should capture (1) approvals for rotation, (2) hash of trust store content shipped, (3) signing logs for first dual-signed release, (4) verification test output. Right now we don’t have a “bundle verification test output artifact” saved anywhere.

Devon Price: On dual-sign: we have two options:
- produce `manifest.sig` and `manifest.sig.next` (two detached sig files)
- produce a single envelope that contains signatures array
Installer currently expects single detached sig file.

Ethan Park: Installer has PRs for “trust store + key rollover” and “detached signature layout” but we didn’t implement multi-sig envelope. Supporting two sig files is easiest. But manifest schema needs to declare which signature file(s) to verify.

Marcus Lin: Multi-sig is safer long-term (explicit threshold / multiple signers), but for rotation we can do “accept any of the trusted keys” with a single sig file. That implies we keep signing with old key until the trust store update propagates.

Connor O'Brien: That seems like the right path for now: ship trust store update first, then move signing key for `manifest.sig` to new key on a later release (not dual-sign). BUT we still want the ability to verify older bundles after rotation, so old key stays trusted for a deprecation period.

Sahana Iyer: Noted. That changes the drill outcome: we can validate (a) trust store can contain multiple keys, (b) installer chooses correct key based on signature key-id, (c) downgrade prevention still works when key changes.

Sean Gallagher: Operational note: any time we flip the signing key used for new bundles, Support will see a spike in `unknown key` errors from customers who didn’t update installer. We need an alert + a canned response + a “check installer version vs bundle version” checklist.

Logan Wright: Also audit event currently logs `verify_success=true/false` but doesn’t include `key_id`. That’s going to be painful during rotation.

Ethan Park: We can add `key_id` and `trust_store_version` to the local audit event. There’s already a field placeholder in the schema. (This came up in PR-24947 too.)

Neha Kapoor: For SRE: we should monitor signing pipeline failures and time-to-issue signed bundle. Rotation days are high risk. Add a “rotation mode” dashboard annotation when we start.

Connor O'Brien: OK, continuing drill with updated sequencing. Action: generate installer build candidate w/ dual trust store.

Devon Price: I made a local branch to add the new pubkey to `trust-store.json` and bumped `trust_store_version: 2025.10-rot1`.

Sahana Iyer: Heads up: when I built installer, preflight still failed with `not-yet-valid` on a test signature where we used the x509-backed key wrapper. The cert NotBefore was set to 10 minutes in the future (clock skew on the build runner?).

ReleaseBot: Test `verify_signature_time_window` failed.
Error: `x509: certificate is not yet valid`
Runner clock: `2025-10-17T03:21:05Z`
Cert NotBefore: `2025-10-17T03:31:12Z`

Hanae Suzuki: That’s from the cert generation defaulting to “NotBefore=now” but the HSM service clock is slightly ahead of the runner clock. For air-gapped customers, this exact scenario happens a lot.

Marcus Lin: We should avoid relying on tight validity windows for the *signing cert* in offline verification. If we keep x509, set NotBefore to something conservative (e.g., now - 24h). Or switch to raw key signatures without x509 validity checks.

Connor O'Brien: For this project we already have that time-skew bugfix PR (24961). The drill confirms it’s real in build infra too, not just customer envs.

Ethan Park: In installer we added “time override for diagnostics only” flag, but default behavior is fail closed. For rotation, we need the release pipeline to not generate certs that fail validation in a normal system.

Sahana Iyer: I can fix in the signing job: when generating the signing cert wrapper, set `not_before = now - 1d`. But that should be in the signing tool itself to avoid drift.

Devon Price: Another thing: the `trust-store.json` is being serialized with different whitespace/order depending on the builder. If we ever sign the trust store itself (we probably should), we need canonicalization.

Connor O'Brien: Adding to follow-ups.

Olga Petrov: For customer comms: we need to explicitly address “time source” and “clock skew” in the rotation docs. Security teams will ask why signatures can be “not yet valid” in an air gap.

Daniel Carter: Evidence note: for the drill, capture screenshots/logs of (1) new key created, (2) approvals, (3) trust store diff, (4) a successful verification run on an offline machine. Right now we have logs sprinkled across Slack/CI.

Sean Gallagher: Also, runbook needs an explicit rollback step: if new key causes widespread failures, revert signing to old key, keep both trusted, and ship a corrective installer update.

Connor O'Brien: Summarizing “what went wrong” so far:
- CI/HSM permissions tied to a fixed alias -> rotation breaks until manual RBAC update
- Runbook sequencing unclear: can’t publish bundles signed by new key until trust store is distributed
- Time skew caused x509 “not yet valid” failures in CI (not just customer env)
- Missing audit fields (`key_id`, trust_store_version) makes rotation triage hard
- Trust store canonicalization / reproducibility concerns (future)

Connor O'Brien: Proposed follow-ups (owners pls confirm):
1) Scripted rotation scaffold: create alias + bind minimal perms + emit audit evidence bundle (Hanae + Sahana)
2) Update runbook sequencing + add rollback section (Connor + Sean)
3) Signing tool: set conservative NotBefore or move away from x509 validity check for bundle signature verification (Hanae + Marcus)
4) Installer audit event additions: include `key_id`, `trust_store_version`, and “break-glass used” marker (Logan + Ethan)
5) Release checklist: require installer version gate before switching active signing key (Connor + Devon)

Hanae Suzuki: Confirm for (1) and (3). For (1) we should also require approval artifact (who approved rotation). I’ll draft a “rotation request” template.

Sahana Iyer: Confirm for (1). I’ll add a CI job that validates the signing operator role has access to the *next* alias before we attempt rotation.

Marcus Lin: Confirm for (3). I’d prefer we don’t treat x509 validity as a hard gate for the signing identity in offline mode; the signature is the integrity mechanism, time validity is optional/fragile offline. We can keep certs for identity/chain, but don’t fail installs because of NotBefore drift.

Ethan Park: Confirm for (4). We can add fields without breaking schema; exporter mapping might need an update too.

Logan Wright: Confirm. I’ll coordinate w/ audit-log-exporter folks so `bundle_verification` includes those fields.

Sean Gallagher: Confirm for (2). I’ll also add a Support note section: how to diagnose `UNKNOWN_SIGNING_KEY` and what to ask customers for (installer version, trust store hash, `rpi bundle inspect` output).

Neha Kapoor: Please add an SRE note: on rotation day, we need an on-call aware handoff + explicit “rotation start/stop” messages in `#eng-releases`.

Devon Price: Confirm for (5). I’ll update the release train checklist so we can’t flip the signing alias unless the installer RC containing both keys is already published.

Olga Petrov: For (2)/(5): loop me in on wording for the customer-facing policy: how long old keys remain trusted, and what constitutes “revocation.”

Daniel Carter: I’ll put together an “evidence packet” outline for the drill so next time we aren’t hunting logs.

Connor O'Brien: Cool. I’ll open/attach tasks to the rotation ticket set (ENG-4825 / ENG-4862) and link back here. Next drill after we land audit fields + fix the NotBefore skew.

ReleaseBot: Reminder set by Connor O'Brien: “Key rotation drill v2” in 14 days.

High level: we need a clearer delegation ladder for processor/subprocessor roles, and we have EU transfer concerns (TheraSys stores some customer records in an Azure EU region but may need US processing for analytics).

Key asks:
- Please confirm whether Redwood can accept our proposed carveout language for controller-controller/subprocessor details (see redline p.3).
- Can you provide the standard audit evidence for cross-border transfers (SOC2 scope, KMS details) and the list of subprocessor locations?
- We may need an explicit Transfer Impact Addendum if transfer to non-EEA is required; are you open to that?

Proposed timeline: legal review this week, finalize DPA next week — customer procurement needs execution by 31 May.

Appreciate a quick confirmation on ownership of these asks so I can coordinate with Procurement.

Thanks,
Sarah
Sarah Lin
Head of Procurement — TheraSys Health Inc.

Thanks for the redlines and checklist. Looping in Karthik (privacy/legal) and Laura (contracts) — they'll lead the review from our side. Ben, keeping you in the loop for procurement timing.

Initial responses:

- Regarding the transfer addendum: Redwood supports SCCs and can sign an addendum for specific transfers, but we need details on the downstream processing (what's processed in the US vs EU) to assess feasibility.

title: Pilot weekly triage: performance contrast - AxiomHealth
content:
Pilot weekly triage: performance contrast - AxiomHealth

Weekly POC sync to triage throughput/latency deltas vs incumbent provider. Team reviewed tail latency incidents, KV/prefix cache priming, routing decisions, and next tuning steps (dedicated slot request + 100k synthetic run). Agreed owner for follow-ups and schedule for final mid-pilot benchmark next Tuesday.
tail latency and p95/p99 deltas
prefix/KV cache priming
routing playbook and fallbacks
dedicated slots vs hosted bursts
quantization tradeoffs
Priya Raman: produce updated routing config (include fallback to small-quant variant) and share link to config repo by 2026-04-16
Dana Liu: run 100k synthetic traffic run on incumbent and attach raw CSV results to the shared bench spreadsheet by 2026-04-15
Ravi Kapoor: provision a dedicated 4-slot pool for two hours on 2026-04-18 for side-by-side run (Jordan to send order form)
Jordan Hayes: share security checklist and short explainer doc on prefix caching and KV priming by 2026-04-14
Evan Cho: schedule mid-pilot readout meeting for 2026-04-21
Send dedicated slot order and booking window
Run side-by-side 2 hour throughput test with KV cache primed vs cold
Compare p50/p95/p99 and unit token cost with incumbent across same test corpus
SE to propose adjusted batching config and recommend quantization profile
[00:00] Jordan Hayes: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 42 minutes, quick agenda--look at last week's bench, triage a couple of tail latency spikes, agree next run.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: Sounds good, Jordan. We saw the big p99 blip at 3pm on Monday, that killed a few user flows. We want to understand root cause and whether that's routing or model cold starts.
[00:35] Priya Raman: Right, looking at traces we saw a pattern where long prefix sequences produced larger KV cache misses, plus one of the routing hops send traffic to the smaller GPU class which added 60-80ms.
[00:50] Dana Liu: To add, the incumbent is using a pinned smaller context model for short prompts which reduced cost but helped our 95th. We're trying to see if Redwood's batching + prefix cache can match p95 without doubling token cost.
[01:12] Ravi Kapoor: Also note our SRE saw CPU throttling on the proxy during burst 10k qps window, might be client side issue too.
[01:28] Priya Raman: Good call, Ravi. For today's triage I pulled the traced requests, annotated where prefix cache was cold. There's a shared spreadsheet link in the chat: https://redwood.share/axh-bench-2026 (note: link may be mis-typed by transcriber).
[01:45] Mel: Quick ask — can you remind us the difference between Redwood Dedicated slot behavior vs hosted burst? Our security team leaning hosted but we need predictable latency.
[02:03] Jordan Hayes: Sure — hosted is the fast path but multi-tenant, bursts are best-effort. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU slots and isolation; we can also schedule short dedicated windows for apples-to-apples runs. We'll send the order form after this call.
[02:25] Dana Liu: When you ran the 50k bench last week, how was KV priming handled? We primed with warm prefixes but saw cold tails.
[02:40] Priya Raman: The bench did a naive primer; we didn't prime every active prefix. For the next run we suggest targeted priming for top-10 prefixes and a background priming worker to reduce cold miss rate. That should knock down some p99s.
[03:05] Carlos Mendez: Is that expensive though? More tokens to prime maybe increases cost.
[03:12] Priya Raman: There's a tradeoff: a short priming phase reduces tail latency and can actually lower overall unit cost because retries/timeouts are costly. We'll model that for your corpus.
[03:29] Dana Liu: Could quantization help? Incumbent uses an 8-bit profile; What's Redwood's quant recommendation?
[03:40] Priya Raman: We have quant profiles — 4-bit and 8-bit. For this workload 8-bit with selective KV layout tends to hit the best latency/cost balance; 4-bit can introduce small quality diffs for longer contexts. We'll recommend a profile after one more eval.
[04:05] Ravi Kapoor: Any weird network hops? We saw one request route through eu-west even though client origin is us-west, which added 70ms.
[04:16] Jordan Hayes: That was from our routing policy test where traffic steered by cost; looks like a mis-config in the canary rules. Priya will include routing policy that pins by region for the next run.
[04:33] Priya Raman: I'll fold that into the routing config and add explicit region pin for steady-state. Also adding a fallback to a lower-cost model variant to avoid errors when dedicated slots are saturated.
[04:49] Mel: On security, our infosec asked about audit logs retention and KMS integration for private deployment. Is that separate?
[04:58] Evan Cho: I captured that. We sent a compliance pack earlier but Jordan will re-share the short security checklist tonight. For any private/prem deployments we support KMS and audit exports.
[05:15] Carlos Mendez: Great. Let's talk numbers — last week's baseline vs Redwood: p50 similar, p95 about +22ms, p99 about +120ms. Cost per 1k tokens was slightly lower on Redwood but variance hurts UX.
[05:34] Jordan Hayes: Exactly. Our hypothesis — tail is from cold KV + cross-region routing + a few requests hitting smaller GPU class during bursts. If we eliminate those factors we expect p99 to approach incumbent.
[05:50] Dana Liu: For the dedicated run, can we replicate exact token distribution and request concurrency? Incumbent used a 2k concurrency window and a heavy tail.
[06:04] Priya Raman: Yes, when you run the synthetic we need the CSV of request lengths and concurrency schedule. Dana, can you attach that?
[06:13] Dana Liu: I'll do that after the call, yes.
[06:20] Priya Raman: Also note that batching config was conservative — we can increase batch max tokens for short prompts to get better throughput without hurting median latency. I'll propose new batch settings in the config.
[06:35] Ravi Kapoor: Side question — does Redwood have a way to pre-warm the KV cache on deploys? We see p99 spikes after model swaps.
[06:46] Priya Raman: There's a prefix priming hook in the runtime; we can run a controlled warm-up before traffic cutover. We'll document recommended priming sequences for model rollouts.
[07:02] Jordan Hayes: Ok let's go through the action owners quickly. Priya will update routing + batching + fallback. Dana will run the 100k synthetic on incumbent and share results. Ravi will provision dedicated slot. Jordan will share order/security docs. Evan will schedule the mid-pilot readout.
[07:22] Mel: Can you put the expected ROI numbers in the routing doc? Our CFO needs a unit-cost delta with assumptions.
[07:31] Jordan Hayes: We'll include token unit cost delta, expected savings with batching and quantization assumptions.
[07:40] Carlos Mendez: On the prior bench, we also noticed a handful of 5xxs during the 8k spike. Are those timeouts or OOMs?
[07:52] Priya Raman: The traces show timeouts at the proxy layer due to backpressure; not OOMs in the model. We'll add backpressure metrics to the shared dashboard and propose a soft-fail fallback to a lower-latency model to keep user flows alive.
[08:12] Dana Liu: That fallback idea is critical for UX. If the fallback changes output a lot we can't use it, need to test.
[08:22] Priya Raman: Totally — we can A/B the fallback variant on a small percent and run a quality check against your evaluation set.
[08:33] Jordan Hayes: Quick note — we'll also try a KV cache heuristic change: evict larger prefix items sooner to favor hot short prefixes. Might improve p95.
[08:46] Ravi Kapoor: Any instrument changes we need to make on our side?
[08:52] Priya Raman: Add the trace-id header to all synthetic runs and ensure timestamps are synced to NTP. That helps correlate.
[09:02] Carlos Mendez: Ok, timeline? We want the mid-pilot readout next Tuesday.
[09:08] Evan Cho: We'll aim for 2026-04-21 for the readout; Jordan will send invite once the dedicated slot is booked.
[09:16] Mel: One last ask — include the incumbent config we used so it's apples-to-apples.
[09:22] Dana Liu: I'll upload the incumbent run config and the raw CSV for the 50k run. Expect that by Friday.
[09:30] Priya Raman: Great, I'll follow up with routing config and batch proposal. Also including a short explainer about quant profiles.
[09:40] Jordan Hayes: Anything else before we wrap?
[09:44] Carlos Mendez: No, thanks all. Looking forward to the side-by-side.
[09:49] Jordan Hayes: Thanks team — we'll recap in email and list owners.
[10:00] [call end — meeting lasted approx 42 minutes — recording clipped by host at 42:12]

title: Add SLO→Customer Impact Classifier & Remediation Workflow doc (v2 scoring + updated comms)
content:
Add SLO→Customer Impact Classifier & Remediation Workflow doc (v2 scoring + updated comms)

Context
We have an internal Confluence page describing the SLO→customer impact tier classifier and the remediation workflow. That page is being referenced during incidents, but the operational details have drifted since the enrichment pipeline shipped score weighting changes (v2) and CS escalation timing was tightened after SUP-19344.

This PR adds the canonical doc to the slo-toolkit repo so it can be versioned alongside the classifier code and reviewed via normal PR workflows. The majority of the content mirrors the Confluence page, but includes the v2 scoring thresholds and updated templates.

What changed (summary)
- Keep: tier definitions (1–4), overall workflow (alert→enrich→score→tier→remediate), evidence retention requirements, and post-incident/error budget reconciliation flow.
- Update: score mapping thresholds (v2), add confidence gating and a human-review fallback, update Tier 1 comms SLA (10 min), and reduce Tier 4 auto-escalation window (4 hours).
- Update: SLO catalog excerpt targets to match current baselines; add explicit note that targets are examples and owners must use the live SLO registry as source of truth.
- Update: capacity knobs table to reflect current CLI commands and pool naming.

Doc content (added under docs/incident-response/)

Title: SLO to Customer Impact Classifier and Remediation Workflow

Overview
This document defines a reproducible classifier that maps SLO signals to a customer-impact tier and a prescriptive remediation workflow. It is intended to: align SRE, Product, and Customer Success during SLO degradations; minimize time-to-customer-remediation; and create consistent inputs for post-incident reviews and error-budget decisions.

Audience
- On-call SREs
- SRE leads and managers
- Incident commanders (ICs)
- Customer Success (CS) and Support for high-impact incidents

Principles
1) Tie every SLO alert to an explicit customer-impact tier (1–4).
2) Automate low-friction routing and remediation for common degradations.
3) Escalate proactively for any Tier 1/2 customer impact.
4) Preserve evidence for postmortems and error-budget reconciliations.

Definitions
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., request_latency_p95 <= 250ms).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over the defined rolling window.
- Customer-impact tier: a 1–4 classification used to route and prioritize incident response.

Customer-impact tiers (quick guide)
| Tier | User-visible symptoms | Business effect | Escalation urgency | Owner to notify |
|------|----------------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------|
| 1 | Multi-region outage OR widespread request failures OR sustained elevated error rate affecting a large portion of traffic | Severe revenue/customer retention impact | Immediate (page) | SRE lead + Product PM + CS Director |
| 2 | Single-region outage, or large subset of customers impacted (major tenants) or major feature down | Significant business disruption for key customers | High (page + slack) | SRE oncall + Product owner + CS manager |
| 3 | Localized errors, degraded latency for non-critical endpoints | Minor customer annoyance, limited support tickets | Medium (slack alert) | On-call SRE + Feature owner |
| 4 | Minor latency increase or transient errors with no customer tickets | No immediate business impact | Low (ticket) | On-call SRE |

SLO catalog excerpt (example mapping; owners must confirm in live SLO registry)
| SLO name | Metric | Target | Error-budget window | Default customer-impact tier |
|----------|--------|--------|--------------------|--------------------------|
| request_latency_p95_public | request_latency_p95{route=~"/v1/.*"} | <= 250ms | 30d | 2 |
| api_error_rate_5m | sum(rate(api_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests_total[5m])) | <= 0.5% | 7d | 1 |
| embedding_throughput_tail | embedding_infer_latency_p99 | < 1.4s | 14d | 3 |
| console_ui_availability | synthetic_check(console_login) | 99.7% monthly | 30d | 3 |

Classification algorithm (operational)
1) Alert receives telemetry: detector alerts on SLI breach or error-budget burn (alerting config).
2) Metrics enrichment: pull impact signals (affected tenant count, region distribution, top N tenants by RPS, open support tickets matching pattern).
3) Heuristics engine evaluates scores (0–100): failure-scope, severity, customer-exposure.
4) Confidence gating (v2): compute confidence (0–100) based on completeness/consistency of enrichment inputs. If confidence < 50, do not auto-upgrade beyond Tier 3; route to on-call for manual triage and re-run enrichment after 5 minutes.
5) Combined score maps to Tier (v2 thresholds): Score >= 85 -> Tier 1; 70–84 -> Tier 2; 35–69 -> Tier 3; < 35 -> Tier 4.
6) Attach classification + confidence to incident and follow the tiered remediation workflow below.

Heuristics inputs (examples)
- affected_tenant_ratio: percent of total tenant RPS impacted.
- p95_latency_delta: percent change vs baseline.
- error_rate_delta: absolute change in error rate vs baseline (preferred over p99_error_spike for API).
- active_cs_tickets: number of open tickets tagged /inference or /api.
- region_blast_radius: number of regions with concurrent impact.

Operational remediations by tier
Tier 1 (Immediate response)
- Page the SRE oncall and SRE lead (PagerDuty service: customer-impact).
- Open an incident in the incident-management system using template tag=CUSTOMER_IMPACT_TIER_1 (auto-created if classifier confidence >= 70).
- Run mitigation playbook: fallback-to-compatible-model-variant.
- If capacity-related: trigger immediate capacity burst policy (see CLI below).
- Notify CS and Product leadership within 10 minutes with templated Slack/Jira.

Tier 2 (High-priority)
- Page on-call (high urgency) and post to #incidents.
- Execute targeted throttles or tenant fair-share configuration.
- Begin canary rollback of recent model or config changes (if correlated).

Tier 3 (Operational handling)
- Create ticket and schedule on-call investigation within 30–60 minutes.
- Apply mitigations from the runbook: restart worker pool, clear KV cache, or disable newly-deployed feature flag.

Tier 4 (Monitoring)
- Monitor metrics and let automated remediation run. If unresolved after SLA window (4 hours), escalate to Tier 3.

Sample alert rule (Prometheus-style YAML)
alert: HighAPIErrorRate
expr: sum(rate(api_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(api_requests_total[5m])) > 0.005
for: 2m
labels: severity: page impact: "possible-customer-impact"
annotations: summary: "API error rate >0.5% over 5m" runbook: "https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/api-error-rate-mitigation"

Enrichment query examples (pseudo-SQL / analytics)
- Tenants affected in last 10m: SELECT tenant_id, count(*) FROM requests WHERE status >= 500 AND timestamp > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 50;
- Support ticket correlation: count tickets where created_at >= now()-10m AND tags IN ('api','inference')

Capacity escalation knobs (examples)
| Trigger | Condition | Automated action | Escalation threshold |
|---------|-----------|------------------|----------------------|
| headroom_exhausted | available_gpu_slots < 7% | trigger-burst-alloc --pool=shared-burst-v2 | immediate (Tier1) |
| model_warm_pool_empty | warm_pool_size < configured_min | scale warm pool by +2 nodes | Tier2 |
| p95_latency_spike | p95 > baseline*1.6 for 10m | enable-prefetch-kv-cache=true | Tier2 |

CLI examples
- Trigger burst capacity (operators only): rcmd infra capacity burst apply --pool shared-burst-v2 --reason "Tier1 SLO breach" --expires 30m
- Re-route traffic to fallback models: rcmd infra routing promote --from model-xyz-v2 --to model-xyz-v1 --weight 100

Communication templates
Slack template (Tier1)
- Channel: #incidents
- Message: [Tier 1 SLO breach] api_error_rate_5m at 1.2% impacting ~32% of tenant RPS across 2 regions. IC: @oncall. Mitigation in progress: promoting fallback routing. Please notify CS lead @renee.zhao. Incident: <INCIDENT_URL>

Jira template fields
- Priority: P0 for Tier1, P1 for Tier2, P2 for Tier3/4
- Components: runtime, routing, capacity, product-feature
- Labels: slo-breach, customer-impact-tier-<n>, automated-enrichment, classifier-v2

Post-incident / Error-budget reconciliation
1) Add classification evidence (metrics, tenant list, tickets) to the incident story.
2) Compute error-budget consumption attributable to the incident window.
3) For Tier1/Tier2 incidents: schedule a joint SRE/Product/CS triage within 72 hours. The triage determines whether to take a governance action (e.g., customer credits, temporary throttle, emergency capacity commit).
4) Document remediation plan and assign owners with due dates.

Postmortem checklist (to include in incident review)
- Summary of classifier result (tier + confidence) and whether the initial tier matched customer reports.
- Timeline of detection -> mitigation -> recovery.
- Root cause and contributing factors including capacity and SLO misconfigurations.
- Action items (owner + due date) and follow-up on error-budget policy.
- Evidence attachments: metrics, logs, enrichment query results.

Automation and operational tooling notes
- The classifier runs in the telemetry enrichment pipeline (owner: telemetry-team). Inputs are Prometheus alerts, request traces, and support ticket API.
- All automated classification decisions must be auditable: store computed scores, confidence, and input summaries in incident metadata.
- Confidence gating exists to prevent false Tier 1/2 upgrades when enrichment is degraded (e.g., ticket API latency, tenant-mapping lag).

Ownership and governance
- SLO owner: Each SLO must list a primary owner (SRE or Product) and a secondary owner. Owners are responsible for maintaining mapping in the SLO registry and ensuring this doc stays consistent.
- Classification engine owner: telemetry-team@redwood.com.
- Incident review owner for Tier1/Tier2: SRE lead on rotation.

Runbook links (examples)
- API error mitigation: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/api-error-rate-mitigation
- Fallback routing: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/fallback-routing-and-rollbacks
- Capacity burst playbook: https://confluence.internal/s/reliability/runbooks/capacity-burst-and-burst-rollback

Change log
- 2026-01-15 — Initial draft published (Priya Natarajan).
- 2026-02-20 — Added capacity knobs and CLI examples (review: Liam O'Connor).
- 2026-03-01 — Finalized communication templates and post-incident checklist (review: Renee Zhao).
- 2026-03-16 — Updated classifier thresholds to v2, added confidence gating, tightened Tier1 notification SLA to 10 min, and reduced Tier4 escalation window to 4 hours (review: Sasha Kim).

Appendix: sample incident evidence payload (illustrative)
- incident_id=INC-2026-0316-014 slo=api_error_rate_5m failure_scope=81 severity=88 customer_exposure=63 confidence=77 mapped_tier=1 top_affected_tenants=[tenant-acme,tenant-vela] evidence_queries=[tenant_impact_query_2026-03-16-10m]

Operator note
If you are an on-call SRE and this workflow appears to misclassify an incident, create a ticket in the SRE backlog and tag telemetry-team for review. Include the incident link and the classifier scores/confidence from incident metadata.

Contact
- Document owner: Priya Natarajan (pri@redwood.com)
- Telemetry owner: telemetry-team@redwood.com
- Incident management: incidents@redwood.com

Testing
- N/A (documentation only).

Rollout
- Once merged, we will link this doc from the internal runbook index and update the Confluence page to point at this repo copy as the source of truth.
Liam O'Connor (review): Please make the v2 threshold change explicit (old vs new) so oncall knows why behavior differs from the Confluence screenshot floating around.
Priya Natarajan (author): Added v2 thresholds in-step (Score >= 85 Tier1 etc) and added confidence gating paragraph. I avoided pasting old thresholds to prevent copy/paste drift, but can add a one-liner callout if you want.
Liam O'Connor (review): One-liner callout is enough. Also the capacity pool is shared-burst-v2 now, right?
Priya Natarajan (author): Updated the capacity table + CLI examples to shared-burst-v2 and added a changelog entry dated 2026-03-16.
Renee Zhao (review): Please change Tier1 CS notification window to 10 minutes (per SUP-19344). Also remove the emoji from the Slack template; our incident tooling strips it and it looks messy.
Priya Natarajan (author): Done: Tier1 comms within 10 minutes; Slack template now uses a bracketed prefix instead of emoji.
Mateo Alvarez (review): Appendix evidence payload: earlier doc showed JSON object with nested computed_scores. This repo doc should avoid implying a strict JSON schema unless we link to the actual schema file.
Priya Natarajan (author): Adjusted appendix to an illustrative key=value format and clarified it's illustrative. The actual schema lives in telemetry-pipeline and will be referenced separately.
Sasha Kim (review): Add a note that if confidence < 50 we should not auto-upgrade beyond Tier3; that’s the key operational change we made after ticket API outages.
Priya Natarajan (author): Added confidence gating rule in the algorithm steps and in automation notes.
Liam O'Connor (final): Approved.
Renee Zhao (final): Approved.
