title: POC scoping: sensitive flow retention & redaction - BlueHarbor Analytics
content:
POC scoping: sensitive flow retention & redaction - BlueHarbor Analytics

Discovery + POC scoping for handling PII in prompts and logs. Discussed redaction, retention windows, scope of data stored for telemetry, benchmarking plan (replay vs synthetic), success criteria (latency SLOs, quality parity, auditability), and a two-week pilot timeline. Agreed to run a 7-day benchmark and provide security docs and a draft quote.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Carlos (CTO), Priya (MLOps), Samir (Security)

Summary: quick scoping call focused on how BlueHarbor routes sensitive prompts through Redwood for a 2-week pilot. Main concerns: PII leakage in logs, configurable retention, redaction automation, and benchmark sizing.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh let's do quick intros and then jump in. We're budgeting 45–60 minutes.
[00:12] Carlos: Hi, Carlos here. CTO. We're looking to test Redwood for our customer support summarization workflow which touches PHI/PII.
[00:20] Priya: Priya — lead on MLOps. We run approx 100k support interactions per month, average prompt length around 120 tokens, peaks are spikier. We're mostly worried about what gets stored and how to prove deletion.
[00:35] Ethan: thanks, yeah so from the platform side we support Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. For POC we usually start on Hosted with strict retention + redaction rules, or a Private control-plane if you need full network isolation.
[00:47] Samir: Quick — are you SOC 2 Type II? And what about key management, do you support customer-managed keys / HSM?
[00:55] Maya: Yes we are SOC2 and have an ISO pack. KMS integration is supported, HSM via our Private deployment — we'll send the docs.
[01:08] Carlos: Good. For the POC success criteria: 1) no raw PII in logs, 2) 95th pct latency under 200ms for the main route, 3) output quality parity with current pipeline — we'll use a fixed eval set.
[01:22] Priya: Also need audit logs that show retention and deletion events for prompt IDs. Right to Erasure is a blocker for us.
[01:33] Ethan: Understood. For redaction we have two approaches: automated inline redaction at ingestion (regex + ML PII classifier), or store hashed prompts and redact the stored copy on write. Both have tradeoffs — inline redaction reduces fidelity for debugging, hashed storage preserves raw tokens off of the main store but is irreversible unless you keep separate vaults.
[01:56] Carlos: Can you walk through an example? Say a prompt contains a SSN and a credit card number. What gets stored?
[02:04] Ethan: Sure. Option A (inline redaction): we scrub and replace detected tokens with <REDACTED> before logging; Option B (hash + ephemeral): we hash the prompt text (sha256) and store only the hash + derived metadata, while routing the raw prompt ephemeral directly to the model but not persisted past X seconds — this helps debugging if you keep ephemeral snapshots guarded by KMS, but it's more operational overhead.
[02:32] Priya: How good is the PII classifier? FPs/ FNs matter to us — a missed SSN is bad.
[02:39] Ethan: The built-in classifier is tuned for common PII types; we recommend a two-stage check: regex for high-confidence patterns (SSN/CC) and ML detector for contextual leaks. We can ship the classifier config used in the POC and you can fine-tune thresholds.
[02:58] Maya: On retention, we expose per-route retention windows: 0 days (no storage), 7 days, 30, 90, 365. You can also mark certain routes as ephemeral: logs are deleted after processing.
[03:12] Carlos: Do deletions provide proof? Audit trail?
[03:15] Ethan: Yes, deletions are recorded in audit logs with event IDs, timestamps, and the requesting principal. Those logs can be exported to your SIEM or S3.
[03:26] Samir: We need proofs for GDPR erasure — is the deletion immediate across all backups?
[03:30] Maya: For Hosted we provide logical deletion and scrub copies in standard backup windows; for legal-level guarantees we recommend Private where backups are customer-managed — we can detail RTO/RPO semantics in the security pack.
[03:44] Priya: Benchmarking — we want to understand latency and cost tradeoffs. Our target is approx 95th percentile <200ms and steady-state throughput ~30 requests/sec for the route.
[03:56] Ethan: For throughput/latency sizing we'll run two benchmarks: replay of your sample set (best) and synthetic traffic that simulates bursts. For replay we need ~2–5k representative prompts and target concurrency. We'll also test with quantized model variants to estimate cost delta.
[04:14] Carlos: What's the expected delta when using int8/quantized models vs full precision in terms of quality? We can't accept >3% drop in summary quality.
[04:22] Ethan: Quality delta depends on model family; for many Llama-based variants we've seen <2% drop on summarization tasks with 8-bit quantization if you tune temperature and sampling. We'll include a small human evaluation on your eval set.
[04:38] Priya: Can Redwood do prefix/KV cache so we get lower tail latency on repeated contexts? Our workflow reuses multiple customer context templates.
[04:46] Ethan: Yes, our runtime supports KV caching and prefix caching per route. That can cut median latency significantly for repeated tokens. We'll include that in the benchmark config.
[05:00] Carlos: For the pilot length — we prefer a 2-week pilot but operationally ok with a 7-day intensive benchmark followed by a 7-day softer integration run. Can Redwood support that timeline in early Jan?
[05:12] Maya: Yes, tentatively Jan 4th start for the 7-day benchmark, Jan 11–18 soft integration. We'll confirm.
[05:20] Samir: Can you also show redaction false positive logs? We need to see examples of when PII is redacted but it wasn't PII.
[05:28] Ethan: We'll capture FP/FN counts and example cases and surface them in the evaluation report.
[05:35] Priya: What about prompt storage for debugging — hashing means we can't replay exact prompts to reproduce issues. Any middle ground?
[05:42] Ethan: Middle ground is encrypted vaults: store raw prompts encrypted with your KMS key and access via RBAC only to approved engineers; deletion still triggers KMS-based wiping procedures. This gives replayability but increases compliance burden.
[06:00] Carlos: Procurement — quote needed. For POC we'd likely want a short-term reserved capacity with burst to Hosted. Any rough estimate for 100k monthly interactions?
[06:10] Maya: We'll run a back-of-envelope after we get sample prompts (token distribution) — Ethan will do an estimate and give a per-1M token estimate and possible Dedicated delta if you choose reserved capacity.
[06:22] Priya: Also, can we configure route-level retention to zero for certain user-facing routes (e.g., password reset flow)?
[06:30] Ethan: Yes, route-level policies are supported. You can attach policy tags like PII:HIGH -> retention=0 and logging=redact.
[06:38] Samir: Audit requirements — we need immutable logs, event signatures?
[06:42] Maya: Audit logs are append-only, stored with event signatures, and exported to your S3 or SIEM. For highest assurance we recommend Private so you manage storage retention end-to-end.
[06:55] Carlos: Ok let's align on success criteria again — latency <200ms 95p, FP/FN PII detection thresholds below 1%/2% respectively, evidence of deletion/audits, and a cost estimate under our target.
[07:12] Priya: We'll provide an eval set of 500 labelled examples for quality checks and 2–5k unlabeled prompts for replay.
[07:20] Maya: Great, here's what we'll do next — send security pack, benchmark plan, and a preliminary quote. We'll also include instructions for uploading prompts securely.
[07:32] Ethan: I'll prepare the synthetic workload template: concurrency, token distribution, KV-cache on/off scenarios, and quantization flags.
[07:40] Carlos: Thanks all — anything else?
[07:42] Priya: One more — can we get SLA terms for Dedicated if we scale?
[07:46] Maya: We'll include Dedicated SLA language in the quote addendum.
[07:50] Samir: Sounds good. End of call.

Meeting close.

title: KV cache compaction experiments tracker (parameter sweeps + defaults)
content:
KV cache compaction experiments tracker (parameter sweeps + defaults)

Owner: Samir
TL: Omar
Scheduler hook: Sofia
Perf harness: Marcus / Rina
SRE guardrails: Sean / Allison

Purpose
- Track the compaction/eviction parameter sweeps and what they did to: fragmentation ratio, bytes moved, compaction time, throughput, p95/p99 decode latency.
- Keep a written record of “safe defaults” we can ship behind feature flags for runtime-1.22 rollout (Hosted first, then Dedicated).
- This is not the final design doc. It’s the messy notebook we’re using while iterating.

Definitions (working)
- Fragmentation ratio (FR): 1 - (largest_free_contiguous / total_free). Higher = worse. 0.0 means free space is fully contiguous.
- Trigger threshold: FR value above which compaction is allowed to run (subject to budget).
- Budget: hard cap on compaction work per scheduling window. We’re testing both:
  - bytes_budget_per_step (KV bytes relocated)
  - time_budget_ms_per_step (wall time)
- Step boundary: when scheduler allows compaction to run (prefill boundary, decode boundary, or background thread).
- Eviction: dropping KV pages for eligible sequences to avoid OOM / pathological churn. Tier-aware + LRU-ish. (Pinned sessions never evicted.)

Test environments used (summary)
- Staging cluster: us-east1, A100-80GB + H100-80GB pools
- “Prod-like” perf lab runs via benchmark-lab generator (PR-881) + perf-canary scenario (PR-412)
- Models tested: llama-70b-ish profile, mixtral-ish MoE profile (names omitted here; see benchmark results sheet)

Workloads (we keep reusing these names)
W1: Mixed-length burst chat
- Prompt length: bimodal (short 128–256 and long 2k–6k)
- Churn: high (cancelled requests, reconnects)
- Burst: 3–5x QPS for 2–3 minutes
- Goal: reproduce p99 spikes + fragmentation growth

W2: Long-lived sessions
- 20–40% sessions persist 30+ minutes with periodic decode
- Low churn
- Goal: check for “slow fragmentation creep” + compaction stability

W3: Streaming + cancellations adversarial
- Frequent mid-decode cancellations
- Goal: correctness + ensure we don’t create stalls or allocator leaks during relocation


Experiment log (chronological)

2026-01-10 — Baseline reproduction (no compaction, no eviction)
Run: W1 on A100
- FR steady climbs to 0.55–0.75 under bursty churn, then never fully recovers
- Symptoms: allocator spends time hunting free blocks; we see short stalls around page alloc
- Tail: p99 decode latency spikes correlate with FR > ~0.60 (not perfect, but consistent)
Notes:
- Confirms this isn’t just “GPU busy” — there are visible allocator overhead spikes
- Action: implement FR metric export (ENG-4822 / PR-19342)

2026-01-14 — Compaction boundary sweep (where to run it)
Variants:
A) background-only worker
B) scheduler boundary only (end of prefill, end of decode step)
C) hybrid (background + scheduler guard)
Findings:
- A (background-only): best FR reduction but worst tail in bursts (p99 spikes) when worker competes w/ decode. Needs strict budgeting + priority.
- B (scheduler boundary): predictable tail, slightly worse FR reduction but “good enough” if budgets aren’t tiny.
- C (hybrid): promising but harder to reason about; easiest way to shoot ourselves during canary.
Decision (tentative): runtime-1.22 use B as primary. A can be gated behind extra flag for later.

2026-01-16 — Budget sweep #1 (bytes_budget_per_step)
Workload: W1
Hardware: A100
Trigger: FR > 0.55
Budgets tested: 0MB, 32MB, 64MB, 128MB, 256MB per step
Observations (approx)
- 0MB: baseline (FR peaks ~0.75, p99 spikes)
- 32MB: FR still peaks ~0.70, p99 slightly improved but spikes remain
- 64MB: FR peaks ~0.60–0.65, noticeable p99 improvement; throughput unchanged within noise
- 128MB: FR peaks ~0.50–0.58, p99 best; BUT saw occasional short decode elongation during burst (likely step taking too long)
- 256MB: FR very good, but increased risk: some steps exceeded our “do no harm” budget and p95 started to wobble
Notes:
- Bytes budget alone is not a stable guard on H100 (copy perf varies with contention)
Action: add time-budget enforcement option + traces around compaction (PR-19405)

2026-01-19 — Budget sweep #2 (time_budget_ms_per_step)
Workload: W1
Hardware: A100
Trigger: FR > 0.55
Time budgets: 0ms, 0.15ms, 0.25ms, 0.5ms, 1.0ms per scheduler window
Observations:
- <=0.15ms: too conservative; FR stays high, p99 spikes reduced but not eliminated
- 0.25ms: good balance; FR moderates, p99 materially better, p95 unchanged
- 0.5ms: FR good, p99 very good, slight p95 cost in worst burst minute (not huge)
- 1.0ms: FR excellent, but p95/p99 both see occasional “compaction-caused” plateaus (copy dominates step)
Notes:
- Time budget is easier to reason about for canary guardrails (“we will not spend more than X ms”)
Decision: prefer time budget as primary guardrail; bytes budget can remain secondary cap (safety).

2026-01-22 — Trigger threshold sweep (when to start compaction)
Workload: W1 + W2
Budget: 0.25ms per step
Thresholds: FR > 0.45, 0.55, 0.65
Results:
- 0.45: compaction runs often, keeps FR low; cost: more background work; risk of “always on” for certain churn patterns
- 0.55: “just in time” behavior; FR stays under ~0.60 most of the time; good p99
- 0.65: too late; we still see p99 spikes before compaction catches up
Notes:
- Hosted traffic seems to hit FR 0.55 quickly under bursts; 0.65 is basically “let it get bad first.”
Decision: default trigger FR 0.55 for Hosted. Consider 0.60 for Dedicated (since more predictable load, but still bursty in some pools).

2026-01-26 — Cooldown / hysteresis experiment (avoid thrash)
Idea: Once FR drops below low watermark, stop compaction for N seconds.
Settings tried:
- Low watermark: 0.45
- Cooldowns: 0s, 10s, 30s
Findings:
- No cooldown: mild thrash (lots of small compaction steps) but tail fine
- 10s: reduced total bytes moved ~10–15% in W2 without harming FR
- 30s: sometimes allowed FR to climb back quickly in W1 burst tail; not ideal
Decision: add 10s cooldown (configurable). Keep off by default until we finish canary.

2026-01-29 — Eviction on/off + threshold sweep
Why: compaction alone can’t save us when we’re near capacity and fragmentation blocks large allocs; eviction is the pressure relief.
Workload: W1 with artificially tight KV arena to simulate high utilization
Eviction modes:
- Off
- On, threshold: “free_kv_bytes < X” (X as % of arena)
Thresholds tried: 1%, 2%, 5% remaining free
Findings:
- Off: periodic OOM / forced shedding in worst churn variant
- 1%: still risky; too late to prevent allocator failure in some runs
- 2%: generally prevented OOM; limited eviction events
- 5%: safe but too aggressive; evicted sessions that would’ve survived; can cause quality-of-service issues for lower tier
Decision: 2% free threshold (as a starting point) + tier-aware eviction. Keep strict pinning rules.
Open: Should threshold be model-size dependent? (probably yes)

2026-02-02 — Tier-aware eviction policy (what gets evicted)
Workload: W1 (high churn) + W2 (long lived)
Policy candidate: tier-aware LRU by “last decode time”, exclude pinned sessions, prefer evicting preemptible prefix-cache entries first.
Observations:
- With eviction enabled, p99 stabilized during near-capacity bursts.
- User-visible effect: in synthetic tests, low-tier sessions occasionally lost cache and had to re-prefill (latency bump on next turn). This is acceptable if bounded + not happening to premium tiers.
Decision: ship tier-aware eviction with these rules (current):
- Never evict pinned sessions.
- Premium tiers: only evict if we’re about to OOM (hard emergency mode).
- Standard tiers: eligible at 2% free threshold.
- Prefer prefix-cache / preemptible entries (if present) before active session KV.

2026-02-05 — Scheduler boundary choice revisited (decode vs prefill)
Workload: W1
Budget: 0.25ms
Result:
- Running compaction at decode boundary only: best for avoiding user-visible streaming jitter, but FR reduction slower.
- Running at prefill boundary only: FR reduction ok, but bursty “chat turn” pattern can starve compaction.
- Mixed boundaries: better FR control; minimal impact if time budget is strict.
Decision: allow both boundaries, but prioritize decode boundary with lower budget, and allow a slightly higher budget at prefill boundary (since prefill already heavy). (Implementation detail still in flux.)

2026-02-09 — H100 rerun + copy kernel sensitivity
Workload: W1
Hardware: H100
Budget: 0.25ms
Observation:
- H100 copy is faster but contention patterns differ; compaction steps sometimes finish early, so we move fewer bytes than A100 but with similar FR improvement.
- Suggests time budget is portable.
Note: we should keep bytes cap to prevent pathological “move too much because it’s fast” causing downstream effects (cache invalidation bursts).

2026-02-12 — Tracing overhead check (compaction spans)
Added spans in PR-19405; some perf regression discussion in Slack (1767741120)
Finding:
- Always-on detailed spans cost is nontrivial in CI perf tests; needs sampling.
Decision: keep spans but sample; ensure oncall can enable verbose tracing temporarily.

2026-02-14 — Canary-style guardrails simulation (auto rollback signals)
Goal: what metrics best predict compaction-caused harm vs “compaction helping.”
Signals tested:
- compaction_time_ms_step p95
- bytes_moved_per_sec
- eviction_rate_per_min
- p99 decode latency delta vs baseline
Findings:
- p99 alone too noisy (traffic mix)
- Better: “p99 up AND compaction_time_ms_step p95 above threshold” to attribute to compaction
- Also: sustained eviction_rate increase may indicate we’re too aggressive / too close to capacity
Proposal (for SRE):
- Alert/rollback if p99 decode > +15% baseline for 10m AND compaction_time_ms_step_p95 > 0.6ms
- Alert if eviction_rate spikes above expected for tier (needs tier breakdown)


Summary table (current best-known settings)
NOTE: these are *proposed* safe defaults for runtime-1.22 canary. Final call after perf-canary + SRE signoff.

Hosted (default-on in limited canary cohort)
- compaction_enabled: true (flag)
- trigger_FR: 0.55
- time_budget_ms_per_step:
  - decode boundary: 0.20ms
  - prefill boundary: 0.35ms
- bytes_budget_per_step: 128MB (secondary cap)
- cooldown: 0s initially (consider 10s after canary)
- eviction_enabled: true (flag)
- eviction_free_threshold: 2% arena free
- eviction_policy: tier-aware LRU; premium = emergency-only

Dedicated (default-off initially; opt-in per pool)
- trigger_FR: 0.60 (tentative)
- time_budget_ms_per_step:
  - decode boundary: 0.15ms
  - prefill boundary: 0.30ms
- bytes_budget_per_step: 128MB
- eviction: enabled only for specific high-churn pools; otherwise off until we have customer messaging


Notes / gotchas collected while running
- The “right” FR threshold depends on allocator page size + model KV shape. If we change layout later, we must rerun.
- Biggest p99 improvements happen when we prevent FR crossing ~0.60 in W1. Once FR is >0.70, compaction can’t catch up without large budgets.
- Beware cancellation edge cases during relocation (fixed in later PR; keep stress tests on).
- Eviction is safer than OOM, but it moves the pain to user-visible extra prefill. Must be tier-correct and observable.

Open questions
- Should trigger_FR be dynamic based on utilization (e.g., lower threshold when utilization is high)?
- How do we treat prefix-cache vs session KV when prefix-cache is “shared-ish” across requests?
- Do we need per-model tuning defaults (at least for the very large KV footprints)?
- Can we estimate “copy cost” better than wall-time to avoid hiding in GPU queueing?

Next steps (as of last edit)
- Rerun W1/W2 on latest runtime branch with PR-19371 (scheduler integration) + PR-19388 (eviction) + kill-switch plumbing (PR-19422).
- Update perf-canary thresholds (PR-412) to include compaction_time + eviction_rate gating.
- Decide canary defaults with SRE (Sean/Allison) and product (Nikhil/Lauren) for Hosted vs Dedicated.

Changelog (manual)
- 2026-02-20: Updated proposed defaults to split budgets by decode vs prefill boundary; added guardrail proposal.
- 2026-02-14: Added canary guardrail simulation notes.
- 2026-01-29: Added eviction sweeps + preliminary threshold.
- 2026-01-19: Switched preference to time-budget guardrail.

title: Prober-driven schema gate with probabilistic function-call diff thresholds and staged unwind
content:
Prober-driven schema gate with probabilistic function-call diff thresholds and staged unwind

Goal: Add a lightweight probing layer that runs parallel (shadow/prober) requests during canaries and A/B slices to detect structured-output and function-call incompatibilities earlier, and automatically trigger a staged unwind when mismatch rates exceed probabilistic thresholds.

Success criteria:
- Detect schema or function-call argument divergence with >90% precision and <2% false positive rate in production-like traffic within first 10k probe events.
- Auto-unwind (canary -> rollback) initiates within configured hysteresis window when the 1-minute rolling mismatch probability exceeds threshold.
- No measurable end-user latency increase for primary traffic (probe traffic is shadowed).

Design overview:
1) Prober agents: small, deterministic probe variants that exercise edge-shaped prompts and typical tool-calling surfaces. Probers run as shadow requests (non-blocking) at a configurable sample rate per route (default 2%).
2) Differential comparator: lightweight sawtooth comparator that computes three signals per invocation: schema-structure-diff (shape/type mismatch), named-arg-diff (missing/extra keys), and semantics-fail (function invoked unexpectedly). Each signal is boolean per probe.
3) Probabilistic gate: instead of hard counts, we maintain exponentially-weighted mismatch probability per route and model-variant; the gate trips when P(mismatch) > configured threshold (default 0.015) sustained for N windows (default 3).
4) Staged unwind actions: on trip, first reduce rollout percentage by 50% and notify canary watchers; if sustained, fully revert to last stable variant and execute incident runbook.

Telemetry & monitoring:
- Metrics: probe.invocations, probe.mismatch.{schema,args,semantics}, probe.mismatch_probability, probe.rollback_trigger_count, probe.latency_p95_shadow.
- Dashboards: canary-compatibility (per-route, per-variant) with a drilldown to failed probes (payload hashes + example diffs).
- Alerts: Pager alert when rollback_trigger_count > 0 for a paid customer route and severity is high. Slack notification to #rollouts for non-prod.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Probabilistic thresholding reduces noisy rollbacks from low-count random divergences but requires careful tuning to avoid delayed detection for high-latency bugs. We prefer EWMA-based probability over fixed counts to adapt across traffic profiles.
- Shadow probes avoid user-facing latency but increase egress and runtime cost; we scope probes to 2% by default and allow burst budgets.
- Comparator must be conservative on schema (type/shape) but aggressive on required named args for tool-calling safety.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for comparator logic + fuzz harness that generates pairwise function-call variants.
- Integration: run prober against model-variants in staging with a replay of production prompt corpus (dataset: canary-prober-replay-2026-02).
- Canary: enable shadow probes at 2% for first 24h then evaluate mismatch_probability; ramp to 5% for second 24h.

Rollout strategy:
- Feature flag gated (canary-compat-prober) plus per-customer opt-out.
- Initial alpha on internal routes and selected non-prod customers.
- Ramp plan: internal -> sandbox customers -> small set of production routes (low-risk) -> global.

Runbook excerpt (automated portion):
1) Gate trips => reduce rollout_pct *= 0.5, send automated Slack message and create a temporary incident channel.
2) If sustained for 3 windows => revert variant, annotate rollout with reason and attach failing probe sample.
3) Post-mortem triggers if rollback happened on >1 route within 24 hours.

Open implementation notes & blockers:
- Need a compact canonical diff format to store probe failures in telemetry without PII; blocked by privacy review (SEC-PRIV-41).
- Runtime integration: lightweight comparator must run in serving path's shadow pipeline; avoid allocating large objects to not perturb GC in host process.
- Edge case: cached responses (KV cache) can mask mismatches for some probes; we're adding a probe header to force no-cache for probe traffic.

Artifacts & references:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/PROBER-GATE-2026
- GitHub sketch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1782 (prober scaffolding)
- Telemetry dashboard (Datadog): https://app.datadog.com/dashboard/canary-compat-2026
- Probe corpus (internal GCS): gs://redwood-canary/probes/2026-02-replay.jsonl

Next steps (this sprint):
- Complete comparator C implementation and land PR for shadow pipeline integration.
- Finalize canonical diff schema with security & product.
- Add alerting rules and dashboard panels for first-run alpha.

Acceptance criteria for this ticket:
- Shadow probe pipeline lives in runtime and can be toggled by per-route config.
- Comparator produces telemetry metrics and example diff payloads (sanitized).
- Automated staged unwind executes on simulated trip in integration tests.
2026-03-03 Sana Iqbal: Initial design is up. Marco to prototype comparator functions; requested PM review from Leila.
2026-03-05 Marco Alvarez: Implemented comparator prototype (C) and added unit tests. PR posted: runtime#1782. Benchmarks show median probe overhead <1ms for shadow path.
2026-03-08 Leila Chen (PM): Reviewed. Request: expose per-customer opt-out and an escalation label for enterprise SLA routes. Also asked to add audit log entry for auto-unwinds.
2026-03-10 Security: flagged privacy note — diff payload must be scrubbed. Proposed scheme: payload-hash + sanitized-diff. SEC-PRIV-41 filed.
2026-03-12 Marco Alvarez: Added EWMA gate logic and hysteresis. Starting integration tests against staging replay. Noted a transient failure due to KV cache — adding no-cache header for probes.

title: Define latency SLO tiers and acceptance gates for tiered batching perf CI/canary
content:
Define latency SLO tiers and acceptance gates for tiered batching perf CI/canary

Goal
Finalize numeric latency targets for the three customer-facing SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient) and codify pass/fail gates used by the perf suite + perf-canary so we can safely roll out workload-aware batching defaults.

Scope
- Provide concrete numeric targets (p50/p95/p99) per tier for:
  - Non-streaming requests (end-to-end latency)
  - Streaming requests (TTFT and per-token cadence; explicitly call out what we gate on)
- Define acceptance gates for:
  - Benchmark-lab suite runs (pre-merge / nightly)
  - Perf-canary (merge blocker) thresholds and baseline refresh policy
- Specify which model families/hardware/regions are in-scope for gating for runtime-1.22 launch.

Non-goals
- We are not defining customer contractual SLAs here (Product will reference these for messaging, but SRE owns SLA docs).
- We are not choosing batching knob values here (that’s the scheduler/profile work); this is the target + gating contract.

Proposed tier definitions (for runtime perf validation)
Units: milliseconds. All numbers are measured at the runtime boundary (request admitted -> response complete) for non-streaming, and at runtime boundary for streaming TTFT (request admitted -> first token emitted). Unless noted, gates are evaluated at steady-state concurrency (see “Gating workload shape”).

A) Non-streaming (end-to-end latency)
Fast tier
- p50 <= 350ms
- p95 <= 900ms
- p99 <= 1400ms
Standard tier
- p50 <= 500ms
- p95 <= 1400ms
- p99 <= 2200ms
Cost-efficient tier
- p50 <= 700ms
- p95 <= 2200ms
- p99 <= 3500ms

B) Streaming
We gate streaming on TTFT and “decode smoothness” (not strict p95 token-to-token, but a regression guard). Rationale: batching defaults mainly move queueing/prefill behavior; customers mostly feel TTFT + long stalls.

Fast tier (streaming)
- TTFT p50 <= 250ms
- TTFT p95 <= 650ms
- TTFT p99 <= 1100ms
- Stall guard: % of responses with >250ms inter-chunk gap after first token must not increase by >0.5pp vs baseline (measured on streaming scenarios only).

Standard tier (streaming)
- TTFT p50 <= 350ms
- TTFT p95 <= 900ms
- TTFT p99 <= 1500ms
- Stall guard: % with >400ms inter-chunk gap must not increase by >0.5pp vs baseline.

Cost-efficient tier (streaming)
- TTFT p50 <= 450ms
- TTFT p95 <= 1200ms
- TTFT p99 <= 2000ms
- Stall guard: % with >600ms inter-chunk gap must not increase by >0.5pp vs baseline.

Notes / clarifications
- These are runtime targets for the tiered batching defaults feature. The platform will still enforce overload behavior (backpressure/load shed) rather than allowing unbounded tail latency. Where overload mode triggers, we treat results separately (see “Overload handling in gates”).
- If a model family cannot meet fast-tier p99 on a given hardware class without unacceptable throughput collapse, the correct path is: model-family compatibility doc marks “fast tier not supported” for that hardware (and selection logic must emit a reason code and downgrade). This ticket defines the targets and gating expectations, not the compatibility matrix.

Gating workload shape (benchmark methodology contract)
To avoid bikeshedding in each perf PR, we standardize the workload parameters used by CI/canary for these gates:
- Prompt length buckets: short (<=256 tok), medium (257–1024), long (1025–4096)
- Output length: fixed per scenario (e.g., 128 tok decode for chat, 256 for summarization) to reduce variance
- Mix for tier validation:
  - Fast: 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long; streaming-heavy (>=70% streaming)
  - Standard: 40% short, 40% medium, 20% long; mixed streaming (50/50)
  - Cost-efficient: 30% short, 45% medium, 25% long; mostly non-streaming (>=70% non-streaming)
- Concurrency ramps: evaluate at 3 points (low/target/high) per model/hardware to catch queueing thresholds (exact numbers owned by benchmark-lab but must include a “near saturation” point).

What we gate in CI vs canary
1) Pre-merge (benchmark-lab / perf suite)
- Soft gate (non-blocking initially for 2 weeks after enabling new scenarios): report deltas, create auto-ticket if exceeding thresholds.
- After warmup period: blocking gate for fast-tier TTFT p99 and non-streaming p99 only (to avoid blocking on high-variance metrics early).

2) Perf-canary (merge blocker)
Hard gates (must pass to merge for runtime-1.22 branches once enabled):
- Fast tier:
  - Streaming TTFT p99 must not regress by >7% vs baseline (per model/hardware), and must remain under the absolute target above.
  - Non-streaming p99 must not regress by >7% vs baseline and must remain under absolute target.
- Standard tier:
  - Non-streaming p95 must not regress by >8% vs baseline and must remain under absolute target.
- Cost-efficient tier:
  - Throughput guard (primary): tokens/sec must not regress by >5% vs baseline on cost-efficient scenarios.
  - Tail-latency guard (secondary): non-streaming p99 must not regress by >10% vs baseline.

Baseline policy
- Baselines are per (model family, hardware class, scenario tier, streaming flag).
- Baseline refresh requires:
  - Two consecutive nightly runs showing improvement and stable variance
  - Approval from Runtime Scheduling EM (Sofia) + SRE (Sean) to avoid “refreshing away” a regression
  - Linked internal ticket (use INT-* or ENG-18428 follow-up) documenting why refresh is safe.

Overload handling in gates
- If overload mode triggers (admission control / shedding), we do not fail solely on latency inflation; instead:
  - Verify overload mode is entered at the expected concurrency point (no earlier than baseline by >10%)
  - Verify shed rate does not increase by >1pp vs baseline for fast tier scenarios
- Any earlier-than-baseline overload triggering is treated as a regression.

In-scope for runtime-1.22 gating (initial)
Model families (top traffic):
- Llama-3.x 8B/70B chat variants (hosted)
- Mistral-family mid-size chat (hosted)
Hardware classes:
- H100 and A100 for hosted; L4 for a single “edge/cheap” lane (standard + cost-efficient only)
Regions:
- us-east-1, eu-west-1 (primary); add us-west-2 once variance is within bounds.

Deliverables
- Numbers and definitions above are mirrored into the SRE/architecture SLO tier doc:
  sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/latency-slo-tiers-definition-fast-standard-cost-efficient.json
- Perf-canary gating spec to be implemented under:
  sources/github/perf-canary/pr-489-gate-on-fast-tier-p99-and-standard-tier-p95.json
- Benchmark-lab scenarios updated under:
  sources/github/benchmark-lab/pr-612-add-mixed-workload-slo-tier-scenarios.json

Open questions (resolved in comments below)
- Whether to gate streaming on p95 TTFT or p99 TTFT for fast tier (decision: p99, with baseline % regression + absolute target).
- Whether to publish absolute numbers externally or keep as internal gates (decision: publish tier intent and ranges externally; keep p99 absolute values as internal gates initially; PM to update copy accordingly).

Acceptance criteria
- Confluence SLO tier doc updated with numeric targets and explicit measurement definitions.
- Perf-canary gate definitions agreed by Runtime + SRE and tracked for implementation.
- Any model/hardware exceptions documented as compatibility constraints (reason-code-driven downgrade) rather than silently failing fast tier.

Risks
- High variance on p99 in GPU-shared environments could cause false positives. Mitigation: baseline regression threshold + require multiple-run confirmation for baseline updates; canary runs pin to dedicated canary capacity.
- Streaming stall guard metric instrumentation is not fully baked. Mitigation: implement as “delta vs baseline only” initially and do not hard-block on it until metrics are stable.

Owners
- Primary: Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling)
- Review/approval: Sean Gallagher (SRE), Jonas Weber (Applied ML / evals), Marcus Reed (perf suite integration)

2025-11-20 (Sofia Ivanova): Drafted initial numeric targets based on recent H100/A100 traces. Pushed p99 targets slightly looser than current best-case to allow batching headroom; will rely on perf-canary regression thresholds to catch unexpected tail regressions.
2025-11-22 (Sean Gallagher): SRE feedback: we need explicit streaming definition. Customers care about TTFT and long stalls more than mean throughput. Requested stall-guard metric but ok to keep non-blocking until telemetry stabilizes.
2025-12-02 (Marcus Reed): Perf suite note: p99 is noisy unless we standardize concurrency ramps and use pinned canary capacity. Added proposal to treat overload separately (don’t fail on high latency if admission control is behaving).
2025-12-08 (Jonas Weber): Applied ML note: please ensure prompt sets include at least one code-ish workload; some models have distinct prefill characteristics that affect TTFT. OK with weighting staying mostly chat/summarization for launch.
2026-01-06 (Allison Grant): Observability constraint: tier label cardinality must be controlled; gates should be per (tier/model/hardware) but avoid per-route. Confirmed baseline keys match proposed dimensions.
2026-01-10 (Sofia Ivanova): Decision: fast tier gates on streaming TTFT p99 (not p95). Reason: tail latency protection is the core risk; p95 can look fine while p99 explodes under mixed prompt lengths.
2026-01-14 (Sean Gallagher): Final pass: targets acceptable. Added baseline refresh approval process to avoid masking regressions. Confirmed this ticket now blocks ENG-18428 enabling merge gates.
2026-01-27 (Sofia Ivanova): Marking done. Numeric targets mirrored into SLO tier doc; perf-canary and benchmark-lab PRs reference this ticket for thresholds.

title: Clarify atomic refill and token-slicing interactions for multiplexed orchestrator causing intermittent 429s
content:
Clarify atomic refill and token-slicing interactions for multiplexed orchestrator causing intermittent 429s

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 429s from a dedicated pool while running orchestrated worker fanouts that multiplex many short-lived sessions. The customer suspects token-slicing and atomic refill semantics are causing groups of parallel workers to collide on refill boundaries.

Impact: Roughly 8–12% of requests are receiving 429s during scheduled flush windows for their background ingest and the rate spikes are correlated with their orchestrator job starts. This is causing delays in their pipeline and some time-sensitive webhook retries to fail.

Environment: MetricFlow dedicated pool in prod-us-west, traffic originates from a fleet of orchestrator workers that open ephemeral sessions and use API keys rotated every 6 minutes. Workload pattern: bursts of ~200 short sessions that call streaming start then immediately push small chunks (~1-3k tokens).

Observed behavior: 429s come in tight waves aligned to the orchestrator job start times. Throttle headers show remaining=0 and x-refill-epoch points to a refill event that applied to a group of sessions simultaneously. Customer believes refill is being computed atomically per-namespace and token-sliced windows allow momentary negative bursts.

Steps to reproduce (customer provided):
1) Create a dedicated pool and provision 2 workers per orchestrator shard.
2) Rotate ephemeral keys every 6 minutes and fanout 200 workers to start within a 30s window.
3) Each worker starts a streaming session and immediately emits a small payload.
4) Observe 429s concentrated within the first 90s of the job.

Request: Customer asks for an explanation of refill semantics when many short-lived sessions start together and guidance on configuration to avoid synchronized 429 waves. They also ask whether splitting refill epochs or changing token-slicing granularity will help and what recommended knob changes are safe for a dedicated pool.
2026-03-12 10:20 UTC - Received initial ticket with customer logs and sample traffic pattern (200 workers, ephemeral keys).
Checked tenant rate limiter logs: refill events recorded at epoch boundaries with batch size consistent with configured burst budget. Noted a cluster of token grants followed by immediate consumption and subsequent remaining=0 for many sessions.
Hypothesis A: Atomic refill per-tenant combined with synchronized session start leads to token allocation granularity causing short-lived sessions to contend and exhaust micro-budgets simultaneously.
Hypothesis B: Token-slicing uses coarse-grain shards (N=8) for this tenant; when many sessions map to same slice the refill appears atomic and causes seen 429 wave. Consider reducing slice size or enabling random jitter on refill mapping.
Observed metric: token_grants_per_epoch spiked from baseline 1200 to 18k during job window; per-slice utilization showed 60% of allocations hitting two slices.
Console trace: route-level latency spiked 5x during event; no 5xxs from serving runtime—rejections are explicit rate rejects.
Customer token rotation pattern (6m TTL) is causing many ephemeral keys to align with refill boundaries due to orchestrator scheduling; recommend reviewing key rotation schedule as well.
Checked linked issue SUP-3141596 for similar refill alignment cases; that ticket implemented refill jitter experiments on staging with positive results.
Action taken so far: increased customer's burst allowance temporarily by +20% for their dedicated pool to provide immediate relief while we evaluate config changes.
Telemetry snapshot saved: s3://redwood-support/telemetry/SUP-527890/epoch-snap-20260312.json (access granted to eng on request).
Priya Agarwal (2026-03-12T11:02Z): Thanks for the report. I've increased a temporary burst buffer on the dedicated pool to reduce immediate impact. Can you send a short window of request IDs and the orchestrator start timestamps so we can correlate?
MetricFlow - Ops (2026-03-12T11:37Z): Provided sample requestIDs and job-start timestamps for two windows (2026-03-11T23:00Z and 2026-03-12T03:00Z). Noted pattern: starts are scheduled by cron jobs in their orchestrator which align closely with system clocks across shards.
Ethan Chen (SRE) (2026-03-12T13:10Z): Observed per-slice hot-spotting. Tentative plan: run a controlled experiment to change slice_count from 8 to 32 for this tenant in staging and add random refill jitter of up to 30s to epoch boundary. Asking Product if jitter change is safe for SLA window accounting.
Product (2026-03-12T14:05Z): Jitter change acceptable at customer-level for non-critical low-latency lanes. For higher tiers would need rollout notes. Suggest start with orchestrator/background lane only.
MetricFlow - Dev (2026-03-12T15:22Z): We can stagger cron starts by introducing per-shard random delay up to 45s. But we'd prefer config guidance on the server side so we don't have to change many orchestrators across fleets.
Ethan Chen (2026-03-13T09:40Z): Deployed slice_count=32 and refill_jitter=20s in staging for a shadow of MetricFlow traffic. Early results: reduction in 429 wave amplitude by ~70% in staging shadow runs. Preparing rollout playbook.
Priya Agarwal (2026-03-14T08:12Z): Noted that customer agreed to a staged rollout: apply slice_count increase + refill jitter to background-lane only, monitor for billing/console effects, then decide on global lane changes. Will coordinate maintenance window.
MetricFlow - Ops (2026-03-14T12:01Z): Thank you, please proceed with background-lane change during our maintenance window 2026-03-15 02:00-03:00 UTC. We'll monitor.
Temporary burst allowance increased +20%; staging experiment with slice_count=32 and refill_jitter=20s reduced 429 wave amplitude by ~70%. Planned staged rollout to customer background lane during maintenance window. Final resolution pending production rollout and 48h monitoring.

Outcome-driven quarterly lanes for Hosted API + Model Catalog

Objective: Create a reusable, outcome-driven quarterly planning lane specifically for the Hosted API + Model Catalog that ties initiatives directly to OKRs, capacity guardrails, and canary rollout windows. Rationale: previous quarters focused heavily on feature lists; this ticket formalizes an outcomes-first template so PMs and Eng can make trade-offs against capacity and measurable KPIs. Scope: define the lane structure (Outcome, Key Results, Initiatives, Risks), cadence (planning, mid-cycle check, canary windows), gating (eval sets, perf regressions, SLO impact), and a lightweight runbook for rollouts and emergency rollback. title: Manual traffic shift: Hosted API regional failover (US/EU)
content:
Manual traffic shift: Hosted API regional failover (US/EU)

# Purpose
This runbook describes how to manually shift (fail over) production inference traffic for the Hosted API between regions or clusters during GPU capacity shortages, elevated error rates, or regional degradation.

# Scope
- Applies to: chat + embeddings endpoints served by Redwood API (Hosted).
- Not for: Redwood Dedicated customer-specific pools (see dedicated incident playbooks).

# Triggers (choose one)
- Sustained 5xx > 1% for 10+ minutes in a region
- p95 latency > 2x baseline for 15+ minutes with correlated GPU saturation
- GPU capacity deficit (queue depth increasing; admission control engaged)
- Cloud provider incident impacting a region

# Preconditions
- Incident declared or oncall lead approval
- Status page draft ready (if customer-visible)
- Confirm target region has headroom (GPU free capacity + router capacity)

# Definitions
- "Traffic shift": changing routing weights so new requests land in a different region/cluster
- "Failover": shift to secondary region and disable new traffic to primary

# Procedure (regional traffic shift)
1) Confirm situation
   - Check dashboards: Hosted API error rate, p95 latency, queue depth, GPU utilization
   - Confirm whether issue is model-specific or region-wide

2) Choose target
   - Preferred: same cloud + secondary region (us-west -> us-east; eu-west -> eu-central)
   - If capacity constrained, pick the region with the most available GPU pool headroom

3) Prepare routing override
   - Open the routing override doc: confluence://eng-platform/router-policy-manual-traffic-shift
   - Identify the "hosted-api-prod" policy and the route group for the impacted endpoint(s)

4) Shift traffic gradually
   - Start with 20% weight to target region for new requests
   - Observe for 5–10 minutes: errors, latency, saturation in target
   - Increase to 50%, then 80% if stable

5) Full failover (if needed)
   - Set impacted region weight to 0% for new requests
   - Keep existing in-flight streams running when possible
   - Confirm rate limiting thresholds in target region are compatible

6) Verification
   - Confirm overall system p95 recovers within 15 minutes
   - Confirm token throughput is stable and no sustained 429 spikes
   - Confirm new incidents are not triggered in the target region

7) Rollback
   - Reverse weights in 20% increments
   - If rollback causes immediate degradation, pause and reassess capacity

# Cluster-level alternative
If the issue is isolated to a single cluster (not whole region), use the infra drain + handoff procedure first: confluence://eng-infra/gpu-cluster-drain-and-traffic-shift-handoff

# Communication
- Use the oncall checklist: confluence://oncall-and-incident-response/initiating-regional-traffic-shift-checklist
- Post updates in #incidents and #eng-sre

# Common pitfalls
- Shifting traffic without confirming tokenizer/model compatibility across regions
- Over-shifting too quickly and saturating the target region
- Forgetting to remove overrides after the incident

# Owners
- Primary: Eng SRE
- Routing changes: Eng Platform (Router/Policy)
- Capacity: Eng Infra (GPU fleet)

title: Dynamic scope binding and privilege resolution spec for RBAC v2
content:
Dynamic scope binding and privilege resolution spec for RBAC v2

Define a deterministic, auditable privilege resolution model for RBAC v2 that supports dynamic scope binding across resource hierarchies, integrates with SSO/SAML assertions, emits rich audit events for every decision, and provides admin controls including emergency breakglass and scoped delegation. This ticket captures design goals, concrete resolution algorithms, example matrices, migration considerations, and operational hooks for the Console and runtime.
Core idea: treat scopes as first-class, namespaced bindings that can be static (tenant-level) or dynamic (request-bound). At request time, the system builds a 'scope stack' by walking the resource hierarchy from requested resource to tenancy root, collecting explicit scope bindings and evaluating them with an ordered algorithm: 1) explicit deny at nearest scope, 2) explicit allow at nearest scope, 3) role-derived permissions (closest scope wins), 4) attribute-based grants (SAML/OIDC claim-driven) as tie-breakers, 5) global defaults. Roles are declarative sets of actions tied to resource classes; role-templates may be parameterized by scope variables (e.g., project_id). For SSO/SAML, attributes map to initial role assignments and to ephemeral request attributes (group, department, external_project). These attributes have a precedence table: direct role assignment > SAML-group assignment > SCIM-synced group > OIDC claim. Audit events must capture the fully expanded permission set and the evaluation trace (scope anchors, rules hit, deny/allow source). Breakglass is implemented as a short-lived override token issued by the Console with mandatory justification recorded; breakglass tokens are revoked automatically and emit both creation and use audit events.
A clear, unambiguous permission evaluation order that covers role inheritance, scope overrides, deny/allow precedence, and attribute-based exceptions.
Mapping rules from SAML attributes / OIDC claims to role assignments and scope anchors with deterministic precedence documented.
Audit event schema defined for: role assignment changes, resolved permissions per request, scope-binding decisions, and breakglass activations.
Admin UI wireframes and API endpoints for scoped delegation, role previews, and one-click breakglass with TTL and justification tracking.
A migration plan with compatibility mode for existing RBAC v1 tokens and a rollout checklist for Dedicated/Private clusters.
Spec review and alignment with Product and Security (1 week): finalize evaluation order and SAML claim mappings.
Schema changes: extend role binding table with 'scope_kind' and 'binding_origin' columns and add 'evaluation_trace' field to audit_events (DB migration + index plan).
Runtime: implement scope stack builder and evaluate permission engine with deterministic logging (feature-flagged).
Console: add Role Preview UI (show expanded permissions for a given user+resource), Breakglass flow, and scoped delegation controls.
E2E tests: policy fuzzing harness that generates random hierarchies and asserts deterministic outcomes; include regression suite for deny/allow precedence.
Migration: compatibility layer for RBAC v1 tokens for 8 weeks, telemetry to track mismatches, and rollback plan.
Should explicit 'deny' be globally highest precedence or scoped-nearest highest? (proposal: nearest-scope deny outranks global allow).
How to represent attribute-based ephemeral grants in audit logs without leaking sensitive attribute values? (proposal: hash attributes and store policy id).
What is the retention period for evaluation_trace in audit_events given storage costs? (proposal: 90 days hot, 365 days cold).
Do we allow nested delegation (A delegates to B, B delegates to C) and how to limit blast radius?
How does breakglass interact with external identity providers' session policies and MFA requirements?
Adopt 'nearest-scope wins' for both allows and denies; explicit deny at a closer scope overrides allows at parent scopes.
SAML/OIDC claim mapping will be configurable per customer; default mappings provided for common IdPs (Okta, Azure AD).
Evaluation trace will include policy identifiers and decision outcomes; raw claim values will be redacted and represented by stable hashes.
Incorrect precedence could accidentally grant access during the migration window; mitigated by compatibility mode and sampling telemetry.
Audit log volume will increase significantly when we log evaluation traces per request; require retention/aggregation plan.
Complex delegation chains introduce escalation paths; require approval workflows and delegation TTLs in UI.
2026-03-06 Marcus Liu: Drafted evaluation order and shared with Security. Need product sign-off on SAML attribute precedence.
2026-03-08 Priya Menon (Product): Recommend adding an explicit 'role preview' step in the Console before applying scoped delegation; this is now included.
2026-03-10 Security Review: Agreed to redact raw attribute values in logs and use SHA-256 with salt for stable hashing. Follow-up: define salt rotation policy.
2026-03-12 Marcus Liu: Added DB migration notes and flagged audit index performance as potential blocker; scheduled spike.

title: Session-aware cost tuning playbook
content:
Session-aware cost tuning playbook

Summary:
This playbook defines the product guidance, internal runbook, and pricing heuristics for session-aware cost tuning. It targets teams building conversational or session-based integrations that need predictable per-session economics while preserving latency and quality SLOs. The document covers when to choose session-aware pricing, how to compute per-session effective cost, recommended fidelity presets and discounts, telemetry signals to monitor, and a staged rollout plan for Hosted and Dedicated customers.

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable method to estimate, present, and bill per-session costs for conversational products.
- Give product and sales concrete presets and negotiation levers for customers migrating from pure per-token billing to session-pricing.
- Ensure fidelity and latency SLOs are respected with clear fallback and rollback steps.

Scope:
- Applies to: Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Redwood Optimize cost recommendations when sessions are the primary billing unit.
- Not in scope: One-off batch embedding jobs, pure vector store billing, or marketplace third-party resale.

When to apply session-aware pricing:
1. Customer wants predictable monthly cost for interactive experiences with variable tokens per conversation.
2. High frequency short sessions (e.g., chat widgets) where token variance creates billing unpredictability.
3. Customers requesting fidelity guarantees per session (response consistency SLO).

Key definitions:
- Session: A logical conversational interaction tied to a session_id maintained by the integrator for up to 30 minutes of inactivity.
- Session unit: Billing unit representing an allocated compute & fidelity envelope for the session (includes kv-cache usage, warmup, and reserved micro-burst capacity).
- Fidelity preset: A named profile (low/medium/high) mapping to model variant, quantization, and max token budget.

Pricing model variants (recommended):
- Fixed session price: flat price per session unit (best for small/consistent interactions).
- Hybrid: base session fee + per-token on overage (best for unpredictable long sessions).
- Tiered fidelity bundles: customers buy bundles of sessions at different fidelity presets with discounts on committed volume.

Recommended baseline presets (example):
- low-fidelity (L1): gpt-like-2s-quant, max_input 512 tokens, max_output 256 tokens, 10 ms tail-latency SLO, recommended for high-volume low-complexity tasks. Price: $0.003 per session.
- medium-fidelity (M1): open-xlarge-1, max_input 2048 tokens, max_output 512 tokens, 30 ms tail-latency SLO, Price: $0.01 per session.
- high-fidelity (H1): open-xxl, max_input 4096 tokens, max_output 1024 tokens, 100 ms tail-latency SLO, Price: $0.04 per session.
(Prices are illustrative; final contract pricing is adjusted by region, commitment, and Dedicated capacity mix.)

Economics calculation (example table):
| Metric | low-fidelity | medium-fidelity | high-fidelity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| avg tokens per session (input+output) | 150 | 600 | 1800 |
| tokens processed per session (incl. caching) | 120 | 420 | 1300 |
| GPU-second equivalent | 0.02 | 0.08 | 0.35 |
| incremental infra cost estimate | $0.0006 | $0.0024 | $0.0105 |
| suggested session price | $0.003 | $0.01 | $0.04 |

Notes on calculation: use 90-day rolling medians for tokens/session, prefix-cache hit-rate, and model-level throughput to avoid over-indexing on spikes. For Dedicated customers, base infra cost should use committed capacity marginal cost rather than public hosted rates.

Telemetry & KPIs to publish in Console:
- sessions.created per minute, sessions.active, median & 95th percentile tokens per session
- session_fidelity_applied metric (enum: L1/M1/H1)
- session_warmup_seconds and session_warmup_success (boolean)
- billing_effective_cost_per_session (derived)
- fidelity_overage_events and fallback_reasons

Customer onboarding checklist (sales & CSM):
1. Collect expected session profile: avg length, peak concurrency, expected monthly sessions, required SLOs.
2. Recommend fidelity presets and simulate economics using the simulator (see Appendix A).
3. Agree on warm-capacity reservation level for peak concurrency and any burst credits.
4. Define rollback trigger thresholds: e.g., cost drift >15% or user-visible latency > target for 24h.

Internal rollout runbook (engineering + product):
1. Feature toggle: enable session-pricing per tenant (console flag: session_pricing_enabled).
2. Implement meter: attach session_id label to telemetry & billing pipeline.
3. Acceptance tests: synthetic traffic generator with 3 session profiles (short, medium, long) and assert billing matches simulator within 5%.
4. Canary: release to <5 customers with auto-rollback if billing_mismatch_rate > 2% or fidelity_fallback_rate > 1%.
5. Scale: open to broader beta after 2-week stability and sign-off from Finance.

Customer-facing docs and UX notes:
- Console should show per-session cost estimate with sliders to alter avg tokens and fidelity preset.
- Provide an exportable simulation report (CSV) with expected monthly cost, peak concurrency recommendation, and recommended commitment tier.
- Show fallback transparency: if a session falls back (quantized variant or lower fidelity) record and expose reason and cost delta.

Rollback and incident playbook (SRE):
1. Detect: alert if billing_effective_cost_per_session drift > 20% vs expected for >1h (PAGE S1).
2. Triage: check recent model variant changes, quantization rollouts, and autoscaler events.
3. Immediate mitigation: switch impacted tenants to hybrid mode (base fee + per-token) and cap session concurrency to last-known-safe level.
4. Postmortem: include cost delta, root cause, customer impact, and required product changes.

Rollout timeline (recommended):
- Q1 2027: Internal alpha (engineering + product) with simulator and console mockups.
- Q2 2027: Beta with up to 10 customers (hosted + dedicated pilot).
- Q3 2027: Public launch with SDK updates, console features, and billing integration.

Ownership and contacts:
- Product lead: Priya Menon
- Engineering owner: Daniel Wu (runtime billing integration)
- Finance steward: Mariana Costa
- SRE contact: Luca Moretti

Appendix A — Quick simulator examples (CLI):
1) Local simulation (example):
$ redwood-sim sessions --preset M1 --avg-input 400 --avg-output 200 --monthly-sessions 250000 --out report.csv
2) Draft JSON payload for pricing API (example):
{
  "tenant_id": "T-12345",
  "pricing_mode": "hybrid",
  "base_session_fee": "0.01",
  "overage_per_token": "0.000002",
  "fidelity_presets": ["M1"]
}

Appendix B — Done criteria for public launch:
- Telemetry shows accurate session attribution for 30 days with <1% unmapped events.
- Finance validates margin model across hosted & dedicated customers with sample contracts.
- Console UX passes accessibility and clarity heuristics with customer testing.

Document history:
- 2026-11-15: Draft created by Priya Menon.
- 2026-12-08: Internal review with Runtime and Finance; updated fidelity presets.
- 2027-01-12: Updated rollout timeline and approval for Beta cohort.

Related links:
