- PRD: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/prd-session-resilience-and-fallback-contract-2026-08-03

Questions or feedback: contact priya.menon@redwood.com

title: Feature-gated traffic shift — internal announce + Q&A (notes)
content:
Feature-gated traffic shift — internal announce + Q&A (notes)

Purpose: quick internal announce and Q&A scaffold for the staged traffic shift to the 'latency-optim' model variant behind a feature gate. This is my working notes — rough, intentionally choppy.

Audience: ENG (serving/runtime, infra, sres), Product ops, CS triage leads, Support L2, Growth (for feature-flag targeting), Execs (brief line). Tailor messaging for each group.

High-level ask: we will enable the new model variant (quantized, smaller KV footprint) behind a feature flag for 10% of host-api requests starting Fri 10/11 18:00 PT. Goal: validate latency improvements and error mode behavior at scale while keeping ability to rollback to stable model within 2 minutes.

What I want to land in the short announce (one-paragraph):
- Why: expected median p50 token latency improvement ~12–18% on p3/gh200 families for common seq lengths (64–256). Also expected token-cost reduction ~8% with negligible quality regression for short-respone queries.
- When: Fri 10/11 18:00 PT, ramp to 10% over 30m.
- Who: monitored by infra SRE and the release owner (Asha).
- Rollback: instant toggle, fallback to stable routing if error rate >1% or latency tail > +40% vs baseline for 5m.

Quick Q&A (draft responses):
Q: How are we defining success?
A: Primary: no regression in end-to-end error rate (API 5xx + model errors) and <10% increase in p99 latency. Secondary: token-cost per request reduction and stability of output (sampled prompts show no hallucination spike on our eval set).

Q: Will this affect enterprise/tiered customers?
A: Not initially. Feature gate excludes dedicated and private deployments; flag applied only to hosted-api free-tier & standard routes. Enterprise customer tokens are pinned to stable model variants.

Q: Who can flip the flag?
A: Asha (release owner) + SRE on-call (primary) + me as fallback. We will use the feature-control service (audit logs enabled).

Q: What monitoring is in place?
A: Dashboard: latency by route/model-variant, error-rate by route, model-quality sampling (prompt subset), alerting: page on 5xx increase >0.5pp or p99 increase >30% sustained 5m. Synthetic golden prompts hit every 2m. Logs: correlation ids for sampled traces.

Q: How do we communicate rollback to customers?
A: No customer-facing change planned. If we rollback due to regressions, ops will send a short post-mortem to #ops-notices and customer-success if any customers were impacted.

Talking points for SRE/infra sync (bullet list for standup):
- Preflight checklist: kernel flags, inference node pool autoscale policies reviewed, canary sample size validated, golden prompt runbook ready.
- Resource check: ensure at least 2 spare p3/gh200 nodes in pool for rollouts.
- KV cache warm-up: schedule pre-warm of top 1000 prefixes for the 2h window prior to shift.
- Emergency rollback procedure: feature-control toggle + routing table restore + drain in-flight tokens to avoid partial outputs.

Open/unknowns (notes to self):
- Need exact query set for the "golden prompts" — coordinate with Applied ML (Benji) to ensure it captures long-tail failure modes.
- Confirm cost accounting tag will surface on billing exports (so finance can see delta for the experiment).
- Double-check that the feature-flag audit includes actor, timestamp, reason, and pre/post-state.
- Validate that hosted-api quota enforcement won't inadvertently block partial rollouts (some customers have route-specific rate limits).

Draft Slack announce copy (short):
"Heads-up: Fri 10/11 18:00 PT we’ll enable the latency-optim model variant behind a feature flag for 10% of hosted-api traffic (30m ramp). Goal: validate p50/p90 improvements and stability. Monitored by infra SRE + Asha. Rollback criteria set; will post updates in #ops-notices. Ping me or Asha for concerns"

Extended internal email / standup note (longer):
- One-paragraph summary (what/why/when) + link to playbook + who to call for rollback.
- Include the preflight checklist and quick runbook steps (attach Confluence playbook link).

Post-launch follow-ups (what I want to collect):
- 1h: sanity check p50/p90 and errors on targeted routes.
- 4h: sampling of outputs for quality review (Benji).
- 24h: cost delta and aggregate error/latency metrics + decision: keep ramping to 25% or roll back.

Fallback language for execs (one-liner):
"Running a limited, monitored test of a latency-optim model variant to validate production performance. No expected customer-visible changes; rollback is immediate if any stability signals show up"

Tasks before send (todo list):
- [ ] Finalize golden prompt set (Benji).
- [ ] Confirm billing tag (Luis).
- [ ] Dry-run toggle with SRE staging (Asha + SRE).
- [ ] Draft Slack + Standup lines and get a quick +1 from Product leadership.

Notes to self (tone/style):
- Keep public-facing lines minimal and low-risk. Avoid technical caveats in initial announce; route those into a follow-up runbook for ENG.
- Make sure CS triage gets an FAQ snippet (3 bullets) so they can answer common questions quickly.

Recent edits / context:
- 10/02: initial idea after bench-run improvements on 64-token median.
- 10/03: added rollback thresholds after SRE feedback.
- 10/04: tightened ramp window to 30m and added cost-tag ask.

Questions I need help closing (assignments):
- Benji: final golden prompts by 10/07.
- Luis: confirm billing tag + finance contact by 10/08.
- Asha: schedule staging dry-run 10/09.

If anyone reads — feedback welcome. If you want to be on the notify list DM me and I'll add you to the release watchlist.

title: Staging validation and publish playbook for Redwood-verified model performance profiles
content:
Staging validation and publish playbook for Redwood-verified model performance profiles

Problem statement:
Redwood needs a reproducible, low-friction playbook that takes a candidate model from a verified bench run to a published Redwood-verified performance profile. Current onboarding is ad-hoc across teams: engineering runs benches, PM curates results, and publishing is manual. This ticket captures a staged validation + publish workflow that can be automated and audited, includes version pinning guidance, canary rollout rules, rollback criteria, and ongoing revalidation cadence.

Goals:
- Define a deterministic staging validation pipeline that mirrors production workload slices (latency P50/P95/P99, throughput, cost/unit).
- Standardize artifacts required for publishing (bench results, sample workload traces, cost model inputs, bias/quality check links).
- Provide a pinning policy for model variants and a default canary rollout with automated metrics gates.
- Create a publish checklist + automated checks to reduce human error and make publishing auditable.
- Specify periodic revalidation cadence and drift triggers to mark profiles stale.

Success metrics:
- Reduce manual review time per profile by 60% (measured as hours spent by PM and Eng per publish).
- 95% of published profiles have full validation artifacts and pass automated gates at publish time.
- Mean time to rollback for a bad profile <= 30 minutes with automated fallback.

Acceptance criteria:
- A documented staging-to-publish playbook in Confluence (link in attachments).
- CI pipeline job (profile-staging-validation) that runs benches and outputs a canonical manifest with latency/throughput/cost and artifact links.
- Canary deployment policy template: 5% traffic -> 25% -> 100% with automated gate at each step based on SLO/delta thresholds.
- Release checklist implemented as checklist file in repo and a lightweight UI action in the Console to trigger publish.
- Periodic revalidation job scheduled (every 30 days) and drift hooks wired to the evals pipeline.

Proposed staging validation flow (high-level):
1) Intake: model PR + model metadata (architecture, weights hash, quantization knobs) and target dataset slices.
2) Bench run: standardized bench harness executes representative workloads (chat, completion, embeddings) at multiple sequence length distributions and concurrency profiles. Outputs: token-level latency histogram, P50/P95/P99, throughput@seqLen, and cost-per-1M-tokens estimate.
3) KV/prefix caching sanity: run prefix cache microbench to verify KV cache scaling characteristics.
4) Quality smoke tests: run PM prompt set to validate basic output quality (contains sample prompts and reference metrics).
5) Artifact bundle: bench JSON, perf plots, run logs, PR link, and verified-model-manifest attached to staging job.
6) Automated gates evaluate deltas versus baseline profile(s) and check absolute thresholds. If gates pass, job creates a DraftProfile in the profile registry and notifies reviewers.
7) Manual review window (24-48 hours) for PM/Eng/Research to comment; minor issues can be remediated and bench re-run.
8) Canary publish: template rollout policy applies; profile pinned to a stable model variant ID that maps to both hosted and dedicated runtimes.

Automated gate rules (examples):
- Latency P95 must not regress >15% relative to pinned baseline for given sequence lengths.
- Throughput per GPU must be within -20% of baseline or a documented capacity tag with justification.
- Cost per 1M tokens must not exceed baseline by >25% unless explicit business justification present.
- No single microbenchmark should exceed historical max P99 by >200ms for interactive models.
- KV cache hit rate must be >70% for workloads that exercise prefix caching.

Pinning policy summary:
- All published Redwood-verified profiles must include a pinned model identifier that includes model name, semantic version, checksum (weights hash), and recommended runtime flags (quantization, kernel hints). Example: 'gpt-small-v2+q4_0+sha256:abcd1234'.
- Minor weight-only changes (same checksum) are allowed as patch updates; any checksum change requires staged revalidation and a new profile version.
- Profiles should support a backward-compatible aliasing system (stable alias vs exact pin) to allow safe rollback to an older pinned fingerprint.

Canary rollout template (automated):
- Stage 0: DraftProfile created, no traffic. Notify reviewers.
- Stage 1: Canary-1: 5% traffic for 2 hours. Gate: no P95 regression >10% and error rate unchanged.
- Stage 2: Canary-2: 25% traffic for 4 hours. Gate: P95 regression <=12% and SLI error budget consumption within expected range.
- Stage 3: Ramp to 100% after automated approval or manual signoff.
- Fallback: immediate rollback to previous pinned fingerprint if any gate fails; trigger incident alert to oncall and update profile status to "rolled_back".

Revalidation and staleness rules:
- Schedule a full revalidation every 30 days for production profiles and every 7 days for Canary profiles in active testing.
- Trigger revalidation on upstream infra changes (runtime-1.*), major kernel updates, or if the model's token distribution shifts by >20% (tracked by console histogram diffs).
- Profiles failing revalidation are marked STALE and moved to a suggested-refresh queue; customers with active usage receive an opt-in email and a 14-day grace period before autoswitching to fallback variants.

Observability / dashboard needs:
- Per-profile dashboard tile (latency histograms, throughput, cost trajectory, last validation timestamp, pinned fingerprint).
- Diff view between candidate profile and baseline with highlighted regressions and cost delta.
- Automated audit log entry for every publish/rollback with links to artifacts and reviewer approvals.

Operational checklist for publishing (short):
- [ ] Bench artifacts uploaded and manifest created.
- [ ] Automated gates green.
- [ ] PM review complete (comments resolved).
- [ ] Security & privacy checklist (data handling) verified if model used customer data.
- [ ] Canary policy applied and scheduled.
- [ ] Release note drafted and changelog entry created.

Integration and automation tasks (engineering):
- New CI job profile-staging-validation that produces canonical artifact bundle and manifest (ENG-27108).
- Console API endpoint to create DraftProfile and kick off canary (ENG-27345).
- Profile registry change to store fingerprint + alias mapping + publish metadata (ENG-26890).
- Hook evals pipeline for revalidation triggers (ENG-27910).

Risks and trade-offs:
- Tight automated thresholds may block useful model variants that are costlier but still acceptable; include a documented override flow with explicit business justification.
- Additional staging runs increase onboarding latency and infra cost; mitigate by sampling adaptive bench sizes for low-impact models.
- Pinning to exact fingerprints increases operational safety but can delay quick fixes; use aliasing and fast rollback for agility.

Owners and reviewers:
- PM owner: Jonah Patel (assignee).
- Eng owners: Performance infra (Riya Kapoor), Runtime (Marcus Li).
- Research / quality reviewer: Clara Nguyen.
- Design reviewer (Console UX): Leo Martinez.

Deliverables & timeline:
- Week 1 (2025-02-12 -> 2025-02-18): Draft playbook and automated gate definitions; prototype bench harness inputs.
- Week 2 (2025-02-19 -> 2025-02-25): Implement CI job and profile manifest; initial console endpoint stub.
- Week 3 (2025-02-26 -> 2025-03-04): Integrate canary template and audit logging; run two internal onboarding trials.
- Week 4 (2025-03-05 -> 2025-03-15): Iterate on reviewer feedback, finalize Confluence playbook, and flip publish to GA for open-model catalog.

Attachments:
- https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/PM-24321+Profile+Staging+Playbook
- https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1abcStagingBenchArtifacts
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness/pull/374
- Draft checklist: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1exampleChecklist

Notes: This ticket intentionally separates gating logic from the Console UI surface — the former must be engine-agnostic and owned by Performance infra, the latter is a thin orchestration layer owned by Console.

Next steps:
- Jonah and Riya to align on gate thresholds and signal definitions (+ meeting scheduled 2025-02-14 11:00 PST).
- ENG owners to open the CI job epic and link back to this ticket.
- Run the first internal onboarding with model 'open-translate-v1' and document learnings as comments below.
2025-02-12 10:03 - Amina Ruiz: Created initial ticket after sync with Research. Added high-level flow and success metrics. Assigned to Jonah.
2025-02-14 11:47 - Jonah Patel: Meeting notes: agreed to start gates conservative (15% latency / 25% cost), Riya to prototype bench harness. Action: ENG to spin up profile-staging CI job (ENG-27108).
2025-02-18 16:22 - Riya Kapoor: Prototype bench harness PR opened (link in attachments). Early run on open-translate-v1 shows P95 +8% but cost +30% against small baseline. Need PM decision on cost tolerance for translation models.
2025-02-20 09:05 - Clara Nguyen: Research review: quality smoke tests passed for prompts in baseline set, recommend adding semantic similarity checks (BLEU/COMET) for translation workloads.

title: Summerset platform activation sync-up
content:
Summerset platform activation sync-up

Initial implementation kickoff to align on activation runway, security constraints, and pilot benchmarks. Customer prefers dedicated/private deployment but needs cost scenarios and VPC design details. Immediate deliverables: pricing scenarios, security pack, and pilot test matrix.
Onboarding runbook and permissions
Dedicated vs hosted deployment tradeoffs
Pilot benchmark scope and metrics
Networking and VPC peering
SAML/SSO, KMS, and audit logging
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-07-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE); Priya Reddy (Redwood CSM); Jasper Liu (Redwood SE); Marina Cole (Summerset Eng Mgr); Omar Aziz (Summerset Cloud Architect); Lena Park (Summerset Security)

Summary: quick kick off to align ops, security, and pilot. Capture next steps for pricing and pilot setup.

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. We'll do quick intros then dive into the activation runway. Priya and Jasper will handle the onboarding timeline and technical plan.
[00:18] Marina: Hi all, thanks, excited. We want to get clear on the timeline - Q4 launch target and a pilot in late July, maybe early August.
[00:35] Priya (CSM): Great. Quick question on success criteria — are you primarily looking at latency SLOs, cost per 1k tokens, or both?
[00:50] Marina: Both, but latency for customer-facing chat is highest priority. Cost matters for scale - we're forecasting 10M tokens/month in steady state.
[01:12] Jasper (SE): Okay, latency SLOs—are you targeting p95 under 300ms? Also, do you have a preference for dedicated vs hosted? Dedicated gives more predictable latency but requires networking.
[01:33] Omar: We prefer dedicated because of data residency and egress controls; also want VPC peering to our GCP project. Security will be a showstopper if we can't do private deployments.
[01:50] Lena (Security): Yep, SOC 2 and audit logs are required. We also need SSO via SAML, role-based access, and KMS integration for key rotation.
[02:10] Alex: That's all supported—Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, and we have audit logs. Jasper will follow up on the specific KMS providers supported. I'll also link the security pack after the call.
[02:40] Jasper: Quick note - we will need an IP allowlist and a short window for peering setup. For benchmarks, do you have a staging VPC with sample traffic patterns we can run against?
[03:05] Marina: We don't yet, but we can spin up a small staging cluster. We'll share estimated QPS and traffic bursts.
[03:22] Alex: Excellent. For the pilot, we usually do a 2-week benchmark: baseline hosted test, then dedicated run, capture p50/p95/p99, token costs, and steady-state throughput. Does that align?
[03:44] Omar: Yes. Also can you simulate prefix caching and session affinity? Our chat workloads keep long context windows.
[04:01] Jasper: We'll include a KV cache warmup and typical session lengths. We'll instrument token-level costs in the report.
[04:18] Marina: What's the expected timeline to get dedicated capacity up? We have compliance review in mid-August.
[04:30] Alex: With our standard process, dedicated can be provisioned in 10-14 business days after contract. If you need faster, there's a priority onboarding add-on.
[04:49] Lena: Pricing—can you provide reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go scenarios? We need budget sign-off.
[05:03] Alex: Absolutely. I'll share a pricing scenarios spreadsheet with reserved commitments, burst rates, and an estimated unit cost. We'll include cost comparisons to hosted.
[05:18] Marina: Any competitors we should consider? We looked at Anthropic's enterprise offering and also evaluated Vertex managed endpoints.
[05:30] Priya: Noted. We'll highlight where Redwood's routing and caching reduce per-token cost compared to standard endpoints.
[05:48] Jasper: A couple technical clarifications: what quantization profiles do you support for the model variants, and can we pin model versions during rollout?
[06:05] Alex: Yes—model pinning and rollout policies are supported. Quantization recommendations will be part of Redwood Optimize suggestions; Jasper will run a quick compatibility check during the pilot.

--- Transcript continues with timestamped back-and-forth ---
[12:10] Marina: We have an internal requirement that any external logs be redacted of PII before leaving our VPC, is that possible?
[12:28] Jasper: By default, log forwarding can be configured to redact fields. We can also route logs to your Splunk via secure collector. We'll document the redaction patterns.
[18:05] Omar: For networking, does Redwood require dedicated peering or is NAT gateway sufficient for private deployments?
[18:22] Alex: We can support both; peering gives lower variance. For regulatory workloads, peering + private deployment is recommended.
[21:03] Lena: About KMS—we use Cloud KMS with customer-managed keys, can Redwood integrate with that or do we need HSM?
[21:18] Jasper: Cloud KMS is supported; we also support HSM integrations for extra assurance. We'll capture the exact cipher suites in the security pack.
[28:40] Marina: Ok, let's talk runbook and roles. Priya, will you own the onboarding runbook?
[28:51] Priya: Yes, I'll own runbook updates. We'll need a primary contact for network and a separate contact for security.
[29:10] Marina: Omar will own networking, Lena will own security. I'll be overall program lead.
[31:55] Jasper: For pilot metrics—what thresholds should we consider pass/fail? E.g., p95 < 400ms and cost delta under 20% versus hosted?
[32:11] Marina: p95 < 350ms would be ideal, but we can be flexible to 400ms for pilot. Cost target: < 25% higher than hosted if latency gains are evident.
[35:00] Alex: Good. We'll provide an initial proposal listing two pilot scenarios: conservative (lower capacity) and full-scale (higher capacity). The conservative plan aims for speed to results.
[39:14] Marina: Regarding SSO and user access—do you require SCIM for user provisioning or can we do manual RBAC?
[39:29] Priya: We support SCIM and manual invites. For enterprise rollouts we recommend SCIM to sync groups.
[42:40] Omar: One more item—data residency. Some tenant data must be kept in EU regions. Can you guarantee region pinning?
[42:55] Alex: Yes we have region pinning for model serving and data at rest. We'll note the available regions for Private deployments in the follow-up.
[46:10] Marina: This is helpful, thanks. Let's recap next steps.
[46:20] Priya: Recap: Alex sends pricing scenarios; Jasper schedules the pilot and shares the test matrix; Marina/Omar will provide traffic samples and provision staging VPC; Priya sends onboarding runbook and permissions checklist.
[46:40] Marina: Agreed. Also please share the security pack and SOC 2 evidence link.
[46:55] Alex: Will do. I'll drop links: security pack (https://redwood-internal.docs/security-pack.pdf), onboarding runbook (https://redwood-internal.docs/onboarding-runbook), pricing gsheet (link will be shared). We'll also create a pilot workspace in Slack.
[47:20] Omar: Expect traffic patterns by 2026-07-20. We want pilot to start week of 2026-07-27 if possible.
[47:40] Jasper: We'll aim to have the benchmark plan by 2026-07-24 and the pilot runbook by 2026-07-26.
[48:05] Lena: I'll follow up with any compliance questions; otherwise we can proceed.
[48:30] Alex: Great thanks — we'll follow up via email and Slack and set the pilot kickoff calendar invite. Thanks everyone.
[48:45] Meeting ends.

Questions captured:
- Do you need HSM or Cloud KMS? (answered)
- Can you do VPC peering or NAT? (answered)

Action items noted above.

title: Proxy + SDK + Observability Onramp - Meridian BioAnalytics Discovery
content:
Proxy + SDK + Observability Onramp - Meridian BioAnalytics Discovery

Exploratory discovery to understand Meridian's constraints for onramp to Redwood: deciding between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; integration via SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex; gateway/proxy patterns, rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks. Customer wants pilot with predictable throughput and audit logs; has strict KMS/HSM requirement for keys used in embeddings. Action: SE to send sample connectors and run a short benchmark; AE to send security docs and pricing.
Current stack and traffic patterns
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
SDKs, LangChain & LlamaIndex compatibility
Gateway/proxy vs sidecar deployment
Rate limits, quotas, burst handling
Observability and telemetry hooks (OpenTelemetry, traces, token-level cost)
Security: KMS/HSM, SSO, audit logs
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros? We have Maya and Carlos from Redwood - Maya is AE, Carlos lead SE. Could you share roles at Meridian?
[00:18] Noah (CTO): Hey, I'm Noah - CTO. Aisha is platform, Derek does SRE. We're evaluating options to run inference for our clinical summaries and search embeddings. Latency matters but cost is also big, so we want to see Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs.
[00:35] Maya: Great, that'll help. Briefly, Redwood offers Hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private VPC or on-prem. Carlos will cover integration patterns - SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy options.
[00:48] Carlos (SE): Hi all. Before we deep dive, quick qual: what's your expected QPS and typical sequence lengths? Also do you need data to stay in your VPC?
[01:04] Aisha: Good question. For search and summarization, avg prompt length ~200 tokens, peaks to 1.5k. Baseline is 15 QPS with occasional spikes to 80 QPS for short bursts. Data needs to stay in our VPC for PHI — so Private or a VPC-hosted option is preferred. We also have HSM-backed keys for encryption.
[01:30] Derek: And we need audit logs and per-request tracing, plus role-based access — SSO/SAML. SOC2 compliance is table stakes.
[01:44] Maya: Understood. Private deployment supports customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations. Dedicated can be in our cloud with private networking; Hosted has some VPC peering options but you'd need to check the data residency flow. We'll send SOC2 and KMS notes.
[02:02] Noah: Okay. For integration, our app uses LangChain and some bespoke orchestration. We also have a LlamaIndex-based vector store. How smooth is integration?
[02:15] Carlos: We have SDKs in Python/Node, plus examples for LangChain agents and LlamaIndex connectors. For LlamaIndex, the vectorstore adapter needs just a small shim; we've seen customers swap the API key for a Redwood client and it works. We'll share a sample repo. Note: some customers use the Redwood gateway sidecar pattern to centralize retries and rate limiting.
[02:45] Aisha: That sidecar idea — can it live in our cluster? We prefer not to run SDKs directly from many microservices.
[02:54] Carlos: Yes, sidecar or gateway. Two main patterns: 1) SDK direct calls inside app, 2) centralized gateway/proxy that handles batching, caching, auth, and quotas. Gateway gives you single place for observability and consistent retries. Sidecar scales with pods but can be heavier operationally.
[03:18] Derek: For quotas and rate limits: we need per-tenant and per-route quotas. Bursting up to 4x baseline is okay but should be throttled gracefully. Any built-in quota enforcement?
[03:33] Maya: Redwood has per-token and route quotas, and per-api-key limits. For Dedicated you can configure reserved throughput and burst policies. Gateway/proxy can enforce tenant-level quotas before hitting the runtime. We'll demonstrate policy configs in the pilot.
[03:50] Noah: Observability — we use OpenTelemetry and DataDog. We want token-level cost attribution, latency percentiles, traces, and KV cache hit rates. Can Redwood emit open spans and telemetry?
[04:05] Carlos: Yes, we support exporting traces via OTLP, plus webhook traces into DataDog. The Console exposes token-level breakdown and per-model tracing. Small caveat: some internal metric names might differ; we can map them. Also there's a sampling option for high-QPS routes to control telemetry volume.
[04:32] Aisha: You mentioned caching — prefix caching or KV cache — how transparent is that to the app? Could it change semantics?
[04:42] Carlos: Automatic prefix/KV caching is opt-in per-route. It preserves response consistency for deterministic prompts, but for non-deterministic sampling you'll want to disable. We'll review your prompt patterns in the pilot. There's also a cache invalidation TTL you can set.
[05:01] Noah: On models, do you support both open models and Redwood-verified variants? We plan to evaluate smaller quantized models to cut cost.
[05:11] Maya: Yes. Hosted includes curated models, Dedicated and Private can host compatible variants. We also provide recommendations for quantization and kernel selection per workload. Our Optimize toolkit gives batch/caching suggestions.
[05:26] Derek: Is model fallback supported? If a Dedicated node is full can calls route to Hosted? We need graceful degradation.
[05:35] Carlos: Yes, smart routing policies allow fallback to compatible model variants or other regions — configurable per-route. For strict offline/on-prem needs you can disable fallback.
[05:46] Aisha: Security — HSM: we manage customer keys via KMS/HSM. How does Redwood integrate?
[05:57] Maya: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSMs. For Dedicated we can set up a KMS integration (cloud KMS or HSM appliances). We'll include specifics in the security pack. Also SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are all available for Enterprise plans.
[06:14] Noah: Great. Practical question: we use LangChain chains with multiple LLM calls per user request; we'd like routing decisions to be policy-driven — e.g., cheap model for embeddings, higher-quality for final summarization. Can Redwood support per-call model selection?
[06:31] Carlos: Absolutely — you can route by route name, header, or cost threshold. The gateway can rewrite requests to route to different model variants and keep the rest of the app unchanged. Many teams use the gateway to inject a 'routing hint' header.
[06:47] Maya: Maybe a quick demo in the pilot: LangChain example showing embeddings on a quantized model and summarization on a larger model in one workflow.
[06:55] Aisha: That would be ideal. Also, what about token accounting across a chain of calls? We need aggregated cost per user action for billing and audit.
[07:06] Carlos: The Console can aggregate per-transaction when you provide a transaction-id header. We also export per-token logs to your S3/URI if you want offline cost recon. There's a small ingestion fee for long-term retention.
[07:22] Noah: On performance — for our 80 QPS spikes we need sub-200ms tail latency on short prompts. What SLAs can you provide?
[07:34] Maya: SLA varies by product. Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime guarantees; Hosted has best-effort but predictable performance for common configs. We'll propose Dedicated for predictable 99th pct latency. Carlos can walk benchmark results from similar customers.
[07:50] Carlos: We have a benchmark sheet we can share. For short prompts we've sustained 120ms p50 and 220ms p99 in a similar setup with batching and KV caching disabled for low latency. I'll attach the sheet.
[08:06] Aisha: About the gateway/proxy — we prefer the gateway approach to centralize telemetry and quotas. What deployment options exist? A single managed gateway in Redwood vs running their gateway in customer VPC?
[08:20] Carlos: Both. Managed gateway is easiest (Hosted) but requires some network peering. You can also deploy our gateway as a sidecar or a central ingress appliance in your VPC. For PHI, customers often run the gateway on-prem or in their VPC so requests never leave their network — then we only provide control plane access.
[08:41] Derek: If we run gateway in our VPC, can we still use Redwood Console for traces and rollouts?
[08:48] Maya: Yes, the control plane can be hybrid: telemetry and rollouts are reported to the Console while preserving PII in your VPC. We can limit what telemetry leaves your network and provide filtered metrics. We'll document telemetry fields and PII redaction options.
[09:05] Noah: Licensing and pricing — how do pilots work? We'd like a 6-8 week pilot with a Dedicated pool and ability to test burst policies. Any minimum commitment?
[09:17] Maya: Pilots are flexible. For Dedicated we typically ask for a 3-month reserved capacity for predictability, but we can do a scoped pilot for 6-8 weeks with capped usage. We'll send a pricing sketch for a small Dedicated pool plus ingress burst credits.
[09:34] Aisha: On the SDKs, does Redwood provide a LangChain Agent integration or do we need to write adapters?
[09:41] Carlos: We provide code samples: a LangChain LLM wrapper, an embeddings client for vectorstores, and a LlamaIndex connector. Most customers copy/paste the wrapper and replace the key. For more complex chains we recommend using the gateway to centralize logic.
[09:57] Derek: Some words get mis-typed by our infra — like KV cache being called 'K V cash' in earlier docs — just flagging we'll want the exact implementation details.
[10:05] Carlos: Haha, noted. We'll make sure to include accurate docs and a short runbook for cache semantics.
[10:12] Maya: Quick pivot — a security question from procurement: can we support audit logs going to their SIEM?
[10:20] Noah: Yes, we need to push logs to Splunk and also have tamper-evident audit trails.
[10:26] Maya: We support log forwarding to Splunk/S3 and have append-only audit logs in Private deployments. We'll include SIEM integration steps.
[10:35] Aisha: Can you talk about data retention and deletion? For compliance we need data purged after 30 days unless flagged for review.
[10:43] Carlos: Retention windows are configurable per-tenant. For Hosted we retain minimal request metadata by default but can set custom retention and deletion via API. For Private, it's under your control.
[10:56] Noah: One more technical: we have an in-house optimizer that does batching across requests — will Redwood's batching add on top of ours and cause unexpected delays?
[11:07] Carlos: Redwood does continuous batching in the runtime; if you already batch upstream, you can set the runtime to bypass additional batching. We have parameters for max-latency windows and batch size to tune for low-latency workloads.
[11:24] Derek: On quotas again — we need per-team, per-route, and per-user quotas, with alerting when thresholds are near. Does Redwood support webhooks for quota breach alerts?
[11:36] Maya: Yes, quota alerts via webhook, email, and Console dashboards. You can configure soft and hard limits and set pre-threshold alarms.
[11:48] Aisha: For the pilot, what do you need from us to get started?
[11:54] Carlos: Ideally: a small sample prompt set, a TM for expected QPS profile, an example LangChain chain you want to run, and confirmation on network pattern (peered vs in-VPC gateway). We'll run a micro-benchmark and demo the LangChain example.
[12:08] Noah: We'll prepare sample payloads and a dev VPC for the gateway. Also we'll need the LangChain sample earlier you mentioned.
[12:16] Maya: Action recap: Carlos will share the LangChain/LlamaIndex repo and benchmark sheet; Maya sends security docs and pricing; Noah confirms stakeholders and VPC details. Schedule pilot kickoff for week of July 6th. Any blockers?
[12:32] Derek: Only internal legal sign-off; procurement may ask for SOC2 and encryption details but should be standard.
[12:38] Maya: We'll add that to the packet. Any other product questions?
[12:42] Aisha: One thing — metrics naming. We use strict tags (team, env, tenant) in OTEL. Will Redwood mapping support custom attributes?
[12:52] Carlos: Yes, you can map your OTEL attributes to Redwood Console fields. We'll include mapping examples in the integration checklist.
[13:02] Noah: Regarding LlamaIndex vectorstore, we store vectors in our managed store. Do we need to rehydrate embeddings in Redwood?
[13:10] Carlos: You can either call embeddings from Redwood and store vectors back in your store, or send precomputed embeddings. For latency-sensitive retrieval, many customers compute locally and only call the LLM for ranking/augmentation.
[13:25] Aisha: Pricing clarity: how granular is per-token billing, and can we get a forecast for cost if we run at average 15 QPS?
[13:36] Maya: Billing is per-token for generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings. We'll run a cost projection in the pricing doc; include your prompt distribution and QPS and we'll model quantized vs full models.
[13:50] Derek: Any experimental features we should be aware of? Like automatic re-try logic that could double-charge?
[13:58] Carlos: Retries are idempotent-aware if you pass an idempotency key. Console will attribute retries separately unless it's deduped by the runtime; we'll explain best practices.
[14:10] Aisha: For audit, we want a binary proof of who called what model when — is that available?
[14:18] Maya: We have append-only request logs with identity and model version. For Private you can host the logs and we can provide a signed manifest if needed.
[14:28] Noah: Any red flags from your side on our architecture?
[14:31] Carlos: Nothing major. Main area: ensure gateway in-VPC has low-latency path to your vectorstore. Also validate HSM connectivity for KMS early in the pilot.
[14:44] Noah: Good to know. Let's talk pilot specifics now: timeline and success criteria. Our success metrics: p99 <300ms for short prompts, cost per user action under X, and secure handling of PHI (auditable).
[14:58] Maya: We'll propose pilot success criteria aligned with that: p99 target, cost modeling, integration completeness (LangChain + LlamaIndex working), and security checklist completion.
[15:08] Aisha: Sounds good. Any dependencies on their side? We'll need RBAC mappings and sample transaction-id header to test aggregated billing.
[15:18] Carlos: We'll provide a small integration test harness that emits transaction-id and demonstrates aggregator in Console. We'll run a short load test to validate quotas and burst behavior.
[15:28] Derek: One last thing — we integrate with an API gateway (Kong). Will that sit in front of Redwood gateway or will Redwood gateway sit behind Kong?
[15:36] Carlos: Either. Common pattern: Kong in edge, Redwood gateway behind for LLM-specific routing and observability. We'll include an example deployment diagram.
[15:47] Maya: Great. Recap of next steps and I'll follow up via email. Thanks everyone, we'll send docs and schedule the kickoff.
[15:56] Noah: Thanks all. Bye.
[16:00] (call ends)

title: Private VPC egress & runtime interop deep dive - OrionHealthTech
content:
Private VPC egress & runtime interop deep dive - OrionHealthTech

Deep technical session focused on private VPC egress patterns for Redwood Private. Covered NAT hairpin issues, PrivateLink binding options, DNS resolver design, KV cache coherence across AZs, batching windows and quantization tradeoffs; agreed to run a staging benchmark and exchange network diagrams.
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-09 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lila Cho (Redwood SE), Damien Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jared Molina (Orion - Platform), Priya Narayan (Orion - Lead SRE), Evan Brooks (Orion - Security)

Summary: quick recap at top, but full transcript below. Note: auto-transcription has small errors (K V cache sometimes written K V cache, PrivateLink sometimes 'private link').

[00:00] Samir: hey everybody, thanks for carving time today. I think agenda is VPC egress, private connectivity, runtime impacts like KV cache and batching. we'll call out known hairpins.
[00:22] Jared: cool, yeah we wanted to understand the network patterns, especially because our regulatory folks want no public egress for PHI. so the question is, can Redwood Private run in our isolated subnets without hitting the internet for model serving?
[00:37] Lila: short answer yes, with caveats. you can either use PrivateLink to expose the inference API into your VPC, or you can deploy Redwood Private inside your VPC‍—in which case egress only needed for optional telemetry or to pull model artifacts. if telemetry is restricted, we support an airgap package.
[01:05] Priya: if we go PrivateLink, how do we handle egress for downloading container images or pulling checkpoints? our current plan is to use an internal artifact repo but some ops still rely on s3 endpoints.
[01:25] Damien: for model onboarding we recommend either a pre-staged S3 in the same region with VPC endpoint or scp transfer into the node. PrivateLink doesn't magically give you S3 access; it's about ingress to the service endpoints. so, commonly customers put a NAT gateway in a controlled egress subnet with tight route tables and egress-only rules.
[01:48] Evan: we have a strict policy - no outbound to public S3, only VPC endpoints allowed. any NAT hairpin or egress path has to be auditable.
[02:02] Samir: understood. one pattern we've used is dedicated isolated subnets for runtime nodes with no Internet gateway. then a separate managed egress subnet with NAT Gateway and a proxy that whitelists IPs for model fetch or telemetry. for PrivateLink specifically, you set up interface endpoints in your VPC and allow traffic to Redwood's private dns.
[02:27] Jared: there's the hairpin issue though — when nodes try to reach PrivateLink-bound endpoints in the same VPC, we saw packets leaving the subnet and failing source/destination checks. any tips?
[02:40] Lila: yeah, that's the classic source/dest check problem. you need to make sure the ENI for the PrivateLink acceptance is in the right AZ and the route tables point to the interface endpoint. if you're using NAT in the same subnet, disable source/dest check on the ENI and ensure the security groups allow the internal CIDR. sometimes Linux host routing also needs policy routing rules so return packets flow correctly.
[03:06] Priya: so is that something Redwood manages on the PrivateLink side, or we have to do infra changes?
[03:12] Samir: Redwood can provide the CloudFormation/Terraform templates that create the endpoint service and show the accept/attach steps. for PrivateLink the customer must accept and attach the interface endpoint; we can automate some of it via our onboarding script but infra changes are typically on the customer side.
[03:28] Jared: got it. moving into DNS — if we enable private DNS, what's the recommended resolver config? split-horizon?
[03:37] Lila: we recommend enabling private DNS for the interface endpoint so your calls to api.redwood.example (our example host) resolve to the interface IPs. for customers with split-horizon, point the VPC resolver to a centralized forwarding resolver — that way internal hostnames still resolve. beware TTLs and our SDK's connection pooling which caches IPs; if endpoint ENIs failover across AZs you might need to flush connections.
[04:03] Damien: small note — our runtime keeps persistent HTTP2 or GRPC connections to reduce cold-start token overhead. if DNS updates mid-stream, existing connections won't pick up new IPs, so we have keepalives and a periodic reconnect policy (default 10s graceful drain) but you can tune that.
[04:23] Evan: that reconnect window concerns us, because we have latency SLOs. if an AZ goes down, we don't want a 10s blackhole. can we shorten that?
[04:32] Lila: yes, we can lower the drain to 2–3s, but you trade off transient increased CPU while reconnecting. for strict SLOs we recommend multi-AZ clients + per-AZ endpoint binding and health checks in the routing policy.
[04:55] Jared: switching to KV cache — our inference workload is chat-like with long context. we rely on KV caching to avoid re-encoding prefix tokens. how do you keep KV cache coherent across nodes in different AZs?
[05:10] Damien: Redwood runtime uses local KV cache with optional remote invalidation messages. simplest pattern: pin requests to the same AZ (session affinity) so the hot KV cache stays warm. if you need cross-AZ resiliency we do a pub/sub invalidation via the control plane; you'll see a slightly higher tail latency on cold miss if the remote cache needs to fetch.
[05:31] Priya: session affinity sounds fine but our traffic is behind an internal load balancer that balances by round-robin. can we do sticky routing?
[05:40] Samir: yep we can set the LB to use least-conn or a cookie-based stickiness. another pattern: use a small shared redis/kv-store for frequently-mutated prefixes, but that adds network latency — usually 1–4ms extra.
[05:53] Jared: any recomms on TTL/eviction? we have variable prompt lengths, sometimes the prefix is huge.
[06:00] Lila: TTL should reflect typical conversation warm period; for chat apps, 30–90s is common before eviction, but memory pressure and KV slot count matter. we provide telemetry to show cache hit ratio and eviction churn so you can size nodes.
[06:12] Evan: are these KV caches encrypted at rest or in transit?
[06:16] Damien: in transit always TLS, at rest depends on deployment — for Redwood Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM or managed volume encryption.
[06:24] Jared: batching — our P99 for token latency needs to be sub-200ms. how much batching can we do without blowing that SLA?
[06:33] Lila: batching is a knob. smaller batching windows (5–15ms) get you decent throughput benefit for short queries without adding too much tail. for strict tail latency we recommend adaptive batching: batch up to N tokens or T ms whichever triggers first. Redwood Optimize can suggest initial N and T based on your token distribution.
[06:55] Priya: what's the CPU/GC impact of very short windows? we've seen JVM-like runtimes thrash if the load is spiky.
[07:02] Damien: true for some runtimes — our engine is largely C++ with controlled memory allocs; still, very small windows increase scheduling overhead. there's a sweet spot at 10–30ms for most conversational workloads. we'll share benchmark graphs.
[07:18] Jared: quantization — Orion is considering int8 quantized models to reduce memory. how does quantization affect latency and batching?
[07:28] Lila: quantization reduces memory footprint so you can fit larger batches on the same GPU, improving throughput. however, quantized kernels sometimes change per-token latency slightly — especially for attention kernel reorderings. expect 5–15% improvement in throughput but tail latency variance may increase slightly. we recommend testing both int8 and int4 profiles.
[07:48] Samir: and note, quantization interacts with KV cache sizes — smaller checkpoints mean faster KV cache restore on cold start.
[07:57] Evan: what about warmup? if we spin new nodes in an AZ, how long to warm the KV and model artifacts?
[08:05] Damien: depends on model size. for a 13B model with quantized weights on NVMe local storage, artifact load is ~20–45s; KV warmup for chat prefixes depends on traffic — we often run synthetic warmers that ping typical prefixes to pre-populate the KV. we can provide a warmup script.
[08:23] Priya: can that warmup traffic be internal-only? we don't want warmed-up data going to telemetry collectors in Redwood.
[08:30] Samir: yes, that can be configured to stay internal. telemetry opt-out is possible for Private deployments; you can either forward metrics to your own collector or allow Redwood to collect anonymized telemetry only.
[08:45] Jared: security check — our InfoSec wants RBAC and audit logs for inference requests. is there request-level logging for who invoked what model?
[08:55] Lila: yes, we support token-level audit logs, request metadata, and can integrate with your SIEM. logs can be stored in your S3 bucket with server-side encryption and an optional redaction layer to avoid storing PHI content.
[09:09] Evan: about network policies: if we put nodes in isolated subnets, what NAT or egress rules are required for model rollouts?
[09:19] Damien: you only need outbound for artifact fetches, optional license verifications, and updates. those can be limited to specific IPs or VPC endpoints. our recommended pattern is a minimal egress host that proxies to allowed endpoints, combined with strict route tables and security group rules.
[09:34] Priya: are there any known issues when using an egress proxy + PrivateLink and DNS resolver forwarding?
[09:42] Lila: proxying can complicate TLS mutual-auth if the proxy rewrites SNI. make sure the proxy preserves SNI and does TCP passthrough for TLS connections unless you intend to terminate TLS at the proxy. for HTTP traffic we support mTLS to Redwood if required.
[09:58] Jared: we are worried about IP churn when we scale nodes up/down, will that break long-lived streams (websockets / streaming outputs)?
[10:08] Damien: long-lived streams are bound to an instance until you drain. our draining policy is graceful — we finish inflight streams and then shutdown, but if the node loses connectivity you'll transiently re-route to another instance and the client may need to reconnect. best practice: client-side reconnect logic with exponential backoff; also use session affinity to reduce mid-stream reassignment.
[10:30] Samir: quick architecture sketch — three subnet tiers: management (api plane for control), runtime (isolated nodes), egress (NAT + proxy). PrivateLink interface endpoints bound into management subnet for control-plane calls. runtime nodes talk to management plane over internal-only paths.
[10:50] Priya: does Redwood require specific MTU settings? we have jumbo MTU and sometimes packet fragmentation messes up GRPC streams.
[10:58] Lila: we recommend standard 1500 MTU on the data plane unless you have tuned your infra. jumbo frames are ok but ensure all hops support it; otherwise you'll get path MTU issues. also watch for AWS ENI limits per instance when you have many network interfaces for PrivateLink.
[11:16] Jared: any guidance on monitoring — how to correlate network-level drops with KV cache misses and inference error rates?
[11:25] Damien: our console exposes per-route latencies, cache hit ratios, and pod-level health. we also ship tracing hooks that emit spans for cache hit/miss, batching windows and egress time. you can send traces to your Jaeger/Zipkin or to our console. correlating via trace IDs makes debugging easy.
[11:43] Evan: we need the SOC2 artifact and any penetration tests for your private deployment package.
[11:50] Samir: we'll attach our SOC2 packaging and the penetration test summary. for Private deployments we also provide an architecture security checklist.
[11:58] Priya: last thing — can we do a quick experiment: mid-call run a tiny benchmark that simulates 200rps, 8 tokens avg, session-affinity vs no affinity, to see cache hit ratio?
[12:09] Lila: we can show a sample script but we shouldn't run heavy loads on your prod account. we can set it up in your staging VPC and run tomorrow.
[12:18] Jared: that works. can Redwood also provide a target config for batch window and KV sizes to start with?
[12:24] Damien: yes, we'll include a suggested config as part of the onboarding bundle — it's what we normally give to other healthcare customers.
[12:31] Samir: ok recap of action items — Samir: share network diagram and security pack; Lila: share warmup script and batching experiment; Jared: provision staging VPC and accept PrivateLink; set meeting to run benchmark next week.
[12:48] Jared: thanks everyone. anything else?
[12:50] Evan: one tiny note — encryption key lifecycle: we want rotation capability without service disruption.
[12:56] Damien: supported — we rotate keys with rolling restarts and you can bring-your-own-KMS. we'll share the rotation playbook.
[13:06] Samir: great, we'll follow up with docs and the templates. thanks all.

End of transcript.

title: Polaris POC — Quality & Hallucination Evaluation Scope
content:
Polaris POC — Quality & Hallucination Evaluation Scope

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05T16:00:00Z
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Polaris ML), Lena Ortiz (Polaris PM), Rajiv Menon (Polaris SRE), Tasha Nguyen (Polaris Regulatory)

Summary:
A scoping session to finalize the POC quality evaluation plan: define golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination and format checks, scoring approach and load/bench timings. Customer prioritized correctness/format over lowest cost but wants latency SLOs.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria and weighting (accuracy, hallucination rate, format compliance, latency, cost)
- Golden prompt set composition and seeding strategy
- Regression test harness and CI gating rules
- Hallucination detection heuristics and patching strategy
- Benchmark load profile (QPS, tokens per request, concurrency) and timeline
- Data privacy, SOC2/SSO, private vs hosted concerns

Action items (discussed): see metadata field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): OK, hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:10] Daniel (Polaris): hi all, Daniel here — head of ML. Lena and Rajiv are with me as well.
[00:14] Lena (Polaris PM): hi, yeah thanks, excited to get this scoped.
[00:17] Arjun (Redwood SE): great, i'll jump into the technical goals after Maya quickly frames the business objectives.
[00:22] Maya: perfect. Polaris told us earlier that the POC success criteria are mostly quality focused — accuracy, low hallucination, and strict response formatting for downstream parsers. cost and latency are secondary but still important. is that right?
[00:36] Daniel: yes that's the short version. we want the model to produce a structured JSON snippet for 95% of queries with less than 3% hallucination on named entities in the finance domain. latency target is 300–500 ms p50 for typical queries.
[00:50] Rajiv: and from infra, we need to validate sustained 40 qps with burst to 120 for 30s windows, so the benchmark plan needs to include load shape.
[01:02] Arjun: ok noted. for the quality eval itself we usually split into automated metrics and human review. automated checks cover schema/format, exact-match fields, fuzzy entity match for named entities, and a hallucination detector; human review covers edge cases and ambiguous prompts.
[01:18] Lena: when you say hallucination detector, is that a heuristic checks, or model-based? how do you measure it?
[01:24] Arjun: good question. we use a mixed approach: rule-based checks (e.g., verifying entities against a provided canonical list), embedding-similarity checks for factual claims against a small knowledge base, and optionally a secondary verification model that flags probable hallucinations. for the POC we can start with rule-based + embedding threshold, then add the verifier if needed.
[01:42] Tasha (Regulatory): will you need any raw customer data to run that? from a compliance perspective we need logs redacted and no PII leaving the VPC if we go private.
[01:50] Sofia (Redwood): we can run both hosted and private sims. for hosted we ask for anonymized examples only, and we keep logs per our SOC2 practices — we'll send the security FAQ.
[01:58] Daniel: ok we'll anonymize, but we also want to test realistic failure modes so we might provide synthetic records for edge cases.
[02:04] Arjun: perfect. partition the dataset into: golden set (200 examples), regression set (1,800 examples), and holdout (200) for final verification — that's a typical split we recommend.
[02:16] Lena: 200 golden seems small; how do you ensure it covers domain variety?
[02:20] Arjun: golden should be curated: 50 canonical positive templates, 30 tricky edge cases, 60 entity-heavy financial tasks, 30 formatting/escape cases, 30 adversarial hallucination examples. we seed golden from your top-traffic intents and historical failures.
[02:33] Daniel: sounds reasonable. for scoring, we want a single composite score to decide pass/fail for the POC, but also component metrics. can you propose a weighting?
[02:40] Maya: typical starting weighting we use is accuracy/format 50%, hallucination penalty 30%, latency/cost 20% combined, with thresholds that must be met for pass. but we can tweak per customer.
[02:50] Lena: we want format compliance to be hard fail: if JSON schema isn't followed, downstream systems break. so even if the score is high, any format schema failure should be a showstopper for that example.
[02:59] Arjun: agree. we'll implement hard gating on schema checks: examples failing schema get flagged and excluded from automated composite score but counted as failures in the report.
[03:09] Rajiv: on hallucination measurement — you mentioned entity canonical lists. we can provide a names/identifier corpus for Polaris securities, tickers, and bank names. would that be sufficient?
[03:19] Arjun: yes, that materially helps. embedding-based checks will compare response claims to the KB and if similarity below threshold we flag it. we'll provide false positive/negative calibration guidance.
[03:29] Daniel: what's a realistic hallucination threshold? 3% across the regression set?
[03:34] Arjun: 3% is aggressive but feasible; depends on prompt engineering and model variant. for early baseline we aim for <=6% then optimize.
[03:41] Lena: ok timeline — how long do you need to run a proper regression?
[03:45] Maya: typical run is one week for initial baseline (hosted) including prompt tuning and one dedicated config run (if you choose Dedicated) the following week for throughput/latency. so about two weeks end-to-end for initial pass.
[03:56] Daniel: do you need a canary or warmup before the dedicated run?
[03:59] Arjun: yes, we'll do warmup sequences and KV cache priming for a 2 hour window and ramp tests for concurrency.
[04:06] Tasha: can you describe what info you capture in logs? i.e., are outputs stored, and how long?
[04:11] Sofia: we'll capture request/response, model id, latency, and scoring signals for the eval; retention policy can be set per agreement. for hosted we retain minimal logs for 30 days by default; for private deployments we follow your retention policy.
[04:24] Daniel: great. on the scoring side, what automated metrics do you produce?
[04:28] Arjun: we produce exact match %, schema pass %, normalized entity F1, embedding-distance hallucination rate, and a cost-per-request metric. we also produce human-review adjustment factors.
[04:38] Lena: do you do BLEU/ROUGE etc? is that useful for us?
[04:42] Arjun: for generative templates BLEU/ROUGE add little value; we prefer exact-match or token-level normalized edit distance for structured outputs. for free-text responses we can compute ROUGE but we'll prioritize human judgments.
[04:55] Daniel: i want to see an example rubric for human review — like severity levels for hallucination and how they map to pass/fail.
[05:01] Maya: we'll include a suggested 3-tier severity: minor (formatting/typo but no factual error), major (incorrect entity values that could cause downstream misprocessing), and critical (materially wrong financial claim). major+critical count as failures in the composite.
[05:15] Lena: ok. regarding golden prompts — who curates them? we expect collaboration.
[05:20] Arjun: Redwood will provide a first-draft golden set curated from your top intents; you review and augment. We iterate until both parties sign off.
[05:28] Rajiv: about the load profile— 40 qps sustained, 120 burst — what hardware footprint do you simulate for dedicated?
[05:34] Arjun: depends on model size and quantization. rough rule: a 7B quantized model can hit that qps on a 2-GPU pool with batching; 13B requires 4 GPUs. we'll propose a baseline config and cost estimate in the bench spreadsheet.
[05:47] Tasha: any privacy concerns for sending the 2k prompts?
[05:50] Maya: redact PII; we also accept synthetic equivalents. if you prefer, we can run on your private deployment image so data never leaves your VPC.
[05:59] Daniel: let's try hosted baseline with anonymized data first, then private if we need on-prem keys.
[06:03] Lena: timeline recap?
[06:05] Maya: plan: Redwood sends draft golden prompts + rubric by 8/10, Polaris provides datasets by 8/12, baseline hosted run week of 8/17, dedicated sim (if requested) week of 8/24, and final report by 8/28.
[06:16] Daniel: that timeline works.
[06:18] Arjun: one more technical note — hallucination detector thresholds will be tuned on your holdout set; we'll share calibration notes and false-positive rate targets.
[06:27] Lena: how will we consume results? dashboard, CSV?
[06:30] Sofia: both. Redwood Console export includes per-example results, summary dashboards, and a regression CSV that you can plug into your CI. we'll share a sample export format.
[06:39] Rajiv: for CI gating, can we set a nightly regression check that fails the build if composite drops 5%?
[06:44] Arjun: yes, we can integrate with your CI (we've done Jenkins/GitLab/GitHub actions hooks) to post pass/fail. we'll document the webhook and payload.
[06:53] Tasha: send over SOC2 cert and SAML SSO setup docs.
[06:56] Maya: will do — action item.
[06:58] Lena: ok thanks everyone, seems actionable.
[07:02] Maya: thanks, i'll follow up with the plan and spreadsheets. bye.

End of transcript.

title: Fix cache hit attribution for metrics under continuous batched prefill
content:
Fix cache hit attribution for metrics under continuous batched prefill

Summary: Fixes incorrect cache hit/miss attribution in runtime metrics when multiple requests share a continuous batch prefill. Previously, the prefill stage could be executed as a single fused prefill for a set of requests (continuous batching). Our cache telemetry code was attributing prefill-derived cache outcomes (prefix reuse / KV reuse) to the batch as a whole, then fan-out incrementing per-request counters using the wrong join keys. This produced two bad effects in dashboards: (1) inflated hit counts for some routes/models (double-ish counting depending on batch shape), and (2) hit-rate distortions that correlated strongly with batch size and prefill coalescing rather than true cache behavior.

Context / why now: We saw a mismatch between span annotations (trace-level) and metrics breakdowns in the canary dashboard for the new cache telemetry. In workloads with high concurrency + similar prompt lengths, prefill batching increased and the hit-rate metrics drifted upward vs expected, while wasted-prefill was noisy. This blocks SRE/Telemetry from trusting the signals for alerts/recommendations.

Root cause: The metric instrumentation was keyed off PrefillBatchId and then tried to map back to RequestContext using the active scheduler queue snapshot. Under continuous batching, requests can enter/leave the fused prefill window, and the mapping is not stable across the entire prefill run. Additionally, the cache result object returned by the cache layer was “batch-aggregated” (reused_tokens_total, misses_by_reason) rather than per-request/per-segment. We were then distributing totals evenly (or per-token heuristic) which is wrong for partial reuse and causes incorrect per-route attribution.

Fix: 1) Introduce an explicit per-request CacheAttributionToken that is minted at request admission to the batch and passed through prefill execution. 2) Change the cache layer’s telemetry hook to emit an event per request segment (request_id + segment_index) with reused_tokens, attempted_tokens, and miss_reason (if any). 3) In the metrics layer, aggregate only along stable keys (request_id, model_version_id, route_id, deployment_mode, region, prompt_len_bucket) and increment counters/histograms exactly once per request segment. 4) Add guards to prevent fan-out duplication when a request spans multiple micro-batches (continuous batch “stitching”).

Implementation notes: - This PR does not change cache policy or scheduler behavior; it only changes how we attribute telemetry. - Event emission remains sampling-aware (respects existing cache telemetry sampling gates) and uses the same allowlisted tag set. - We keep batch-level debug stats behind a trace-only annotation (no new high-cardinality metric labels).

Illustrative snippet (simplified): Before: metrics.kv_cache_hits_total.add(batch.reused_tokens_total, tags=tags_for(requests[0])) // wrong: tags derived from an arbitrary request; fan-out adds again per request. After: for seg in prefill_result.request_segments: metrics.kv_cache_reused_tokens_total.add(seg.reused_tokens, tags=tags_for(seg.request_ctx)); metrics.kv_cache_attempted_tokens_total.add(seg.attempted_tokens, tags=tags_for(seg.request_ctx))

Tests: - Added integration test that drives two routes concurrently such that they fuse into a single prefill batch (forced by scheduler test harness). Asserts that attempted_tokens_total equals the sum of both requests, and reused_tokens_total matches only the request that should hit (based on seeded prefix cache). - Added regression test covering “stitching”: request A starts in batch1 and continues in batch2; ensures we don’t double-count attempted tokens. - Updated an existing unit test for the prefill metrics aggregator to validate segment-index semantics.

Performance/overhead: No measurable change in the perf-canary p95; the per-request event is emitted from already-available per-request prefill accounting. The new attribution token is an integer stored in RequestContext and passed by value.

Rollout: Safe to ship behind existing flags. No config changes required. Dashboards should show a small correction (downward) in hit counts for routes that heavily rely on continuous batching.

Related: ENG-4822 (KV cache hit/miss counters). This also unblocks dashboard correctness work in observability-pack (PR-612).

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration test for batched prefill attribution - [x] Verified tags comply with cardinality policy - [x] Verified trace annotations still line up with metrics on canary

Notes for reviewers: The key behavioral change is that hit-rate is now computed off per-request attempted/reused tokens, not batch totals. This should align with the ADR semantics for partial hits and avoid batch-size artifacts.
Omar El-Sayed: Can you clarify what exactly was getting double-counted? From the diff it looks like we were incrementing both tokens_total and requests_total multiple times, but the graphs I saw were mostly hit-rate inflation, not request volume inflation.
Samir Qureshi (author): Yep. request counters were usually OK because they were incremented on request completion, not in prefill. The inflation was primarily in token-based numerators/denominators: attempted_tokens_total and reused_tokens_total. We were taking a batch-level attempted/reused summary and then fanning out per request. For a batch of N, each request got credited with the full batch totals (or a heuristic split), which made hit-rate correlate with N. This PR changes attempted/reused accounting to be per-request segment so sums across requests equal the batch totals exactly once.
Sofia Ivanova: I’m concerned about the stability of the mapping. Continuous batching isn’t a single static list; requests can be admitted mid-prefill depending on the microbatch boundaries. How do we guarantee the attribution token stays correct if a request is “stitched” across two prefill microbatches?
Samir Qureshi (author): Good call. The token is minted at request admission to the scheduler and stored on RequestContext; it doesn’t rely on the batch snapshot. For stitching, the cache telemetry callback now emits (request_id, segment_index). The metrics aggregator dedupes by (request_id, segment_index, stage=prefill) so if a request is processed in multiple microbatches, we count each segment once. Added test_cache_metrics_batched_prefill_stitching to cover this.
Noah Patel: Why introduce segment_index rather than just request_id? Also, do we risk increasing event volume (one event per segment) beyond what sampling expects?
Samir Qureshi (author): segment_index is to model partial hits and partial attempts within a single request. With streaming + tool calls we can have multiple prefill segments per logical request; also, in continuous batching we can split prompt processing. Without segment_index, we either undercount (only first segment) or overcount (sum without dedupe). On volume: worst case events ~= prefill segments, which is already bounded by our internal segmentation logic. Sampling gate is still applied at request admission; if a request isn’t sampled, we emit no segment events. So we’re not multiplying sampled requests; we’re giving more accurate accounting within sampled requests.
Nadia Rahman: Please confirm labels don’t change. The metrics naming/cardinality policy explicitly forbids per-request labels and anything derived from prompt content. I see you mention request_id in the telemetry hook.
Samir Qureshi (author): Confirmed: request_id/segment_index only exist in the internal event struct used to aggregate; they never become metric labels. Exported labels remain model_version_id, route_id (allowlisted), deployment_mode, region, prompt_len_bucket, plus miss_reason enum where applicable. I added a comment in cache_metrics.cc and a unit test asserting the tag allowlist is unchanged.
Omar El-Sayed: One more: how does this interact with the fix in PR-18428 (stream retries double counting)? Any chance we’re reintroducing a retry path that counts twice because the same segment is retried?
Samir Qureshi (author): I audited the retry path. Retries now carry a new logical attempt_id but the same request_id; however, segment_index is assigned per attempt. In the retry case we want to count attempted_tokens (because we actually did work again) but we must avoid counting reused_tokens as a “hit” when the retry is due to transport. The existing guard from PR-18428 ensures we don’t treat retry-prefill as cache-hit attribution unless the cache layer explicitly reports reuse. I also ensured segment_index increments on a new prefill compute, so metrics reflect real work while staying consistent with hit semantics.
Sofia Ivanova: Can we add a note in the description that this is expected to lower hit-rate in workloads with big batches? SRE will get nervous if graphs change.
Samir Qureshi (author): Added to rollout section + pinged Allison/Sean to expect correction in canary dashboards.
Omar El-Sayed: Approved after test coverage + explanation. Thanks for the detailed breakdown.
Nadia Rahman: Approved. Please make sure downstream dashboards use attempted/reused tokens, not request counts, for hit-rate; otherwise this won’t fix their graphs.
Samir Qureshi (author): Ack. I linked this PR in the dashboard ticket notes and added a short note to the internal metrics README follow-up PR.

title: Handoff Harmony: Eviction and Transfer Playbook
content:
Handoff Harmony: Eviction and Transfer Playbook

Summary:

This playbook codifies a deterministic, observable approach for transferring in-flight requests and gracefully reclaiming runtime resources. It balances user-visible correctness (avoiding aborted responses and consistency loss) with operator needs for fast resource reclamation during scale events, maintenance, or kernel failures.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs on-call for runtime clusters
- Platform owners planning canaries or capacity changes

Goals and guardrails:
- User-visible aborts from planned or forced handoffs should be < 0.05% monthly.
- Typical handoff commit latency: median <= 150 ms; p99 <= 2.5s for short requests.
- Eviction flows must reclaim a node within configured eviction_window while providing final best-effort completion for affected sessions.

Core terminology (short):
- handoff_token: single-use opaque identifier with expiry ISO8601 timestamp. Appears in traces.
- drain_epoch: the short wait after marking sessions to allow running kernels to finish naturally (configurable).
- eviction_window: hard timeout for completing a transfer or executing graceful eviction.
- kv-sync: optional asynchronous synchronization of minimal KV state to target. Marks session degraded if incomplete.
- preempt_credit: a small retry allowance given to callers during transfer to reduce client-visible failures.

Architecture components involved:
- runtime-dispatcher (dispatcher): selects destination node/shard and initiates handoff intents.
- node-agent: per-host service orchestrating local drain, KV exports, kernel lifecycle, and final commit/eviction actions.
- handoff-orchestrator (leader): optional distributed coordinator for multi-shard transfers and conflict resolution. Data store: etcd.
- telemetry-agent: annotates traces with handoff_token and emits events for Handoff:started, Handoff:committed, Handoff:evicted.

Protocol (ordered steps):
1) Dispatcher detects transfer reason: planned drain, OS maintenance, GPU error, preemption, or capacity balancing. It calculates candidate target(s) and issues an Intent to node-agent: {token, targets, reason, ttl}.
2) Node-agent marks sessions in drain set and enters drain_epoch. It sets internal state to DRAINING and begins non-blocking kv-sync for streaming sessions.
3) Handoff-orchestrator (if present) attempts to reserve a receive slot on the target node. Reservation response includes acceptance, backoff recommendation, or alternate node list.
4) Target node verifies compatibility (model variant, quantization profile, KV shard affinity) and responds. If accepted, it returns a receive_handle with a short TTL.
5) Source node streams session metadata and small KV chunks (if supported). Only metadata required to resume decoding is streamed; secrets and raw user payloads are never proxied.
6) Target node writes session metadata to local cache, acknowledges, and telemetry records Handoff:committed. Source node marks session COMPLETE_LOCAL_CLEANUP and releases kernel resources.
7) If the sequence fails to finish before eviction_window, node-agent triggers graceful-eviction: attempt a synthetic completion (fast-fallback generation), then issue final kernel teardown and emit Handoff:evicted.

Configuration reference (defaults):
| key | default | note |
| .handoff.eviction_window_secs | "30" | applies to short non-stream sessions |
| .handoff.stream_eviction_window_secs | "120" | applies to chat/stream sessions |
| .handoff.drain_epoch_ms | "1500" | small wait to let kernels finish naturally |
| .handoff.max_parallel_transfers | "6" | per-node outgoing transfer concurrency |
| .handoff.preempt_credit_tokens | "1" | number of ephemeral retries clients may consume |
| .handoff.kv_sync_enabled | "true" | best-effort; false disables KV transfer attempts |

Observed failure patterns and recommended mitigations:
- reservation_timeouts (common): when requests queue at dispatcher due to oversubscription. Actions: reduce dispatcher weight, scale dedicated capacity, or reroute to compatible fallback variant. Metric: handoff_reserve_timeout_total.
- kernel_stall during drain: identified by kernel.active_ms spikes and no progress markers. Action: extend drain_epoch up to a soft cap once for kernels flagged as idempotent; otherwise escalate to forced eviction. Metric: kernel_blocked_handoff_total.
- kv_sync_partial: KV sync completed partially. Action: mark session degraded; downstream resume will perform token re-priming. Metric: handoff_kv_partial_total.
- oscillation between nodes: rapid flip-flops identified by repeated commits for same session token. Action: insert randomized cooldown (2m) and raise handoff priority to avoid future oscillations.

Operational runbook (triage):
Alert triggers:
- handoff_reserve_timeout_rate > 5/min sustained for 3m
- handoff_evicted.rate spikes > 1/min for 5m
- handoff_kv_partial.rate > baseline by 200%

Initial responder steps (SRE):
1) Confirm alerts and scope: query Prometheus examples:
   - sum(rate(handoff_reserve_timeout_total[5m])) by (cluster)
   - sum(rate(handoff_evicted_total[5m])) by (node)
2) Inspect dispatcher and node-agent dashboards: dispatcher.route_failures, node.queue_depth_p95, node.kv_sync_errors.
3) If a single node is overloaded: cordon it via node-agent API (dry-run first), allow existing handoffs to proceed, and unfavour new routing to it. Example API:
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -d '{"cordon": true, "eviction_window_secs": 60, "dry_run": true}' \
     https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/cordon
4) If topology-level saturation: scale up dedicated pools or adjust dispatcher routing policies to prefer fallback variants.
5) If KV sync errors: collect node-agent logs (tag: handoff.kv), and export traces from telemetry-service for the handoff_token.
6) Follow recovery verification checklist: handoff_commit_rate returns to baseline, handoff_evicted_total is flat, and canary synthetic workload p99 latency within expected tolerance.

Profiling and benchmarking guidance:
- Synthetic profiles to include in PRs changing handoff logic:
  * Short-request profile: 100k reqs, seq=64, concurrency=800. Report: handoff_commit_success, handoff_latency_p50/p95/p99.
  * Streamed-session profile: 3k sessions, avg_tokens=1500, concurrency=250. Report: kv_sync_success_rate, stream_handoff_commit_latency_p99.
- Profiling tips:
  - Correlate GPU kernel timeline (Nsight/trace) with handoff telemetry. Capture 2s samples across drain_epoch.
  - Sample node-agent state machine transitions and annotate traces with kernel ids to root-cause blockages.

Benchmark pass criteria for merge (non-exhaustive):
- handoff_success_rate >= 99.5% under 75% traffic;
- handoff_latency_p99 degradation <= 25% vs baseline;
- kv_sync_success_rate >= 98% for streaming workloads.

Release & rollout guidance:
- Any protocol change must publish a compatibility matrix and automated migration plan.
- Use feature-flagged canaries: 1% x24h, then 5% x48h, instrument both v1/v2 events.
- Provide explicit rollback actions: disable feature flag and allow existing tokens to expire over one eviction_window cycle.

Telemetry and SLOs (recommended):
- Metrics to emit: handoff_commit_total, handoff_evicted_total, handoff_reserve_timeout_total, handoff_kv_partial_total, handoff_latency_ms(quantiles), handoff_kv_sync_success_ratio.
- Example SLOs (hosted & dedicated):
  * Handoff commit success >= 99.5% monthly
  * User-visible aborts due to handoff <= 0.05% monthly
  * Handoff median latency <= 150ms, p99 <= 2.5s (non-stream workloads)

Debugging snippets:
- Node status (jq):
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/status | jq '.'
- Extract recent handoff traces via telemetry API:
  curl -s "https://telemetry-agent.internal/api/traces?tag=handoff_token&from=-10m" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.samples[] | {token: .token, events: .events}'
- Force a dry-run cordon (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"cordon": true, "eviction_window_secs": 45, "dry_run": true}' \
    https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/cordon

Owner and contacts:
- Primary owner: runtime-platform team (runtime-platform@redwood.com)
- Primary engineers: Marissa Cheng (author), Andrej Kove1cs (handoff/orchestrator), Priya Raman (SRE lead)

Rollout checklist for protocol changes:
1) Unit tests + integration with simulated drain & blocked kernels.
2) PR-level synthetic benchmark comparisons saved to artifacts.
3) Canary rollout (1% -> 5%) with automated alert gates.
4) Full rollout with 30-minute pause windows between increments.

Related resources:
- Runtime dashboards: "Handoff Overview" (Grafana)
- Tools: tools/runtime-canary, synthetic-benchmark-generator
- See also: session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Created (initial playbook and runbook).
- 2026-07-20: Added kv_sync and profiling guidance.
- 2026-12-14: Updated SLO targets and release guidance.
