Subject: Renewal, capacity needs, and a new vendor at the table

Monica,

Thanks for the check-in earlier this week. We are approaching our platform renewal (contract end 2026-12-31) and I wanted to flag two things on our side:

1) Usage growth: Q4 forecasts now show a potential 60% increase in peak concurrent tokens due to a planned personalization rollout. We need guidance on whether our current Dedicated pool can scale to meet that without re-architecting.

2) Competitive pressure: Our infra team ran a short benchmark with Altai AI; they surfaced a managed offer that promises similar latency at ~20% lower unit cost if we commit 12 months. They also propose a migration assistance package.

We value the stability Redwood has provided, but the procurement team is asking for a concrete upsell/price-capacity proposal and a short remediation plan if performance gaps appear. Can you put together an operational playbook and a delta-cost model this week? Evan is looping procurement on next steps.

—Alyssa
Director, Platform Engineering
SummitWorks Inc

Alyssa

title: Add cross-stage cost flare visualization and observability playbook
content:
Add cross-stage cost flare visualization and observability playbook

Motivation: When investigating cost spikes we frequently saw noisy, stage-local metrics (tokenization, model_forward, kv_fetch, decode) that were individually unhelpful. This PR introduces a cross-stage visualization ('Cost Flare') that aligns per-stage token-cost and latency signals to surface correlated flares across the inference pipeline and provides an SRE playbook with automated alert suggestions to speed triage. What changed: 1) A new dashboard JSON for the Cost Flare visualization that aggregates rollups from per-stage telemetry and renders a radial heat/flare view to highlight stages with simultaneous cost/latency deviations; 2) A lightweight cost-annotation agent (telemetry/cost_annotator.go) that tags spans with stage_cost_breakdown and emits compact provenance keys so the dashboard can do low-cardinality joins; 3) An auto-suggester (telemetry/thresholds/auto_suggester.py) that examines correlated anomalies across stages and proposes an alerting bundle (thresholds + priority) in the console; 4) A playbook runbook (observability/playbooks/cost_flare_playbook.md) with reproducible triage steps and recommended SLO actions. Backwards compatibility: All new fields are optional and safely ignored by older dashboards; the annotator falls back to emitting legacy token-cost labels if per-stage data is unavailable. Testing & rollout: Unit tests and integration tests added; deployed to staging with a 24h synthetic replay; gradual canary rollout to production with a kill-switch metric. Security & perf: The annotator operates asynchronously and adds a bounded amount of metadata (<= 128 bytes per invocation) to avoid increasing downstream costs. Links: ENG-1190 for design notes, SUP-2213 for customer incident that motivated this work.

title: Deadline-aware microburst packer for streaming chat to reduce tail latency and GPU memory churn
content:
Deadline-aware microburst packer for streaming chat to reduce tail latency and GPU memory churn

Problem: Streaming chat workloads show microbursts of short requests interleaved with longer generations. Our current continuous batcher either (a) dispatches immediately and pays heavy tail latency during high contention, or (b) waits too long to coalesce and harms P50. Additionally, KV cache allocation and slab reserves jitter under bursty arrivals, causing opportunistic GPU OOMs and frequent small evictions that hurt throughput.

Goal: Implement a deadline-aware microburst packing heuristic that: (1) respects per-request streaming latency budgets, (2) opportunistically coalesces short windows of arrivals into low-jitter microbatches, (3) stabilizes KV slab reservations and eviction patterns to reduce memory churn, and (4) preserves fairness across sessions/tenants. Target SLO: P95 generation token latency <= 160ms for short-turn chat completions under 95th-percentile load, and reduce small-eviction frequency by >= 40% on stress traces.

Approach summary:
- Introduce soft-deadlines per incoming chunk derived from client-declared latency preference (fast/standard) and historical session pacing.
- Maintain a short lookahead buffer (configurable 2-15ms) and a microburst aggregator that holds requests until either the soft-deadline expires or the microbatch reaches a size heuristic.
- Use a deadline-weighted packing score to rank coalescing candidates: score = alpha*(remaining_deadline_ms) + beta*(predicted_token_length) + gamma*(session_priority). Lower score -> higher packing priority.
- For KV cache: implement slot pre-reservation for requests expected to touch KV (chat continuations) and a slab smoothing policy that increments reserves in small deltas instead of immediate full expansion. This reduces transient OOMs and evictions.
- GPU memory policy: maintain a headroom watermark per GPU (configurable, default 12%) and evaluate speculative quantized execution (int8 fallback) when headroom is low and request can tolerate small quality delta.
- Fairness: ensure that long-running, greedy sessions cannot starve microburst aggregation by capping per-session tokens-in-flight used for batch decisioning.

Why unique: This ticket focuses on deadline-first packing for streaming chat (not purely latency-first or throughput-first) and couples the batch formation heuristic with KV reservation smoothing and GPU headroom-aware fallbacks — a coordinated cross-layer strategy rather than independent knobs.

Risks/Unknowns:
- Client-declared latency preferences may be missing or abused; need conservative defaults and rate limits.
- Predicted token-length model needs training/tuning on production traces to avoid mispack.
- Interaction with distributed routing: when routing across capacity tiers we must preserve deadlines or risk inter-region tail spikes.

Success metrics (see acceptance_criteria): P95/P99 latency, small-eviction frequency, GPU OOM incidence, throughput impact.
P95 generation token latency for short completions (<= 8 tokens) under 95th-percentile arrival trace <= 160ms
Small-eviction events (slab < 4MB triggers) reduced by >= 40% on replay of 2026-02 production bursts
No increase in overall cost-per-token > 5% compared to baseline simulated load
Feature gated and can be rolled back at runtime; config flags for lookahead_ms and headroom_pct
Integration tests that simulate interleaved microbursts and long sessions with assertions on batch sizes and reservation deltas
High-level algorithm (prototype):
1) On chunk arrival, attach a computed soft_deadline_ms = client_latency_pref_ms * deadline_scale(session_history).
2) Insert into microburst_buffer indexed by affinity_key (model + tenant + session_shard).
3) Periodically (every scheduler_tick_ms = 1ms) consider buffer: compute packing_score for candidate set and attempt to form microbatch up to gpu_token_budget or until any candidate's soft_deadline <= tick_slack_ms.
4) Before dispatch, call kv_pre_reserve(batch) which calculates incremental slab growth: delta = min(max_delta_bytes, predicted_kv_bytes - current_reserve). Apply in small increments; if global_mem_headroom < headroom_pct, mark requests with speculative_quantize=true.
5) Dispatch: update per-session tokens-in-flight counters and start per-request deadline timers; collect runtime telemetry for observed latency and kv_eviction events.

Notes on parameters to tune: lookahead_ms ∈ [2,15], alpha/beta/gamma weight grid search, headroom_pct default 12%, max_delta_bytes default 8MB.

Prototype artifacts: initial simulator (python) generates synthetic traces of short microbursts + long sessions. Use replay harness to drive dedicated dev cluster with small-scale GPUs to validate eviction frequency changes.
2026-03-10: Triage and spec by Maya. Decided to scope initial rollout to hosted API paths for streaming chat only (no private runtime yet).
2026-03-11: Simulator prototype finished (python harness). Ran 5k trace replays; microburst packing reduced average batch creation events by ~28% in synthetic load. Logged simulator code in /confluence/runtime/2026/deadline-microburst/simulator and added sample traces to drive-tests bucket.
2026-03-12: Implemented microburst_buffer and packing_score in batcher-v2 branch. Initial CI unit tests green. Hooked kv_pre_reserve stub; added feature flag runtime.deadline_microburst = false by default.
2026-03-13: Benchmarked on dev-gpu-4 (A10x4) with replay trace; observed P95 drop for short completions from 220ms -> 150ms, small-eviction delta -36% (below target but promising). Identified jitter in slab growth under heavy concurrent demands.
2026-03-14: Updated slab smoothing to use additive-increase cap and introduced per-tenant reserve ceiling to avoid noisy neighbor expansion. Preparing PR for internal review (see prs).
PM (Rosa Alvarez): prefer conservative defaults for lookahead_ms; user-facing latency settings must be exposed in Console as 'streaming_preference'
SRE (Liam O'Connor): add observability for kv_pre_reserve events and GPU headroom transitions; surface alerts when speculative_quantize > 10%
Design (Priya Nair): when clients fall back to speculative_quantize, we need a UI signal in console and include quality-regression metric in Optimize dashboards
Eng (Kenji Matsuda): ensure packer respects existing priority-aware allocator to avoid regressions for enterprise reserved capacity customers; suggested integration test with Dedicated pool routing

title: Automated scenario-based retention composer and attested evidence workflow for prompt/response/log/metric artifacts
content:
Automated scenario-based retention composer and attested evidence workflow for prompt/response/log/metric artifacts

Problem: Customers need clear, auditable retention controls for the four primary artifact classes (prompts, responses, request logs, metrics) that can be composed into scenario presets (e.g., 'Regulated PII flow', 'GDPR minimize', 'Audit-ready full retention'). Current retention UI and APIs require manual per-route configuration and produce brittle evidence exports that are hard for legal/compliance teams to validate.

Goal: Deliver a scenario-driven Retention Composer that: (1) lets operators pick or author scenario presets which map to per-tenant/per-route retention rules across artifact classes; (2) produces tamper-evident attested evidence bundles (signed metadata + chained hashes) suitable for audits; (3) enables residency-aware retention rules (region pinning + cross-region export); and (4) provides a preview/simulator to estimate storage impact and evidence size.

Scope: UX + API for editor and presets, backend policy engine to translate scenarios into per-route TTLs and sampling rules, evidence exporter format and signer integration (KMS/HSM), residency-aware routing hooks for exports, and CI gating to ensure no scenario rollback breaks SLOs. Excludes: automatic legal approval workflows (out of scope for initial release).
Retention Composer UI: create/edit/save scenario presets that set TTLs and sampling rates for prompts, responses, request logs, metrics
API: POST/GET endpoints for scenario presets and per-tenant binding; changes are versioned and immutable once released
Evidence Bundles: exported bundles contain signed manifest, chained SHA-256 digests for artifact shards, and a human-readable audit summary
Residency: scenario can require region pinning for stored artifacts and the system prevents cross-region exports unless explicitly authorized
Preview Simulator: shows estimated monthly storage, expected export bundle size, and sample evidence timeline for a sample traffic profile
Security: evidence signing uses customer KMS when available; fallback to Redwood attestation; security sign-off obtained
Backward Compatibility: existing per-route TTLs remain honored; binding a scenario should not silently change per-route settings without a preview and confirmation
Operational: rollout supports canary binding (10% of routes) and automatic rollback on retention-export errors
Design note: composer should support both policy-first (RPEL-like) and template-first workflows — operators choose which UI path to use
Implementation idea: translate scenario presets into a small set of primitive rules (TTL, sample_rate, residency_region, export_schedule) which the runtime can enforce without expensive lookups
Evidence format: ZIP with manifest.json, artifacts/*.ndjson (sharded), chainlinks.txt (hash chain), signature.sig; manifest must include per-shard offsets and schema version
KMS integration: prefer EKM/HSM customer keys; when unavailable include a Redwood-produced attestation header and key-rotation metadata
Telemetry: emit retention-affecting config change events to audit log with actor, diff, and before/after preview
Edgecases: handling deleted/retained metrics derived from aggregated counters vs raw time-series—documented in runbook
2026-02-20 Maya Chen: Initial ticket created after workshop with Legal and Platform Security. Scope drafted.
2026-02-28 Anika Patel: Aligned on required artifacts format with Security. Requested evidence signing approach—added KMS fallback.
2026-03-03 Engineering sync: ENG flagged complexity around seamless per-route overrides (ENG-21278). Decided to add canary binding and simulation first.
2026-03-07 Design review: mocked compact manifest format to reduce bundle size; asked PM for schema examples from live tenants.
2026-03-10 Legal review: acceptable for initial release with the signed manifest; legal wants additional identity attestations baked into next iteration. Marked security_review_required=true.

title: On-prem restore fails during manifest apply: missing CRDs / resource ordering causes "no matches for kind" errors
content:
On-prem restore fails during manifest apply: missing CRDs / resource ordering causes "no matches for kind" errors

Issue summary
- Customer attempted a control-plane restore for Redwood Private in an air-gapped on-prem environment.
- `restore apply` fails when applying Kubernetes resources from the backup artifact.
- Errors indicate missing CRDs and/or incorrect ordering (CustomResources applied before CRDs are installed).

Impact
- Customer blocked from completing restore validation for internal DR readiness review.
- No production outage (this was a planned restore drill into a new cluster), but DR timeline at risk.

Customer context
- Customer: MedData Systems
- Deployment: Redwood Private (on-prem, air-gapped)
- Restore target: new Kubernetes cluster (fresh install)
- Backup artifact source: previous cluster (same environment) created via installer `backup create`.

What the customer expected
- Restore should bootstrap required components in a deterministic order and fail fast with clear remediation steps if prerequisites are missing.

What happened
- Restore job attempts to apply Kubernetes manifests (including CRs for cert-manager / external-secrets / redwood control-plane CRs) before the corresponding CRDs exist on the target cluster.

Steps to reproduce (as reported)
1) Stand up a fresh Kubernetes cluster (air-gapped, no external repos).
2) Install Redwood Private base prerequisites (customer believed CRDs would be included in restore bundle).
3) Run: `redwood-private restore apply --from /mnt/backup/backup_2025-02-17T0312Z`.
4) Restore fails during "Apply Kubernetes objects" stage.

Observed errors (snippets)
- kubectl apply output from restore logs:
  - "error: resource mapping not found for name: \"redwood-control-plane\" namespace: \"redwood-system\" from \"manifest.yaml\": no matches for kind \"RedwoodTenant\" in version \"platform.redwood.ai/v1\" ensure CRDs are installed first"
  - "error: unable to recognize \"manifest.yaml\": no matches for kind \"ExternalSecret\" in version \"external-secrets.io/v1beta1\""
  - "error: unable to recognize \"manifest.yaml\": no matches for kind \"Certificate\" in version \"cert-manager.io/v1\""
- Restore summary:
  - "stage=apply_k8s_objects status=failed applied=214 failed=17 skipped=0"
  - "hint: install required CRDs and re-run restore"

Notes
- The customer’s baseline cluster did not have cert-manager and external-secrets CRDs preinstalled in the restore target.
- In air-gapped mode, the customer is using the offline bundle and does not have access to pull charts/images during restore.

Request
- Provide a clear supported workaround for installing required CRDs (and in what order) prior to re-running restore.
- Confirm whether Redwood’s restore workflow should install CRDs automatically (from bundle) or explicitly require them as prerequisites.
- Update customer-facing runbook to prevent recurrence.
2025-02-18 09:14 PT — Fatima Noor (Reporter): Created from customer escalation in #support. Customer blocked on restore drill; attaching initial error snippets and requesting logs + exact installer version.
2025-02-18 10:02 PT — Support (Fatima Noor): Requested: (1) installer version (`redwood-private version`), (2) backup manifest header (format/version), (3) full restore log, (4) list of preinstalled CRDs on target cluster (`kubectl get crd | wc -l` plus grep for cert-manager/external-secrets/platform.redwood.ai).
2025-02-18 13:37 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): Provided logs. Installer: 1.9.3-private (offline bundle). Backup created 2025-02-17. Target cluster has no cert-manager CRDs. Error repeats for ExternalSecret and RedwoodTenant kinds. They assumed restore would include everything required.
2025-02-18 14:10 PT — Sean Gallagher (Assignee, SRE): Confirmed symptom aligns with ordering: restore applying CRs before CRDs are present. In air-gapped mode, CRDs must come from the offline bundle (not fetched). Looping in Ethan Park for control-plane restore sequencing expectations.
2025-02-18 15:03 PT — Ethan Park (Control plane eng lead): Restore workflow currently assumes prerequisite operators/CRDs exist (cert-manager, external-secrets, and Redwood platform CRDs via helm install of control-plane chart). If customer ran restore on a completely fresh cluster without running the "bootstrap" step, CRDs will be missing. We should improve preflight to detect and provide a deterministic checklist, and optionally extract CRDs from bundle for install-first.
2025-02-18 16:22 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Sent interim workaround to customer: install prerequisite CRDs first (from offline bundle) then re-run restore. Asked customer to confirm whether they can run helm from bundle and whether images are already loaded into their registry.
2025-02-19 09:05 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): They can run helm from the bundle; images are preloaded. They need exact commands and ordering. Also asked whether Redwood secrets are restored or only references.
2025-02-19 10:18 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE): Provided ordered workaround (below). Also clarified secrets handling: restore rehydrates secret references/config; secret material depends on customer’s secret manager and must be available post-restore (no raw secret export).
2025-02-19 10:20 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE) — Workaround details shared:
1) Verify CRDs missing:
   - `kubectl get crd | egrep '(cert-manager|external-secrets|platform.redwood.ai)' || true`
2) From the offline bundle, install prereq charts WITH CRDs enabled (do not use `--skip-crds`):
   - cert-manager: `helm upgrade --install cert-manager ./charts/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set installCRDs=true`
   - external-secrets: `helm upgrade --install external-secrets ./charts/external-secrets -n external-secrets --create-namespace`
3) Install Redwood control-plane chart to lay down Redwood CRDs before applying CR instances:
   - `helm upgrade --install redwood-control-plane ./charts/redwood-control-plane -n redwood-system --create-namespace`
4) Confirm CRDs exist:
   - `kubectl get crd | egrep '(cert-manager.io|external-secrets.io|platform.redwood.ai)'`
5) Re-run restore:
   - `redwood-private restore apply --from /mnt/backup/backup_2025-02-17T0312Z --continue-on-preflight=false`
6) Validation:
   - `kubectl -n redwood-system get pods`
   - run the post-restore health check in the runbook (control-plane API ready, tenant config present, routing policy objects present).

Notes: If the cluster has partially-applied CRs, delete the failed CRs before re-run to avoid immutable field conflicts.
2025-02-19 13:44 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): Workaround succeeded after installing CRDs/operators first. Restore completed, but they noted the installer error message was generic and the runbook didn’t emphasize CRD prerequisites for a brand new cluster.
2025-02-20 08:55 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Requested customer confirm final validation checklist results (tenant config restored, routing policies present, control-plane endpoints healthy).
2025-02-20 12:11 PT — Customer (MedData Ops): Validation looks good. They asked Redwood to document "fresh cluster" prerequisites and add a preflight check that fails with specific missing CRDs listed.
2025-02-21 09:32 PT — Sean Gallagher (SRE): Logged follow-up requests for Eng: add explicit preflight CRD checks + improve ordering (CRDs before CRs). Referencing ongoing restore workflow improvements and helm hook work. Linking internal work to ENG-9822/ENG-9830/ENG-9828.
2025-02-22 10:05 PT — Fatima Noor (Support): Marking Resolved. Customer unblocked with documented workaround; awaiting doc patch in next runbook refresh.
Restore failure was due to missing prerequisite CRDs (cert-manager, external-secrets, Redwood platform CRDs) on a fresh on-prem cluster, causing "no matches for kind" during manifest apply. Workaround: install prerequisite charts/CRDs from the offline bundle first, then re-run `restore apply`. Follow-ups filed to improve restore preflight and documentation to explicitly cover fresh-cluster ordering.
Install prerequisite CRDs/operators from the offline bundle (cert-manager with installCRDs=true, external-secrets, then Redwood control-plane chart to install Redwood CRDs) before running `redwood-private restore apply`. If partial CRs were applied, delete failed CR objects prior to re-run to avoid conflicts.
Redwood will update the customer-facing restore runbook to add a "fresh cluster prerequisites" section and enhance installer preflight to list missing CRDs explicitly (targeting the next Private installer + docs release).
This ticket is consistent with recent restore drill feedback: restore should (a) detect missing CRDs and stop early with actionable output, and (b) optionally offer a "bootstrap prerequisites" step in air-gapped mode using bundle-contained CRD manifests. Coordinate with docs owner (Elliot Price / Kira Thompson) and control-plane eng (Ethan Park).
Slack: #support escalation (see internal thread linked from SUP-18421)
Confluence: runbook-control-plane-restore (add prereq CRD section; emphasize ordering for fresh clusters)
GitHub: pr-489 (restore workflow + validation), pr-138 (restore job template/hooks), pr-512 (compatibility/versioning messaging)

title: Consolidate pre-install probe templates and introduce tenant-scoped init-rate profiles
content:
Consolidate pre-install probe templates and introduce tenant-scoped init-rate profiles

Context: Private installer customers run into protracted cluster preflight phases when multi-tenant on-prem installs execute large numbers of tenant init jobs concurrently. This causes API server saturation and sporadic timeouts during pre-install health checks.

Motivation: provide a safer, opt-in default for helm charts that (1) centralizes pre-install and readiness probe templates to reduce duplication, (2) exposes tenant-scoped init-rate profiles (concurrency + burst) so operators can trade install speed for API stability, and (3) add a lightweight migration path so existing values are not broken.

Checklist:
- [x] Add unified probe template library for preflight and init jobs
- [x] Introduce tenant.initRateProfiles map in values.yaml with profiles (low/medium/high)
- [x] Implement values merging precedence and deprecation warnings
- [x] Add integration tests for staggered init behavior and preflight liveness
- [x] Documentation: update values.example and migration guide
- [x] CI: lint, unit tests, helm template, and an e2e job that runs a 6-tenant dry-run

Changes (high level):
- chart/templates/_probes.tpl: new consolidated probe helper (preflightProbe, initLiveness, initReadiness) that takes profile and overrides
- chart/values.schema.json: extended schema for tenant.initRateProfiles and probeOverrides with strict types and examples
- chart/values.example.yaml: new examples showing per-tenant overrides and recommended profiles
- chart/templates/init-job.yaml: wiring to read initRateProfile and apply rate controller annotations (init.kubernetes.io/concurrency, init.kubernetes.io/burst)
- chart/templates/preflight-hook.yaml: use preflightProbe helper and dynamically compute timeouts based on profile
- scripts/migrate-values.sh: helper that rewrites deprecated top-level initRate fields into the new tenant-scoped map (used in upgrade notes)
- tests/helm/staggered-init.test.yaml: unit-style helm template test showing annotation presence for each profile

Commits:
- 9c3f7d8 Add probe template helpers and initial tests
- b14a0fe Add tenant.initRateProfiles schema and example values
- e2f4c1a Wire init-job and preflight-hook to profile annotations and timeouts; add migrate-values script
- 4f5b2d0 Fix: revert flaky e2e timeout and tune medium profile
- d3a71b2 Docs: write migration guide and values examples

Files touched (selective):
- chart/templates/_probes.tpl (new)
- chart/templates/init-job.yaml (modified)
- chart/templates/preflight-hook.yaml (modified)
- chart/values.schema.json (modified)
- chart/values.example.yaml (new examples added)
- scripts/migrate-values.sh (new)
- tests/helm/staggered-init.test.yaml (new)

Small snippet (probe helper usage): {{"{{- include \"redwood._preflightProbe\" (dict \"profile\" \"medium\" \"overrides\" .Values.probeOverrides) -}}"}}

Testing & CI:
- Local lint + helm template passed
- Unit-style Helm tests (kubeval + schema checks) added and passed in CI
- E2E job initially failed due to tight timeouts; fixed by adjusting medium profile defaults and rerunning.

Final CI: all checks green (lint, unit, helm-template, e2e-dryrun).

Review conversation (high level):
- Marco Chen (reviewer): "Nice consolidation. Two asks: 1) make sure default medium profile is conservative for older clusters, 2) add a clear deprecation message in values.schema.json for the old initRate keys."
- Author (Aisha): "Addressed both: medium profile defaults dialed back (see commit b14a0fe) and deprecation warnings added in schema and migration script."
- Lena Fischer (reviewer): "Can we add a knob to completely opt-out of the rate controller annotations for customers who use external init orchestration?"
- Author: "Added tenant.initRateProfiles.<profile>.enabled boolean and documented opt-out in values.example.yaml."
- Diego Alvarez (approver): "Verified on internal testbed with 8 tenants, medium profile helps prevent apiserver saturation. Approving for merge."

Migration notes for operators:
- This change is backwards-compatible: existing top-level initRate fields are still supported but deprecated. Use scripts/migrate-values.sh to automatically convert to the new tenant.initRateProfiles map during upgrades.
- Default behavior: if tenant-specific profile not supplied, chart falls back to global initRate profile, then to 'medium' safe defaults.
- If you previously relied on aggressive concurrency, review new 'high' profile and adjust quotas accordingly.

Observability:
- Added two new Helm chart metrics labels for init profile (chart.k8s.redwood/init_profile) so Console dashboards can correlate init-phase latency with configured profiles.

Security and compliance:
- No secrets introduced. Rate-control annotations are purely metadata; no RBAC changes required.

Merge outcome: squashed and merged via GitHub web UI after approvals (merge method: squash).

Post-merge follow-ups:
- ENG-1248 follow-up created to evaluate adaptive-init autoscaler in next sprint
- Documentation PR queued to redwood-docs that imports values.example snippets and upgrade instructions

Notes: kept changes intentionally conservative to avoid surprises for Private customers running in constrained air-gapped environments. The migration script is minimal and prints a dry-run by default.
Add tenant-scoped init-rate profiles and unified pre-install probe templates. Backwards-compatible values; adds migration guide and example values for Private installs.

title: Spectra Bridge SaaSWorks
content:
Spectra Bridge SaaSWorks

Short-form account notes + technical/ops details:
- Company profile: mid-market B2B SaaS (product analytics toolbox). Multi-tenant product, heavy embeddings-backed search + contextual chat for product discovery.
- Trial summary (Hosted API): running ~14 days, ingestion of 30k tokens/day avg, peak day 95k tokens. Observed baseline QPS: 3-6 sustained, peak QPS bursts up to 12 for short windows. Average tokens/req ~450 (mix of short UI prompts ~120 tokens and deep summarization ~1.2k tokens). Streaming used ~40% of requests (real-time UI).
- POC findings we captured: p95 latency on hosted -> 220–320ms for small prompts; long-run completions push >800ms. Electro-ops: concurrency observed during peak ~12 concurrent requests per node; they expect concurrency to rise as product scales.
- Desired Dedicated sizing targets (customer asks): sustained QPS target 15 (peak 45), p95 latency <250ms for typical UI flows, support for long-context sessions up to 8k tokens, ability to handle 3x growth within 6 months. They want reserved baseline capacity + 2-tier burst policy.
- Token mix and forecasting notes: current mix ~60% short (<256 tokens), 30% mid (256-1024), 10% long (>1024). Forecast: projected product launch -> 3x token volume in 6 months, peak concurrency x3. They want model of costs for 1x / 3x / 5x scenarios and GPU equivalence guidance (what dedicated pool size maps to expected QPS/concurrency).
- Architecture preferences & constraints: prefer VPC peering for Dedicated, KMS integration for key management, SSO (SAML) mandatory, audit logs retention 1 year, EU data residency for subset of customers.
- Commercial: price-sensitive vs performance — willing to commit to reserved capacity if we can guarantee cost per token and burst capacity behavior. Looking for clear comparison hosted vs dedicated TCO and uplift for 99.9% SLA.
- Quote ask: two flavors — (A) small dedicated pool to meet baseline QPS 15 with 3x headroom; (B) larger reserved for predictable throughput and lower per-token cost. Also want options for autoscale/burst credits.
- Risks / objections: procurement timeline (budget closes end of Q1), still evaluating OpenAI + Vertex + potential in-house inference build, SOC2 evidence required before procurement, need legal review for data residency clauses.
- Direct quote from product lead: "If latency spikes we lose flow — need consistent 200–300ms for key flows. Pricing needs to make sense at 3x scale or we'll stay hosted."
- Stubs/links: shared POC CSV with token-by-request breakdown (drive link above), Fireflies meeting ff-4f3a9b2e has full transcript.
- Immediate ask from AE: SE to produce dedicated-capacity spreadsheet mapping QPS/concurrency/token-mix -> GPU pool size (N GPUs of X spec) + estimated monthly cost windows (1x, 3x, 5x). Also send dedicated pricing template and SLA language to procurement.

title: Ignite Labs — Developer Onboard: SDK + Auth Runbook
content:
Ignite Labs — Developer Onboard: SDK + Auth Runbook

Intro + live walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, auth patterns for CI and multiple environments, demo of Console sandbox, and Optimize suggestions for latency/cost tradeoffs. Agreed to follow-up poc scoping and get a sandbox API key and sample repo.
Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-16 14:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Desai, Daniel Park, Sofia Martinez, Lina Zhou

00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, Alex from Redwood — thanks for making time. Um, we'll do a quick agenda, then dive into a hands-on SDK quickstart for Python and TypeScript, cover auth patterns and the Console sandbox, and end with Optimize tips and next steps. Sound good?

00:14 Daniel Park: Yeah that sounds great. Quick note — Sofia's joining for the first 20 minutes and then she has another meeting.

00:21 Sofia Martinez: Hi all — jumping in. We're really keen to understand how this will fit into our CI/CD workflows and data residency stuff.

00:30 Priya Desai: Awesome — we'll call out the CI secrets patterns and the VPC/private options too. Um, for the demo I'll share my screen and run both the Python quickstart and a small TypeScript example.

00:45 Alex Chen: Quick qualification — can you remind us where you're planning to run inference today? Hosted, on-prem, or hybrid?

00:53 Daniel Park: Right now it's all in-house, we run a kube cluster and an internal model-serving layer. We're evaluating whether to keep serving models ourselves or move to managed inference. Main constraints are latency under 120ms p95 for short prompts and tight cost control.

01:10 Priya Desai: Got it. That latency target is reasonable — we'll show how batching and cache policies can be tuned so you don't lose that SLO. Also we'll discuss Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs.

01:28 Lina Zhou: Question — we have strict secrets policies, CI can't see long-lived API keys. How do you recommend rotating keys and integrating with our Vault?

01:36 Priya Desai: Good question. Typical pattern is to use short-lived tokens via our sandbox or exchange tokens from your KMS. We support KMS/HSM integration and recommend storing long-lived credentials in the Vault, then issuing ephemeral tokens in CI using the Redwood token exchange API. We'll share an example GitHub Actions step.

01:58 Alex Chen: Ok jumping into the code. I'm going to paste the Python quickstart command in chat: pip install redwood-sdk (note: the package name here might be a placeholder in transcript).

02:10 Priya Desai: I'm running a tiny script: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_KEY')); resp = client.generate('Write a one-sentence summary of product usage'); print(resp.text)

02:28 Daniel Park: Cool. Does the SDK stream events? We need streaming for our chat UI.

02:35 Priya Desai: Yes, the SDK supports streaming. In Python you can iterate over client.stream_generate(...) and in TypeScript it's event-based with async iterators. Streaming works with our Console so you can debug token timing too.

02:45 Sofia Martinez: I saw in the docs something about function calling and structured outputs — is that stable? We're going to rely on a schema to fill forms.

02:54 Priya Desai: Function/tool calling is supported — we call it tool-calls in some older places in the docs, so you might see variant names. It lets you return JSON and map to your schema. There's also a validation layer in the Console for outputs.

03:10 Alex Chen: Switching to the TypeScript example; I'll open a basic node project. npm install @redwood/sdk (again package name fuzzy in transcribe) and here's a snippet: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY }); const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'rwd-3-small', input: 'Summarize...' });

03:38 Daniel Park: That model name — rwd-3-small — is that a hosted Redwood model? We plan to bring our own model sometimes.

03:44 Priya Desai: Yes rwd-3-small is one of the verified catalog models. You can also point the SDK at a private model in your Dedicated or Private deployment. There's a model alias layer so you can switch models without changing code.

04:02 Lina Zhou: For private deployments, do you manage the control plane or is it customer-managed?

04:08 Alex Chen: For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane option. You get the Console and telemetry but you host the runtime in your VPC or on-prem; we integrate with your KMS and audit logs.

04:22 Daniel Park: Good. Walk us through the auth example for CI.

04:27 Priya Desai: Sure. Typical pattern: store long-lived credential in HashiCorp Vault; CI job requests an ephemeral token via an internal service or via Redwood's token exchange endpoint; that token is short-lived (e.g., 1 hour) and injected as REDWOOD_KEY into the job. For local dev, devs can use a local short-lived key from the Console or a developer sandbox key. We'll attach a sample GitHub Actions snippet in the follow-up.

04:55 Sofia Martinez: Any RBAC? We need to limit which services can call generation endpoints and which can only create embeddings.

05:02 Priya Desai: Yes we support token scoping and role-based policies. In the Console you can create route-level permissions, and tokens can be limited to only embeddings, or only certain models, and you can also scope to rate limits.

05:18 Alex Chen: Okay, next I'm going to bring up the Redwood Console sandbox we provisioned for Ignite. One moment — sharing screen.

05:30 [screen share noise]

05:36 Priya Desai: Here in the Console you can see the Sandbox project: Activity, API keys, Quickstart links. I'm clicking the Quickstart repo which contains a mono-repo with py and ts examples and a GitHub Actions workflow. That repo link will be in the follow-up email.

06:02 Daniel Park: Nice — I see usage limits and a token breakdown. Does the Console show per-route latency percentiles?

06:09 Priya Desai: Yes, per-route dashboards with p50/p95/p99, cost per token, and you can correlate with request tracing IDs. We also surface KV cache hit rates when enabled.

06:22 Lina Zhou: About caching — can prefix caching be used without violating user privacy with PII? We need to ensure we don't cache any user-identifying strings across tenants.

06:33 Priya Desai: Absolutely — caching policies are configurable by route and you can redact sensitive fields before caching. For multi-tenant setups we'd recommend tenant-scoped caches or disabling prefix caching for PII routes.

06:48 Sofia Martinez: We have a questions about model rollouts. If a new quantized model is cheaper but lower quality, can Redwood do canary rollouts?

06:57 Alex Chen: Yes, rollouts are built-in: you can do traffic splits per model version or fallbacks to a higher-quality variant if quality degrades. The Console will alert regressions tied to a prompt set.

07:10 Daniel Park: Great. Let's talk about Optimize — you're recommending batching/caching — any heuristics for our chat-like workload?

07:20 Priya Desai: For chat where latency is important, use small micro-batches (e.g., 8-16) and aggressive KV caching for repeated context. For embedding-heavy pipelines, batch larger with async pools. We'll give a recommended profile based on the sample traffic you provide.

07:38 Alex Chen: Quick demo of a small benchmark script I run in the repo: it uses the SDK and hits the sandbox with a tokenized payload distribution that matches a 3-turn chat. Results show 95ms median, 140ms p95 with default settings — we can tune batching to hit your 120ms p95.

07:58 Lina Zhou: You've mentioned quantization — do you handle quantized models in Hosted? Any lock-in?

08:06 Priya Desai: We support quantized variants in both Hosted and Dedicated; quantized models are model variants so it's easy to switch. There's no lock-in — you can export model configs and run them in your private infra if you choose.

08:22 Daniel Park: Ok, stopping screen share. For the code samples, what about telemetry and logging? We need request IDs to tie back to our logs.

08:30 Priya Desai: The SDK automatically returns a request_id header and you can attach custom metadata. The Console ingest shows traces and lets you search by request_id and user token. We'll show an example log snippet: RequestID: rwd-abc123, model: rwd-3-small, latency_ms: 118

08:50 Sofia Martinez: (overlap) also audit logs for admin actions — we need them to go into our SIEM.

08:55 Alex Chen: Audit logs can be exported via syslog or S3 and you can plug them into your SIEM. For Private deployments you have full control.

09:05 Daniel Park: Let's talk about limits — sandbox vs prod. If we start with sandbox and then move to Dedicated, what is the onboarding time?

09:12 Priya Desai: Sandbox is immediate. Dedicated provisioning is typically 2-4 weeks depending on region and GPU availability; Dedicated also includes reserved capacity and SLA. We'll put a timeline in the follow-up.

09:25 Lina Zhou: Are there any compliance certs we should be aware of? SOC2? ISO?

09:30 Alex Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II and are working on ISO 27001 for certain regions; we'll share our security package.

09:36 Daniel Park: (note of transition) okay Sofia needs to drop now — thanks for joining.

09:40 Sofia Martinez: Thanks everyone — follow-up with the security packet would be great. Bye.

09:45 [Sofia leaves]

09:50 Alex Chen: Back to the demo — Priya, can you run the TypeScript streaming example to show how message-by-message comes through?

09:58 Priya Desai: Sure — running node stream-demo.js. This will stream tokens for a 50-token response. (background typing) You'll see in the console it prints partial chunks, then final event. There's also a callback hook so you can send partial render events to your UI.

10:25 Daniel Park: Looks good. One more question — do you have limits on max context length and how to handle long documents?

10:32 Priya Desai: Max context varies by model family. For long documents we recommend chunking + retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Redwood has built-in embeddings endpoints and you can use our reranker to filter candidate passages. For very long context we also support model-specific streaming of KV cache to disk in Dedicated environments.

10:55 Daniel Park: Let's cover billing. How granular is usage reporting? We need per-team cost chargeback.

11:03 Alex Chen: The Console has token-level billing and you can tag routes and API keys to map usage to teams. We also expose an API for exports so you can run chargeback scripts nightly.

11:18 Lina Zhou: Quick follow — are there example policies for redaction we can apply?

11:24 Priya Desai: Yes, the repo includes a small redaction middleware for Node + Python that strips PII patterns before sending. We'll attach it.

11:35 Daniel Park: Ok, I think that's a solid demo. For the follow-up POC scoping, we'll share expected qps, typical prompt lengths, and required compliance items.

11:45 Alex Chen: Great. Recap of next steps: Priya will send sandbox key and repo; Alex will draft a pilot price; Ignite will provide traffic profile; we'll schedule POC scoping the week of 10/27. Any final questions?

11:58 Lina Zhou: No, thanks — this was helpful.

12:05 Priya Desai: I'll also include the GitHub Actions snippet and the token exchange example.

12:12 Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in the email.

12:18 [meeting ends]

title: Tailback pressure causes 504 timeout for hyperlength single-turn generation with streaming
content:
Tailback pressure causes 504 timeout for hyperlength single-turn generation with streaming

Customer reports 504 Gateway Timeout when issuing a single-turn generation with an extremely long prompt (large context + large max_tokens) using streaming: connection closes before final chunks are emitted. Customer is on a Dedicated cluster in us-east. They reported this started after a spike in similar requests last week and is reproducible for one specific job id. The request uses the /v1/generate endpoint with streaming=true and max_tokens=150000. Impact: Podscribe's nightly ingestion job fails intermittently, causing downstream indexing delays and backfills.
1) Use customer API key on prod-us-east cluster. 2) POST to /v1/generate with model=redwood-open-6B-quant, streaming=true, max_tokens=150000, and a ~180k-token priming prompt (concatenated customer documents). 3) Keep TCP connection open and allow streaming chunks. 4) Observe 504 or connection reset after ~115-125s; occasional partial chunks delivered then finalizer error. Example curl provided to customer during triage: curl -i -N -X POST https://api.redwood.com/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"redwood-open-6B-quant","stream":true,"max_tokens":150000,"prompt":"<very long priming text>"}'
HTTP/1.1 504 Gateway Timeout or connection reset by peer. When a partial stream is returned, the final bytes are delayed then cut off. On successful-but-slow runs the finalizer queue length climbs and worker handoff latency spikes, then the connection is closed without finalization. No increased 5xx rate for other customers in the same cluster during most occurrences.
Streamed chunks continue until generation completes and finalizer emits final chunk; no client-visible 504 for requests that fit within resource quotas for Dedicated customers. If system must reject, return a clear 429 with a recommended fallback model/shorter max_tokens guidance.
Relevant logs for request_id=req_0a1b2c3d4e: 
[2026-03-12T03:18:57Z] api-gateway: accept request req_0a1b2c3d4e client_ip=54.210.12.34
[2026-03-12T03:19:00Z] scheduler: queued job job_99877 priority=normal queue_pos=17
[2026-03-12T03:19:12Z] scheduler: dispatch job job_99877 -> worker pool dedicated-eu? (chosen us-east)
[2026-03-12T03:19:48Z] serving-runtime: pool-alloc-delay=36s kernel-swap=true req=req_0a1b2c3d4e model=redwood-open-6B-quant sequence_len_est=180000
[2026-03-12T03:20:30Z] kv-cache: hit_ratio=0.18 resident=22% attempting-evict=true evict_rate=78%
[2026-03-12T03:20:50Z] finalizer: queue_length=12 headroom_tokens=0 backlog_ms=13450
[2026-03-12T03:21:57Z] finalizer: emit_chunk seq=last error=deadline_exceeded connection_closed=client_reset
[2026-03-12T03:21:57Z] api-gateway: 504 Gateway Timeout req=req_0a1b2c3d4e
Additional metrics: grafana panel: https://metrics.redwood.com/d/abc123/cluster-finalizer?var=cluster=prod-us-east
Initial hypothesis: finalizer queueing + pool allocation delay caused by resource headroom exhaustion under spike of hyperlength jobs. Data points: sustained high kv-cache eviction and large pool-alloc-delay for this job; finalizer queue length correlates with 504 events in the cluster. Further checking: autoscaler logs show burst_capacity_remaining=0 at time of request; node-provisioning latency of ~28s causing delay in new worker attach. No immediate OOMs on worker; CPU on router pods spiked but not saturated. We saw several concurrent jobs with similar token budgets from the same customer window (backfill). The serving runtime stalls around kernel-swap for very long sequences — older kernel path selection causes higher mem copies leading to slower throughput; this cluster is using an older runtime image (runtime v2.14) not yet updated to the optimized kernel selection introduced in v2.18.
Combination of (a) cluster exhausted burst headroom due to multiple hyperlength jobs from the same customer, (b) scheduler allocation delay + autoscaler cooldown preventing timely worker provisioning, and (c) older serving runtime kernel path that increases CPU-bound handoff latency for very long-sequence workloads, which created a finalizer backlog and ultimately triggered gateway-level 504s.
1) Temporarily scoped rate-limit: applied per-customer concurrency cap for Podscribe to 2 concurrent hyperlength jobs to prevent further backlog. 2) Manually increased cluster burst_capacity for prod-us-east and forced a scale-up (nodes added, new workers attached). 3) Enabled fallback policy on the customer's routes to route to redwood-open-6B-quant-smaller (token-window-limited) when headroom < 5%. 4) Restarted a subset of router pods to clear TCP stale connections. These actions reduced immediate 504s and allowed most queued jobs to finish within 90s after scale-up.
Recommend customers split monolithic priming into smaller chunks and use incremental generation + rerank instead of single hyperlength generation. For now we advised Podscribe to reduce max_tokens to <= 50k or switch to a dedicated private deployment with reserved capacity for their nightly backfills. Support provided a script to chunk prompts and stitch outputs client-side.
1) Backport kernel-selection and memory-copy optimizations from runtime v2.18 to v2.14 and roll to affected Dedicated clusters. 2) Improve autoscaler heuristics to detect hyperlength job spikes and pre-warm workers when queue length and estimated sequence length exceed thresholds. 3) Add explicit API-level guardrail: return 429 with explanatory body when estimated token+context cost exceeds dynamic headroom threshold rather than letting requests queue to finalizer. 4) Update docs + quickstart with best practices for large priming workloads. Timeline: hotfix (kernel backport) targeted within 2 weeks; autoscaler heuristics in 6 weeks.
Work in progress. Immediate mitigation reduced customer impact and suggested workaround accepted by customer. Engineering is tracking kernel backport PR and autoscaler changes. Customer asked to keep ticket open until backport is deployed to their dedicated cluster and they validate nightly success for one week.
2026-03-12 04:05 UTC - Support (Ava Martinez): Collected request_id=req_0a1b2c3d4e and sample prompt from customer, asked for exact timing and whether they had concurrent jobs. Customer confirmed 3 parallel backfills at time of failure.
2026-03-12 07:30 UTC - SRE (Liam Chen): Scaled cluster manually and observed worker attach completed at 2026-03-12T07:47Z; finalizer queue drained. Created temporary per-customer concurrency cap. Investigating autoscaler cooldown behavior.
2026-03-13 12:15 UTC - Eng (Priya Nair): Found that runtime v2.18 kernel selection reduces memcopy for long sequences by ~35% in benchmarks. Opening backport PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2145
2026-03-14 09:10 UTC - Customer (Samir Dogra, Podscribe): Confirmed that after temporary concurrency cap and reducing max_tokens to 40k their nightly runs completed successfully. They will trial the chunking script and report results next week.
1) Merge and deploy backport PR to prod-us-east dedicated clusters for Podscribe (owner: Priya). 2) Implement autoscaler heuristic change and test on staging with synthetic hyperlength workload (owner: SRE team). 3) Keep ticket open; validate one week of successful nightly backfills from Podscribe; schedule a check-in on 2026-03-21.

title: Day-2 Automation, Upgrade & Rollback Runbook for Private Deployments
content:
Day-2 Automation, Upgrade & Rollback Runbook for Private Deployments

Summary:

This document is the canonical Day-2 operations runbook for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It combines: the operational checklist for steady-state, automated workflows for common tasks, verified upgrade and rollback procedures for releases, packaging validation for air-gapped installs, and a customer requirements checklist used during sales/onboarding. Target audience: SREs, platform engineers, and solutions engineers executing upgrades or troubleshooting production private deployments.

Goals:
- Ensure upgrades are repeatable, observable, and reversible.
- Minimize customer downtime and manual intervention via automation.
- Provide a single source of truth for safety checks, SLAs, and escalation.

Owner & Contacts:
- Primary owner: Platform SRE (team: eng-private-deployments)
- On-call escalation: private-deployments oncall rotation (pager: #infra-oncall)
- Escalation matrix: Marcus Li (SRE Lead), Priya Nair (Solutions Eng), Daniel Morales (Product).

Prerequisites (preflight):
1) Validated customer topology: list of control-plane endpoints, worker subnets, routing tables, and CIDRs.
2) KMS/HSM configuration verified and accessible (or pre-staged for air-gapped).
3) Current deployment manifest and image digests stored in the release artifact registry.
4) Backups: KV cache snapshot + model artifact snapshot + database backup stored off-host.
5) SLOs & maintenance window agreed with customer and recorded in the SA notes.

Customer Requirements Library (minimum set):
| Requirement | Expected value / action | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------------|-------|
| Supported OS | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS or RHEL 8 | Kernel >= 5.15 recommended |
| Network | Static routing for control plane + NAT for egress | BGP optional for large customers |
| Storage | NFS or Ceph for model artifacts, 1 TB per shard baseline | Validate IOPS against perf profile |
| KMS | AWS KMS / CloudHSM / Onprem HSM | Provide key ARN or cert bundle |
| Air-gap | Installer tarball + SHA256 + signed manifest | See packaging section |

Day-2 steady-state checklist (daily/weekly tasks):
- Verify control-plane health: /health endpoint for each service (latency < 200ms p50).
- Check autoscaling events and GPU pool utilization. Target: 60-75% average utilization for efficiency.
- Review error-rate dashboard: requests with 5xx should < 0.05% of total requests over 1h.
- Verify cache hit-rate: prefix/KV cache hit-rate target >= 80% for production traffic.
- Confirm backups completed and verify restore on a staging cluster monthly.
- Rotate TLS certs and KMS keys per customer policy (at least quarterly for test keys, annual for production keys).

Automations & Scripts (examples):
- Preflight automation: terraform plan + custom manifest diffs to detect incompatible changes.
- Canary automation: scripted canary rollout that updates 10% of pods and runs synthetic traffic checks.
- Rollback automation: safe-rollback script that restores previous image digests and replays KV cache warmup.

Example preflight script snippet (bash):

#!/bin/bash
# preflight-check.sh - run from CI or operator machine
set -euo pipefail
RELEASE=$1
# 1. Validate digests
jq -r '.images[] | .name + @"@" + .digest' manifests/$RELEASE.json
# 2. KMS smoke test
curl -sSf "https://kms-check.local/v1/unwrap" -H "Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN"
# 3. Run perf profile validation (local binary)
./perf-validate --manifest manifests/$RELEASE.json --thresholds perf_thresholds.yaml

Packaging & air-gapped install notes:
- Distribution: signed .tar.gz with release manifest (manifest.json), SHA256SUMS, and a detached GPG signature.
- Verification steps for customer: verify SHA256, verify GPG signature, compare manifest image digests with internal inventory.
- Example verification commands:
  - sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
  - gpg --verify manifests/$RELEASE.manifest.sig manifests/$RELEASE.manifest
- Offline registries: prior to install, push images to customer local registry and update manifest image URLs. Provide a registry-sync script.

Upgrade procedure (recommended safe path):
0) Schedule: define a maintenance window; notify customer with the runbook and rollback plan.
1) Preflight checks: run the automation from CI and ensure no failing checks.
2) Snapshot: trigger artifact snapshots and DB backup; verify completion.
3) Canary rollout (10%):
   a) Deploy canary using the orchestration tool (Helm or kustomize).
   b) Run the automated synthetic test suite for at least 15 minutes. Key tests: token latency, throughput, correctness on canonical prompts.
   c) If any synthetic test fails or error-rate > 3x baseline, abort and rollback.
4) Staged rollout (50%): expand to 50% and run 1 hour of traffic; monitor heatmaps and P99 latency. Thresholds: P99 < 2x baseline and 5xx < 0.2% absolute.
5) Full rollout: if staged checks pass, complete rollout.
6) Post-upgrade validation: run customer smoke tests and confirm SLAs.
7) Mark release: update inventory and release notes; capture model-variant compatibility matrix if changed.

Rollback procedure (fast revert):
1) Trigger: any of the following triggers rollback:
   - Canary synthetic suite failed
   - Error-rate > configured abort threshold
   - Operator judgement during staged rollout
2) Actions:
   a) Pause trafﬁc to the updated pods (service weight to previous).
   b) Execute rollback automation: restore previous image digests + restart pods. Example Helm command: helm rollback <release> <revision> --namespace redwood-private || kubectl rollout undo deployment/<svc> -n redwood-private
   c) Rehydrate cache: replay cached prefixes from snapshot to minimize cold-start latencies.
   d) Validate health endpoints and synthetic tests before re-opening traffic.
3) Post-rollback: create postmortem, notify customer, and schedule a follow-up patch release.

Observability & SLOs (what to track during upgrades):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 per route; abort if p99 > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes.
- Errors: 5xx absolute threshold and relative increase; abort if 5xx > 0.2% or >3x baseline increment.
- Resource usage: GPU/memory per-pod; abort if OOM or GPU saturation detected.
- Synthetic tests: pass rate must be >= 95% during canary.

Runbook for common Day-2 incidents:
- degraded-control-plane: reduce client timeouts to protect control-plane; scale control-plane out by +1 replica per 10% increase in cpu.
- high-error-rate-after-upgrade: trigger rollback if error-rate persists > 15 minutes; capture traces and core dumps to support debugging.
- model-serving-slowdowns: validate KV cache hit-rates and warm caches using cached-prefix-replay tool.

Templates & customer comms (use these verbatim or adapt):
- Pre-upgrade notice (48h): "We plan to perform a non-disruptive upgrade on <DATE>. Expected impact: brief rolling restarts; no data loss. Contact: <SRE_CONTACT>."
- Post-rollback notification: "An automated rollback to version <REV> was performed on <DATE> due to <REASON>. Incident ticket: <TICKET_ID>. We will follow up with a root-cause analysis within 5 business days."

Change log & audit trail requirements:
- All upgrade actions must be recorded in the deployment audit: operator, timestamp, release manifest digest, preflight result ID, and canary run-id.
- Store artifacts and logs in the customer-specific retention bucket for 90 days (default) or customer-specified retention.

Appendix A: Example Terraform pattern (snippet):

# module: redwood_private_cluster/main.tf
# - uses provider aliases for customer accounts
module "control_plane" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/redwood/terraform//modules/control-plane"
  cluster_name = var.cluster_name
  vpc_id = var.vpc_id
}

Appendix B: Common failure modes and mitigations:
- Image digest mismatch: abort and verify signed manifest.
- KMS transient failures: fall back to wrapped key cache if available, otherwise pause upgrade.
- Storage I/O degradation: throttle model loading, increase replicas temporarily.

Appendix C: Post-upgrade checklist (within 24h):
- Confirm synthetic test coverage for customer-critical prompts.
- Verify billing/usage counters for anomalies.
- Close the maintenance ticket and attach upgrade artifact digests.

Notes & references:
- See related reference architecture for hybrid-control-plane considerations.
- For air-gapped installs, consult the onprem packaging guide for pre-staging images and KMS cert exchange.

If you find any missing steps or make improvements, update this document and add yourself to the reviewers list.

title: Usage Insights API Contract (v1)
content:
Usage Insights API Contract (v1)

h1. Overview

This document defines the v1 API contract for *Usage Insights* in Redwood Console.

The API provides:
* Cost/usage breakdowns attributed by *route + model* (and optional dimensions: project, env, deployment mode, region).
* “Top cost drivers” and “What changed?” insights.
* CSV export job lifecycle (async generation + signed downloads).

This is an *API standards* contract. Service-specific implementation details (warehouse tables, cache strategy, dependencies) live in the system doc.

h2. Goals

* Provide stable, predictable request/response shapes for console and external tooling.
* Support cursor-based pagination and consistent filter semantics.
* Ensure time bucket boundaries are deterministic and well-defined with time zone handling.
* Provide a robust export job model (create → poll → download) with RBAC and audit logging.
* Maintain consistent totals vs billing, with documented rounding/tolerance.

h2. Non-goals

* Fully automated optimization actions (API may include recommendations as links only).
* Arbitrary customer-defined dimensions beyond the fixed allowlist.

h2. Versioning and compatibility

* All endpoints are under */v1/*.
* Backwards compatibility policy:
  * Additive changes (new fields) are allowed without version bump.
  * Renames/removals require a new major version.
  * Enums may gain new values; clients must handle unknown enum values.

h1. Authentication and authorization

h2. AuthN

* Standard Redwood API auth: *Authorization: Bearer <token>*.
* Requests must include *X-Request-Id* (client-generated UUID) when possible; otherwise the server will generate one.

h2. AuthZ (RBAC)

Usage Insights contains cost data and must be gated.

* Read breakdowns:
  * Requires permission: *insights.cost:read* (or workspace setting that allows cost visibility).
* Create/download exports:
  * Requires permission: *insights.cost:export*.
* Shareable links (if enabled) are governed by the same permission checks at time of access.

If a workspace is configured to *Hide cost data*, endpoints return 403 even if the user can view non-cost usage metrics elsewhere.

h1. Common conventions

h2. Content types

* Requests: JSON
  * Content-Type: application/json
* Responses: JSON
  * Content-Type: application/json
* Export downloads: text/csv (via signed URL)

h2. Time handling

* All timestamps in responses are RFC 3339 in UTC (e.g., 2026-02-16T18:42:11Z).
* Requests accept a *tz* parameter (IANA time zone, e.g., America/Los_Angeles) used only to compute *bucket boundaries* and to interpret *date-only* ranges.
* If *tz* is omitted:
  * Default tz = UTC.

h3. Range semantics

Requests can specify either:
* Explicit timestamps (*start_at*, *end_at*) in RFC 3339, OR
* A relative window (*lookback*) like 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d.

Rules:
* *start_at* is inclusive.
* *end_at* is exclusive.
* If both explicit and lookback are provided, the server returns 400.

h2. Freshness semantics

Most responses include:
* *as_of*: the latest event timestamp fully included.
* *data_lag_seconds*: estimated lag from “now” to *as_of*.

Clients should render warnings when data_lag_seconds is above the UI threshold.

h2. Cardinality and filter allowlist

To keep query latency predictable, only the following dimensions are queryable and/or groupable:
* workspace_id (required)
* project_id (optional)
* environment (optional; enum: prod | staging | dev | unknown)
* deployment_mode (optional; enum: hosted | dedicated | private | unknown)
* region (optional; Redwood region string)
* route (optional; *normalized* route, see ADR)
* model (optional; stable model identifier)
* model_family (optional)
* model_version (optional; reporting bucket)

Route normalization and model bucketing MUST follow:
* ADR: *Route normalization and attribution*

h2. Standard error format

All non-2xx responses return:

{code}
{
  "error": {
    "code": "invalid_argument",
    "message": "end_at must be after start_at",
    "request_id": "3f8b3a2a-9e1f-4e6b-8c2a-3fd0fbfe7e0d"
  }
}
{code}

Common error codes:
* invalid_argument (400)
* unauthorized (401)
* forbidden (403)
* not_found (404)
* conflict (409)
* too_many_requests (429)
* internal (500)

h1. Endpoint summary

* GET /v1/usage-insights/breakdown
* GET /v1/usage-insights/top-drivers
* POST /v1/usage-insights/exports
* GET /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}
* POST /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}/cancel

Notes:
* Export download is via a signed URL returned by GET export status when ready.
* Some installations may additionally support: GET /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}/download-url (alias) for clarity.

h1. GET /v1/usage-insights/breakdown

Returns a paginated breakdown table grouped by one or more dimensions, with per-group cost and usage metrics.

h2. Query parameters

Required:
* workspace_id (string)

Time window (choose one):
* start_at (RFC3339)
* end_at (RFC3339)
* lookback (string: 1h | 24h | 7d | 30d)

Optional filters:
* project_id (string)
* environment (prod | staging | dev | unknown)
* deployment_mode (hosted | dedicated | private | unknown)
* region (string)
* route (string; normalized)
* model (string)
* model_family (string)
* model_version (string)

Grouping:
* group_by (repeatable query param; allowed values: route, model, model_family, model_version, region, deployment_mode, environment, project_id)
  * Default: group_by=route&group_by=model

Bucketing:
* granularity (string; enum: hour | day)
  * Default: day
* tz (IANA time zone)
  * Default: UTC

Sorting/pagination:
* order_by (string; enum: total_cost | tokens_in | tokens_out | requests | p95_latency_ms)
  * Default: total_cost
* order (asc | desc)
  * Default: desc
* page_size (int; 1–500)
  * Default: 100
* cursor (opaque string)

h2. Response shape

{code}
{
  "as_of": "2026-02-16T18:00:00Z",
  "data_lag_seconds": 420,
  "currency": "USD",
  "granularity": "day",
  "tz": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "range": {
    "start_at": "2026-02-09T08:00:00Z",
    "end_at": "2026-02-16T08:00:00Z"
  },
  "group_by": ["route", "model"],
  "rows": [
    {
      "dimensions": {
        "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
        "model": "llama-3.1-70b"
      },
      "metrics": {
        "requests": 182341,
        "successful_requests": 181902,
        "errored_requests": 439,
        "retries": 1203,
        "fallback_requests": 881,
        "streaming_requests": 176210,
        "tokens_in": 934820112,
        "tokens_out": 1120938812,
        "cache_hit_tokens": 402881920,
        "cache_miss_tokens": 1532877004,
        "total_cost": 28432.17,
        "avg_latency_ms": 812.4,
        "p50_latency_ms": 691,
        "p95_latency_ms": 1612
      }
    }
  ],
  "page": {
    "next_cursor": "eyJvZmZzZXQiOjEwMH0=",
    "has_more": true
  },
  "totals": {
    "requests": 401223,
    "tokens_in": 1900012211,
    "tokens_out": 2219001123,
    "total_cost": 51210.44
  }
}
{code}

h2. Notes on fields

* dimensions: Only includes keys specified by group_by.
* retries: Count of server-side retry attempts attributable to the request lifecycle.
* fallback_requests: Number of requests that were served by a fallback policy/model after the originally selected model could not serve.
* cache_*_tokens: Token attribution follows the metering pipeline definition; for prefix/KV cache, token accounting is based on “billed tokens avoided” vs “billed tokens processed” as standardized in telemetry.

h2. Billing consistency and rounding

* total_cost is returned as a decimal number in the workspace billing currency.
* Totals are expected to reconcile with billing within tolerance:
  * Daily range: <= 0.5%
  * Hourly range: <= 1.0% (more sensitive to late events)
* The API returns *unrounded* values to 1/10000 currency unit internally; clients should display with 2 decimal places.

h1. GET /v1/usage-insights/top-drivers

Returns top cost drivers and “what changed” explanations for the selected window compared to a prior period.

h2. Query parameters

Required:
* workspace_id

Time window (choose one):
* start_at + end_at OR lookback

Optional:
* project_id, environment, deployment_mode, region
* route (if set, provides drivers within a route)
* model/model_family/model_version (if set, provides drivers within a model bucket)

Comparison:
* compare_to (string; enum: previous_period | previous_week)
  * Default: previous_period
* tz (IANA time zone; default UTC)

Pagination:
* page_size (1–200; default 50)
* cursor

h2. Response shape

{code}
{
  "as_of": "2026-02-16T18:00:00Z",

h2. Explainability requirements

Top drivers MUST:
* Include a plain-language headline.
* Provide at least one measurable signal (delta) tied to user-visible metrics.
* Avoid causal claims that cannot be supported (use “correlates with” when appropriate).

h1. POST /v1/usage-insights/exports

Creates an async export job for a breakdown dataset (CSV). Exports are used for engineering and finance workflows (chargeback, BI ingestion).

h2. Request body

Notes:
* filters keys are optional; unknown keys return 400.
* columns may be:
  * "default" (server-defined stable default set)
  * "all" (includes extended metrics)

h2. Response (201)

{code}
{
  "export_id": "exp_01HTY5Q7K2Y0A0N6ZK3Z0K9P0M",

}
{code}

h2. Constraints and limits

* Max time range: 31 days (server may reject larger ranges with 400).
* Max rows (post-grouping): 2,000,000 (returns 413 or 400 with guidance).
* Export jobs are rate limited per workspace and per user.

h2. Audit logging requirements

Export creation and download MUST emit audit events (see security guidance). Minimum fields:
* actor_user_id
* workspace_id
* export_id
* requested_range
* filters hash (not raw prompt/data)
* created_at / downloaded_at
* client_ip (if available)

h1. GET /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}

Returns export job status, progress, and download link when ready.

h2. Response shape

{code}
{
  "export_id": "exp_01HTY5Q7K2Y0A0N6ZK3Z0K9P0M",
  "status": "ready",
  "created_at": "2026-02-16T18:10:00Z",

    "content_type": "text/csv",
    "size_bytes": 18299331
  },
  "download": {
    "url": "https://downloads.redwood.example/signed/....",
    "url_expires_at": "2026-02-16T19:12:44Z"
  },
  "failure": null
}
{code}

Status enum:
* queued
* running
* ready
* failed
* canceled

If failed:

{code}
{
  "export_id": "...",
  "status": "failed",
  "failure": {
    "code": "query_timeout",
    "message": "Export exceeded time limit for the selected range. Try reducing the range or grouping by fewer dimensions."
  }
}
{code}

h1. POST /v1/usage-insights/exports/{export_id}/cancel

Cancels an export job if it is queued or running.

h2. Response

{code}
{
  "export_id": "exp_...",
  "status": "canceled"
}
{code}

h1. Pagination standard (cursor-based)

All list endpoints in Usage Insights use cursor pagination.

Rules:
* *cursor* is opaque; clients must not parse it.
* *page_size* defaults and maximums are endpoint-specific.
* Responses include:
  * page.next_cursor (string|null)
  * page.has_more (boolean)

If the underlying dataset changes between pages (late events/backfill), the API may return slightly inconsistent ordering; clients should treat results as best-effort for interactive exploration.

h1. Filter semantics

h2. Multi-value filters

v1 supports single-valued filters for route/model dimensions. Multi-select may be added later as additive fields (e.g., routes=[...]).

h2. Route matching

* route filter matches the *normalized* route string.
* Unnormalized paths (high-cardinality) are aggregated under the sentinel value: "/__unattributed__/untemplated" when applicable.

h2. Model matching

* model is the stable Redwood model identifier used in metering events.
* model_family/model_version are reporting buckets and may map multiple model identifiers.

h1. Caching and HTTP semantics

* Breakdown and top-drivers endpoints may return:
  * Cache-Control: private, max-age=30
* Exports:
  * Status endpoints are not cached.
  * Signed download URLs are short-lived and must not be stored long-term.

h1. Security and compliance notes

* Exports are subject to retention constraints and workspace restrictions (e.g., restricted workspaces may disallow exports entirely).
* Download URLs must be signed, single-purpose, and time-bound.
* API responses must not include raw prompts, completions, or customer payloads; only aggregated usage/cost metrics.

h1. Open questions / follow-ups

* Multi-select filters for route/model in v1.1 (console UX may require it).
* Optional “shareable link” object for exports/reports (requires expanded security review).
* Standardization of retry vs replay definitions across gateway/runtime telemetry.

h1. Changelog

* 2026-02-16: Clarified tz behavior for bucket boundaries; added export cancellation endpoint; documented billing tolerance expectations.
* 2026-02-06: Added freshness fields (as_of, data_lag_seconds) to all interactive endpoints.
* 2026-01-29: Initial v1 contract published.

title: Arcadia Merchant Foundry
content:
Arcadia Merchant Foundry

Summary: Arcadia is an omni-channel e-comm platform (home/gear vertical) planning a migration from hybrid BM25 + heuristics to a semantic-first catalog search with a small LLM reranker. Primary goal: reduce false positives and lift add-to-cart; secondary goal: lower average cost per query during sustained seasonal peaks.

Key constraints / voice from the buyer: 
- "I can't trade 10% relevance for 30% cost savings during peak weekends" — Director of Search.
- Must support multi-region failover (NA primary, EU for data residency option).
- Target p95 generation + rerank latency under 200ms for core product browse queries; willing to accept up to 400ms for complex cross-sell flows.
- Cost target: $0.002–$0.01 per query (depending on rerank depth); current vendor TCO is ~ $0.015/query at scale.
- Indexing scale: ~12M active SKUs, embeddings stored for all SKUs (~3–4B embedding dims total estimated), daily delta updates ~50k SKU changes.
- Recovery and warm-start: worried about KV cache cold starts during region failover and large afternoon flash sales. Asking about prefix caching, warm-up policies, and continuous batching.
- Security: SAML SSO + SCIM for admin; audit logs retention 1 year; must integrate with Azure Key Vault (KMS) or on-prem HSM.

Current POC scope & asks: 
- Ingest subset (1.2M SKU) + produce 768-dim embeddings, evaluate recall + rerank lift on labeled queries (700 query testset).
- Measure end-to-end p95 latency and cost-per-query with canary traffic that simulates 6x seasonal spike.
- Provide Dedicated burst pricing and autoscale policy that caps spend while meeting latency SLOs.

title: Audit log pipeline dashboards + alerts (ingestion latency, drop rate) with runbook links
content:
Audit log pipeline dashboards + alerts (ingestion latency, drop rate) with runbook links

Context: As part of the audit logging standardization effort we’re tightening operational visibility for the audit event ingestion/export path. We’ve had a couple of near-misses where ingestion lag spiked without a clear on-call landing page, and early alert drafts lacked enough context to triage quickly.

This PR adds:
- A Grafana dashboard for the audit-log ingestion pipeline (end-to-end delivery latency, ingest backlog, drop rate, retry/429/5xx, DLQ growth).
- Alert rules for delivery latency and drop rate with sane defaults + per-environment routing.
- Runbook links embedded in alert annotations and dashboard panel descriptions.

Key signals / definitions:
- delivery_latency_seconds: time from event emission at producer to ack at ingestion sink (measured via audit-ingest gateway metrics + exporter timestamps).
- drop_rate: fraction of events not successfully delivered after retry budget (from ingest and exporter counters).
- backlog: queued events in buffer (when enabled) + ingestion consumer lag.

Alert thresholds (initial):
- AuditLogDeliveryLatencyP99High: p99(delivery_latency_seconds) > 60s for 10m (page: enterprise tiers; ticket: others).
- AuditLogDropRateHigh: drop_rate > 0.10% for 5m (page; includes per-region breakdown).
- AuditLogIngestBacklogGrowing: backlog > 50k AND increasing for 15m (ticket; pages if > 200k).

Cardinality guardrails:
- Dashboard panels group primarily by region, deployment_mode (hosted|dedicated|private), and service. We intentionally do not group by raw tenant_id/project_id. event_type is only used in a single table panel with top-N + allow-listed types.

Runbooks:
- Incident runbook: sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/audit-log-pipeline-incident-runbook.json
- Coverage regression runbook is linked from the dashboard “Coverage” row for follow-up when events are missing but pipeline is healthy.

Testing:
- jsonnetfmt + dashboards render in CI.
- promtool rules tests added for the new alert expressions.

Notes:
- This is intended to be the “default landing page” linked from paging alerts. We can iterate thresholds after a week of production data; see INT-3984 for noise tuning follow-ups.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Thresholds look OK but we should avoid paging on backlog alone. Can we gate backlog alert on backlog increasing + delivery latency elevated?

Aisha Bello (author): Updated AuditLogIngestBacklogGrowing to require backlog increasing for 15m and changed paging behavior: backlog alert is ticket-only unless backlog > 200k. Delivery latency + drop rate remain paging.

Allison Grant (Observability standards): Please add panel descriptions for metric definitions and ensure runbook links use the canonical Confluence path. Also, avoid grouping by tenant_id.

Aisha Bello: Added metric definitions to the top row and removed the one panel that was grouping by tenant_id (replaced with deployment_mode + region). Runbook links updated to the canonical path.

Kevin Osei (SIEM/export): Can we include exporter-side 429/5xx and retry saturation signals? That’s what we saw on VectorGrid.

Aisha Bello: Added a new “Exporter health” row with 429/5xx rate, retry queue depth, and a panel for “duplicates detected (dedupe key collisions)” where supported.

Rafael Mendes (Runbooks): Please include direct links to the incident comms template section in the runbook and add an annotation that we treat delivery as at-least-once (duplicates possible).

Aisha Bello: Added alert annotation: “Delivery is at-least-once; dedupe on event_id in downstream SIEM.” Added deep link to runbook comms templates.

Approvals:
- Sean Gallagher: Approved
- Allison Grant: Approved
- Kevin Osei: Approved
- Rafael Mendes: Approved
