title: eng-ml
content:
eng-ml

maria: Bringing up cumulus15b-int4 on canary GPUs (a100). Hitting repeated OOMs on cold starts + memory fragmentation spikes. Default max_new_tokens=1024. Logs below, any quick ideas?

maria: Logs: ```OOM on alloc of 104857600, kv_cache reserve failed, memfrag: 78% used, available contiguous: 60MB```

sam: which kernel/runtime build? any recent kernel patches?

alex: saw similar on a different model — int4 pack layout + large max_new_tokens can frag GPU memory on cold start. temporarily fixed by setting batch_size=1 and max_new_tokens=256.

maria: tried batch_size=1 + max_new_tokens=256, still saw one cold-start OOM at first warmup, then stable. But throughput drop is large.

raj: two quick knobs: reduce reserve_slots (we default to 256 for 15b), try reserve_slots=96 or 64; and disable kv-prefetch on cold starts so we don't pre-allocate full prefix. Also try setting `gc_threshold=0.6` in runtime to force earlier compaction.

emma: (from infra-bot) deploy canary started for cumulus15b-int4 -> canary-3 on a100.

maria: I flipped reserve_slots=96 and disabled kv-prefetch for the canary. Reproduced OOM cleared, memfrag dipped to ~42%. Perf: tail latency increased ~12ms.

elaine: int4 quant layout sometimes increases allocator pressure because of alignment differences. Running quant-eval with warm snapshots helps. Can you run `python infra/evals/onboard_eval.py --model=cumulus15b --quant=int4 --warm_snap=1 --batch=1` and post the results?

maria: Ran eval, snippet: ```avg_latency: 182ms, p95: 412ms, mem_peak: 33.2GB, kv_frag_after_warm: 41%```. Quality checks passed (perplexity within expected).

sam: if int4 stable but latency penalty unacceptable, fallback plan: ship int8 canary for prod while we iterate int4 tunings. int8 seemed fine on our previous runs.

raj: also add a warmstart snapshot step to canary rollout pipeline: pre-warm kv cache with synthetic prefix to avoid cold allocation spikes. Example script: `./scripts/warm_cache.sh --model cumulus15b --tokens 1024` — this reduces cold OOMs in tests.

maria: Plan: rollback int4 canary for now, start int8 canary + add warmstart snapshot + set operator defaults: max_new_tokens=512, reserve_slots=96, batch_size_default=1 for canary traffic. Will create a follow-up PR with config. cc @oncall

sam: SGTM. opened ticket INC-7123 and assigned to eng-ml.

maria: executing rollback in 10m and will re-run quant-eval with warm snapshots after int8 canary is stable. Thanks for the quick input everyone :thumbsup:

deploy-bot: Canary rollback triggered for cumulus15b-int4 by maria (reason: cold-start OOMs).

title: Archipelago MedData Solutions
content:
Archipelago MedData Solutions

High-level: want private VPC deployment for PHI workflows. Very strict residency + audit requirements.
Encryption posture is primary ask — detailed notes from SecDeepDive:
- In-transit: require mutual TLS between customer LB and Redwood ingress. TLS 1.3 preferred, TLS1.2 acceptable with strong cipher suites.
- mTLS: customer will provision client certs; Redwood to validate client certs against customer CA OR offer mutual-auth with customer-managed certs via ACM in customer's account.
- Service-to-service: internal mTLS between runtime components for zero-trust, cert rotation handled by control plane with cert expiry <90 days.
- At-rest: AES-256-GCM envelope encryption for model KV cache and user data; per-tenant data keys wrapped by customer CMK when BYOK selected.
- Key rotation: recommend two-tier rotation: data-key rotation every 90 days, CMK rotation policy annually (customer can trigger rotation). Rewrap flow documented; no downtime for POC.
- KMS integration: support for AWS KMS (cross-account), AWS CloudHSM, and external HSM via PKCS#11 (enterprise package). BYOK model preferred.
- Secrets management: recommend HashiCorp Vault in customer VPC (auto-unseal with KMS) or AWS Secrets Manager; Redwood control plane will not persist plaintext keys for private VPC.
- Audit logging: immutable write-once logs forwarded to customer SIEM (Splunk/Datadog/Elastic). Retention policy requested: 7 years for audit trails; must include request metadata + token usage (redacted PII).
- Data residency: all inference inputs/outputs must remain in us-east-1; no cross-region backups without explicit consent.
- Network topology: private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) only; no NAT egress for inference traffic. Customer will provide VPC peering/VPN terms.
- Operational controls: RBAC via SSO/SAML, granular route-level policies, per-route key binding (bind a CMK to a model route).
- Compliance asks: provide SOC2 Type II evidence, ISO27001 cert, results of recent pen test + remediation plan.
Customer quotes / call fragments:
- 'We cannot have keys managed by a vendor control plane unless wrapped by our CMK.'
- 'Audit logs must be tamper-evident and stored in our SIEM; we will supply log ingestion credentials.'
POC scope notes: sample dataset de-identification pipeline + RAG with customer KMS BYOK; latency target 200ms P50 for short prompts; throughput 60 QPS burstable to 200 for evaluation.
Cost sensitivity: medium — willing to pay for isolation and BYOK HSM but want clear unit economics for heavy embedding batches.

title: Progressive Tool Fusion and Client Surface — Lab Notes
content:
Progressive Tool Fusion and Client Surface — Lab Notes

Exploratory PRD-like lab notes proposing a streaming-first approach where tool calls and tool results are progressively fused into the client-visible stream. Focus is on ergonomics for SDKs, lightweight typed frames, resume semantics, and observability required to iterate safely in production.
Context:

This doc captures an ideation run for 'progressive tool fusion' — an approach where hosted inference can emit interleaved partial text, tool-call intents, and tool results in a single stream and the client-side SDK performs deterministic fusion of those pieces into a final structured output. The hypothesis: pushing a small, well-documented amount of fusion logic into SDKs (instead of heavy server-side transactions) produces lower tail latency, better incremental UX, and more deterministic developer ergonomics for tool-heavy workflows (e.g., multi-tool data enrichment, stepwise actions).

Why now:
- Increasing demand for tool-calling workflows with low-latency interactive UX (chatbots that call search, calculators, code-run, db lookups)
- Customers want structured, typed outputs to be accessible incrementally (partial lists, progressive tables)
- Platform has mature streaming primitives; next step is a well-scoped contract for tool-call interleaving and client fusion that scales across mobile/desktop/server SDKs.

Goals:
- Define a minimal streaming frame vocabulary for partial_text, tool_call, tool_result, fusion_marker, and typed_blob that SDKs can implement easily.
- Specify an SDK-facing API contract for deterministic fusion that is resilient to reconnects and duplicate tool results.
- Define telemetry and SLOs to safely roll out fusion-enabled streams (observe per-tool latency, fusion-completion time, and reconstruction mismatch rates).
- Deliver migration guidance for existing non-interleaved hosted-api customers and a toggle/flag-based rollout plan.

Non-goals:
- Full server-side orchestration of multi-tool transactions with ACID semantics (we aim for best-effort correctness with idempotency tokens, not distributed two-phase commits).
- Replacing existing typed-output endpoints (we provide a complementary streaming surface).

User personas and flows:
1) Product engineer embedding a chat assistant in a web app: wants partial answers quickly, and a single final card containing aggregated tool outputs (search snippets + db rows).
2) Platform integrator on mobile: must support intermittent connectivity and resume semantics without duplicating tool side effects (e.g., avoid double-run of a code execution tool).
3) SRE/ops: cares about per-request cost, tool invocation counts and partial-stream error modes.

Streaming frame vocabulary (proposal):
- partial_text: raw incremental tokens (string) with sequence_id and offset.
- tool_call: metadata describing the intended tool (tool_id, invocation_id, schema_hint, input_preview). Sent when model decides to call a tool.
- tool_result: result payload produced by tool (invocation_id, result_id, checksum, maybe typed_blob). May be streamed itself if large.
- fusion_marker: annotation that signals a stable boundary where the SDK should emit a fused output to the app (fusion_id, expected_parts).
- typed_blob: compact typed payload (schema_id, json_schema_version, base64 payload) for high-confidence structured outputs.

Each frame includes minimal routing metadata: request_id, session_id, sequence_number, timestamp, and optional resume_token. Tool frames MUST carry an invocation_id to correlate calls and results across reconnects.

SDK ergonomics (guiding principles):
- Determinism: SDKs should implement a deterministic fusion algorithm given the ordered stream of frames; meaning two identical frame sequences yield identical fused outputs.
- Progressive delivery: SDK surfaces incremental fused candidates (non-blocking) and a final fused commit event when fusion_marker is received or a timeout elapses.
- Safety: SDK must expose hooks for the host app to control 'materialization' of tool side effects (e.g., provide onToolMaterialize callback; default: do not auto-materialize in mobile low-bandwidth mode).
- Resume-friendly: SDK must persist a lightweight resume token map (invocation_id -> result_id/checksum) to avoid duplicate tool replays after reconnect.
- Configurable heuristics: provide tunables for buffer_size, fusion_timeout_ms, allow_partial_on_disconnect (default: true for UX).

SDK API sketch (for JS-like pseudocode):
- createStream({requestId, sessionId, options}) -> stream
- stream.on('frame', (f) => {}) // raw frames
- stream.on('fusionCandidate', (candidate) => {}) // candidate fused partial
- stream.on('fusionCommit', (commit) => {}) // final fused output
- stream.materializeToolResult(invocation_id) // optional manual materialize for idempotency control
- stream.resumeFromToken(token)

Behavioral examples:
- Model emits partial_text x3, then tool_call(invA), then partial_text x2, then fusion_marker expecting invA. SDK should: show progressive text; when tool_result for invA arrives, incorporate into fused structure and emit fusionCommit. If tool_result doesn't arrive before deadline, SDK emits fusionCommit with placeholder and a post-hoc update when result arrives.

Low-bandwidth and offline heuristics:
- If connection degrades, SDK should prefer progressive partial_text deliveries and suppress heavy typed_blob auto-materialization (e.g., large images, file attachments).
- allow_partial_on_disconnect setting controls whether SDK exposes incomplete fused outputs to the app.

Observability and telemetry needs:
- Per request: time_to_first_token, time_to_fusion_commit, number_of_tool_calls, number_of_tool_results_missing, fusion_mismatch_rate (cases where server produces a final authoritative structure different from SDK-fused final after reconciliation).
- Per tool: mean_latency, p95_latency, error_rate, duplicate_invocations_detected.
- SDK-instrumented counters: local_resume_successes, local_resume_failures, pending_invocations_at_disconnect.

SLOs and acceptance criteria:
- Under normal network: median time_to_fusion_commit <= baseline + 120ms (baseline is plain streaming text commit).
- Fusion mismatch rate < 0.3% in canary window.
- Duplicate tool invocation rate (post-resume) < 0.1% in canary.
- SDK must provide a deterministic rehydration flow that passes unit/integration tests included in the SDK test harness.

Migration and backward compatibility:
- Default behavior: streams without fusion_marker are treated as plain streaming text (no fusion).
- Provide an API flag on requests: enable_progressive_fusion=true. Start with invite-only canary customers and an SDK opt-in.

Rollout plan (proposal):
- Phase 0: internal lab tests with simulated tool latencies and reconnect patterns.
- Phase 1: Alpha release to internal Redwood apps + 3 trusted customers (feature flagged). Monitor telemetry.
- Phase 2: Public SDK beta for JS + mobile with opt-in toggle; collect mismatch metrics and developer feedback.
- Phase 3: Gradual default-on for new request workflows with migration docs and 'compat' header to request original stable-only behavior.

Open implementation risks and questions:
- Tool side-effects: we must guarantee an idempotency story for tools where replays can cause side-effects (webhooks, chargeable actions). Recommendation: tool integrations must advertise idempotency_token support and SDK must prefer 'do-not-replay' default unless tool confirms idempotent semantics.
- Contract evolution: will typed_blob schema changes require version negotiation? We propose including schema_version in frames and refusing to auto-parse unknown majors.
- Server authoritative reconciliation: if server later decides to rewrite fused output (e.g., correct hallucinated tool_call), how are SDKs expected to reconcile? We propose final authoritative fusion frames with authoritative=true; SDK should emit a correction event and the app can reconcile.

Testing and validation plan:
- SDK unit tests for fusion determinism across permutations of frame interleavings.
- Integration harness that simulates: lost frames, delayed tool results, duplicate tool_result with different checksums, reordered partial_text chunks.
- E2E with a mock tool that has both idempotent and non-idempotent modes to validate resume heuristics.

Developer docs and UX examples to produce:
- Quickstart: enabling progressive fusion in a single line and sample code to display incremental fused cards.
- Troubleshooting guide: common mismatch causes and how to instrument.
- Migration checklist: what to do before turning on fusion for production traffic.

Next steps (concrete):
1) Team alignment session (product + applied-ml + SDK + platform) to validate vocabulary and heuristics (target week of 2025-02-17).
2) Prototype JS SDK fusion algorithm and a simple mock server within 2 sprints.
3) Build telemetry dashboards (fusion mismatch, per-tool latency) and a canary alert.
4) Draft integration guide and safe defaults for mobile clients.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a lab-level PRD sketch: please challenge the assumptions about pushing fusion to clients vs doing more server-side commit logic.
- Look for edge cases where deterministic recomposition cannot be guaranteed due to lossy network or intentionally lossy model behavior.

References and inspiration:
- Internal hosted-api streaming patterns (see linked artifacts)
- Typical idempotency design patterns from payment gateways (applicability for tool integrations)

End of notes.

title: Stuck model pin after canary throttle suppression causes routing to legacy variant
content:
Stuck model pin after canary throttle suppression causes routing to legacy variant

Issue summary: During a staged canary rollout of pf-3b-v2 for PathFinder Analytics (dedicated pool), a rate-adaptive canary throttle triggered 'suppression' mode which prevented the orchestrator from committing the per-tenant pin. The tenant traffic continued to be routed to the legacy pf-3b-v1 variant, causing inconsistent responses and elevated cost when some requests fell back to the hosted dequantized variant. Impact: customer reports mixed model outputs, degraded quality for ~12% of requests for a critical endpoint and a sudden spike in token usage due to fallback to a higher-cost variant.

Observed window: 2025-02-18 03:05 - 03:50 UTC.

Context: This customer is on a dedicated pool with explicit model version pin requested via API header X-Model-Pin, and a canary rollout (20% weight) was configured with adaptive-rate throttle enabled (adaptive-canary-throttle v2). The edge-proxy applied a transient rate-shed tag which the orchestrator interpreted as a health suppression and did not persist the pin commit in the cluster snapshot.
1) On a dedicated tenant with pinned header X-Model-Pin: pf-3b-v2, begin a weighted canary rollout (20%) via console rollout API.
2) Simulate a spike of short-lived concurrent requests to the canary slice to trigger adaptive-canary-throttle thresholds on the edge-proxy.
3) Observe orchestrator logs for pin commit path; confirm whether pin commit RPC returns 202 vs 200.
4) Inspect routing decisions returned by the edge (x-routing-variant header) and compare to requested pin.
5) Verify if snapshot store contains the committed pin entry for the tenant after rollout slice stabilizes.
edge-proxy logs (us-east-1) 2025-02-18T03:06:12Z: INFO rate-shed applied: tenant=pf-tenant-88 action=suppress reason=adaptive-throttle threshold=0.2
orchestrator logs 2025-02-18T03:06:15Z: WARN pin-commit-suppressed tenant=pf-tenant-88 snapshot_write_status=skipped reason=health-suppression
serving-runtime logs 2025-02-18T03:06:20Z: DEBUG route-eval tenant=pf-tenant-88 selected_variant=pf-3b-v1 (pin requested pf-3b-v2)
snapshot-store: last_written_epoch=8420 (pre-rollout), attempted_commit_epoch=8421 (skipped)
kvcache-metrics: prefix-hit-rate unchanged; no prewarm observed for pf-3b-v2 in tenant pool
2025-02-18 04:00 UTC - Triage: Confirmed customer reproduced discrepancy; initial hypothesis: edge suppression flag prevented snapshot commit path.
Checked rollout controller: commit flow returns 'skipped' when health suppression present (code path introduced in adaptive-throttle v2).
Reproduced in internal staging by enabling adaptive-canary-throttle and simulating 200rps spike; observed identical 'pin-commit-suppressed' logs.
Hypothesis refined: edge-proxy annotates requests with suppression metadata which the orchestrator treats as 'abort commit' instead of 'defer commit'. This leaves the tenant in a half-committed state where routing remains bound to previous snapshot epoch.
Temporary mitigation tested: manually forcing a snapshot write via admin endpoint produced a committed entry and restored pinned routing for the tenant.
Risk: If adaptive throttle suppression remains aggressive during low-latency window, automatic commit may never persist leading to rolling inconsistencies across tenants.
Support (Maya Chen) 2025-02-18T05:12Z: Reached out to PathFinder contact (ops@pathfinder.io) to request request IDs and sample traces. Customer confirms ~12% of calls returned different output shape.
Customer (Alex Rivera, PathFinder) 2025-02-18T05:40Z: Provided sample request IDs: req-9832, req-9841, req-9910. They noted risk to production analytics pipeline; asking for ETA on fix.
SRE (Diego Alvarez) 2025-02-18T06:10Z: Confirmed we can force a snapshot commit as a short-term fix. Will coordinate to apply to the dedicated tenant after approval.
Eng (Priya Nair) 2025-02-18T09:30Z: Reproduced locally. Root cause: orchestrator treat_suppressed_as_abort flag default true; change would be to treat suppression as 'defer' and schedule commit after suppression clears. Drafting PR to adjust logic and add metric for suppressed-commits.
Support (Maya Chen) 2025-02-19T14:22Z: Customer approved manual snapshot write at 2025-02-19 15:00 UTC. Applied forced commit; customer confirms traffic now reaches pf-3b-v2 for pinned requests.
Customer (Alex Rivera) 2025-02-19T15:30Z: Verified outputs normalized; thanked team and asked for postmortem and permanent fix timeline.
Manual snapshot commit applied 2025-02-19 15:00 UTC for tenant pf-tenant-88; pinned routing restored. Engineering merged PR to change suppression handling (orchestrator PR #1223) which treats adaptive-throttle suppression as defer instead of abort and schedules a follow-up commit when suppression clears. Patch scheduled for rollout to prod-us-east on 2025-02-21 during maintenance window.
1) Postmortem doc: create Confluence page documenting root cause, timeline, and customer impact (owner: Priya Nair, due 2025-02-24)
2) Add telemetry: metric suppressed_pin_commits and alert if rate > 1/min for any tenant (owner: SRE team)
3) QA: add regression test to rollout controller simulating adaptive throttle suppression to ensure defer-path commits succeed after suppression clears (owner: rollout-controller team)
4) Customer comms: send summary and offered credit for elevated token cost during incident (owner: CS manager)
5) Monitor: keep a 72-hour watch on pf-tenant-88 routing logs and suppressed-commit metric after patch rollout.

title: SLO-driven chaos curriculum and capacity simulation guidelines
content:
SLO-driven chaos curriculum and capacity simulation guidelines

Overview

This document defines a repeatable curriculum and operational guidelines for SLO-driven chaos/gameday exercises and capacity simulations. The goal is to exercise realistic multi-tenant inference failure modes, validate SLOs and error-budget controls, and collect forensic evidence suitable for incident review and actionable remediation. This guide is intentionally lightweight so teams can run 1–2 hour labs or full-day rehearsals with equivalent outcomes.

Goals

- Validate that production SLOs reflect customer-impacting outcomes.
- Confirm autoscale and capacity policies behave under realistic traffic and model-serving degradations.
- Exercise fallback and graceful degradation (model variants, region failover, cache priming).
- Collect structured evidence and metrics for post-event analysis tied to deployments, rollouts, and model changes.
- Train on controlled abort and rollback criteria to avoid customer harm.

Scope and audience

- Audience: SREs, runtime engineers, platform owners, and on-call partners.
- Systems: Redwood inference serving runtime, request router, cache layer, autoscaler, and per-tenant priority controls.
- Not covered: billing/accounting reconciliation (separate finance runbook).

Prerequisites

1. Testbed environment with traffic replay capability (see Tooling).
2. Canary dataset and representative token-length distribution for workload.
3. Owner sign-off and scheduled maintenance window (if exercises touch production).

Key definitions (for this curriculum)

- Target SLOs: 99.9%% p95 latency for short-text generation routes; 99%% p99 for embedding batch jobs; availability SLOs per-tenant remain as defined in SLO registry.
- Error budget window: 30 days rolling; exercise will consume a controlled percentage (target 5–15%%) for tabletop calibration.
- Capacity simulation run: a synthetic traffic injection with stepwise load, introduced faults, and validation windows.

Curriculum overview (modular)

1. Quick warm-up (30–45 minutes)
   - Objective: Ensure team familiarity with telemetry dashboards and evidence collection.
   - Activities: Walk the SLO dashboards, confirm alert subscriptions, run a 10-minute synthetic baseline replay.

2. Mini chaos lab (1 hour)
   - Objective: Simulate a single-fault cascade and validate graceful degradation.
   - Faults injected (choose one): KV cache eviction, model quantization path misconfiguration, or network routing flapping between regions.
   - Expected outcomes: Fallback to smaller model variant, increased token cost but preserved critical responses, clear SLO delta.

3. Capacity simulation (1.5–2 hours)
   - Objective: Measure autoscaler headroom and service tail-latency under increasing concurrency and long-context traffic.
   - Steps: Stepped traffic ramp: 25%%, 50%%, 75%%, 100%% of projected peak; hold intervals 10 minutes. Introduce a 10-minute throttling event at 75%% to validate token-priority arbitration.

4. Complex multi-tenant scenario (2–4 hours)
   - Objective: Validate tenant isolation, fair-share heuristics, and emergency eviction procedure.
   - Scenario: One tenant spikes with emergent batch embedding jobs while other tenants run steady low-latency requests; test backpressure and eviction policies.

5. Post-exercise tabletop & evidence handoff (45–60 minutes)
   - Objective: Capture lessons, map root causes, and generate remediation tickets with owners and SLO impact.

Tooling and artifacts

- Traffic replay: load-generator with token-length and event-time fidelity (recommended: replayer v2). Example CLI: replayer run --trace sample.json --scale 1.4 --duration 20m
- Failure injection: failctl (network, process, latency, and memory faults). Example: failctl inject --target runtime-node-3 --type socket-delay --ms 250
- Telemetry dashboards: SLO overview, p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap, per-tenant error budget burn, request-router traces, KV hit/miss.
- Evidence collection: standardized evidence bundle (see Evidence Matrix). Script: evidence-collector --scope exercise --output /tmp/evidence-<YYYYMMDD>.tgz

SLOs and error budget policy for exercises

- Pre-declare the error budget allocation for the exercise: annotate the SLO registry with an exercise token and approval.
- Target consumption: small labs 1–5%%, full-day rehearsals 10–15%%.
- Hard abort: if cumulative error budget > 25%% for any production tenant without explicit exec approval, abort exercise and roll back injected faults.

Capacity simulation configuration table (recommended baseline)

| Parameter | Recommended value | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Baseline multiplier | 1.0 | Normal traffic profile |
| Peak multiplier | 1.5–2.0 | Simulate high demand bursts |
| Ramp step | 25%% increments | Small enough to observe inflection points |
| Hold duration | 10 minutes | Capture steady-state metrics for each step |
| Long context ratio | 10–20%% | Models with KV-cache pressure show different tails |

Runbook: executing a standard simulation (checklist)

1. Pre-checks (15–30 minutes)
   - Confirm owners, communication channel (pager, slack), and maintenance windows.
   - Snapshot current SLO status and evidence baseline.
   - Ensure replay traces and canary keys loaded.

2. Start baseline replay and validate dashboards (10 minutes)

3. Execute traffic ramp (operators: run replayer with step schedule)

4. Inject single-point faults at planned time markers; observe autoscaler and fallback behavior

5. Collect evidence bundle at each stage and tag with step id and timestamp

6. If abort criteria triggered: run abort procedure (see Abort & Rollback)

7. Post-run verification: validate services restored, caches re-primed, and model-variants pinned back if changed.

Abort & Rollback (safety gates)

- Abort triggers (any of the following):
  - Tenant-level error budget > 25%%
  - Uncontrolled memory pressure causing OOM restarts across > 10%% of serving nodes
  - Data-plane errors that corrupt persisted KV cache state
- Immediate steps on abort:
  1. Halt traffic generator and failctl scripts.
  2. Revert injected network/process faults.
  3. Verify core runtime health, then escalate to on-call SRE lead if not recovered within 10 minutes.

Evidence Matrix (minimal fields)

Each evidence bundle must include the following items and be named consistently:
- exercise-id: string (e.g., slo-chaos-20260112-01)
- dashboard-snapshots: list of png/csv exports with timestamps
- trace-exports: tracing spans correlated to exercise windows
- node-metrics: cpu/mem/gpu-utilization CSV
- autoscaler-events: raw events log
- injected-faults-log: failctl output
- sample-requests: 50 raw request/response pairs from each affected tenant (sanitized)

Attachment naming convention: <exercise-id>_<artifact-type>_<YYYYMMDDTHHMMZ>

Post-exercise retro template (minimum required fields)

- Summary (one paragraph): what we set out to test and the outcome.
- SLO impact: quantifiable delta and error-budget consumption.
- Root cause hypothesis: top 1–3 contributors.
- Evidence pointers: artifact filenames and timestamps.
- Action items: owner, priority, due date.

Ownership and run cadence

- Exercise owner: service steward listed in SLO registry (primary contact).
- Recommended cadence: team-level mini-labs quarterly; full cross-functional rehearsals semi-annually.

Measurement and success criteria

- Success: clear mapping from injected faults to SLO telemetry where mitigation patterns performed as designed (fallback invoked, degradation prioritization enforced).
- Secondary success: reproducible remediation steps and closed action items for the top remediation tickets within 30 days.

References and related pages

- See: Chaos exercises library: /confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/chaos-exercises-and-failure-hypothesis-library-2026
- See: Capacity rehearsal runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/capacity-rehearsal-decision-playbook-2026

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call (cheat sheet)

- Before exercise: publish exercise id, start time, and abort thresholds to #sre-gameday.
- During: stream evidence bundle to shared storage every 15 minutes.
- After: file retro within 48 hours and annotate SLO registry with consumed budget.

Contact

For questions or to schedule a cross-team rehearsal, contact Marco Reynolds (marco@redwood.example) or the eng-sre scheduling channel.
